title: argument
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When calling a function, you pass actual values - arguments - that fill the parameter slots.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`add(3, 5)` - here 3 and 5 are the arguments. They fill parameters `a` and `b`.

## 🔗 Analogy

The ingredients you actually bring to the kitchen. The recipe (function) says 'bring flour and sugar' (parameters); you bring 200g flour and 100g sugar (arguments).

## Related Concepts

- [[parameter|Parameter]]
- [[function-call|Function Call]]
- [[keyword-argument|Keyword Argument]]

title: arithmetic-operator
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Math is fundamental to programming - adding scores, multiplying prices, dividing portions.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`5 + 3 = 8`, `10 / 3 = 3.333`, `10 // 3 = 3` (floor division), `2 ** 10 = 1024` (power).

## 🔗 Analogy

The buttons on a calculator - each one does a specific math operation on the numbers you give it.

## Related Concepts

- [[integer|Integer]]
- [[float|Float]]
- [[expression|Expression]]
- [[operator-precedence|Operator Precedence]]

title: array
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When performance matters (games, science, AI), a fixed-size array stores data more efficiently than a list.

## 📋 Concrete Example

In C: `int scores[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};`. All elements must be the same type and the size is fixed.

## 🔗 Analogy

A tray of labelled compartments - each slot is exactly the same size, lined up in a row, and you can't add more slots.

## Related Concepts

- [[list|List]]
- [[index|Index]]
- [[fixed-size|Fixed Size]]

title: assignment-operator
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

You need a way to put a value into a variable. The assignment operator does exactly that.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`x = 5` puts 5 into x. `x += 3` adds 3 to x (same as `x = x + 3`).

## 🔗 Analogy

An arrow pointing into a box - the value on the right goes into the box labelled on the left.

## Related Concepts

- [[variable|Variable]]
- [[augmented-assignment|Augmented Assignment]]
- [[expression|Expression]]

title: augmented-assignment
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Updating a variable based on its current value is so common that Python has shortcuts: +=, -=, *=, /=.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`score += 10` is the same as `score = score + 10` but shorter. `count -= 1` decrements. `total *= 2` doubles.

## 🔗 Analogy

Refilling a water bottle - instead of pouring out the old water, measuring it, adding more, and pouring back (x = x + y), you just top it up (x += y).

## Related Concepts

- [[assignment-operator|Assignment Operator]]
- [[expression|Expression]]
- [[variable|Variable]]

title: base-case
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Recursion needs a stopping point - without it, the function calls itself forever. The base case is that stop.

## 📋 Concrete Example

In `factorial(n)`, the base case is `if n <= 1: return 1`. Without this, factorial(0) calls factorial(-1) calls factorial(-2)... forever.

## 🔗 Analogy

The smallest nesting doll that doesn't open - it's solid inside. When you reach it, you stop opening. That's the base case.

## Related Concepts

- [[recursion|Recursion]]
- [[call-stack|Call Stack]]
- [[infinite-recursion|Infinite Recursion]]

title: block
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Related statements are grouped into blocks - the body of a function, the code inside an if, etc.

## 📋 Concrete Example

In Python, blocks are defined by indentation: the lines after `if x > 0:` indented by 4 spaces form one block.

## 🔗 Analogy

A paragraph in an essay - sentences that belong together are grouped. In Python, indentation (like paragraph indenting) shows grouping.

## Related Concepts

- [[indentation|Indentation]]
- [[function|Function]]
- [[conditional|Conditional]]

title: boolean
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Programs constantly make yes/no decisions - is the game over? Is the user logged in? Booleans capture this.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`is_logged_in = True` or `game_over = False`. Used in `if` conditions: `if is_logged_in: show_dashboard()`.

## 🔗 Analogy

A light switch - it's either ON (True) or OFF (False), nothing in between.

## Related Concepts

- [[conditional|Conditional]]
- [[logical-operator|Logical Operator]]
- [[truth-value|Truth Value]]

title: break
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Sometimes you need to exit a loop early - you found what you were looking for, or something went wrong.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`for item in items: if item == target: print('Found!'); break` - stops the loop immediately.

## 🔗 Analogy

Finding your keys in a bag - you dig through items one by one, and the moment you find the keys, you stop searching.

## Related Concepts

- [[for-loop|For Loop]]
- [[while-loop|While Loop]]
- [[continue|Continue]]

title: call-stack
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Every function call adds a frame to the call stack. When functions return, frames are removed. Too many = overflow.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Calling `f()` which calls `g()` which calls `h()` - the stack is [f, g, h]. When h returns, it's [f, g]. When g returns, it's [f].

## 🔗 Analogy

A stack of plates - you add a plate on top (call) and remove from the top (return). Last plate on is the first off. Too many plates = the stack falls over (overflow).

## Related Concepts

- [[recursion|Recursion]]
- [[stack-overflow|Stack Overflow]]
- [[function-call|Function Call]]

title: character
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Text is made up of individual characters - letters, digits, punctuation, symbols. Each character is a building block of strings.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`'A'` is a character, `'7'` is a character, `'!'` is a character. `len('Hello') = 5` because it has 5 characters.

## 🔗 Analogy

Individual tiles in a Scrabble game - each tile is one letter. You arrange them to spell words.

## Related Concepts

- [[string|String]]
- [[ascii|ASCII]]
- [[unicode|Unicode]]

title: class
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When you have data and the functions that operate on it tightly coupled, a class bundles them together.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`class Dog: def __init__(self, name): self.name = name; def bark(self): return self.name + ' says woof!'` - data (name) and behaviour (bark) together.

## 🔗 Analogy

A blueprint for a house - the blueprint (class) defines the structure. You can build many houses (objects) from the same blueprint, each with different paint (data).

## Related Concepts

- [[object|Object]]
- [[constructor|Constructor]]
- [[method|Method]]
- [[object-oriented-programming|Object-Oriented Programming]]

title: comment
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Code tells the computer what to do, but comments tell humans (including yourself) why. They're ignored by the computer.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`# This calculates the final price after discount` - the # makes it a comment. Python skips this line.

## 🔗 Analogy

Sticky notes on a recipe - 'this is the spicy version!' or 'grandma trick: add a pinch of salt'. The oven doesn't read them, but you do.

## Related Concepts

- [[documentation|Documentation]]
- [[code-readability|Code Readability]]

title: comparison-operator
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Programs need to compare values - is the score high enough? Are two strings the same?

## 📋 Concrete Example

`5 > 3` is True. `'a' == 'a'` is True. `10 != 20` is True. `age >= 18` checks if old enough to vote.

## 🔗 Analogy

A balance scale comparing two weights - it tells you which side is heavier, or if they're equal.

## Related Concepts

- [[boolean|Boolean]]
- [[conditional|Conditional]]
- [[expression|Expression]]

title: conditional
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Programs must make decisions - if the score is high enough, show 'You win!'. Conditionals branch the flow.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`if score >= 100: print('You win!') elif score >= 50: print('Try again') else: print('Game over')`

## 🔗 Analogy

A fork in a hiking trail - a sign tells you which path to take based on your destination. The condition is the sign.

## Related Concepts

- [[boolean|Boolean]]
- [[if-statement|If Statement]]
- [[else|Else]]
- [[elif|Elif]]

title: constant
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Some values should never change - pi, the speed of light, a max score. Constants are variables you agree not to modify.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`MAX_LEVELS = 50` or `PI = 3.14159`. By convention, uppercase names mean `don`t change this'.

## 🔗 Analogy

A carved stone sign at a park entrance - 'Park Hours: 6am-10pm' is fixed and permanent. Everyone agrees not to change it.

## Related Concepts

- [[variable|Variable]]
- [[naming-convention|Naming Convention]]
- [[global-variable|Global Variable]]

title: constructor
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When creating an object, you need to set up its initial data. The constructor is the method that runs on creation.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`def __init__(self, name): self.name = name` - when you call `Dog('Rex')`, this method runs automatically and sets `name` to `Rex`.

## 🔗 Analogy

The setup crew for a new restaurant - before opening day, they stock the kitchen, set the tables, and train the staff. The restaurant is ready to operate.

## Related Concepts

- [[class|Class]]
- [[object|Object]]
- [[initialization|Initialization]]

title: context-manager
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Managing resources (files, connections) safely is error-prone. Context managers (the `with` statement) handle setup and cleanup automatically.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`with open('data.txt') as f: data = f.read()` - the file is automatically closed when the block ends, even if an error occurred.

## 🔗 Analogy

A self-cleaning paint roller - when you're done painting (exit the `with` block), it automatically cleans itself. You don't have to remember to clean up.

## Related Concepts

- [[file-i-o|File I-O]]
- [[finally|Finally]]
- [[resource-management|Resource Management]]

title: continue
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Sometimes you want to skip the rest of the current loop iteration and jump to the next one.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`for n in range(10): if n % 2 == 0: continue; print(n)` - skips even numbers, only prints odd ones.

## 🔗 Analogy

Skipping songs on a playlist - if you don't like a song, you skip to the next one without finishing the current one.

## Related Concepts

- [[for-loop|For Loop]]
- [[while-loop|While Loop]]
- [[break|Break]]

title: data-type
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Computers need to know what kind of data they're working with - text, whole numbers, decimals - because they handle each differently.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`name = 'Alice'` is a string, `age = 14` is an integer, `height = 1.65` is a float.

## 🔗 Analogy

Different shaped containers - you wouldn't put soup in a pencil case. Each data type is a container shaped for its content.

## Related Concepts

- [[variable|Variable]]
- [[string|String]]
- [[integer|Integer]]
- [[float|Float]]
- [[boolean|Boolean]]

title: default-parameter
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Sometimes a parameter usually has the same value. Default parameters let callers skip it when they want the default.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`def greet(name, greeting='Hello'): return greeting + ', ' + name`. `greet('Alice')` uses `Hello`. `greet('Alice', 'Hi')` uses `Hi`.

## 🔗 Analogy

A restaurant menu - 'comes with chips by default (default parameter). If you want salad instead, just say so (override the default).'

## Related Concepts

- [[parameter|Parameter]]
- [[argument|Argument]]
- [[function|Function]]

title: dictionary
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Sometimes you want to look up a value by a name rather than a position - like finding a phone number by name.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`phone_book = {'Alice': '555-1234', 'Bob': '555-5678'}`. Look up: `phone_book['Alice']` returns the number.

## 🔗 Analogy

A real phone book or dictionary - you look up a word (key) to find its definition (value), not by page number.

## Related Concepts

- [[key-value-pair|Key-Value Pair]]
- [[hash-table|Hash Table]]
- [[lookup|Lookup]]

title: docstring
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A docstring is a special comment right after a function/class definition that documents what it does. Tools can extract them.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`def add(a, b): '''Return the sum of a and b.''' return a + b` - the triple-quoted string is a docstring. `help(add)` shows it.

## 🔗 Analogy

A label on a filing cabinet drawer - 'Tax documents 2023' tells you what's inside without opening it. Docstrings tell you what a function does without reading its code.

## Related Concepts

- [[comment|Comment]]
- [[documentation|Documentation]]
- [[help-function|Help Function]]

title: duck-typing
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Python doesn't check types strictly - if an object walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`def quack(thing): thing.quack()` - any object with a `.quack()` method works, whether it's a Duck, a Toy, or a Person imitating a duck.

## 🔗 Analogy

Judging by behaviour, not identity - if someone can swim and quack convincingly, you treat them as a duck. You don't check their DNA.

## Related Concepts

- [[type-checking|Type Checking]]
- [[polymorphism|Polymorphism]]
- [[interface|Interface]]

title: elif
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When there are more than two possibilities, elif (else-if) lets you chain multiple conditions.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`if grade >= 90: print('A') elif grade >= 80: print('B') elif grade >= 70: print('C')`

## 🔗 Analogy

A series of toll booths - at each one, if you meet the condition you exit; otherwise you continue to the next.

## Related Concepts

- [[conditional|Conditional]]
- [[if-statement|If Statement]]
- [[else|Else]]

title: else
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When the `if` condition is false, you often want a backup plan. `Else` provides that alternative.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`if age >= 18: print('Adult') else: print('Minor')` - if age is under 18, `Minor` is printed.

## 🔗 Analogy

If it's raining, take an umbrella; otherwise (else), wear sunglasses. The `else` is the otherwise.

## Related Concepts

- [[conditional|Conditional]]
- [[if-statement|If Statement]]
- [[elif|Elif]]

title: encapsulation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Hiding internal details and only exposing a clean interface prevents other code from accidentally breaking things.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A `BankAccount` class hides its `balance` variable. You can only change it through `deposit()` and `withdraw()` methods that check rules.

## 🔗 Analogy

A car's engine - you don't directly control the spark plugs. You press the gas pedal (interface), and the engine's internals (encapsulated details) handle the rest.

## Related Concepts

- [[class|Class]]
- [[private-attribute|Private Attribute]]
- [[interface|Interface]]

title: error-handling
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Things go wrong - files don't exist, network fails, division by zero. Error handling keeps your program from crashing.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`try: result = 10 / 0 except ZeroDivisionError: print('Cannot divide by zero!')` - the program continues instead of crashing.

## 🔗 Analogy

Wearing a seatbelt - you hope you won't crash, but if you do, the seatbelt (try/except) protects you from disaster.

## Related Concepts

- [[exception|Exception]]
- [[try-except|Try-Except]]
- [[error-message|Error Message]]

title: exception
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When something goes wrong in Python, it raises an exception - a special error object with a type and message.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`ValueError`, `TypeError`, `KeyError` are common exceptions. `int('abc')` raises `ValueError: invalid literal for int()`.

## 🔗 Analogy

A fire alarm - when something goes wrong, the alarm (exception) sounds. If nobody handles it (no try/except), the building evacuates (program crashes).

## Related Concepts

- [[error-handling|Error Handling]]
- [[try-except|Try-Except]]
- [[stack-trace|Stack Trace]]

title: expression
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An expression is any piece of code that produces a value - math, function calls, comparisons.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`3 + 4` is an expression (value 7). `x > 5` is an expression (value True). `len('hello')` is an expression (value 5).

## 🔗 Analogy

A math problem on a test - when you solve it, you get an answer (a value). The problem itself is the expression.

## Related Concepts

- [[operator|Operator]]
- [[statement|Statement]]
- [[evaluation|Evaluation]]

title: f-string
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Building strings by concatenation is clunky. F-strings let you embed variables directly into text.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`name = 'Alice'; age = 14; print(f'My name is {name} and I am {age}')` - variables are inserted right into the string.

## 🔗 Analogy

A fill-in-the-blanks story - 'My name is ___ and I am ___' where the blanks are automatically filled with your variable values.

## Related Concepts

- [[string|String]]
- [[string-concatenation|String Concatenation]]
- [[template-string|Template String]]

title: file-i-o
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Programs need to save and load data - reading a config file, saving game progress, writing a log.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`with open('scores.txt', 'w') as f: f.write('Alice: 100')`. Reading: `with open('scores.txt') as f: data = f.read()`.

## 🔗 Analogy

A notebook - you write down information (write to file) so you don't forget it. Later, you open the notebook and read it back (read from file).

## Related Concepts

- [[file-handle|File Handle]]
- [[context-manager|Context Manager]]
- [[serialization|Serialization]]

title: filter
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Selecting only items that meet a condition from a collection is what `filter` does.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`list(filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0, [1,2,3,4,5,6]))` gives [2, 4, 6]. Only even numbers pass through.

## 🔗 Analogy

A sieve in the kitchen - you pour mixed ingredients through it. Only items smaller than the holes (passing the condition) get through.

## Related Concepts

- [[higher-order-function|Higher-Order Function]]
- [[lambda|Lambda]]
- [[predicate|Predicate]]

title: finally
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

In error handling, sometimes you need cleanup code to run whether or not an error occurred - finally always runs.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`try: f = open('file') ... finally: f.close()` - the file closes whether the try succeeded or raised an error.

## 🔗 Analogy

Cleaning up after a party - whether the party was a success or a disaster (exception), you still have to clean up (finally).

## Related Concepts

- [[try-except|Try-Except]]
- [[error-handling|Error Handling]]
- [[context-manager|Context Manager]]

title: float
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Some values aren't whole - like distances, temperatures, or money. Floats store numbers with decimal points.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`price = 9.99` or `pi = 3.14159`. But `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004` - floats are slightly imprecise!

## 🔗 Analogy

A ruler with tiny markings - you can measure fractions, but if you look very closely, the marks aren't perfectly even.

## Related Concepts

- [[integer|Integer]]
- [[floating-point-error|Floating Point Error]]
- [[precision|Precision]]

title: for-loop
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When you need to repeat something for each item in a collection - process every student, check every file.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`for name in ['Alice', 'Bob']: print(name)` prints each name. `for i in range(5): print(i)` prints 0,1,2,3,4.

## 🔗 Analogy

A teacher calling roll - they go through the class list, one name at a time, doing the same thing (calling the name) for each.

## Related Concepts

- [[loop|Loop]]
- [[iterable|Iterable]]
- [[range|Range]]
- [[break|Break]]

title: function-call
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

To use a function, you call it by name with any needed arguments. This executes the function's code.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`greet('Alice')` calls the greet function with `Alice` as the argument. The function runs and may return a value.

## 🔗 Analogy

Pressing the button on a microwave - you've set up the program (function), and pressing the button (calling it) starts it running.

## Related Concepts

- [[function|Function]]
- [[argument|Argument]]
- [[call-stack|Call Stack]]

title: function
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When you do the same thing multiple times, wrapping it in a function avoids repetition and makes code readable.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`def greet(name): return 'Hello, ' + name`. Call it: `greet('Alice')` returns 'Hello, Alice'.

## 🔗 Analogy

A recipe card - you write the steps once, then whenever you want that dish, you just follow the card. You can give it different ingredients (arguments) each time.

## Related Concepts

- [[parameter|Parameter]]
- [[return-value|Return Value]]
- [[function-call|Function Call]]
- [[def|Def]]

title: global-variable
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Some variables need to be accessible everywhere - configuration settings, game state.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`MAX_HEALTH = 100` at the top of the file is global. Any function can read it. But modifying it from inside a function requires `global` keyword.

## 🔗 Analogy

A school notice board - anyone in any classroom can read it. But if you want to change it, you need special permission.

## Related Concepts

- [[scope|Scope]]
- [[local-variable|Local Variable]]
- [[side-effect|Side Effect]]

title: hash-function
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A hash function converts any input into a fixed-size number. It's the engine behind dictionaries and much more.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`hash('hello')` gives a number like `-599545696`. Same input always gives same output. Different inputs usually give different outputs.

## 🔗 Analogy

A librarian's cataloguing system - you give them a book title (input), and they compute a shelf number (hash). Same title always goes to the same shelf.

## Related Concepts

- [[hash-table|Hash Table]]
- [[hash-code|Hash Code]]
- [[deterministic|Deterministic]]

title: hash-table
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Dictionaries use a hash table internally - it converts keys to numbers (hashes) for lightning-fast lookups.

## 📋 Concrete Example

When you do `d['name']`, Python hashes `name` to a number, jumps to that slot, and finds the value. O(1) - constant time, no matter how big the dict.

## 🔗 Analogy

A coat check at a event - you give your coat, they put it on a numbered hanger (hash). When you return with your ticket (key), they go straight to that number. Very fast.

## Related Concepts

- [[dictionary|Dictionary]]
- [[hash-function|Hash Function]]
- [[collision|Collision]]

title: higher-order-function
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Functions that take other functions as arguments (or return them) let you write very flexible, reusable code.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`map(str.upper, ['a','b'])` applies `str.upper` to each element. `filter(lambda x: x > 0, [-1, 0, 1])` keeps only positives.

## 🔗 Analogy

A manager who assigns tasks to workers - the manager (higher-order function) doesn't do the work; it decides which worker (function) does what.

## Related Concepts

- [[lambda|Lambda]]
- [[map|Map]]
- [[filter|Filter]]
- [[reduce|Reduce]]

title: if-statement
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The most basic decision in code - do something only if a condition is true.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`if temperature > 30: print('It is hot!')` - the message only prints when it is above 30 degrees.

## 🔗 Analogy

A bouncer at a club door - they check your ID (the condition), and only let you in if it passes.

## Related Concepts

- [[conditional|Conditional]]
- [[boolean|Boolean]]
- [[block|Block]]

title: import
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Python has a huge ecosystem of pre-written code. Importing lets you use code others have written.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`import random` gives you `random.randint(1, 6)` to roll a die. `from math import sqrt` gives you `sqrt(16) = 4`.

## 🔗 Analogy

Borrowing books from a library - instead of writing your own encyclopedia, you borrow one that's already written and use the parts you need.

## Related Concepts

- [[module|Module]]
- [[package|Package]]
- [[standard-library|Standard Library]]

title: indentation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

In Python, indentation isn't just for looks - it defines which statements belong together in a block.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`if True:` then 4 spaces then `print('a')` on the next line - the print is inside the if because of indentation.

## 🔗 Analogy

The way paragraphs work in writing - indenting shows 'this belongs together'. In Python, it's mandatory, not optional.

## Related Concepts

- [[block|Block]]
- [[syntax|Syntax]]
- [[whitespace|Whitespace]]

title: 01-programming
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

To access a specific element in a list or string, you need a position number - an index.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`name = 'Alice'` - `name[0]` is `A`, `name[1]` is `l`. Python also counts from the end: `name[-1]` is `e`.

## 🔗 Analogy

House numbers on a street - each house has a number, and you find it by counting from the start (or from the end if using negatives).

## Related Concepts

- [[list|List]]
- [[string|String]]
- [[zero-based-indexing|Zero-Based Indexing]]

title: infinite-loop
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A loop that never ends because its condition never becomes false. Usually a bug, but sometimes intentional (servers).

## 📋 Concrete Example

`while True: print('forever')` never stops. `while x > 0: x += 1` (if x starts positive) - x keeps growing, condition stays true.

## 🔗 Analogy

A hamster wheel - the hamster keeps running and the wheel keeps spinning. There's no exit condition. Sometimes useful (generating power), often a trap.

## Related Concepts

- [[while-loop|While Loop]]
- [[break|Break]]
- [[bug|Bug]]

title: inheritance
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When multiple classes share behaviour, inheritance lets a child class reuse a parent's code without duplicating it.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`class Cat(Animal):` - Cat inherits all of Animal's methods. You can add cat-specific methods or override inherited ones.

## 🔗 Analogy

A family business - the child inherits the business knowledge and assets from the parent, then adds their own new ideas or changes some practices.

## Related Concepts

- [[class|Class]]
- [[method-overriding|Method Overriding]]
- [[subclass|Subclass]]

title: integer
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Many programs count things - steps, lives, items in inventory. Integers are whole numbers without decimals.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`lives = 3` or `temperature = -5`. You can do arithmetic: `3 * 4 = 12`.

## 🔗 Analogy

A counter on a scoreboard - it clicks up or down by whole clicks, never half a click.

## Related Concepts

- [[float|Float]]
- [[arithmetic-operator|Arithmetic Operator]]
- [[modulo|Modulo]]

title: iterable
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Anything you can loop over with a `for` loop is iterable - lists, strings, dictionaries, files, and more.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`for x in [1,2,3]` - list is iterable. `for c in 'hi'` - string is iterable. `for k in {'a':1}` - dict is iterable (iterates over keys).

## 🔗 Analogy

A conveyor belt of items - as long as items keep coming, you can process them one at a time. The belt is the iterable.

## Related Concepts

- [[iteration|Iteration]]
- [[iterator|Iterator]]
- [[for-loop|For Loop]]

title: iteration
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Going through items one by one is one of the most common programming patterns - iteration makes this possible.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`for x in [1, 2, 3]: print(x)` iterates over the list. `for ch in 'Hello': print(ch)` iterates over each character.

## 🔗 Analogy

Reading a book page by page - you don't read all pages at once; you go through them one at a time (iterate), processing each before moving to the next.

## Related Concepts

- [[for-loop|For Loop]]
- [[iterable|Iterable]]
- [[iterator|Iterator]]

title: json
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Different programs and languages need to exchange data. JSON is a universal text format everyone can read and write.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`{'name': 'Alice', 'age': 14, 'hobbies': ['coding', 'chess']}` - this is JSON. Python: `import json; json.loads(data)` converts it to a dict.

## 🔗 Analogy

A universal language like Esperanto - no matter what language you normally speak (Python, JavaScript, Java), everyone can read and write in this format.

## Related Concepts

- [[dictionary|Dictionary]]
- [[serialization|Serialization]]
- [[api-response|API Response]]

title: key-value-pair
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Dictionaries store data as key-value pairs: you use the key to find the value, like a word and its definition.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`{'apple': 3, 'banana': 5}` - `apple` is the key, 3 is the value. You look up `apple` to get 3.

## 🔗 Analogy

A name tag at a conference - the name (key) identifies the person (value). You find someone by looking for their name tag.

## Related Concepts

- [[dictionary|Dictionary]]
- [[hash-table|Hash Table]]
- [[lookup|Lookup]]

title: keyword-argument
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When a function has many parameters, passing them by name (keyword) makes calls clearer and order-independent.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`greet(name='Alice', greeting='Hi')` - order doesn't matter. Compare with positional: `greet('Alice', 'Hi')` where order matters.

## 🔗 Analogy

Ordering food by naming what you want: `I`ll have the burger with extra cheese, no onions' (keyword args) vs. just 'burger, extra, none' (positional).

## Related Concepts

- [[parameter|Parameter]]
- [[default-parameter|Default Parameter]]
- [[argument|Argument]]

title: lambda
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Sometimes you need a tiny function without bothering to name it - lambda creates anonymous functions.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`sorted(names, key=lambda x: len(x))` sorts names by length. The lambda is a mini function: takes `x`, returns `len(x)`.

## 🔗 Analogy

A disposable cup - you use it once for a specific purpose (sorting, filtering) and throw it away. No need to give it a name or wash it.

## Related Concepts

- [[function|Function]]
- [[anonymous-function|Anonymous Function]]
- [[higher-order-function|Higher-Order Function]]

title: list-comprehension
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Creating lists with loops is verbose. List comprehensions do it in one clean line.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`squares = [x**2 for x in range(10)]` creates [0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81] in one line.

## 🔗 Analogy

A cookie cutter - instead of shaping each cookie by hand (loop), you press the cutter and get them all at once.

## Related Concepts

- [[list|List]]
- [[for-loop|For Loop]]
- [[filter|Filter]]

title: list
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

You often need to store many related items together - a deck of cards, a class list, a shopping cart.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']`. Access by position: `fruits[0]` is `apple`. Add items: `fruits.append('date')`.

## 🔗 Analogy

A shopping list written on paper - items are in order, you can cross things off, add new ones, or look at any item by its position.

## Related Concepts

- [[array|Array]]
- [[index|Index]]
- [[append|Append]]
- [[list-comprehension|List Comprehension]]

title: local-variable
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Variables created inside a function only exist while that function runs - they're local.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`def greet(): msg = 'Hi'` - `msg` exists only inside `greet()`. After `greet()` finishes, `msg` is gone.

## 🔗 Analogy

A whiteboard in a meeting room - you write on it during the meeting, but when you leave, the next meeting erases it.

## Related Concepts

- [[scope|Scope]]
- [[global-variable|Global Variable]]
- [[function|Function]]

title: logical-operator
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

You often need to combine conditions - age over 13 AND has permission, OR is an adult.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`age > 13 and has_permission` - both must be True. `is_admin or is_teacher` - either one being True is enough. `not is_banned`.

## 🔗 Analogy

Filtering at a theme park: you can ride if (tall enough) AND (not pregnant) OR (have a VIP pass). AND, OR, NOT combine the rules.

## Related Concepts

- [[boolean|Boolean]]
- [[conditional|Conditional]]
- [[truth-table|Truth Table]]

title: map
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Applying the same operation to every item in a collection is so common that `map` makes it a one-liner.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`list(map(lambda x: x**2, [1,2,3]))` gives [1, 4, 9]. Each element is squared.

## 🔗 Analogy

A factory assembly line - each item passes through the same machine (function), and comes out transformed.

## Related Concepts

- [[higher-order-function|Higher-Order Function]]
- [[list-comprehension|List Comprehension]]
- [[iterable|Iterable]]

title: method
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A method is a function that belongs to a class - it operates on the object's data.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`my_dog.bark()` - bark is a method of the Dog class. It uses `self.name` (the object's data) to produce its output.

## 🔗 Analogy

A skill that a dog knows - `sit`, `fetch`, `bark`. Each dog (object) has the same skills (methods) from the same training (class), but does them in their own way.

## Related Concepts

- [[class|Class]]
- [[function|Function]]
- [[self|Self]]

title: module
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A module is a file of Python code you can import - it groups related functions and classes together.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`import math` - the math module has `math.pi`, `math.sqrt()`, `math.cos()`, etc. All math-related functions in one place.

## 🔗 Analogy

A toolbox - the math toolbox has a ruler, compass, and protractor. You open the box (import) and use the tool you need.

## Related Concepts

- [[import|Import]]
- [[package|Package]]
- [[standard-library|Standard Library]]

title: modulo
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

You often need the remainder after division - checking if a number is even, cycling through positions.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`7 % 3 = 1` (7 divided by 3 is 2 remainder 1). `8 % 2 == 0` means 8 is even.

## 🔗 Analogy

Sharing 7 sweets among 3 friends - each gets 2, and 1 is left over. That leftover is the modulo.

## Related Concepts

- [[arithmetic-operator|Arithmetic Operator]]
- [[integer|Integer]]
- [[even-number|Even Number]]

title: namespace
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When programs get large, name collisions happen. Namespaces keep names organised so they don't clash.

## 📋 Concrete Example

The `math` module has `pi`. The `numpy` package also has `pi`. `math.pi` and `numpy.pi` are in different namespaces, so no clash.

## 🔗 Analogy

Phone extensions in an office - Bob in Sales is extension 101, Bob in Engineering is also 101. The department (namespace) tells you which Bob.

## Related Concepts

- [[scope|Scope]]
- [[module|Module]]
- [[import|Import]]

title: object-oriented-programming
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Organising code around objects (data + behaviour) makes large programs easier to manage and understand.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A game might have Player, Enemy, and Item classes. Each manages its own data (health, position) and behaviour (move, attack).

## 🔗 Analogy

Organising a school by departments - the Science department handles labs and science teachers, the Music department handles instruments and music teachers. Each manages its own area.

## Related Concepts

- [[class|Class]]
- [[object|Object]]
- [[inheritance|Inheritance]]
- [[encapsulation|Encapsulation]]

title: object
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An object is a specific instance of a class - it has its own data but shares the class's behaviour.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`my_dog = Dog('Rex')` creates an object. `my_dog.bark()` returns 'Rex says woof!'. Another `Dog('Buddy')` is a different object.

## 🔗 Analogy

A specific house built from the blueprint - it has its own paint colour and furniture (data) but the same layout (structure) as the blueprint defined.

## Related Concepts

- [[class|Class]]
- [[instance|Instance]]
- [[constructor|Constructor]]

title: operator-precedence
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When an expression has multiple operators, which goes first? Precedence rules decide, like math's PEMDAS.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`2 + 3 * 4 = 14` not 20, because * happens before +. Use parentheses to override: `(2 + 3) * 4 = 20`.

## 🔗 Analogy

Priority lanes at immigration - diplomats (higher precedence) go first, then regular passengers. Parentheses are like a VIP pass - they jump the queue.

## Related Concepts

- [[arithmetic-operator|Arithmetic Operator]]
- [[expression|Expression]]
- [[parentheses|Parentheses]]

title: package
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When a project has many modules, they're organised into a package - a folder of modules.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`import numpy.random` - numpy is a package, random is a module inside it. `numpy.random.randint(0, 10)` generates a random integer.

## 🔗 Analogy

A tool chest with drawers - each drawer (module) holds related tools. The whole chest (package) organises everything.

## Related Concepts

- [[module|Module]]
- [[import|Import]]
- [[pip|Pip]]

title: parameter
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Functions need inputs to work with - parameters are the named slots that receive those inputs.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`def add(a, b): return a + b` - `a` and `b` are parameters. When you call `add(3, 5)`, 3 goes into `a`, 5 into `b`.

## 🔗 Analogy

The blanks on a form - 'Name: ____' and 'Age: ____'. When someone fills in the form (calls the function), those blanks get values.

## Related Concepts

- [[function|Function]]
- [[argument|Argument]]
- [[default-parameter|Default Parameter]]

title: pip
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Pip is Python's package manager - it downloads and installs packages from PyPI (Python Package Index).

## 📋 Concrete Example

`pip install requests` downloads the requests package. `pip list` shows what's installed.

## 🔗 Analogy

An app store for Python - you search for what you need, tap `install` (pip install), and it downloads and sets it up for you.

## Related Concepts

- [[package|Package]]
- [[pypi|PyPI]]
- [[virtual-environment|Virtual Environment]]

title: polymorphism
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Different classes can have methods with the same name, and code can call them without knowing which class it is.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`for animal in [Dog(), Cat(), Duck()]: animal.speak()` - each speaks differently (woof, meow, quack) but the code is the same.

## 🔗 Analogy

A universal remote control - the `play` button works on a TV, a stereo, and a DVD player, even though each does something different internally.

## Related Concepts

- [[duck-typing|Duck Typing]]
- [[inheritance|Inheritance]]
- [[method-overriding|Method Overriding]]

title: recursion
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Some problems are naturally self-similar - a smaller version of the same problem. Recursion solves these elegantly.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`def factorial(n): if n <= 1: return 1; return n * factorial(n-1)` - factorial(4) = 4 * 3 * 2 * 1 = 24.

## 🔗 Analogy

Russian nesting dolls - to open the biggest doll, you open it and find a smaller one inside. You keep opening until you reach the tiniest doll (base case).

## Related Concepts

- [[base-case|Base Case]]
- [[call-stack|Call Stack]]
- [[stack-overflow|Stack Overflow]]

title: reduce
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Combining all items in a collection into a single value - summing, multiplying, finding the max - is what reduce does.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`from functools import reduce; reduce(lambda a,b: a+b, [1,2,3,4])` gives 10. It folds the list into one number.

## 🔗 Analogy

Making a smoothie - you put in many fruits (the list), blend them all together (the reducing function), and get one smoothie (the single result).

## Related Concepts

- [[higher-order-function|Higher-Order Function]]
- [[map|Map]]
- [[accumulator|Accumulator]]

title: return-value
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Functions often need to give back a result - the return value is what the function hands back to the caller.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`def square(x): return x * x`. `result = square(4)` - `result` now holds 16, the returned value.

## 🔗 Analogy

A vending machine - you put in money (arguments), it processes, and returns a drink (return value). You can then use that drink.

## Related Concepts

- [[function|Function]]
- [[expression|Expression]]
- [[void-function|Void Function]]

title: scope
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Variables created inside a function shouldn't leak outside - scope controls where variables are visible.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`def f(): x = 10`. Outside `f`, `x` doesn't exist - it's local scope. Global variables are visible everywhere but can cause bugs.

## 🔗 Analogy

Rooms in a house - a variable in the kitchen (local scope) can't be seen from the bedroom. A note on the front door (global) is visible to everyone.

## Related Concepts

- [[variable|Variable]]
- [[local-variable|Local Variable]]
- [[global-variable|Global Variable]]
- [[namespace|Namespace]]

title: serialization
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Objects in memory are complex. Serialization converts them to a simple format (text/bytes) for saving or sending.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`import json; json.dumps({'a': 1})` produces the string `'{"a": 1}'` - the dict is now text that can be saved to a file or sent over a network.

## 🔗 Analogy

Vacuum-packing clothes for travel - you compress your clothes (objects) into flat packages (serialized) so they fit in a suitcase (file/network). At your destination, you unpack them (deserialize).

## Related Concepts

- [[json|JSON]]
- [[deserialization|Deserialization]]
- [[file-i-o|File I-O]]

title: set
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When you need to track unique items and don't care about order - like collecting unique tags or checking membership.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`tags = {'python', 'ai', 'code'}`. Adding `python` again does nothing - duplicates are ignored. `tags.add('web')` adds it.

## 🔗 Analogy

A bucket of unique marbles - you can toss one in, but if an identical one is already there, it bounces out. No order, no duplicates.

## Related Concepts

- [[list|List]]
- [[membership-test|Membership Test]]
- [[set-operations|Set Operations]]

title: stack-overflow
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When recursion goes too deep or the call stack gets too big, the program crashes - stack overflow.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Calling `factorial(1000000)` without optimisation - the stack grows until it exceeds memory limits and crashes.

## 🔗 Analogy

Stacking too many plates - eventually the tower gets too tall and topples over. The crash is the stack overflow.

## Related Concepts

- [[call-stack|Call Stack]]
- [[recursion|Recursion]]
- [[memory-limit|Memory Limit]]

title: statement
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A statement is a complete instruction that does something - it's a full sentence of code.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`x = 5` is a statement (assignment). `if x > 3: print(x)` is a statement (conditional). Statements don't produce values.

## 🔗 Analogy

A command from a teacher - 'Open your books' or 'Stand up'. It's a complete instruction, not a question with an answer.

## Related Concepts

- [[expression|Expression]]
- [[block|Block]]
- [[syntax|Syntax]]

title: string-concatenation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

You often need to join text together - combining a first name and last name, or building a message.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`'Hello, ' + name + '!'` joins the strings. In Python, f-strings are easier: `f'Hello, {name}!'`

## 🔗 Analogy

Gluing paper strips together - each piece of text is a strip, and `+` is the glue that joins them into one long strip.

## Related Concepts

- [[string|String]]
- [[f-string|F-String]]
- [[string-formatting|String Formatting]]

title: string
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Almost every program deals with text - names, messages, passwords. A string is how computers store text.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`greeting = 'Hello, World!'` - the text in quotes is a string. You can join strings: `first + ' ' + last`.

## 🔗 Analogy

A row of letter tiles - each tile is one character, and you string them together to make words and sentences.

## Related Concepts

- [[character|Character]]
- [[string-concatenation|String Concatenation]]
- [[text-encoding|Text Encoding]]

title: truth-table
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A truth table shows the result of logical operators (and, or, not) for all possible input combinations.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`True and False = False`, `True or False = True`, `not True = False`. A table with all combinations makes it clear.

## 🔗 Analogy

A referee's rulebook for combinations - 'foul AND card = red' (AND), 'rain OR snow = postpone' (OR), 'NOT home = away' (NOT). The table lists every scenario.

## Related Concepts

- [[logical-operator|Logical Operator]]
- [[boolean|Boolean]]
- [[conditional|Conditional]]

title: try-except
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The mechanism for catching exceptions and handling them gracefully instead of crashing.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`try: file = open('data.txt') except FileNotFoundError: print('File missing!')` - catches the error and prints a friendly message.

## 🔗 Analogy

A safety net under a tightrope walker - if they slip (error), the net (except) catches them instead of letting them fall (crash).

## Related Concepts

- [[error-handling|Error Handling]]
- [[exception|Exception]]
- [[finally|Finally]]

title: tuple
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Some data shouldn't change after creation - coordinates, dates, RGB colour values. Tuples are immutable lists.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`rgb = (255, 128, 0)` for orange. You can't change `rgb[0]` - it's locked. But it's faster and safer than a list.

## 🔗 Analogy

A sealed envelope - once you seal it, the contents can't be changed. You can read what's inside, but not swap it.

## Related Concepts

- [[list|List]]
- [[immutability|Immutability]]
- [[unpacking|Unpacking]]

title: type-hint
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Type hints annotate variables and functions with expected types, making code clearer and enabling tool support.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`def greet(name: str) -> str: return 'Hello, ' + name` - hints say name should be a string and the function returns a string.

## 🔗 Analogy

Labels on containers - 'this jar is for sugar, this one for salt'. The label doesn't stop you from putting salt in the sugar jar, but it helps you avoid mistakes.

## Related Concepts

- [[type-checking|Type Checking]]
- [[static-analysis|Static Analysis]]
- [[data-type|Data Type]]

title: variable
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

You need a way to store information that can change while your program runs, like a player's score in a game.

## 📋 Concrete Example

In Python: `score = 0` stores the number 0. Later, `score = score + 10` updates it.

## 🔗 Analogy

A labelled box on a shelf - you write `score` on the box and put a number inside. You can swap the number anytime.

## Related Concepts

- [[data-type|Data Type]]
- [[assignment-operator|Assignment Operator]]
- [[constant|Constant]]

title: virtual-environment
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Different projects need different packages and versions. A venv keeps them isolated so they don't conflict.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`python -m venv myenv` creates an isolated environment. `source myenv/bin/activate` turns it on. Packages installed here don't affect other projects.

## 🔗 Analogy

Separate lockers for each sport - football gear in one locker, swimming gear in another. They don't mix up or interfere.

## Related Concepts

- [[pip|Pip]]
- [[package|Package]]
- [[dependency-management|Dependency Management]]

title: while-loop
text:
> **Domain:** [[_programming-fundamentals-moc|Programming Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When you don't know how many times to repeat, but you know when to stop - keep going until a condition changes.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`while lives > 0: play_round()` - keeps playing as long as the player has lives left.

## 🔗 Analogy

Running laps around a track - you keep running while you still have energy. When energy hits zero, you stop.

## Related Concepts

- [[loop|Loop]]
- [[conditional|Conditional]]
- [[infinite-loop|Infinite Loop]]

title: 2d-array
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When data has two dimensions -- a chessboard, a spreadsheet, an image -- a 2D array stores it as rows and columns.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`board = [[0,0,0], [0,1,0], [0,0,0]]`. Access `board[1][2]` gives row 1, column 2. A tic-tac-toe board is a 3x3 2D array.

## 🔗 Analogy

A cinema seating chart. Rows are letters (A, B, C), columns are numbers (1, 2, 3). Seat B5 is at row B, column 5.

## Related Concepts

- [[array|Array]]
- [[matrix|Matrix]]
- [[grid|Grid]]
- [[nested-list|Nested List]]

title: adjacency-list
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

For sparse graphs (few edges relative to nodes), an adjacency list stores each node's neighbours separately, saving memory.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`graph = {'A': ['B', 'C'], 'B': ['A', 'D'], 'C': ['A'], 'D': ['B']}`. Each key lists only its direct neighbours.

## 🔗 Analogy

A contacts list on your phone. Each person's name has a list of their direct friends. You do not store every possible friendship, only the ones that exist.

## Related Concepts

- [[graph|Graph]]
- [[adjacency-matrix|Adjacency Matrix]]
- [[sparse-graph|Sparse Graph]]
- [[space-complexity|Space Complexity]]

title: adjacency-matrix
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

For dense graphs (many edges) or when you need to check edge existence instantly, a matrix stores all possible connections as a table.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A 4x4 grid where `matrix[i][j] = 1` means node i connects to node j, `0` means no connection. Checking `matrix[2][3]` is O(1).

## 🔗 Analogy

A seating chart for a classroom showing who sits next to whom. Every possible pair has a yes or no in a grid. Quick to look up but wastes space if few students sit together.

## Related Concepts

- [[graph|Graph]]
- [[adjacency-list|Adjacency List]]
- [[dense-graph|Dense Graph]]
- [[matrix|Matrix]]

title: array
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When you need to store many items of the same type in order and access them quickly by position, arrays are the simplest choice.

## 📋 Concrete Example

In Python: `scores = [85, 92, 78, 90]`. Access `scores[0]` to get 85. You can change `scores[1] = 95` instantly.

## 🔗 Analogy

A row of numbered lockers in a school hallway. Each locker has a number (index) and holds one item. You walk straight to locker 0 or locker 3 without checking the others.

## Related Concepts

- [[index|Index]]
- [[fixed-size-array|Fixed-Size Array]]
- [[dynamic-array|Dynamic Array]]
- [[linked-list|Linked List]]

title: avl-tree
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A plain BST can become unbalanced (like a linked list) after many insertions. AVL trees self-balance to guarantee fast operations.

## 📋 Concrete Example

After inserting nodes that tilt the tree, AVL performs rotations to keep the height difference between left and right subtrees at most 1.

## 🔗 Analogy

A mobile (hanging sculpture) that rebalances itself. If you add weight to one side, it rotates to keep both sides roughly equal so it never tilts too far.

## Related Concepts

- [[binary-search-tree|Binary Search Tree]]
- [[self-balancing-tree|Self-Balancing Tree]]
- [[rotation|Rotation]]
- [[red-black-tree|Red-Black Tree]]
- [[tree-height|Tree Height]]

title: b-tree
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When data is too large for memory and lives on disk -- databases, file systems -- B-trees minimise disk reads by storing many keys per node.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A B-tree node might hold 100 keys and 101 child pointers. This means fewer levels, fewer disk reads. Database indexes use B-trees extensively.

## 🔗 Analogy

A library where each shelf holds 100 books (not just 1). You find the right shelf in 2-3 steps instead of 10, saving time walking through the stacks.

## Related Concepts

- [[self-balancing-tree|Self-Balancing Tree]]
- [[database-index|Database Index]]
- [[disk-i-o|Disk I-O]]
- [[external-sorting|External Sorting]]

title: binary-heap
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A heap implemented as a complete binary tree stored in an array. Parent at index i has children at 2i+1 and 2i+2.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Array `[10, 5, 3, 1, 2]` represents a max-heap: index 0 (10) has children at index 1 (5) and 2 (3). No gaps in the tree.

## 🔗 Analogy

A fully packed stadium where every row is filled left to right before the next row starts. You know exactly where row i's seats are without a map.

## Related Concepts

- [[heap|Heap]]
- [[complete-binary-tree|Complete Binary Tree]]
- [[min-heap|Min-Heap]]
- [[max-heap|Max-Heap]]

title: binary-search-tree
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A BST keeps data sorted so you can search, insert, and delete efficiently: left child is smaller, right child is larger.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Searching for 25 in a BST with root 50: 25 < 50, go left; 25 > 20, go right; found 25. Each step eliminates half the tree.

## 🔗 Analogy

A phone book organised by surname. If you are looking for `Chan`, you open to the middle, see `Lee`, know C comes before L, and flip to the left half.

## Related Concepts

- [[binary-tree|Binary Tree]]
- [[in-order-traversal|In-Order Traversal]]
- [[search|Search]]
- [[avl-tree|AVL Tree]]
- [[red-black-tree|Red-Black Tree]]

title: binary-tree
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When data has a natural hierarchy -- file systems, family trees, organisation charts -- trees organise it with parent-child relationships.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A root node with up to two children (left and right). Each child can itself be a root of a smaller tree. A file folder containing subfolders is a tree.

## 🔗 Analogy

A family tree. Each person (node) has up to two parents, and each branch leads to more relatives. The oldest ancestor is the root at the top.

## Related Concepts

- [[tree-node|Tree Node]]
- [[root|Root]]
- [[binary-search-tree|Binary Search Tree]]
- [[avl-tree|AVL Tree]]

title: bloom-filter
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When you need to quickly check if an item might be in a huge set without storing the full set, a bloom filter gives a fast `possibly` or 'definitely not'.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A bloom filter for a million URLs uses a few hundred KB. `might_contain(url)` returns True (maybe) or False (definitely not). No false negatives, some false positives.

## 🔗 Analogy

A bouncer with a blurry photo list. If someone is not on the list, they are definitely not VIP. If they seem to match, they might be VIP (worth a closer check).

## Related Concepts

- [[hash-function|Hash Function]]
- [[false-positive|False Positive]]
- [[probabilistic-structure|Probabilistic Structure]]
- [[bit-array|Bit Array]]

title: bounds-checking
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Accessing an index outside the array's range causes errors or crashes. Bounds checking prevents this dangerous mistake.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`arr = [1, 2, 3]`. `arr[5]` raises `IndexError: list index out of range` in Python. Some languages like C silently read garbage memory.

## 🔗 Analogy

A building with floors 1 to 10. If you press button 15 in the lift, nothing happens -- there is no floor 15. Bounds checking is that safety lock.

## Related Concepts

- [[index|Index]]
- [[array|Array]]
- [[indexerror|IndexError]]
- [[buffer-overflow|Buffer Overflow]]

title: chaining
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A collision resolution strategy where each bucket holds a linked list of all entries that hashed to that index.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Index 5 has a linked list: Ada -> Bob -> Charlie. To find Bob, hash to index 5, then scan the small list. If the list is short, it is still very fast.

## 🔗 Analogy

A shared locker used by all students whose surnames start with `C`. Their bags are lined up inside on hooks (a chain). You look through the hooks to find yours.

## Related Concepts

- [[collision|Collision]]
- [[open-addressing|Open Addressing]]
- [[hash-table|Hash Table]]
- [[linked-list|Linked List]]

title: circular-buffer
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When you need a fixed-size buffer that overwrites old data when full -- audio streams, log rotation, sensor data -- a circular buffer cycles back to the start.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Buffer of size 4: positions [0,1,2,3]. After filling all 4, the next write goes back to position 0, overwriting the oldest data. A write pointer cycles around.

## 🔗 Analogy

A circular running track with 4 lanes. When the runner in lane 4 finishes, the next runner starts again in lane 1, replacing the oldest runner. The track never grows.

## Related Concepts

- [[ring-buffer|Ring Buffer]]
- [[fixed-size-buffer|Fixed-Size Buffer]]
- [[fifo|FIFO]]
- [[deque|Deque]]

title: circular-linked-list
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When the last node points back to the first, the list forms a circle. This is useful for round-robin scheduling and turn-based games.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A -> B -> C -> A (back to start). There is no null end. You keep cycling through the same nodes endlessly.

## 🔗 Analogy

A clock face. After 12 comes 1 again. There is no `end` to the hours -- they cycle forever in a circle.

## Related Concepts

- [[linked-list|Linked List]]
- [[round-robin|Round-Robin]]
- [[cyclic-structure|Cyclic Structure]]

title: collision
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Two different keys hash to the same index. Collisions are inevitable and must be handled for the hash table to work correctly.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Keys `Ada` and `Bob` both hash to index 5. The table must store both. Common fixes: chaining (linked list at index 5) or open addressing (find the next empty slot).

## 🔗 Analogy

Two students whose surnames start with `C` are assigned the same locker. The school handles this by putting a divider in the locker (chaining) or finding the next empty locker nearby (probing).

## Related Concepts

- [[hash-table|Hash Table]]
- [[chaining|Chaining]]
- [[open-addressing|Open Addressing]]
- [[hash-function|Hash Function]]

title: degree
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The degree of a node is the number of edges connected to it. In directed graphs, we distinguish in-degree and out-degree.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Node Alice with edges to Bob, Carol, and Dave has degree 3. In a directed graph, if 2 people follow Alice and Alice follows 1, in-degree is 2 and out-degree is 1.

## 🔗 Analogy

The number of friends someone has on social media. If Alice has 50 friends, her degree is 50. More friends means more connections (edges).

## Related Concepts

- [[graph|Graph]]
- [[node|Node]]
- [[in-degree|In-Degree]]
- [[out-degree|Out-Degree]]

title: deque
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A deque (double-ended queue) lets you add and remove from both ends, combining stack and queue flexibility.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`from collections import deque; d = deque([1,2,3]); d.appendleft(0); d.pop()` gives 3. You can operate on both ends.

## 🔗 Analogy

A train with doors on both ends. Passengers can board or exit from either the front or the back of the train.

## Related Concepts

- [[queue|Queue]]
- [[stack|Stack]]
- [[double-ended|Double-Ended]]
- [[circular-buffer|Circular Buffer]]

title: dequeue
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Dequeue is the operation of removing and returning the front item from a queue.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`q.popleft()` removes and returns the item at the front. The next item moves up to become the new front.

## 🔗 Analogy

The person at the front of the queue gets their food and leaves. The second person steps up to the counter.

## Related Concepts

- [[queue|Queue]]
- [[enqueue|Enqueue]]
- [[fifo|FIFO]]

title: directed-graph
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When relationships have a direction -- one-way streets, followers on social media, prerequisites -- edges point from one node to another.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Instagram follows: Alice follows Bob, but Bob does not follow Alice. The edge goes A -> B, not B -> A.

## 🔗 Analogy

One-way streets in a city. You can drive from street A to street B, but not back. The arrow shows the legal direction of travel.

## Related Concepts

- [[graph|Graph]]
- [[undirected-graph|Undirected Graph]]
- [[edge|Edge]]
- [[in-degree|In-Degree]]
- [[out-degree|Out-Degree]]

title: disjoint-set
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When you need to track which elements belong to the same group -- connected components, network connectivity, Kruskal algorithm -- disjoint sets manage merging efficiently.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Friends: Alice-Bob, Bob-Carol. After union operations, Alice, Bob, and Carol are in the same group. Asking `find(Alice) == find(Carol)` returns True.

## 🔗 Analogy

A school club fair. Students start alone. As they join clubs, they merge into groups. You can instantly check if two students are in the same club.

## Related Concepts

- [[union-find|Union-Find]]
- [[find-operation|Find Operation]]
- [[union-operation|Union Operation]]
- [[path-compression|Path Compression]]
- [[kruskal-algorithm|Kruskal Algorithm]]

title: doubly-linked-list
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When you need to move both forward and backward through a sequence, each node holds two pointers: next and previous.

## 📋 Concrete Example

None <- [A|<->] <-> [B|<->] <-> [C|<->] -> None. From B, you can go to A (prev) or C (next). Python is actually built on doubly linked concepts in some structures.

## 🔗 Analogy

A two-way street. You can drive forward or reverse. This is more flexible but requires more road surface (memory) than a one-way street.

## Related Concepts

- [[linked-list|Linked List]]
- [[singly-linked-list|Singly Linked List]]
- [[bidirectional-traversal|Bidirectional Traversal]]

title: dynamic-array
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Fixed arrays cannot grow. A dynamic array automatically resizes when full, giving you flexibility without manual memory management.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Python lists are dynamic arrays: `nums = [1]; nums.append(2); nums.append(3)` -- the list grows as needed. Under the hood it may copy to a bigger buffer.

## 🔗 Analogy

A stretchy notebook. You start with 10 lines, but when you fill the page a new page with more lines is glued on so you never run out of space.

## Related Concepts

- [[array|Array]]
- [[capacity|Capacity]]
- [[amortized-cost|Amortized Cost]]
- [[vector|Vector]]

title: edge
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An edge is the connection between two nodes in a graph. It can be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted.

## 📋 Concrete Example

In a social graph, an edge between Alice and Bob means they are friends. In a road graph, an edge between two intersections means there is a road connecting them.

## 🔗 Analogy

A bridge connecting two islands. The bridge (edge) links the islands (nodes). Some bridges are one-way, some are two-way, some have tolls (weights).

## Related Concepts

- [[graph|Graph]]
- [[node|Node]]
- [[directed-graph|Directed Graph]]
- [[weighted-graph|Weighted Graph]]

title: enqueue
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Enqueue is the operation of adding an item to the back of a queue.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`q.append('task3')` adds `task3` to the end of the queue. It will be processed after all earlier items.

## 🔗 Analogy

A new person joining the back of the lunch queue. They stand at the end and wait their turn.

## Related Concepts

- [[queue|Queue]]
- [[dequeue|Dequeue]]
- [[fifo|FIFO]]

title: fenwick-tree
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Also called a Binary Indexed Tree. A compact array-based structure for prefix sums and point updates, using less memory than a segment tree.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Array [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]. `prefix_sum(3)` = 3+1+4 = 8 in O(log n). Updating index 2 also takes O(log n). Implemented with bit tricks.

## 🔗 Analogy

A running total column in a spreadsheet. Instead of re-adding all rows, you keep partial sums at power-of-two intervals and combine them cleverly.

## Related Concepts

- [[segment-tree|Segment Tree]]
- [[prefix-sum|Prefix Sum]]
- [[range-query|Range Query]]
- [[binary-indexed-tree|Binary Indexed Tree]]

title: fifo
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

First-In-First-Out describes the access order of a queue: the earliest added item is the first to be removed.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Queue: enqueue A, enqueue B, enqueue C. Dequeue gives A (first in). Dequeue gives B. Dequeue gives C (last in, last out).

## 🔗 Analogy

A conveyor belt sushi restaurant. The first plate put on the belt is the first one a customer picks up at the other end.

## Related Concepts

- [[queue|Queue]]
- [[lifo|LIFO]]
- [[enqueue|Enqueue]]
- [[dequeue|Dequeue]]

title: fixed-size-array
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Sometimes you know exactly how many items you will store and want the speed and memory efficiency of a fixed buffer.

## 📋 Concrete Example

In C: `int seats[6] = {0,0,0,0,0,0};` reserves exactly 6 integer slots. You cannot add a 7th seat.

## 🔗 Analogy

A six-seater car. You cannot magically add a seventh seat. If you need more passengers, you need a bigger vehicle.

## Related Concepts

- [[array|Array]]
- [[static-allocation|Static Allocation]]
- [[buffer|Buffer]]

title: forest
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A collection of separate trees. Sometimes data naturally forms multiple disconnected trees rather than one unified tree.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A file system with two separate drives C: and D: -- each is a tree, and together they form a forest. A company with multiple divisions, each with its own org chart, is a forest.

## 🔗 Analogy

A national park with several separate wooded areas. Each grove is a tree, but they are not connected to each other. The whole park is a forest of separate groves.

## Related Concepts

- [[tree|Tree]]
- [[disjoint-set|Disjoint Set]]
- [[connected-components|Connected Components]]
- [[graph|Graph]]

title: graph
text:
> **Domain:** [[_data-structures-moc|Data Structures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When relationships between items are not hierarchical but network-like -- social networks, maps, dependencies -- a graph is the right structure.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A graph of friends: Alice is friends with Bob and Carol, Bob is friends with Dave. Each person is a node, each friendship is an edge.

## 🔗 Analogy

A map of Hong Kong MTR stations. Each station is a node, each train line connecting stations is an edge. You can travel in any direction.
