title: http-header
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Metadata sent with HTTP requests and responses: content type, authentication, caching, CORS.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Headers: 'Content-Type: application/json' (data is JSON). 'Authorization: Bearer token123' (authenticated). 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *' (CORS: any website can access). Metadata about the request.

## 🔗 Analogy

HTTP headers are like labels on a package - `Fragile` (handle carefully), `Refrigerate` (storage instruction), 'Return Address' (sender). Headers give the server instructions about how to handle the request.

## Related Concepts

- [[http|HTTP]]
- [[cors|CORS]]
- [[content-type|Content-Type]]

title: http-method
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Verbs that define what to do with a resource: GET (read), POST (create), PUT (update), DELETE (remove).

## 📋 Concrete Example

GET /users: list all users. POST /users: create a new user. PUT /users/123: update user 123. DELETE /users/123: delete user 123. The method tells the server what action to perform.

## 🔗 Analogy

HTTP methods are like verbs in a sentence - GET (read), POST (create), PUT (update), DELETE (destroy). The resource (users) is the noun. Together, they form a complete instruction.

## Related Concepts

- [[rest-api|REST API]]
- [[http|HTTP]]
- [[api-endpoint|API Endpoint]]

title: internet
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The internet connects billions of devices worldwide. Understanding it is essential because AI agents live on the internet - they fetch data, call APIs, and serve users globally.

## 📋 Concrete Example

You type google.com. Your request travels through undersea cables, reaches Google's server, and returns results in 50ms. The internet makes this possible for billions of people simultaneously.

## 🔗 Analogy

The internet is like a global postal system - your letter (data) goes from your house to a post office (router) to another post office to the destination. Billions of letters travel simultaneously, each reaching the right address.

## Related Concepts

- [[network|Network]]
- [[tcp-ip|TCP-IP]]
- [[world-wide-web|World Wide Web]]

title: javascript
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The programming language of the web. Runs in the browser. Adds interactivity: clicks, animations, dynamic content.

## 📋 Concrete Example

JavaScript: button.addEventListener(`click`, () => { alert('Hello!'); }). When the user clicks the button, a popup appears. JavaScript makes web pages interactive, not just static.

## 🔗 Analogy

JavaScript is like electricity in a house - the frame (HTML) and decoration (CSS) are static. Electricity (JS) makes things move: lights turn on, the doorbell rings, the TV works. JavaScript brings web pages to life.

## Related Concepts

- [[html|HTML]]
- [[web-browser|Web Browser]]
- [[dom|DOM]]

title: json
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

JavaScript Object Notation - a lightweight data format. The standard for API data exchange.

## 📋 Concrete Example

JSON: {"name": "Alice", "age": 14, "hobbies": ["coding", "gaming"]}. Easy for humans to read, easy for machines to parse. The lingua franca of web APIs.

## 🔗 Analogy

JSON is like a standardized form - everyone fills it out the same way: name, age, hobbies. Any system can read it. JSON is the standard form for data exchange on the web.

## Related Concepts

- [[rest-api|REST API]]
- [[api|API]]
- [[data-format|Data Format]]

title: jwt
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

JSON Web Token - a standard for tokens. Contains user info, signed for security.

## 📋 Concrete Example

JWT: three parts - header, payload, signature. Payload: {user_id: 123, role: `admin`, exp: 1690000000}. Signature: verifies it has not been tampered with. Compact, self-contained, widely used.

## 🔗 Analogy

JWT is like a sealed letter of recommendation - it contains information about you (payload), is sealed by the sender (signature), and anyone can verify the seal. No one can tamper with it without breaking the seal.

## Related Concepts

- [[token|Token]]
- [[authentication|Authentication]]
- [[json|JSON]]

title: nginx
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A popular web server and reverse proxy. Handles high traffic efficiently. Used for load balancing and serving static files.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Nginx: receives 10,000 requests/second. Serves static files (images, CSS) directly - fast. For dynamic content, forwards to the backend application. Also load balances across multiple backend instances.

## 🔗 Analogy

Nginx is like an efficient traffic cop - they handle simple requests (static files) themselves instantly. Complex requests (dynamic content) are forwarded to specialists (backend). They also direct traffic to less busy lanes (load balancing).

## Related Concepts

- [[web-server|Web Server]]
- [[load-balancer|Load Balancer]]
- [[reverse-proxy|Reverse Proxy]]

title: offline-mode
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When a web app works without internet. Achieved through caching and service workers.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Offline mode: you open the app. No internet. The service worker serves cached files. You can read saved articles, see cached data. When internet returns, the app syncs.

## 🔗 Analogy

Offline mode is like a downloaded movie - you download it once (online), then watch it anytime (offline). No internet needed. Offline mode lets web apps work like downloaded content.

## Related Concepts

- [[service-worker|Service Worker]]
- [[progressive-web-app|Progressive Web App]]
- [[caching|Caching]]

title: pagination
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Splitting large lists into pages. API returns 20 items per page instead of 10,000 at once.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Pagination: GET /api/users?page=2&per_page=20. Returns users 21-40. Not all 10,000 at once. Faster, less memory, better UX. User clicks `Next` for page 3.

## 🔗 Analogy

Pagination is like pages in a book - instead of one long scroll (10,000 items), you have pages (20 items each). Easier to read, faster to load. You turn pages instead of scrolling endlessly.

## Related Concepts

- [[rest-api|REST API]]
- [[json|JSON]]
- [[user-experience|User Experience]]

title: progressive-web-app
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A web app that works like a native app: offline, push notifications, home screen icon.

## 📋 Concrete Example

PWA: you visit a website. Browser asks: 'Add to home screen?' You accept. Now it has an icon, works offline, and sends push notifications - like a real app. But it is still a website.

## 🔗 Analogy

A PWA is like a food truck that becomes a restaurant - it starts mobile (website) but can set up a permanent location (home screen), serve customers even when the road is closed (offline), and send promotions (push notifications).

## Related Concepts

- [[responsive-design|Responsive Design]]
- [[web-development|Web Development]]
- [[service-worker|Service Worker]]

title: rate-limiting
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Restricting how many API requests a user can make per time period. Prevents abuse.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Rate limit: 100 requests per minute per user. User A: 50 requests -> OK. User A: 101st request -> '429 Too Many Requests.' Prevents abuse and ensures fair usage.

## 🔗 Analogy

Rate limiting is like a speed limit on a highway - you can only go 80 km/h, not 200. It prevents dangerous behavior and ensures everyone gets fair use of the road. Rate limiting ensures fair API access.

## Related Concepts

- [[api|API]]
- [[security|Security]]
- [[throttling|Throttling]]

title: react
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A JavaScript library for building user interfaces. Component-based, declarative. Very popular.

## 📋 Concrete Example

React: build a Button component. Reuse it everywhere: <Button color=`red` onClick={handleClick}>. Components are like Lego bricks - build once, reuse everywhere. React manages the UI efficiently.

## 🔗 Analogy

React is like Lego - you build small pieces (components) and combine them into complex structures (UIs). Each piece is reusable. Change one piece, and React efficiently updates only what changed.

## Related Concepts

- [[frontend|Frontend]]
- [[component|Component]]
- [[virtual-dom|Virtual DOM]]

title: real-time-communication
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Exchanging data instantly, with minimal delay. Chat, gaming, live streaming, collaborative editing.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Real-time: you type a message. Your friend sees it in 50ms. You move a game character. Other players see it instantly. No page refresh, no delay. WebSocket enables this.

## 🔗 Analogy

Real-time communication is like a walkie-talkie - you speak and the other person hears instantly. No waiting, no delays. Essential for chat, gaming, and live collaboration.

## Related Concepts

- [[websocket|WebSocket]]
- [[latency-in-networks|Latency in Networks]]
- [[streaming|Streaming]]

title: rendering
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The process of generating the visual output from code. Browser rendering: HTML + CSS -> pixels on screen.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Rendering: browser receives HTML, builds DOM tree. Applies CSS styles. Lays out elements. Paints pixels on screen. 60 times per second for smooth animation. The browser's core job.

## 🔗 Analogy

Rendering is like a painter translating a sketch into a finished painting - they take the outline (HTML), apply colors (CSS), and produce the final artwork (pixels on screen). The browser renders web pages.

## Related Concepts

- [[web-browser|Web Browser]]
- [[virtual-dom|Virtual DOM]]
- [[css|CSS]]

title: responsive-design
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Designing websites that work on all screen sizes: phone, tablet, desktop.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Responsive: CSS media queries: '@media (max-width: 768px) { .menu { display: none; } }'. On mobile, the menu is hidden; a hamburger icon appears. On desktop, the full menu shows. One website, all devices.

## 🔗 Analogy

Responsive design is like a transformer toy - it changes shape depending on the situation. On a small screen (phone), it is compact. On a large screen (desktop), it expands. Same toy, different forms.

## Related Concepts

- [[css|CSS]]
- [[frontend|Frontend]]
- [[mobile-design|Mobile Design]]

title: rest-api
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Representational State Transfer - a style of API design using HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) on resources.

## 📋 Concrete Example

REST API: GET /books (list), POST /books (create), GET /books/123 (detail), PUT /books/123 (update), DELETE /books/123 (delete). Standard, predictable, widely used.

## 🔗 Analogy

REST is like a library system - GET (read a book), POST (add a new book), PUT (update a book), DELETE (remove a book). Standard operations on resources (books). Clear and predictable.

## Related Concepts

- [[api-endpoint|API Endpoint]]
- [[http-method|HTTP Method]]
- [[json|JSON]]

title: reverse-proxy
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A server that sits in front of other servers, forwarding requests. Provides security, load balancing, and caching.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Reverse proxy: all requests go to proxy.example.com. Proxy forwards to backend1, backend2, or backend3. Users never see the backend servers directly. Security + load balancing + caching.

## 🔗 Analogy

A reverse proxy is like a building receptionist - all visitors go to reception first. Reception directs them to the right office (backend server). Visitors never know the actual office number. Security and organization.

## Related Concepts

- [[nginx|Nginx]]
- [[load-balancer|Load Balancer]]
- [[web-server|Web Server]]

title: service-worker
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A script that runs in the background, enabling offline functionality, push notifications, and caching for PWAs.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Service worker: intercepts network requests. If offline: serves cached files. If online: fetches fresh data. Runs even when the page is closed. Enables push notifications.

## 🔗 Analogy

A service worker is like a night security guard - they work even when the store (page) is closed. They handle incoming requests (visitors), check inventory (cache), and call for backup (fetch from network) when needed.

## Related Concepts

- [[progressive-web-app|Progressive Web App]]
- [[caching|Caching]]
- [[offline-mode|Offline Mode]]

title: session
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A period of interaction between user and server. The server remembers the user across multiple requests.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Session: user logs in at 2pm. Session starts. User browses for 30 minutes. Server remembers: this is Alice, she is logged in, she has items in her cart. Session ends at 2:30pm (timeout or logout).

## 🔗 Analogy

A session is like a gym membership - you check in (login), use the gym (browse), and the staff knows who you are the whole time. When you leave (logout), the session ends. Next visit, you check in again.

## Related Concepts

- [[cookie|Cookie]]
- [[authentication|Authentication]]
- [[state-management|State Management]]

title: single-page-application
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A web app that loads once and updates dynamically without page reloads. Smooth, app-like experience.

## 📋 Concrete Example

SPA: you click `Profile`. Instead of loading a new page, JavaScript: 1) fetches profile data (API). 2) Updates the DOM. 3) URL changes to /profile. No page reload. Smooth, instant.

## 🔗 Analogy

SPA is like a magic book - you turn to a new chapter, but the book does not close and reopen. The content changes instantly. No loading screen. Smooth transitions between `pages`.

## Related Concepts

- [[react|React]]
- [[frontend|Frontend]]
- [[virtual-dom|Virtual DOM]]

title: ssl-certificate
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A digital certificate that proves a website's identity and enables HTTPS encryption.

## 📋 Concrete Example

SSL certificate: issued by a Certificate Authority. Contains: domain name, owner, expiration. Browser checks: is this certificate valid? Yes -> shows the lock icon. No -> warns the user.

## 🔗 Analogy

An SSL certificate is like a passport - it proves identity (this is really google.com) and is issued by a trusted authority (Certificate Authority). The browser checks it, just like immigration checks your passport.

## Related Concepts

- [[tls|TLS]]
- [[https|HTTPS]]
- [[security|Security]]

title: static-site
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A website with fixed content. No server-side processing. Fast, cheap, secure.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Static site: HTML, CSS, JS files on a server. No database, no server code. Just files. Extremely fast (no processing), cheap (no server needed), secure (no server to hack). Good for blogs and portfolios.

## 🔗 Analogy

A static site is like a printed brochure - the content is fixed. Everyone sees the same thing. No interactivity, but fast, cheap, and reliable. Contrast with a dynamic site, which is like a live conversation.

## Related Concepts

- [[web-development|Web Development]]
- [[frontend|Frontend]]
- [[dynamic-site|Dynamic Site]]

title: streaming
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Sending data continuously rather than all at once. Used for video, audio, and AI token streaming.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Streaming: instead of waiting for the full AI response (10 seconds), stream tokens as they are generated. User sees words appearing one by one. Feels instant, even though total time is the same.

## 🔗 Analogy

Streaming is like a water tap - instead of delivering a bucket of water all at once, water flows continuously. You start drinking immediately. Streaming delivers data continuously for a better experience.

## Related Concepts

- [[real-time-communication|Real-Time Communication]]
- [[token-stream|Token Stream]]
- [[latency-in-networks|Latency in Networks]]

title: token-stream
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When an LLM generates tokens one at a time and sends each immediately. The user sees text appearing progressively.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Token stream: model generates `The` -> send. ' capital' -> send. ' of' -> send. ' France' -> send. ' is' -> send. ' Paris.' -> send. User sees the sentence building up, word by word. Feels faster.

## 🔗 Analogy

Token streaming is like a typist typing a letter while you watch - each letter appears as they type. You start reading immediately, before the letter is finished. Token streaming shows AI output as it is generated.

## Related Concepts

- [[streaming|Streaming]]
- [[next-token-prediction|Next-Token Prediction]]
- [[user-experience|User Experience]]

title: token
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A piece of data that proves authentication. Sent with each request instead of re-entering passwords.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Token: after login, server gives a JWT token: `eyJhbG...`. Client stores it. Each API request includes the token. Server verifies: is this token valid? Yes -> authenticated. No -> rejected.

## 🔗 Analogy

A token is like a festival wristband - you show your ticket once (login), get a wristband (token). For the rest of the festival, you just show the wristband. No need to show your ticket again. Tokens work the same way.

## Related Concepts

- [[authentication|Authentication]]
- [[jwt|JWT]]
- [[session|Session]]

title: virtual-dom
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

React's internal representation of the DOM. Enables efficient UI updates by comparing changes.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Virtual DOM: React keeps a copy of the DOM in memory. When data changes, React: 1) updates the virtual DOM. 2) Compares with the real DOM. 3) Updates only the changed parts. Efficient.

## 🔗 Analogy

The virtual DOM is like a draft blueprint - the architect (React) sketches changes on a draft first, compares with the current blueprint, and only sends the differences to the builder (browser). Efficient, no wasted work.

## Related Concepts

- [[react|React]]
- [[dom|DOM]]
- [[rendering|Rendering]]

title: web-api
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An API accessed over HTTP. The most common way for applications to communicate on the internet.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Web API: your app calls 'GET https://api.weather.com/today?city=HongKong'. Returns JSON: {temp: 28, condition: `sunny`}. Your app uses this data to show weather. APIs connect applications.

## 🔗 Analogy

A web API is like a restaurant's takeout window - you (application) ask for food (data) through the window (API). The kitchen (server) prepares it and hands it out. You do not need to go inside.

## Related Concepts

- [[rest-api|REST API]]
- [[api-endpoint|API Endpoint]]
- [[json|JSON]]

title: web-browser
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A program that fetches and displays web pages. Chrome, Safari, Firefox are browsers.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Browser: you type `google.com`. Browser sends HTTP request, receives HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and renders the page. It interprets the code and displays the visual result.

## 🔗 Analogy

A web browser is like a translator and decorator - it fetches raw materials (HTML, CSS, JS) from a server, translates them, and presents a beautifully decorated page. Without the browser, web code is just text.

## Related Concepts

- [[world-wide-web|World Wide Web]]
- [[html|HTML]]
- [[rendering|Rendering]]

title: web-development
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Building websites and web applications. Involves frontend, backend, databases, and deployment.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Web development: 1) Design UI (frontend). 2) Build API (backend). 3) Set up database. 4) Deploy to server. 5) Maintain and update. The full process of creating a web application.

## 🔗 Analogy

Web development is like building a house - design the layout (frontend), install plumbing and electricity (backend), set up storage (database), get permits (deployment), and maintain it. A complete construction project.

## Related Concepts

- [[full-stack|Full-Stack]]
- [[frontend|Frontend]]
- [[backend|Backend]]

title: web-scraping
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Extracting data from web pages by parsing HTML. Useful when no API is available.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Scraping: fetch 'https://news.com', parse HTML, extract all <h2> tags (headlines). Return: ['AI Breakthrough', 'New Phone Released', ...]. Get data from any website, even without an API.

## 🔗 Analogy

Web scraping is like clipping newspaper articles - you go to the newsstand (website), find the articles you want (headlines), and clip them (extract). No subscription (API) needed, but you must do the work yourself.

## Related Concepts

- [[html-parsing|HTML Parsing]]
- [[web-api|Web API]]
- [[data-collection|Data Collection]]

title: web-server
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Software that receives HTTP requests and sends HTTP responses. Apache, Nginx are web servers.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Web server: receives 'GET /index.html'. Finds the file. Sends '200 OK' + HTML. Receives 'GET /api/data'. Calls the application. Sends JSON. The middleman between client and application.

## 🔗 Analogy

A web server is like a restaurant host - they greet customers (requests), find them a table (route to the right resource), and bring the menu (response). They handle the flow of customers.

## Related Concepts

- [[http|HTTP]]
- [[backend|Backend]]
- [[nginx|Nginx]]

title: webhook
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A URL that receives HTTP POST requests when an event occurs. Like a callback for web services.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Webhook: when a GitHub push happens, GitHub sends a POST to your webhook URL: https://yourapp.com/webhook. Your app receives it and triggers a build. Automated, event-driven.

## 🔗 Analogy

A webhook is like an automatic phone call from a store - 'Your order is ready.' You do not need to call and ask; they call you when it is ready. Webhooks call your app when events happen.

## Related Concepts

- [[http|HTTP]]
- [[event-driven-architecture|Event-Driven Architecture]]
- [[api|API]]

title: websocket
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A protocol for real-time, two-way communication between client and server. Unlike HTTP, the connection stays open.

## 📋 Concrete Example

WebSocket: chat app. Client connects to server. Connection stays open. Client sends message -> server receives instantly. Server sends new message -> client receives instantly. Real-time, bidirectional.

## 🔗 Analogy

WebSocket is like a phone call - once connected, both sides can talk anytime. No need to dial again. HTTP is like a text message - each message is separate. WebSocket keeps the line open for real-time chat.

## Related Concepts

- [[http|HTTP]]
- [[real-time-communication|Real-Time Communication]]
- [[socket|Socket]]

title: world-wide-web
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The Web is the part of the internet accessed through browsers. Websites, web apps, and web APIs. Not the same as the internet (which also includes email, gaming, etc.).

## 📋 Concrete Example

The internet: roads, bridges, tunnels. The Web: shops and buildings on those roads. Email, online games, and file transfers use the internet but are not the Web.

## 🔗 Analogy

The internet is the road network; the Web is the buildings along the roads. You use roads (internet) to reach buildings (websites). But roads also reach places that are not buildings (email servers, game servers).

## Related Concepts

- [[internet|Internet]]
- [[http|HTTP]]
- [[web-browser|Web Browser]]

title: yaml
text:
> **Domain:** [[_internet-web-moc|Internet & Web]]

## 🎯 Motivation

YAML Ain't Markup Language - a human-friendly data format used for configuration files.

## 📋 Concrete Example

YAML: name: Alice\nage: 14\nhobbies:\n  - coding\n  - gaming. Clean, readable, uses indentation for structure. Common for config files and CI-CD pipelines.

## 🔗 Analogy

YAML is like a neatly organized outline - indentation shows hierarchy, no brackets or commas. Clean and readable. Perfect for configuration files that humans need to read and edit.

## Related Concepts

- [[data-format|Data Format]]
- [[json|JSON]]
- [[configuration|Configuration]]

title: agile
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An approach to software development: iterative, flexible, customer-focused. Deliver working software in short cycles.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agile: 2-week sprints. Each sprint: plan -> build -> test -> demo -> reflect. Deliver a small, working feature every 2 weeks. Adapt based on feedback. Flexible, not rigid.

## 🔗 Analogy

Agile is like cooking a meal one course at a time - you make the appetizer, serve it, get feedback, then make the soup, adjust based on feedback, then the main course. You adapt as you go, rather than cooking everything at once and hoping for the best.

## Related Concepts

- [[scrum|Scrum]]
- [[sprint|Sprint]]
- [[iterative-development|Iterative Development]]

title: backlog
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A prioritized list of tasks, features, and bug fixes waiting to be worked on.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Backlog: 1) [HIGH] Fix login crash. 2) [HIGH] Add password reset. 3) [MED] Dark mode. 4) [LOW] Change button color. Prioritized by importance. Tasks are pulled from the top during sprint planning.

## 🔗 Analogy

A backlog is like a to-do list sorted by priority - the most urgent tasks at the top, nice-to-haves at the bottom. You work from the top down. The backlog keeps track of everything that needs to be done.

## Related Concepts

- [[sprint-planning|Sprint Planning]]
- [[scrum|Scrum]]
- [[task-prioritization|Task Prioritization]]

title: backward-compatibility
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

New versions should work with old code. Breaking compatibility forces all users to update.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Compatible: v2.0 can read files from v1.0. Users upgrade smoothly. Breaking: v2.0 cannot read v1.0 files. All users must convert. Avoid breaking compatibility unless necessary.

## 🔗 Analogy

Backward compatibility is like a new phone supporting old chargers - you can use your old charger (backward compatible) or you must buy a new one (breaking). Compatible upgrades are smooth; breaking ones are painful.

## Related Concepts

- [[version-pinning|Version Pinning]]
- [[dependency|Dependency]]
- [[version-control|Version Control]]

title: branch
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A parallel line of development. You can experiment on a branch without affecting the main code.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Branch: 'git checkout -b feature/dark-mode'. You are now on the dark-mode branch. Changes here do not affect main. When dark mode is ready, merge it into main. Safe experimentation.

## 🔗 Analogy

A branch is like a copy of a document - you edit the copy freely. If it turns out great, replace the original. If not, throw away the copy. The original is safe. Branches let developers experiment safely.

## Related Concepts

- [[git|Git]]
- [[merge|Merge]]
- [[pull-request|Pull Request]]

title: breakpoint
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A marker in code where execution pauses. Lets you inspect variables and step through code.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Breakpoint: set at line 10. Run code. It pauses at line 10. Inspect: x = 5, y = 3, result = 15 (wrong, should be 8). Step to line 11. result = 15 + 3 = 18. Found the bug: wrong calculation on line 10.

## 🔗 Analogy

A breakpoint is like a pause button on a video - you freeze the action at a specific frame and examine everything: 'What is the score? Where are the players? What just happened?' A breakpoint freezes code for inspection.

## Related Concepts

- [[debugging|Debugging]]
- [[debugger|Debugger]]
- [[step-through|Step Through]]

title: bug
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An error in code that causes wrong behavior. Bugs range from cosmetic to critical.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Bug: sort function returns [3, 1, 2] instead of [1, 2, 3]. The code has a bug. Debug: find the cause (wrong comparison), fix it, test. Bugs are inevitable; the goal is to find and fix them quickly.

## 🔗 Analogy

A bug is like a flat tire - it stops you from reaching your destination. You must find the hole (root cause), patch it (fix), and continue. Bugs are software flat tires.

## Related Concepts

- [[debugging|Debugging]]
- [[testing|Testing]]
- [[error-handling|Error Handling]]

title: clone
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Making a local copy of a remote repository. You get all files and full history.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Clone: 'git clone https://github.com/user/project.git'. You now have a full copy on your computer. You can edit, commit, and push changes back. Full local copy of the remote repo.

## 🔗 Analogy

Cloning is like borrowing a book from the library - you get a complete copy. You can read it, write notes, and when you return it, your notes are shared (push). You have the full book locally.

## Related Concepts

- [[repository|Repository]]
- [[git|Git]]
- [[push|Push]]

title: code-review
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Having teammates review your code before it is merged. Catches bugs, improves quality, shares knowledge.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Code review: Bob reviews Alice's PR. 'Line 15: no error handling. Line 30: variable name is unclear. Line 45: good test coverage.' Alice addresses feedback. Better code through peer review.

## 🔗 Analogy

Code review is like peer grading - a classmate reads your essay and gives feedback: 'unclear thesis, great conclusion.' You improve it before submitting. Code review improves code before merging.

## Related Concepts

- [[pull-request|Pull Request]]
- [[code-quality|Code Quality]]
- [[collaboration|Collaboration]]

title: cohesion
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

How focused a module is on one task. High cohesion = does one thing well. Good.

## 📋 Concrete Example

High cohesion: auth.py only does authentication - login, logout, token verification. Focused. Low cohesion: utils.py does authentication, database, formatting, and email. Unfocused. High cohesion is better.

## 🔗 Analogy

Cohesion is like a specialist doctor vs a generalist - a cardiologist (high cohesion) focuses on hearts. A general practitioner (low cohesion) handles everything. Specialists are better at their one thing. Modules should be specialists.

## Related Concepts

- [[coupling|Coupling]]
- [[modular-design|Modular Design]]
- [[single-responsibility|Single Responsibility]]

title: collaboration
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Multiple people working on the same project. Version control, code review, and communication tools enable this.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Collaboration: Alice works on the frontend, Bob on the backend, Carol on tests. They use Git for version control, Slack for communication, GitHub for code review. Parallel work, combined results.

## 🔗 Analogy

Collaboration is like a group project - each person does their part, they communicate, combine their work, and review each other's contributions. Software collaboration tools make this possible for code.

## Related Concepts

- [[code-review|Code Review]]
- [[version-control|Version Control]]
- [[team-workflow|Team Workflow]]

title: comment
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Notes in code for humans. Explain why something is done, not what (the code shows what).

## 📋 Concrete Example

Good comment: '# Use binary search because the list is sorted - O(log n) instead of O(n).' Bad comment: '# increment i by 1.' The first explains why; the second is obvious from the code.

## 🔗 Analogy

A comment is like a margin note in a textbook - 'This formula is used in physics.' The note explains why, not what. The textbook (code) already shows what. Comments explain the reasoning behind the code.

## Related Concepts

- [[docstring|Docstring]]
- [[documentation|Documentation]]
- [[code-readability|Code Readability]]

title: commit-message
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A description of what a commit does. Good messages explain why, not just what.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Good: 'Fix: sort function crashes on empty list. Added check for len(list) == 0.' Bad: 'fixed stuff.' The message helps teammates (and future you) understand the change.

## 🔗 Analogy

A commit message is like a diary entry for your code - 'Today I fixed the sort function because it crashed on empty lists.' Future developers read these entries to understand why changes were made.

## Related Concepts

- [[commit|Commit]]
- [[git|Git]]
- [[documentation|Documentation]]

title: commit
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A saved snapshot of changes in Git. Each commit has a message describing what changed and why.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Commit: 'git commit -m "Fix: handle empty list in sort function"'. This saves the change with a message. History: commit a1b2c3, 'Fix: handle empty list in sort function', Alice, 2025-08-01.

## 🔗 Analogy

A commit is like saving a video game - your progress is saved at this point. You can continue, and if you make a mistake, reload this save. Each commit is a save point for your code.

## Related Concepts

- [[git|Git]]
- [[version-control|Version Control]]
- [[commit-message|Commit Message]]

title: coupling
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

How much modules depend on each other. Low coupling = modules are independent. Good.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Low coupling: auth.py and data.py communicate through a clear interface. Change data.py's internals without affecting auth.py. High coupling: auth.py directly accesses data.py's variables. Change one, break the other. Low coupling is better.

## 🔗 Analogy

Coupling is like the links in a chain - if each link is independent (low coupling), you can replace one without affecting others. If they are welded together (high coupling), you must replace the whole chain. Low coupling is more maintainable.

## Related Concepts

- [[modular-design|Modular Design]]
- [[cohesion|Cohesion]]
- [[separation-of-concerns|Separation of Concerns]]

title: debugger
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A tool that lets you pause code, inspect variables, and step through execution. Essential for debugging.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Debugger (pdb in Python): set breakpoint, step line by line, inspect variables, evaluate expressions. 'Why is x = 15 instead of 8?' Step through to find where it went wrong. Far better than print statements.

## 🔗 Analogy

A debugger is like a slow-motion camera for code - you replay the execution frame by frame, seeing exactly what happens at each step. Where did the value change? Why? The debugger shows you.

## Related Concepts

- [[breakpoint|Breakpoint]]
- [[debugging|Debugging]]
- [[step-through|Step Through]]

title: debugging
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Finding and fixing bugs. Involves reproducing the bug, finding the cause, and fixing it.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Debugging: 1) Reproduce: run the code, see the wrong output. 2) Isolate: which function is wrong? 3) Inspect: add print statements or use a debugger. 4) Fix: change the code. 5) Test: verify the fix. 6) Check: did the fix break anything else?

## 🔗 Analogy

Debugging is like detective work - find the crime scene (bug), gather evidence (logs, state), identify the suspect (root cause), and fix the problem. Systematic investigation.

## Related Concepts

- [[bug|Bug]]
- [[testing|Testing]]
- [[breakpoint|Breakpoint]]

title: dependency
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

External code your project relies on. Libraries, frameworks, packages. Must be managed carefully.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Dependencies: requests (HTTP), flask (web), pytest (testing). Your code imports and uses them. If requests has a bug, your code has a bug. If requests updates and breaks compatibility, your code breaks.

## 🔗 Analogy

Dependencies are like subcontractors on a construction site - you rely on the electrician, plumber, and painter. If the electrician does bad work, your building has electrical problems. Dependencies are your code's subcontractors.

## Related Concepts

- [[dependency-management-in-code|Dependency Management in Code]]
- [[requirements-file|Requirements File]]
- [[version-pinning|Version Pinning]]

title: docstring
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A documentation string inside code. Explains what a function does, its parameters, and return value.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Docstring: '''Calculate the average of a list of numbers. Args: numbers (list): List of numbers. Returns: float: The average. Raises: ValueError: If list is empty. ''' Right inside the code, above the function.

## 🔗 Analogy

A docstring is like a label on a kitchen spice jar - 'Salt - for cooking, not baking soda.' It tells you what it is and how to use it, right where you need it. Docstrings label functions in the code.

## Related Concepts

- [[documentation|Documentation]]
- [[comment|Comment]]
- [[code-quality|Code Quality]]

title: documentation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Written guides for code: README, API docs, inline comments, tutorials. Essential for maintainability.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Documentation: README.md (project overview, setup, usage), API.md (endpoints, parameters, examples), docstrings (each function explained), CONTRIBUTING.md (how to contribute). Without docs, code is incomprehensible.

## 🔗 Analogy

Documentation is like a manual for a board game - without it, no one knows how to play. With it, anyone can learn. Code documentation is the manual for developers using or maintaining the code.

## Related Concepts

- [[readme|README]]
- [[docstring|Docstring]]
- [[code-quality|Code Quality]]

title: edge-case
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Unusual or extreme inputs that might break the code: empty lists, zero, negative, very large, null.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Edge cases for sort(): empty list [], single item [5], all same [3, 3, 3], very large [1M items], null input, negative [-5, -1, -10]. The code must handle these correctly. Edge cases are where bugs hide.

## 🔗 Analogy

Edge cases are like extreme weather tests for a building - what happens in a typhoon? In an earthquake? In flooding? Normal conditions (common inputs) are easy; extreme conditions (edge cases) reveal weaknesses.

## Related Concepts

- [[test-case|Test Case]]
- [[unit-test|Unit Test]]
- [[robustness|Robustness]]

title: end-to-end-test
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Testing the entire application from user's perspective: click button -> see result. Most realistic but slowest.

## 📋 Concrete Example

E2E test: 1) Open browser. 2) Navigate to login page. 3) Enter username and password. 4) Click login. 5) Verify dashboard appears. 6) Click `Profile.` 7) Verify profile page. Tests the real user experience.

## 🔗 Analogy

An E2E test is like a full preview performance - real audience, real stage, real lighting. Everything is tested as the audience (user) would experience it. Most realistic, but takes the most effort.

## Related Concepts

- [[integration-test|Integration Test]]
- [[testing|Testing]]
- [[user-experience|User Experience]]

title: error-handling
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Code that anticipates and handles errors gracefully: try/except, error messages, fallbacks.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Error handling: try: result = 10 / 0. except ZeroDivisionError: result = 'Error: cannot divide by zero.' The program does not crash; it handles the error gracefully. Better user experience.

## 🔗 Analogy

Error handling is like having a spare tire - if you get a flat (error), you do not abandon the car. You put on the spare (handle the error) and continue. Error handling lets programs survive problems.

## Related Concepts

- [[bug|Bug]]
- [[exception|Exception]]
- [[graceful-degradation|Graceful Degradation]]

title: exception
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An error that occurs during execution. In Python: ValueError, TypeError, ZeroDivisionError, etc.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Exception: int(`abc`) -> ValueError: invalid literal for int(). The code stops unless you handle it: try: int(`abc`) except ValueError: print('Please enter a number.'). Handled gracefully.

## 🔗 Analogy

An exception is like a fire alarm - something went wrong, and the program stops unless someone handles it. try/except is the fire drill: you know what to do when the alarm sounds.

## Related Concepts

- [[error-handling|Error Handling]]
- [[bug|Bug]]
- [[try-except|Try-Except]]

title: fallback
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A backup plan when the primary approach fails. Keeps the system running.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Fallback: primary AI model is down. Fallback to a simpler model. Fallback to cached response. Fallback to a default message. The system keeps responding, even if not perfectly.

## 🔗 Analogy

A fallback is like a spare key - if you lose your main key (primary fails), the spare key (fallback) gets you in. Not as convenient, but it works. Systems need fallbacks for reliability.

## Related Concepts

- [[graceful-degradation|Graceful Degradation]]
- [[error-handling|Error Handling]]
- [[robustness|Robustness]]

title: git
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The most popular version control system. Distributed: every developer has a full copy of the repository.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Git: 'git init' (start), 'git add' (stage changes), 'git commit' (save), 'git push' (upload), 'git pull' (download). Every change is tracked. Branches allow parallel work. Merges combine work.

## 🔗 Analogy

Git is like a sophisticated library system - every book (file) has a history of edits. You can see any past version. Multiple authors can work on different chapters (branches) and combine them (merge).

## Related Concepts

- [[version-control|Version Control]]
- [[repository|Repository]]
- [[branch|Branch]]

title: github
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A platform for hosting Git repositories online. Adds collaboration features: pull requests, issues, code review.

## 📋 Concrete Example

GitHub: push your repo. Others can: clone it, suggest changes (PRs), report bugs (issues), review code. Collaboration platform built on Git. Used by most open-source projects.

## 🔗 Analogy

GitHub is like a collaborative workspace - your project is there, and anyone you invite can view, suggest changes, discuss, and contribute. It is the office for code collaboration.

## Related Concepts

- [[repository|Repository]]
- [[git|Git]]
- [[pull-request|Pull Request]]

title: graceful-degradation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When something fails, the system continues to work with reduced functionality instead of crashing.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Graceful: API is down. Instead of crashing, the app shows cached data with a 'Offline mode' banner. Reduced functionality, but still usable. Better than a blank screen.

## 🔗 Analogy

Graceful degradation is like a restaurant running out of chicken - instead of closing, they offer beef and pork. Reduced menu, but still serving. The system degrades gracefully instead of failing completely.

## Related Concepts

- [[error-handling|Error Handling]]
- [[robustness|Robustness]]
- [[fallback|Fallback]]

title: impact-vs-effort
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A framework for prioritization: high impact + low effort = do first. Low impact + high effort = skip.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Matrix: Fix login bug (high impact, low effort) = DO NOW. Rewrite architecture (high impact, high effort) = PLAN. Change font (low impact, low effort) = MAYBE. Add chat (low impact, high effort) = SKIP.

## 🔗 Analogy

Impact vs effort is like choosing which homework to do first - math assignment (high impact on grade, low effort) = do first. Rewrite notes (low impact, high effort) = skip. Maximize impact per effort.

## Related Concepts

- [[task-prioritization|Task Prioritization]]
- [[backlog|Backlog]]
- [[roi|ROI]]

title: integration-test
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Testing how multiple components work together. Catches issues that unit tests miss.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Integration test: test_login_flow(): 1) Create user in database. 2) Send login request. 3) Check response token. 4) Use token to access protected page. Tests the full flow: database + API + authentication.

## 🔗 Analogy

An integration test is like a dress rehearsal with all actors - each actor (component) was checked individually (unit test), but now they perform together. Chemistry, timing, and flow are tested. Integration tests check the whole system.

## Related Concepts

- [[testing|Testing]]
- [[unit-test|Unit Test]]
- [[end-to-end-test|End-to-End Test]]

title: merge-conflict
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When two branches change the same code. Git cannot auto-merge. The developer must resolve it.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Conflict: Alice changed line 5 to 'return a + b'. Bob changed line 5 to 'return a * b'. Git: 'CONFLICT on line 5.' Developer must choose: addition or multiplication? Resolve and commit.

## 🔗 Analogy

A merge conflict is like two people editing the same sentence - Alice: 'The sky is blue.' Bob: 'The sky is gray.' You must decide: blue or gray? Someone has to choose. Git flags the conflict; the developer resolves it.

## Related Concepts

- [[merge|Merge]]
- [[git|Git]]
- [[branch|Branch]]

title: merge
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Combining changes from one branch into another. Git automatically merges, or flags conflicts.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Merge: 'git merge feature/dark-mode' into main. Git combines the changes. If both branches changed the same line, conflict! Git asks you to resolve it. Otherwise, automatic merge.

## 🔗 Analogy

Merging is like combining two people's edits on a group project - if Alice edited page 1 and Bob edited page 2, just combine them. If both edited page 3, line 5, you must decide which version to keep. Git does this for code.

## Related Concepts

- [[branch|Branch]]
- [[git|Git]]
- [[merge-conflict|Merge Conflict]]

title: modular-design
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Breaking a system into independent modules. Each module does one thing well. Easier to build, test, and maintain.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Modules: auth.py (login), data.py (database), api.py (endpoints), utils.py (helpers). Each is independent, well-defined, and testable. Change auth.py without affecting data.py. Clean separation.

## 🔗 Analogy

Modular design is like a Lego city - each building (module) is separate. You can rebuild the police station without touching the hospital. Independent, interchangeable, maintainable.

## Related Concepts

- [[architecture|Architecture]]
- [[coupling|Coupling]]
- [[separation-of-concerns|Separation of Concerns]]

title: mvc
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Model-View-Controller - an architecture pattern. Model: data. View: UI. Controller: business logic.

## 📋 Concrete Example

MVC: Model: User database. View: login page. Controller: handles login request, checks model, returns view. Each part is separate. Change the view (redesign login page) without touching the model or controller.

## 🔗 Analogy

MVC is like a restaurant: Model (kitchen/ingredients), View (menu/dining area), Controller (waiter). The waiter takes orders, the kitchen prepares food, the dining area displays it. Each part is separate but works together.

## Related Concepts

- [[separation-of-concerns|Separation of Concerns]]
- [[architecture|Architecture]]
- [[design-pattern|Design Pattern]]

title: pull-request
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A request to merge your branch into the main code. Enables code review before merging.

## 📋 Concrete Example

PR: Alice opens 'PR: Add dark mode feature.' Team reviews the code: 'Looks good, but add a test for the toggle button.' Alice adds the test. Team approves. PR is merged. Code is reviewed before it goes live.

## 🔗 Analogy

A pull request is like submitting an article to a magazine - you write the article (branch), submit it (PR), the editor reviews it (code review), suggests changes, you revise, and when approved, it is published (merged).

## Related Concepts

- [[github|GitHub]]
- [[code-review|Code Review]]
- [[merge|Merge]]

title: pull
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Downloading the latest changes from a remote repository. Keeps your local copy up to date.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Pull: 'git pull origin main'. Downloads Alice's latest commits from GitHub. Your local code is now up to date with the remote. You have Alice's changes.

## 🔗 Analogy

Pulling is like checking the class bulletin board - you read the latest announcements (commits) so you are up to date. If you do not pull, you miss your teammates' changes.

## Related Concepts

- [[git|Git]]
- [[push|Push]]
- [[fetch|Fetch]]

title: push
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Uploading your local commits to a remote repository. Shares your changes with the team.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Push: 'git push origin main'. Your local commits are uploaded to GitHub. Teammates can now pull them. Your changes are shared.

## 🔗 Analogy

Pushing is like submitting homework - you did the work locally (commit), now you submit it to the teacher (remote repo). The teacher and classmates can see your work.

## Related Concepts

- [[git|Git]]
- [[clone|Clone]]
- [[pull|Pull]]

title: readme
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The first file people read in a project. Explains what the project is, how to set it up, and how to use it.

## 📋 Concrete Example

README.md: '# Todo App. A simple task manager built with React. ## Setup. npm install. npm start. ## Usage. Click Add to create a task. ## Features. - Add, edit, delete tasks. - Categories. - Due dates.'

## 🔗 Analogy

A README is like a book's back cover and first chapter - it tells you what the book is about and how to get started. Without it, people do not know what the project does or how to use it.

## Related Concepts

- [[documentation|Documentation]]
- [[repository|Repository]]
- [[project-overview|Project Overview]]

title: red-green-refactor
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The TDD cycle: Red (test fails), Green (test passes), Refactor (improve code quality).

## 📋 Concrete Example

Cycle: 1) Red: write test, run, fail. 2) Green: write minimal code to pass, run, pass. 3) Refactor: improve code without breaking tests. Repeat. Each cycle adds one piece of functionality.

## 🔗 Analogy

Red-green-refactor is like sculpting - rough shape (red: test defines the goal), refine until it looks right (green: code works), then polish (refactor: clean up). Cycle by cycle, the sculpture (code) takes shape.

## Related Concepts

- [[test-driven-development|Test-Driven Development]]
- [[testing|Testing]]
- [[refactoring|Refactoring]]

title: refactoring
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Improving code structure without changing behavior - making it cleaner, faster, or more maintainable.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Before: 50-line function with nested ifs. After (refactored): 3 smaller functions, each 15 lines, clear names, same behavior. Easier to read and maintain. No new features, just better structure.

## 🔗 Analogy

Refactoring is like reorganizing your room - same furniture, same stuff, but better arranged. It functions the same but is more pleasant and efficient. Refactoring reorganizes code for better maintainability.

## Related Concepts

- [[technical-debt|Technical Debt]]
- [[code-quality|Code Quality]]
- [[code-smell|Code Smell]]

title: repository
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A storage location for a project. Contains all files, history, and metadata. Often called a repo.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Repository: 'my-project/' contains: source code, tests, documentation, .git/ (history). Hosted on GitHub, GitLab, or local. The complete project with full history.

## 🔗 Analogy

A repository is like a project folder with a built-in time machine - it contains all current files and every past version. You can travel back to any point in the project's history.

## Related Concepts

- [[git|Git]]
- [[github|GitHub]]
- [[clone|Clone]]

title: scrum
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A specific Agile framework: sprints, daily standups, sprint planning, retrospectives.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Scrum: 2-week sprints. Daily 15-minute standup: 'What did I do? What will I do? Any blockers?' Sprint planning: choose tasks. Retrospective: what went well, what to improve. Structured Agile.

## 🔗 Analogy

Scrum is like a basketball team's practice system - daily practice (standup), game plan (sprint planning), post-game analysis (retrospective). Structured, repetitive, focused on continuous improvement.

## Related Concepts

- [[agile|Agile]]
- [[sprint|Sprint]]
- [[standup|Standup]]

title: separation-of-concerns
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Different concerns (UI, business logic, data) should be in separate modules. Like MVC.

## 📋 Concrete Example

MVC: Model (data), View (UI), Controller (logic). Each concern is separate. Change the UI without touching data logic. Change the database without affecting the UI. Clean separation.

## 🔗 Analogy

Separation of concerns is like organizing a kitchen - raw ingredients (data), cooking (logic), and plating (UI) are in separate areas. Change the plating style without changing the recipe. Each concern is independent.

## Related Concepts

- [[modular-design|Modular Design]]
- [[coupling|Coupling]]
- [[mvc|MVC]]

title: single-responsibility
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Each module/class/function should do one thing. Easier to understand, test, and maintain.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Good: calculate_tax() only calculates tax. format_receipt() only formats. send_email() only sends. Each does one thing. Bad: process_order() calculates tax, formats receipt, sends email, and updates inventory. Too many responsibilities.

## 🔗 Analogy

Single responsibility is like a factory assembly line - each station does one thing: put on the wheels, paint the body, install the seats. Focused, efficient, replaceable. One thing per station (module).

## Related Concepts

- [[cohesion|Cohesion]]
- [[modular-design|Modular Design]]
- [[separation-of-concerns|Separation of Concerns]]

title: software-engineering
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Writing one function is easy; building a large system is hard. Software engineering provides methods to design, build, test, and maintain complex software reliably.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A team of 10 developers building a banking app: they need architecture, version control, code review, testing, CI-CD, documentation. Without engineering practices, the project collapses into chaos.

## 🔗 Analogy

Software engineering is like city planning - building one house is simple, but planning a city requires zoning, infrastructure, traffic management, and building codes. Software engineering plans and builds large software systems.

## Related Concepts

- [[version-control|Version Control]]
- [[testing|Testing]]
- [[ci-cd|CI-CD]]

title: sprint-planning
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Choosing which tasks to work on in the next sprint. Based on priorities and capacity.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Planning: 10 tasks in the backlog. Team capacity: 6 tasks in 2 weeks. Choose the top 6 by priority. Assign owners. Sprint starts. Focused, realistic plan.

## 🔗 Analogy

Sprint planning is like planning a road trip - you have 10 destinations (tasks) but only 5 days (capacity). You pick the 5 best destinations and plan the route. Realistic, prioritized.

## Related Concepts

- [[sprint|Sprint]]
- [[scrum|Scrum]]
- [[backlog|Backlog]]

title: sprint
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A fixed period (usually 1-4 weeks) for completing a set of tasks. At the end, working software is delivered.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Sprint: 2 weeks. Tasks: implement login, write tests, fix 3 bugs. At the end: all done, demoed, deployed. Next sprint: new tasks. Predictable, iterative delivery.

## 🔗 Analogy

A sprint is like a study week before exams - you plan what to study, study intensively for a week, take the exams (demo), and then review what worked (retrospective). Focused, time-boxed effort.

## Related Concepts

- [[scrum|Scrum]]
- [[agile|Agile]]
- [[sprint-planning|Sprint Planning]]

title: standup
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A short daily meeting: what did you do, what will you do, any blockers? Keeps the team aligned.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Standup (15 min): Alice: 'Finished login UI, starting API integration, no blockers.' Bob: 'API is ready, need to write tests, blocked by missing test data.' Quick, focused, action-oriented.

## 🔗 Analogy

A standup is like a hockey team's quick huddle between periods - 'I played defense, next I am on offense. Our goalie needs rest.' Quick update, everyone aligned, back to work.

## Related Concepts

- [[scrum|Scrum]]
- [[sprint|Sprint]]
- [[communication|Communication]]

title: step-through
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Executing code one line at a time in a debugger. See exactly what happens at each step.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Step through: line 1: x = 5. line 2: y = 3. line 3: result = x * y (result = 15). line 4: return result. You see: the bug is on line 3: it multiplies instead of adds. Found it by stepping.

## 🔗 Analogy

Stepping through is like replaying a video one frame at a time - you see exactly what happens in each frame (line). 'Frame 3: the player kicks the ball.' 'Frame 4: the ball goes in the wrong direction.' Stepping through reveals the exact moment things go wrong.

## Related Concepts

- [[debugger|Debugger]]
- [[breakpoint|Breakpoint]]
- [[debugging|Debugging]]

title: task-prioritization
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Deciding which tasks are most important. Urgent vs important, impact vs effort.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Prioritization: Fix security bug (urgent + important) = do now. New feature (important, not urgent) = next sprint. Change button color (not important) = maybe never. Focus on high-impact tasks.

## 🔗 Analogy

Task prioritization is like triage in an emergency room - the most critical patients (urgent + important) are seen first. Minor issues wait. Prioritization ensures the most important work gets done first.

## Related Concepts

- [[backlog|Backlog]]
- [[scrum|Scrum]]
- [[impact-vs-effort|Impact vs Effort]]

title: team-workflow
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

How a team organizes work: who does what, how changes are reviewed, how releases happen.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Workflow: 1) Pick a task from the board. 2) Create a branch. 3) Code. 4) Write tests. 5) Open PR. 6) Code review. 7) Merge. 8) Deploy. Structured, repeatable process.

## 🔗 Analogy

A team workflow is like a kitchen brigade system - the head chef assigns tasks, each cook prepares their dish, the sous-chef checks quality, and the expediter sends orders out. Everyone has a role; the process is structured.

## Related Concepts

- [[collaboration|Collaboration]]
- [[agile|Agile]]
- [[scrum|Scrum]]

title: technical-debt
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Quick-and-dirty code saves time now but creates debt that must be paid back later with interest (harder maintenance).

## 📋 Concrete Example

Rushing: copy-paste code 5 times (fast now). Debt: when you need to change the logic, you must change 5 places (slow later). The model can identify and help pay down debt.

## 🔗 Analogy

Technical debt is like using a credit card - buy now (fast), pay later with interest (expensive). Quick code is like credit card debt: convenient now, costly later. Pay it down by refactoring.

## Related Concepts

- [[refactoring|Refactoring]]
- [[code-quality|Code Quality]]
- [[code-smell|Code Smell]]

title: test-case
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A specific scenario to test: input + expected output. Many test cases cover different scenarios.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Test cases for sort(): 1) Empty list -> []. 2) One item -> same. 3) Sorted list -> same. 4) Reverse sorted -> sorted. 5) Duplicates -> sorted. 6) Negative numbers -> sorted. 7) Large list -> sorted. Each case checks a scenario.

## 🔗 Analogy

A test case is like a specific exam question - 'Solve x + 5 = 10.' One question, one expected answer. Many questions (test cases) cover the full topic. Each case checks one specific scenario.

## Related Concepts

- [[unit-test|Unit Test]]
- [[testing|Testing]]
- [[edge-case|Edge Case]]

title: test-driven-development
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Write tests before code. Red (test fails) -> Green (code passes) -> Refactor (improve). TDD cycle.

## 📋 Concrete Example

TDD: 1) Write test: assert is_prime(7) == True. 2) Run: FAIL (function does not exist). Red. 3) Write code: def is_prime(n): return True. 4) Run: PASS. Green. 5) Write more tests, fix code. Cycle.

## 🔗 Analogy

TDD is like writing the exam before studying - you write the test (what should the code do?), then learn (write code) until you pass. It ensures you know the goal before you start coding.

## Related Concepts

- [[testing|Testing]]
- [[unit-test|Unit Test]]
- [[red-green-refactor|Red-Green-Refactor]]

title: testing
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Verifying that code works correctly. Unit tests, integration tests, end-to-end tests. Essential for quality.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Testing: write test_add(): assert add(2, 3) == 5. Run it. Pass! Now test edge cases: assert add(0, 0) == 0, assert add(-1, 1) == 0. Each test verifies a specific behavior. Catches bugs early.

## 🔗 Analogy

Testing is like a dress rehearsal before a play - you practice everything to find problems before the real performance (production). Each test checks one aspect. Finding bugs in rehearsal is better than during the show.

## Related Concepts

- [[unit-test|Unit Test]]
- [[integration-test|Integration Test]]
- [[test-coverage|Test Coverage]]

title: try-except
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Python's error handling: try something, except catch the error. Prevents crashes.

## 📋 Concrete Example

try: file = open(`data.txt`) except FileNotFoundError: print('File not found. Creating a new one.') file = open(`data.txt`, `w`). The error is caught and handled. No crash.

## 🔗 Analogy

try-except is like wearing a seatbelt - you try to drive safely, but if something goes wrong (exception), the seatbelt (except) protects you. The program survives the error.

## Related Concepts

- [[exception|Exception]]
- [[error-handling|Error Handling]]
- [[python|Python]]

title: unit-test
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Testing the smallest unit of code (a function) in isolation. Fast, specific, numerous.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Unit test: test_sort_empty_list(): assert sort([]) == []. test_sort_one_item(): assert sort([5]) == [5]. test_sort_duplicates(): assert sort([3, 1, 3]) == [1, 3, 3]. Each function tested separately.

## 🔗 Analogy

A unit test is like checking each ingredient before cooking - is the egg fresh? Is the flour dry? Each ingredient (function) is checked individually. If all pass, the dish (program) has a good foundation.

## Related Concepts

- [[testing|Testing]]
- [[test-coverage|Test Coverage]]
- [[test-case|Test Case]]

title: version-control
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Tracking changes to code over time. Who changed what, when, and why. Essential for team collaboration.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Git: Alice changes line 10. Bob changes line 20. Both commit. Git merges the changes. History: 'Alice: fixed login bug, 2025-08-01 14:00.' Full traceability. Rollback if needed.

## 🔗 Analogy

Version control is like a time machine for your code - you can see what the code looked like at any point in history, who made each change, and why. If something breaks, you can go back in time.

## Related Concepts

- [[git|Git]]
- [[commit|Commit]]
- [[branch|Branch]]

title: version-pinning
text:
> **Domain:** [[_software-engineering-moc|Software Engineering]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Specifying exact versions of dependencies to prevent unexpected breaks.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Pin: 'requests==2.31.0' (exactly this version). If requests releases 2.32 with breaking changes, your code is safe. You upgrade deliberately, not accidentally.

## 🔗 Analogy

Version pinning is like locking in a flight price - you pay exactly the price you saw. If prices go up, you are not affected. Pinning locks dependency versions to prevent unexpected breaks.

## Related Concepts

- [[dependency|Dependency]]
- [[requirements-file|Requirements File]]
- [[backward-compatibility|Backward Compatibility]]

Adds non-linearity so the network can learn complex patterns, not just straight-line rules.

ReLU turns negative inputs to zero and keeps positives. Sigmoid squashes values to between 0 and 1.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a gate that only opens if you push hard enough - without it, the network would only draw straight lines.

title: ai-vs-ml-vs-dl
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Computers can do smart things in different ways. Knowing the difference helps you pick the right tool.

## 📋 Concrete Example

AI is the big umbrella (any program that seems smart). ML is a subset where the program learns from data. DL is a subset of ML using neural networks with many layers.

## 🔗 Analogy

AI is like cooking food in general. ML is cooking by tasting and adjusting. DL is cooking with a fancy multi-layer oven that learns recipes itself.

## Related Concepts

- [[supervised-learning|Supervised Learning]]
- [[unsupervised-learning|Unsupervised Learning]]

title: attention
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Lets the model focus on the most relevant parts of the input when making each prediction.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Translating the bank of the river, attention links bank to river not to money-bank.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a student skimming a long article and highlighting only the sentences relevant to the question.

## Related Concepts

- [[self-attention|Self-Attention]]
- [[transformer-architecture|Transformer Architecture]]
- [[embedding|Embedding]]

title: backpropagation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Calculates how much each weight contributed to the error, so we can adjust them. The learning step.

## 📋 Concrete Example

The model predicted cat with 60% but the true label is dog. Backprop computes gradients telling each weight how to change.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a coach reviewing a lost game with each player, telling them exactly what to fix for next time.

## Related Concepts

- [[forward-pass|Forward Pass]]

title: batch
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A small chunk of data processed before updating weights. Makes training faster and more stable.

## 📋 Concrete Example

With 1000 images and batch size 50, each batch has 50 images, giving 20 updates per epoch.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like eating a big meal in small bites instead of all at once - easier to digest.

## Related Concepts

- [[epoch|Epoch]]
- [[mini-batch-gradient-descent|Mini-Batch Gradient Descent]]
- [[training|Training]]

title: biases
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A bias shifts the neuron output so it can fire even when inputs are zero, giving the model flexibility.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A neuron with bias = -2 will not fire easily. Changing bias to +3 makes it fire more often for the same inputs.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a thermostat offset - even if the room temperature reading is the same, you can nudge the system to heat earlier.

## Related Concepts

- [[weights|Weights]]
- [[neuron|Neuron]]
- [[activation-function|Activation Function]]

Predicting a category label from a fixed set of options.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Given an email, predict spam or not spam. Given a photo, predict which of 10 animals.

Like sorting mail into labeled bins - each item goes into exactly one category.

Grouping similar items together without labels. A key unsupervised task.

Group shoppers by buying habits into clusters like weekly groceries, luxury, impulse buyers.

Like organizing a big box of mixed buttons into piles by color and size, with no labels given.

text:

## 🎯 Motivation

A loss function for classification that rewards confident correct predictions and punishes wrong confident ones.

## 📋 Concrete Example

If the model says 0.9 probability for the correct class, loss is small. If it says 0.1, loss is large.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like an exam that gives full marks only if you are both correct and confident - guessing right by luck gives little credit.

The collection of examples used to train and test a model. Bigger and cleaner is usually better.

ImageNet is a dataset with over 14 million labeled images across 1000 categories.

Like a library - the bigger and better organized it is, the more you can learn from it.

Machine learning using neural networks with many layers. Deep means many layers.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A 50-layer network classifying medical X-rays is deep learning. A 2-layer network is shallow.

Like a multi-story factory: the more floors (layers), the more complex the product it can make.

Squeezing data with many features into fewer dimensions while keeping the important info.

Reduce 1000-pixel images to a 50-number summary that still captures the key shapes.

Like summarizing a 300-page book into a 1-page synopsis that keeps the main plot.

Randomly turns off some neurons during training so the network does not rely too much on any one path.

During each training step, 20% of neurons are randomly dropped. At inference, all neurons are used.

Like a sports coach benching random players during practice so the team learns to work together, not depend on one star.

Turning things like words or images into lists of numbers so a computer can compare them.

Like giving each student a ID badge with numbers - students with similar interests get similar numbers.

One full pass through the entire training dataset. Training runs for many epochs.

Like reading a textbook cover to cover once. You read it many times to really learn it.

Creating useful new features from raw data to help the model learn better.

Like a chef prepping ingredients before cooking - cutting and seasoning well makes the dish better.

An individual measurable property used as input. Good features make learning easier.

For predicting house price, features might be area, number of rooms, age, and location.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the clues a detective collects - each clue (feature) helps solve the case.

Take a model already trained on a big general dataset and train it a bit more on your specific data.

Start with a model trained on general English text, then fine-tune on Hong Kong legal documents.

Like a general mechanic taking a short course to specialize in electric cars - building on existing skills.

Pushing input through the network to get a prediction. The everyday use of a trained model.

Input image -> hidden layers compute -> output layer says 92% cat, 8% dog.

Like sending a letter through sorting stations until it arrives at the destination address.

How well a model performs on new unseen data, not just the data it trained on.

Like a student who truly understands the topic can solve new problems, not just the ones they memorized.

Adjusts weights step by step downhill on the loss surface to reduce error.

If the loss goes down when you increase weight A, gradient descent increases weight A a little. Repeat.

Like hiking down a foggy mountain by always stepping in the steepest downward direction.

Layers between input and output where the network learns internal representations.

A hidden layer might detect edges in an image; a deeper one might detect shapes like ears or eyes.

Like the kitchen of a restaurant - customers do not see it, but that is where the real work happens.

Settings chosen by the human before training, not learned from data.

Learning rate, number of layers, batch size, and number of epochs are hyperparameters you set before training starts.

Like the rules of a game set before playing - the players (parameters) play within those rules.

Using a trained model to make predictions on new, unseen data.

After training, you upload a new photo and the model says cat with 95% confidence.

Like sitting the actual exam after all your studying is done.
