text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Receives the raw data, one neuron per feature. No computation - just passes values in.

## 📋 Concrete Example

For a 28x28 image, the input layer has 784 neurons, one per pixel.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the front desk of a company - it receives visitors (data) and routes them inside.

## Related Concepts

- [[layers|Layers]]
- [[feature|Feature]]
- [[hidden-layer|Hidden Layer]]

title: k-means
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A clustering algorithm that assigns each point to the nearest of K centers, then updates centers.

## 📋 Concrete Example

K-means on customer data with K=3 finds three customer types based on spending patterns.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like choosing 3 meeting points in a city and asking everyone to go to the nearest one, then re-centering.

## Related Concepts

- [[clustering|Clustering]]
- [[unsupervised-learning|Unsupervised Learning]]

title: l1-l2-regularization
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

L1 adds a penalty based on absolute weight values (can zero out weights). L2 adds a penalty based on squared weights.

## 📋 Concrete Example

L1 can shrink unimportant weights to exactly zero, doing feature selection. L2 keeps all weights small but nonzero.

## 🔗 Analogy

L1 is like a strict editor who deletes whole paragraphs. L2 is like one who trims every word a little.

## Related Concepts

- [[regularization|Regularization]]
- [[overfitting|Overfitting]]
- [[weights|Weights]]

title: label
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The correct answer paired with input features in supervised learning.

## 📋 Concrete Example

In a spam dataset, each email (features) has a label: spam or not spam.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the answer key next to each practice question - tells the model what to aim for.

## Related Concepts

- [[feature|Feature]]
- [[supervised-learning|Supervised Learning]]
- [[dataset|Dataset]]

title: layers
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A neural network is built from stacked layers, each transforming the data step by step.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A cat classifier might have an input layer (pixels), 3 hidden layers (features), and an output layer (cat or dog).

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a relay race: each runner (layer) takes the baton (data), transforms it, and hands it to the next runner.

## Related Concepts

- [[input-layer|Input Layer]]
- [[hidden-layer|Hidden Layer]]
- [[output-layer|Output Layer]]
- [[neural-network|Neural Network]]

title: learning-rate
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Controls how big each weight update step is. Too big diverges, too small is slow.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Learning rate 0.001 means each step changes weights by a tiny amount. 0.5 might overshoot and explode.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like adjusting a shower tap: tiny turns find the right temperature; big turns scald or freeze you.

## Related Concepts

- [[gradient-descent|Gradient Descent]]
- [[hyperparameters|Hyperparameters]]
- [[training|Training]]

title: loss-function
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Measures how wrong the predictions are. Training tries to make this number as small as possible.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Mean squared error: average of (prediction - true value) squared across examples.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a scoreboard that shows your mistakes - the lower the score, the better you are doing.

## Related Concepts

- [[gradient-descent|Gradient Descent]]
- [[cross-entropy|Cross-Entropy]]
- [[mean-squared-error|Mean Squared Error]]

title: mean-squared-error
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A loss function for regression: average of squared differences between predictions and true values.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Predict house price 4.2M, actual 4.0M. Error = 0.2M. Squared = 0.04. Average over all houses gives MSE.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like measuring how far your darts land from the bullseye, squaring the distances so big misses hurt more.

## Related Concepts

- [[loss-function|Loss Function]]
- [[regression|Regression]]
- [[variance|Variance]]

title: mini-batch-gradient-descent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Update weights using small batches of data - a balance between speed and stability.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Batch size 32: each update uses 32 examples. Faster than full-batch, smoother than one-at-a-time.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a teacher grading 32 papers at a time to estimate the class average, instead of all at once or one by one.

## Related Concepts

- [[gradient-descent|Gradient Descent]]
- [[batch|Batch]]
- [[epoch|Epoch]]

title: model-capacity
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

How complex a pattern the model can learn. More parameters usually means higher capacity.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A linear model has low capacity (straight lines only). A 100-layer network has very high capacity.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a toolbox: a small kit can fix simple things, a big workshop can build complex machines.

## Related Concepts

- [[overfitting|Overfitting]]
- [[underfitting|Underfitting]]
- [[parameters|Parameters]]

title: neural-network
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A model inspired by the brain that can learn very complex patterns when given enough data.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A network with layers of connected neurons takes pixel values of a photo and outputs the probability it is a cat.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a factory assembly line: each station (layer) processes the product a bit and passes it on until the final station gives the answer.

## Related Concepts

- [[neuron|Neuron]]
- [[layers|Layers]]
- [[forward-pass|Forward Pass]]
- [[backpropagation|Backpropagation]]
- [[deep-learning|Deep Learning]]

title: neuron
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The basic unit of a neural network. It combines inputs and decides how much signal to pass forward.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A neuron takes 3 numbers, multiplies each by a weight, adds a bias, then applies ReLU. Output goes to the next layer.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a single voter who weighs different rumors (inputs), adds their own bias, and decides whether to shout (activate).

## Related Concepts

- [[weights|Weights]]
- [[biases|Biases]]
- [[activation-function|Activation Function]]
- [[neural-network|Neural Network]]

title: non-linearity
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The ability to model curved, complex relationships, not just straight lines. Comes from activation functions.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Without non-linearity, a 100-layer network collapses to the equivalent of one linear layer.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like being able to draw curves and squiggles, not just rulers-straight lines, on a graph.

## Related Concepts

- [[activation-function|Activation Function]]
- [[neural-network|Neural Network]]
- [[deep-learning|Deep Learning]]

title: output-layer
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The final layer that produces the prediction or decision.

## 📋 Concrete Example

For 10-digit classification, the output layer has 10 neurons, one per digit, with softmax probabilities.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the cash register - it gives you the final answer after all the behind-the-scenes work.

## Related Concepts

- [[layers|Layers]]
- [[softmax|Softmax]]
- [[classification|Classification]]

title: overfitting
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The model memorizes training data including noise, so it fails on new data.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A student memorizes past-paper answers word for word but cannot solve a slightly different exam question.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like memorizing a map of your own neighborhood so well that you get lost anywhere else.

## Related Concepts

- [[underfitting|Underfitting]]
- [[regularization|Regularization]]
- [[validation-set|Validation Set]]
- [[generalization|Generalization]]

title: parameters
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The numbers inside the model (weights and biases) that get learned from data.

## 📋 Concrete Example

GPT-3 has about 175 billion parameters. Each is a number adjusted during training.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the knobs and dials on an old radio - millions of them, tuned until the signal comes in clear.

## Related Concepts

- [[weights|Weights]]
- [[hyperparameters|Hyperparameters]]
- [[model-size|Model Size]]

title: pca
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Principal Component Analysis finds the directions of most variance and projects data onto them.

## 📋 Concrete Example

PCA on 3D data might find that most variation lies on a flat 2D plane, so you can plot it in 2D.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like photographing a 3D sculpture from the angle that shows the most detail - you capture the essence in 2D.

## Related Concepts

- [[dimensionality-reduction|Dimensionality Reduction]]
- [[embedding|Embedding]]
- [[variance|Variance]]

title: perceptron
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The simplest neural unit - a single neuron that makes a yes/no decision. The ancestor of modern networks.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A perceptron takes exam score and homework score, multiplies by weights, and outputs pass or fail.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a strict teacher who adds up weighted scores and says pass or fail based on a cutoff.

## Related Concepts

- [[neuron|Neuron]]
- [[activation-function|Activation Function]]
- [[classification|Classification]]

title: policy
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

In reinforcement learning, the strategy the agent uses to choose actions based on the current state.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A self-driving car policy might say: if the light is red, brake; if green and clear, go.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a personal rulebook the agent follows, which it keeps rewriting to get more rewards.

## Related Concepts

- [[reinforcement-learning|Reinforcement Learning]]
- [[reward-signal|Reward Signal]]

title: pre-training
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Training a model on a huge general dataset before fine-tuning on a specific task.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Pre-train a language model on all of Wikipedia, then fine-tune it for answering science questions.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a student doing general reading for years before specializing in a university major.

## Related Concepts

- [[fine-tuning|Fine-Tuning]]
- [[transfer-learning|Transfer Learning]]
- [[training|Training]]

title: regression
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Predicting a continuous number instead of a category.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Predict the price of a house (a number like 4.5 million) from its features.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a weather forecast predicting tomorrow temperature will be 27.3 degrees - a number, not a category.

## Related Concepts

- [[classification|Classification]]
- [[mean-squared-error|Mean Squared Error]]
- [[supervised-learning|Supervised Learning]]

title: regularization
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Techniques that prevent overfitting by keeping the model simple or robust.

## 📋 Concrete Example

L2 regularization adds a penalty for large weights, encouraging the model to spread importance out.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like packing only essentials for a trip so you do not overpack and get slowed down.

## Related Concepts

- [[overfitting|Overfitting]]
- [[dropout|Dropout]]
- [[l1-l2-regularization|L1 L2 Regularization]]
- [[generalization|Generalization]]

title: reinforcement-learning
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An agent learns by trying actions and getting rewards or penalties, improving over time.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A robot learns to walk: each step forward gives reward, falling gives penalty. Over many tries it learns a good walking policy.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like training a dog with treats and scolding - it figures out good behavior by trial and error.

## Related Concepts

- [[supervised-learning|Supervised Learning]]
- [[reward-signal|Reward Signal]]
- [[policy|Policy]]

title: relu
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A simple, fast activation that keeps positives and zeroes negatives. Used in most deep networks.

## 📋 Concrete Example

ReLU(5) = 5, ReLU(-3) = 0. It is just max(0, x).

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a bouncer who lets in guests with positive vibes and turns away negative ones, no questions asked.

## Related Concepts

- [[activation-function|Activation Function]]
- [[sigmoid|Sigmoid]]
- [[neural-network|Neural Network]]

title: reward-signal
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

In reinforcement learning, the feedback (positive or negative) the agent receives after each action.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A game-playing agent gets +1 reward for winning a level and -1 for losing a life.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a video game score - the player adjusts strategy to maximize points.

## Related Concepts

- [[reinforcement-learning|Reinforcement Learning]]
- [[policy|Policy]]

title: sigmoid
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Squashes any number into the range 0 to 1, useful for probabilities and binary outputs.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Sigmoid(0) = 0.5, Sigmoid(10) is about 0.99995, Sigmoid(-10) is about 0.00005.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a dimmer switch that can only go from off (0) to fully on (1), no matter how hard you twist.

## Related Concepts

- [[activation-function|Activation Function]]
- [[softmax|Softmax]]
- [[classification|Classification]]

title: softmax
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Turns a list of numbers into probabilities that sum to 1. Used in classification output layers.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Raw scores [2.0, 1.0, 0.1] become probabilities [0.7, 0.2, 0.1] after softmax.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a teacher converting raw test scores into percentages that add up to 100%.

## Related Concepts

- [[sigmoid|Sigmoid]]
- [[classification|Classification]]
- [[cross-entropy-loss|Cross-Entropy Loss]]

title: supervised-learning
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

We want the computer to learn a rule from labeled examples so it can predict on new data.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Show 100 photos of cats and dogs each labeled. The model learns to tell cats from dogs. Then it can label a new photo.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a student doing past papers with answer keys - they learn the pattern, then tackle the exam.

## Related Concepts

- [[unsupervised-learning|Unsupervised Learning]]
- [[reinforcement-learning|Reinforcement Learning]]
- [[classification|Classification]]
- [[regression|Regression]]
- [[label|Label]]

title: tanh
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Like sigmoid but outputs range -1 to 1, centered at zero. Often works better in hidden layers.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Tanh(0) = 0, Tanh(2) is about 0.964, Tanh(-2) is about -0.964.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a steering wheel that can turn left (negative) or right (positive) but only so far each way.

## Related Concepts

- [[activation-function|Activation Function]]
- [[sigmoid|Sigmoid]]
- [[relu|ReLU]]

title: train-validation-test-split
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Divide data into three parts: train to learn, validation to tune, test to final-check.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Split 10000 examples: 8000 train, 1000 validation, 1000 test. Only touch test once at the end.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like splitting your study time: past papers (train), mock exam (validation), real exam (test).

## Related Concepts

- [[dataset|Dataset]]
- [[overfitting|Overfitting]]
- [[generalization|Generalization]]

title: training
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The phase where the model adjusts its weights by looking at data and reducing loss.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Train a cat-dog classifier on 10000 labeled photos for 20 epochs.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a student studying with past papers and answer keys to prepare for an exam.

## Related Concepts

- [[inference|Inference]]
- [[epoch|Epoch]]
- [[loss-function|Loss Function]]
- [[backpropagation|Backpropagation]]

title: transfer-learning
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Reuse knowledge learned on one task to help learn another task faster and better.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A model trained to recognize cars can be adapted to recognize trucks with much less data.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like learning to ride a bicycle first - that balance skill transfers when you learn a motorcycle.

## Related Concepts

- [[fine-tuning|Fine-Tuning]]
- [[pre-training|Pre-Training]]
- [[embedding|Embedding]]

title: transformer-architecture
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A neural network design based on attention that powers modern language models like GPT.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A transformer reads a whole sentence at once and uses attention to figure out which words matter for each other.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a team meeting where everyone listens to everyone and each person decides who to pay attention to.

title: underfitting
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The model is too simple to capture the pattern, doing poorly even on training data.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Trying to fit a straight line to data that is clearly curved - it misses the shape entirely.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like using a blunt knife to carve a fine sculpture - you just cannot capture the detail.

## Related Concepts

- [[overfitting|Overfitting]]

title: unsupervised-learning
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Sometimes data has no labels. We still want to find hidden structure or groups.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Give a shop customer purchase data with no labels. The algorithm groups customers into clusters (e.g. bargain hunters vs big spenders).

## 🔗 Analogy

Like sorting a big pile of mixed Lego bricks into piles by shape and color without anyone telling you the categories first.

## Related Concepts

- [[supervised-learning|Supervised Learning]]
- [[clustering|Clustering]]
- [[dimensionality-reduction|Dimensionality Reduction]]

title: weights
text:
> **Domain:** [[_ai-fundamentals-moc|AI Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Weights decide how important each input is. Learning means adjusting weights to reduce errors.

## 📋 Concrete Example

If predicting house price, the weight on location might be large (important) and the weight on paint color small.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like volume sliders on a mixing desk - you turn up the inputs that matter and turn down the ones that do not.

title: argmax
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Returns the index of the largest value. Used to pick the predicted class.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Scores [0.1, 0.7, 0.2]. Argmax = 1 (index of 0.7), so the prediction is class 1.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like picking the tallest student in class by their position in line, not by their height value.

## Related Concepts

- [[softmax|Softmax]]
- [[classification|Classification]]
- [[prediction|Prediction]]

title: backpropagation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The algorithm that computes gradients for all weights by applying the chain rule backward through the network.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Loss is computed at the output. Backprop sends the error backward, computing each layer contribution using the chain rule.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a factory quality control running backward through the line, blaming each station for its share of defects.

## Related Concepts

- [[chain-rule|Chain Rule]]
- [[gradient-descent|Gradient Descent]]
- [[forward-pass|Forward Pass]]

title: bayes-theorem
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Updates our belief when we see new evidence. The backbone of many reasoning systems.

## 📋 Concrete Example

If 1% of people are sick, and a test is 99% accurate, a positive test does not mean 99% chance of being sick - Bayes adjusts it.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a detective updating the suspect list each time a new clue arrives.

## Related Concepts

- [[conditional-probability|Conditional Probability]]
- [[probability|Probability]]

title: boolean-algebra
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Algebra of true/false values. The math behind computer logic gates and binary operations.

## 📋 Concrete Example

true AND false = false. true OR false = true. NOT true = false.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like light switches - two switches in series (AND) need both on; in parallel (OR) need at least one on.

## Related Concepts

- [[logic|Logic]]
- [[set-theory|Set Theory]]

title: calculus
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The math of continuous change. Derivatives measure change; integrals accumulate it.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Calculus lets us compute how loss changes as weights change, which is how neural networks learn.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the math of motion - derivatives are speed (instant change), integrals are distance (total accumulation).

## Related Concepts

- [[derivative|Derivative]]
- [[gradient|Gradient]]
- [[chain-rule|Chain Rule]]

title: chain-rule
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Lets us compute derivatives of composite functions. Essential for backpropagation in neural networks.

## 📋 Concrete Example

If y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f-prime(g(x)) times g-prime(x). This is how backprop propagates gradients layer by layer.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like tracking a rumor through a chain of friends - each person changes it a bit, and you multiply all the changes.

## Related Concepts

- [[derivative|Derivative]]
- [[backpropagation|Backpropagation]]
- [[function-composition|Function Composition]]

title: conditional-probability
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The probability of an event given that another event has already happened.

## 📋 Concrete Example

P(rain | dark clouds) is much higher than P(rain) in general. Knowing clouds change the odds.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the probability your bus is late changes once you hear there was an accident on the road.

## Related Concepts

- [[probability|Probability]]
- [[bayes-theorem|Bayes Theorem]]

title: convex-function
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A bowl-shaped function with one global minimum. Easy to optimize - any downhill path reaches the bottom.

## 📋 Concrete Example

f(x) = x squared is convex. Gradient descent always finds the bottom, no matter where you start.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a smooth bowl - a marble rolled from anywhere will settle at the lowest point.

## Related Concepts

- [[optimization|Optimization]]
- [[global-minimum|Global Minimum]]
- [[local-minimum|Local Minimum]]

title: correlation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Measures how two variables move together. Correlation is not causation.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Ice cream sales and drowning deaths both rise in summer - correlated, but ice cream does not cause drowning.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like two dancers moving together - they might be following the same music, not one leading the other.

## Related Concepts

- [[statistics|Statistics]]
- [[covariance|Covariance]]

title: cosine-similarity
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Measures the angle between two vectors, ignoring their length. Great for comparing meaning.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Vectors for king and queen have a small angle (high cosine similarity, about 0.7). King and banana have a large angle.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like comparing the direction two people are walking - same direction means similar, regardless of speed.

## Related Concepts

- [[dot-product|Dot Product]]
- [[vector|Vector]]
- [[embedding|Embedding]]

title: covariance
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Measures how two variables change together. Positive means they rise together; negative means one rises as the other falls.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Study hours and grades have positive covariance. TV hours and grades might have negative covariance.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like two friends on a seesaw - if one goes up while the other goes down, that is negative covariance.

## Related Concepts

- [[correlation|Correlation]]
- [[variance|Variance]]
- [[statistics|Statistics]]

title: cross-entropy
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Measures the difference between two probability distributions. Used as a loss function in classification.

## 📋 Concrete Example

If the true label is cat but the model predicts only 10% cat, cross-entropy loss is high. If 90%, it is low.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a penalty for being wrong and confident - you lose points for assigning low probability to the truth.

## Related Concepts

- [[entropy|Entropy]]
- [[loss-function|Loss Function]]
- [[softmax|Softmax]]
- [[kl-divergence|KL Divergence]]

title: derivative
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Measures how fast a function changes at a point. The slope of the tangent line.

## 📋 Concrete Example

For f(x) = x squared, the derivative is 2x. At x=3, slope is 6.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a speedometer showing how fast your position changes at this instant.

## Related Concepts

- [[gradient|Gradient]]
- [[chain-rule|Chain Rule]]
- [[calculus|Calculus]]

title: dimension
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The number of independent directions in a space. Each feature adds a dimension.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A 3-feature dataset (height, weight, age) is 3-dimensional. An image with 784 pixels is 784-dimensional.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the axes on a graph - 2 axes is a flat plane, 3 axes is a 3D space, more axes are beyond what we can picture.

## Related Concepts

- [[vector|Vector]]
- [[dimensionality-reduction|Dimensionality Reduction]]
- [[pca|PCA]]

title: dot-product
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Multiplies two vectors element-wise and sums the result. Measures how aligned two vectors are.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Dot of [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6] = 1*4 + 2*5 + 3*6 = 4 + 10 + 18 = 32.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like two people pulling a cart - if they pull in the same direction, their effort adds up; if opposite, it cancels.

## Related Concepts

- [[vector|Vector]]
- [[matrix-multiplication|Matrix Multiplication]]
- [[cosine-similarity|Cosine Similarity]]

title: eigenvalue-eigenvector
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Special vectors that only stretch or shrink under a transformation (eigenvectors), by a factor (eigenvalues).

## 📋 Concrete Example

PCA finds eigenvectors of the covariance matrix. The largest eigenvalues mark the most important directions.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like finding the natural grain of a piece of wood - along the grain (eigenvector) it stretches evenly, by the eigenvalue amount.

## Related Concepts

- [[pca|PCA]]
- [[linear-algebra|Linear Algebra]]
- [[matrix|Matrix]]

title: entropy
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Measures uncertainty or randomness. Higher entropy means more chaos, less predictability.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A fair coin has entropy of 1 bit. A loaded coin with 99% heads has much lower entropy.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the messiness of a bedroom - a tidy room (predictable) has low entropy, a chaotic one has high.

## Related Concepts

- [[cross-entropy|Cross-Entropy]]
- [[kl-divergence|KL Divergence]]
- [[information-theory|Information Theory]]

title: euclidean-distance
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The straight-line distance between two points. Used to measure similarity in feature space.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Distance between [0,0] and [3,4] = square root of (9+16) = 5.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like measuring with a ruler between two dots on a map - the direct straight line.

## Related Concepts

- [[hypotenuse|Hypotenuse]]
- [[vector|Vector]]
- [[cosine-similarity|Cosine Similarity]]

title: expected-value
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The long-run average of a random variable. What you would expect on average over many trials.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Rolling a fair 6-sided die: expected value = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5. You won't roll 3.5, but over many rolls the average approaches it.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the average score you would get playing a game many, many times - not any single game's score.

## Related Concepts

- [[mean|Mean]]
- [[probability|Probability]]
- [[statistics|Statistics]]

title: exponent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Repeated multiplication. The inverse of logarithm. Growth can be explosive.

## 📋 Concrete Example

2 to the power 10 = 1024. Exponential growth doubles each step: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, ...

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a rumor spreading where each person tells 2 new people - the numbers explode quickly.

## Related Concepts

- [[logarithm|Logarithm]]
- [[exponential-growth|Exponential Growth]]
- [[sigmoid|Sigmoid]]

title: exponential-growth
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Growth that multiplies by a constant each step, not adds. How things go viral.

## 📋 Concrete Example

If followers double each day: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... After 20 days, over 1 million.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a chain letter - each person who gets it sends it to more, and the numbers explode.

## Related Concepts

- [[exponent|Exponent]]
- [[logarithm|Logarithm]]

title: function-composition
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Applying one function after another. Neural networks are deep compositions of simple functions.

## 📋 Concrete Example

If f(x) = x+1 and g(x) = x*2, then g(f(x)) = (x+1)*2. A 10-layer network composes 10 functions.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a series of filters on a photo app - each filter feeds into the next, building the final image.

## Related Concepts

- [[chain-rule|Chain Rule]]
- [[neural-network|Neural Network]]
- [[forward-pass|Forward Pass]]

title: global-minimum
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The absolute lowest point of the function. The goal of optimization.

## 📋 Concrete Example

For f(x) = x squared, the global minimum is at x=0, f(x)=0.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the deepest point in the ocean - the true bottom, not just a local trench.

## Related Concepts

- [[local-minimum|Local Minimum]]
- [[convex-function|Convex Function]]
- [[optimization|Optimization]]

title: gradient
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A vector pointing in the direction of steepest increase. Negative gradient points toward decrease.

## 📋 Concrete Example

On a hill, the gradient points uphill. To descend, you go in the opposite direction.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a compass that always points to the steepest way up a mountain; flip it to find the way down.

## Related Concepts

- [[derivative|Derivative]]
- [[gradient-descent|Gradient Descent]]
- [[partial-derivative|Partial Derivative]]

title: hypotenuse
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The longest side of a right triangle, opposite the right angle. Foundation of distance calculations.

## 📋 Concrete Example

For sides 3 and 4, the hypotenuse is 5 (Pythagorean theorem: 3 squared + 4 squared = 5 squared).

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the shortcut across a rectangular field - longer than either side, but the direct route.

## Related Concepts

- [[euclidean-distance|Euclidean Distance]]
- [[vector|Vector]]

title: identity-matrix
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A matrix with 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere. Multiplying by it changes nothing.

## 📋 Concrete Example

The 3x3 identity is [[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]]. Any matrix times identity equals itself.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like multiplying a number by 1 - the value stays exactly the same.

## Related Concepts

- [[matrix|Matrix]]
- [[matrix-multiplication|Matrix Multiplication]]

title: independent-events
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Two events are independent if one happening does not change the probability of the other.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Coin flips are independent - getting heads on flip 1 does not change the odds for flip 2.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like two friends flipping coins separately - neither result affects the other.

## Related Concepts

- [[conditional-probability|Conditional Probability]]
- [[probability|Probability]]

title: information-theory
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The study of quantifying information, uncertainty, and communication. Foundation of modern ML loss functions.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Shannon entropy measures the average bits needed to encode messages from a source.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a postal pricing system - it costs more bits to send surprising news than predictable news.

## Related Concepts

- [[entropy|Entropy]]
- [[cross-entropy|Cross-Entropy]]
- [[kl-divergence|KL Divergence]]

title: inverse-matrix
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A matrix that undoes another matrix. Multiplying them gives the identity matrix.

## 📋 Concrete Example

If A times B = identity, then B is the inverse of A. Used to solve linear systems.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like an undo button - apply matrix A, then its inverse, and you are back where you started.

## Related Concepts

- [[matrix|Matrix]]
- [[identity-matrix|Identity Matrix]]

title: kl-divergence
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Measures how one probability distribution differs from another. Not symmetric - direction matters.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Compare a predicted word distribution to the true one. KL divergence quantifies the gap.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like measuring how different your map is from the real city layout - useful for knowing how much to correct.

## Related Concepts

- [[entropy|Entropy]]
- [[cross-entropy|Cross-Entropy]]
- [[information-theory|Information Theory]]

title: linear-algebra
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The study of vectors, matrices, and linear transformations. The language of data in AI.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Representing 1 million images as a matrix and multiplying by a weight matrix to classify them.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the grammar of multi-dimensional space - it lets us describe and manipulate data efficiently.

## Related Concepts

- [[vector|Vector]]
- [[matrix|Matrix]]
- [[eigenvalue-eigenvector|Eigenvalue Eigenvector]]

title: linear-model
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The simplest model: output is a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias. A straight-line or flat-plane relationship.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Predict house price = 10000*area + 5000*rooms - 1000*age + 50000. A linear combination of features.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a recipe: a fixed amount of each ingredient gives the result. No complex interactions.

## Related Concepts

- [[logistic-regression|Logistic Regression]]
- [[regression|Regression]]
- [[weights|Weights]]

title: linear-separability
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When classes can be separated by a straight line (or flat plane). Simple models can handle this; complex data needs more.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Cats vs dogs on a height-weight graph might be separable by a line. Cats vs dogs photos cannot.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like sorting coins by drawing a line - easy if they are clearly separated, impossible if mixed.

## Related Concepts

- [[linear-model|Linear Model]]
- [[classification|Classification]]
- [[perceptron|Perceptron]]

title: local-minimum
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A low point that is not the lowest overall. Gradient descent can get stuck here.

## 📋 Concrete Example

On a bumpy loss surface, the gradient might lead to a small valley that is not the deepest point.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like resting in a small ditch on a mountainside - you are low locally, but not at the valley floor.

## Related Concepts

- [[global-minimum|Global Minimum]]
- [[convex-function|Convex Function]]
- [[gradient-descent|Gradient Descent]]

title: logarithm
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The inverse of exponentiation. Compresses huge ranges into manageable numbers. Used in loss functions and probabilities.

## 📋 Concrete Example

log base 10 of 1000 = 3, because 10 to the power 3 = 1000. log turns multiplication into addition.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a zoom lens that shrinks vast distances so you can see them on one map.

## Related Concepts

- [[exponent|Exponent]]
- [[entropy|Entropy]]
- [[cross-entropy|Cross-Entropy]]

title: logic
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The formal rules of reasoning. AND, OR, NOT combine statements to reach conclusions.

## 📋 Concrete Example

If it is raining AND I have an umbrella, then I go out. If NOT raining, I go out without one.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the rules of a board game - clear yes/no decisions that combine to determine the outcome.

## Related Concepts

- [[set-theory|Set Theory]]
- [[boolean-algebra|Boolean Algebra]]

title: logistic-regression
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A simple classification model using sigmoid to predict probabilities. The building block before neural networks.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Predict whether a student passes (1) or fails (0) based on study hours, using a sigmoid on a linear combination.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a bouncer with a sliding scale - the more study hours you have, the higher your chance of getting in.

## Related Concepts

- [[sigmoid|Sigmoid]]
- [[classification|Classification]]
- [[linear-model|Linear Model]]

title: matrix-multiplication
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Combines two matrices to produce a new one. The core operation in every neural network layer.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A 3x2 matrix times a 2x4 matrix gives a 3x4 matrix. Each output cell is a dot product of a row and column.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a factory assembly line where each station combines parts from two supply lines to make a new product.

## Related Concepts

- [[matrix|Matrix]]
- [[dot-product|Dot Product]]
- [[forward-pass|Forward Pass]]

title: matrix-transpose
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Flips a matrix over its diagonal, swapping rows and columns. Used everywhere in ML computations.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Transpose of [[1,2],[3,4],[5,6]] (3x2) becomes [[1,3,5],[2,4,6]] (2x3).

## 🔗 Analogy

Like turning a photo sideways - rows become columns and columns become rows.

## Related Concepts

- [[matrix|Matrix]]
- [[matrix-multiplication|Matrix Multiplication]]

title: matrix
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A grid of numbers. Used to store data and perform many calculations at once.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A class of 30 students each with 5 subject scores is a 30-row by 5-column matrix.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a spreadsheet - rows are students, columns are subjects, each cell holds a number.

## Related Concepts

- [[vector|Vector]]
- [[tensor|Tensor]]
- [[matrix-multiplication|Matrix Multiplication]]

title: maximum-likelihood
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Choose parameters that make the observed data most probable. The principle behind many ML training procedures.

## 📋 Concrete Example

If data looks bell-shaped, pick the mean and variance that make that bell curve fit best.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a detective picking the story that best explains all the evidence - the most likely scenario.

## Related Concepts

- [[probability|Probability]]
- [[optimization|Optimization]]
- [[loss-function|Loss Function]]

title: mean-squared-error
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The average of squared errors. Penalizes large errors more than small ones.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Errors of 2 and 4: squared to 4 and 16, averaged to 10. The 4-error dominates.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a test that punishes big mistakes extra hard - a 10-point miss hurts more than five 2-point misses.

## Related Concepts

- [[loss-function|Loss Function]]
- [[variance|Variance]]
- [[regression|Regression]]

title: mean
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The average of a set of numbers. The simplest summary of the center of data.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Scores [70, 80, 90]. Mean = (70+80+90)/3 = 80.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like sharing all the class candy equally - everyone gets the average amount.

## Related Concepts

- [[median|Median]]
- [[mode|Mode]]
- [[statistics|Statistics]]

title: median
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The middle value when data is sorted. Not affected by extreme outliers.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Salaries sorted: [10k, 20k, 25k, 30k, 1M]. Median = 25k. Mean would be dragged up by the 1M.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the middle person in a line sorted by height - one giant at the end does not change them.

## Related Concepts

- [[mean|Mean]]
- [[mode|Mode]]
- [[statistics|Statistics]]

title: mode
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The most frequently occurring value in a dataset.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Shoe sizes sold: [36, 37, 38, 38, 38, 39]. Mode = 38 because it appears most.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the most popular dish at a canteen - the one ordered most often.

## Related Concepts

- [[mean|Mean]]
- [[median|Median]]
- [[statistics|Statistics]]

title: norm
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The length or magnitude of a vector. L2 norm is the Euclidean length; L1 norm is the sum of absolute values.

## 📋 Concrete Example

L2 norm of [3, 4] = 5. L1 norm of [3, 4] = 7.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like measuring the total length of a route - L2 is the crow-flies distance, L1 is the city-block distance.

## Related Concepts

- [[vector|Vector]]
- [[euclidean-distance|Euclidean Distance]]
- [[l1-l2-regularization|L1 L2 Regularization]]

title: normal-distribution
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The bell curve. Most data clusters around the mean, with fewer values at the extremes.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Heights of students: most near the average, few very short or very tall. Classic bell shape.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a sand pile - most sand heaps in the middle, with thinner slopes on the sides.

## Related Concepts

- [[uniform-distribution|Uniform Distribution]]
- [[mean|Mean]]
- [[standard-deviation|Standard Deviation]]

title: one-hot-encoding
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Represents a category as a vector with a single 1 and the rest 0s. Lets models handle categorical data.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Three colors red, green, blue become [1,0,0], [0,1,0], [0,0,1]. No implied ordering.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a multiple choice answer sheet - you fill exactly one bubble, leaving the rest blank.

## Related Concepts

- [[softmax|Softmax]]
- [[classification|Classification]]
- [[cross-entropy|Cross-Entropy]]

title: optimization
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Finding the best solution from many options. Training a model is an optimization problem.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Gradient descent optimizes weights to minimize the loss function.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like tuning a radio dial to find the clearest signal among many positions.

## Related Concepts

- [[gradient-descent|Gradient Descent]]
- [[loss-function|Loss Function]]
- [[convex-function|Convex Function]]

title: partial-derivative
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The derivative with respect to one variable while keeping others fixed. Used when functions have many inputs.

## 📋 Concrete Example

For f(x, y) = x*y, partial derivative with respect to x is y (treat y as constant).

## 🔗 Analogy

Like adjusting only the volume on a mixing desk while leaving all other sliders alone, to see the effect.

## Related Concepts

- [[gradient|Gradient]]
- [[derivative|Derivative]]
- [[gradient-descent|Gradient Descent]]

title: probability
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Measures how likely an event is, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). The language of uncertainty in AI.

## 📋 Concrete Example

The probability of rolling a 6 on a fair die is 1/6, about 0.167.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a weather forecast saying 70% chance of rain - a number between 0 and 1 for how likely.

## Related Concepts

- [[conditional-probability|Conditional Probability]]
- [[bayes-theorem|Bayes Theorem]]
- [[distribution|Distribution]]

title: relu
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Max(0, x). Simple, fast, and avoids the vanishing gradient problem for positive inputs.

## 📋 Concrete Example

ReLU(5)=5, ReLU(-3)=0. Gradient is 1 for positive, 0 for negative.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a one-way valve - positive flow passes through unchanged, negative flow is blocked.

## Related Concepts

- [[activation-function|Activation Function]]
- [[vanishing-gradient|Vanishing Gradient]]
- [[neural-network|Neural Network]]

title: sampling
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Picking items from a distribution. Used to generate text, augment data, and estimate statistics.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A language model samples the next word from its probability distribution, adding variety to outputs.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like drawing names from a hat - you pick one based on the probabilities, not always the most likely.

## Related Concepts

- [[probability|Probability]]
- [[distribution|Distribution]]
- [[language-model|Language Model]]

title: set-theory
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The study of collections of objects. Foundation for logic, probability, and data operations.

## 📋 Concrete Example

The set of students who like math intersected with the set who like music gives students who like both.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like sorting toys into labeled boxes and then finding what is in common or different between boxes.

## Related Concepts

- [[logic|Logic]]
- [[probability|Probability]]

title: sigmoid-derivative
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The slope of sigmoid, used in backpropagation. Maxes at 0.25, which causes vanishing gradients in deep networks.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Sigmoid derivative at x=0 is 0.25 (steepest). At extremes it approaches 0, meaning gradients vanish.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a hill that is flattest at the top and bottom - hard to slide down when there is no slope.

## Related Concepts

- [[sigmoid|Sigmoid]]
- [[derivative|Derivative]]
- [[vanishing-gradient|Vanishing Gradient]]

title: sigmoid
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Squashes any real number into (0, 1). Historically popular, now mostly replaced by ReLU in hidden layers.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Sigmoid(0) = 0.5. Very positive input goes to ~1, very negative goes to ~0.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a dimmer switch smoothly going from off (0) to fully on (1).

## Related Concepts

- [[activation-function|Activation Function]]
- [[softmax|Softmax]]
- [[logistic-regression|Logistic Regression]]

title: softmax
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Converts a vector of scores into probabilities that sum to 1. The standard output for multi-class classification.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Scores [1, 2, 3] become probabilities [0.09, 0.24, 0.67] after softmax. The biggest score gets the most probability.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like an election that converts vote counts into percentages - all percentages add up to 100%.

## Related Concepts

- [[sigmoid|Sigmoid]]
- [[cross-entropy|Cross-Entropy]]
- [[classification|Classification]]

title: standard-deviation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The square root of variance, in the same units as the data. Easier to interpret.

## 📋 Concrete Example

If variance is 25, standard deviation is 5. Most data falls within 2 standard deviations of the mean.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a margin of error - plus or minus 5 marks tells you how spread out exam scores typically are.

## Related Concepts

- [[variance|Variance]]
- [[mean|Mean]]
- [[normal-distribution|Normal Distribution]]

title: statistics
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The science of collecting, summarizing, and interpreting data. Essential for understanding ML results.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Computing mean, median, and standard deviation of student test scores to understand class performance.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a sports commentator summarizing a match with stats - possession, shots, passes - to tell the story.

## Related Concepts

- [[mean|Mean]]
- [[variance|Variance]]
- [[probability|Probability]]
- [[distribution|Distribution]]

title: tensor
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A generalization of vectors and matrices to any number of dimensions. The data format deep learning uses.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A color image is a 3D tensor: height x width x 3 color channels (RGB). A batch of 32 images is a 4D tensor.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a cube of data, or even a hypercube - you can keep adding dimensions as needed.

## Related Concepts

- [[vector|Vector]]
- [[matrix|Matrix]]
- [[neural-network|Neural Network]]

title: uniform-distribution
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Every outcome has equal probability. No value is more likely than another.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Rolling a fair 6-sided die: each face has exactly 1/6 chance. Flat, not bell-shaped.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a lottery where every ticket has the same chance of winning - no favorites.

## Related Concepts

- [[normal-distribution|Normal Distribution]]
- [[probability|Probability]]

title: vanishing-gradient
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When gradients shrink to near zero as they propagate back through layers, stopping deep networks from learning.

## 📋 Concrete Example

In a 20-layer network with sigmoid, gradients in early layers may be 0.25 to the power 20, essentially zero.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a whisper passed through 20 people - by the end, the message has faded to nothing.

## Related Concepts

- [[sigmoid-derivative|Sigmoid Derivative]]
- [[backpropagation|Backpropagation]]
- [[deep-learning|Deep Learning]]
- [[relu|ReLU]]

title: variance
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Measures how spread out the data is from the mean. High variance means data is scattered widely.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Two classes both average 70. Class A scores range 65-75 (low variance). Class B ranges 40-100 (high variance).

## 🔗 Analogy

Like measuring how far arrows spread from the bullseye - tight cluster is low variance, scattered is high.

## Related Concepts

- [[standard-deviation|Standard Deviation]]
- [[mean|Mean]]
- [[statistics|Statistics]]

title: vector
text:
> **Domain:** [[_math-logic-for-ai-moc|Math & Logic for AI]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A list of numbers that represents a point or direction in space. The basic building block of data in AI.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A student can be represented as a vector: [Math=85, English=72, Science=90]. Each number is a feature.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a GPS coordinate with three numbers (lat, long, altitude) that pinpoints a spot.

## Related Concepts

- [[matrix|Matrix]]
- [[tensor|Tensor]]
- [[dot-product|Dot Product]]
- [[embedding|Embedding]]
