title: attention-mechanism
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Lets the model focus on the most relevant input words when producing each output word.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Translating The bank of the river, attention links bank to river (not to money-bank) to translate correctly.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a student highlighting key sentences in a textbook before answering a question.

## Related Concepts

- [[self-attention|Self-Attention]]
- [[transformer-architecture|Transformer Architecture]]
- [[machine-translation|Machine Translation]]

title: bag-of-words
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Represents text as a count of each word, ignoring order. Simple but loses meaning and structure.

## 📋 Concrete Example

I love AI and AI loves me becomes {I:1, love:1, AI:2, and:1, loves:1, me:1}. Order is gone.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like tossing all words from a sentence into a bag - you know what words are there but not the order.

## Related Concepts

- [[n-gram|N-Gram]]
- [[tf-idf|TF-IDF]]
- [[vectorization|Vectorization]]

title: beam-search
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

At each step, keeps the top K most promising partial outputs instead of just the best one. Improves generation.

## 📋 Concrete Example

With beam width 3, the decoder keeps 3 best partial translations at each step and expands all of them.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a chess player thinking several moves ahead and keeping multiple promising lines of play.

## Related Concepts

- [[greedy-decoding|Greedy Decoding]]
- [[decoder|Decoder]]
- [[language-model|Language Model]]

title: bert
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. Reads text in both directions for deep understanding.

## 📋 Concrete Example

BERT is trained with masked language modeling. It is great for classification and question answering, not generation.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a reader who can look at the whole page at once, both left and right, to understand each word.

## Related Concepts

- [[masked-language-modeling|Masked Language Modeling]]
- [[encoder|Encoder]]
- [[transformer-architecture|Transformer Architecture]]

title: bleu-score
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Measures how close machine translation output is to human reference translations. Higher is better.

## 📋 Concrete Example

If the model output matches the reference exactly, BLEU = 1.0. Partial matches give partial scores.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like grading a translation essay by comparing it to the teacher reference answer.

## Related Concepts

- [[evaluation|Evaluation]]
- [[machine-translation|Machine Translation]]

title: bpe
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Byte-Pair Encoding starts with characters and merges the most frequent pairs step by step. Used by GPT models.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Start with characters. low + est merge to lowest if seen often. Build a vocabulary of frequent subwords.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a factory that starts with tiny parts and keeps gluing the most common pairs together until it has useful modules.

## Related Concepts

- [[subword-tokenization|Subword Tokenization]]
- [[wordpiece|WordPiece]]
- [[vocabulary|Vocabulary]]
- [[tokenization|Tokenization]]

title: causal-language-modeling
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Predicts the next token given all previous tokens. How GPT models are trained.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Given The cat sat on the, predict mat. The model can only look left, never right.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like writing a story one word at a time - you can only use what you have already written.

## Related Concepts

- [[language-model|Language Model]]
- [[gpt|GPT]]
- [[next-token-prediction|Next Token Prediction]]
- [[decoder|Decoder]]

title: character-level-tokenization
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Splits text into individual characters. No out-of-vocabulary problem, but sequences get very long.

## 📋 Concrete Example

AI becomes [A, I]. Every character is a token.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like spelling out a word letter by letter - no word is unknown, but it takes a long time to say.

## Related Concepts

- [[tokenization|Tokenization]]
- [[word-tokenization|Word Tokenization]]
- [[subword-tokenization|Subword Tokenization]]

title: chunking
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Grouping tokens into meaningful phrases (noun phrases, verb phrases). A step between tokens and full parsing.

## 📋 Concrete Example

The big red car becomes [The big red car] as one noun phrase chunk.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like grouping words into Lego blocks - each block is a phrase you can move around.

## Related Concepts

- [[part-of-speech-tagging|Part of Speech Tagging]]
- [[syntax|Syntax]]
- [[tokenization|Tokenization]]

title: context-length
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

How many tokens of conversation the model remembers at once. Beyond this, old messages are forgotten.

## 📋 Concrete Example

If context length is 4096 tokens and the chat exceeds that, the earliest messages drop out of memory.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a goldfish bowl - there is only so much room. New water pushes old water out.

## Related Concepts

- [[context-window|Context Window]]
- [[tokenization|Tokenization]]
- [[transformer-architecture|Transformer Architecture]]

title: context-window
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The maximum number of tokens a model can see at once. Larger windows mean longer memory but more cost.

## 📋 Concrete Example

GPT-4 has a 128K token context window. It can read a whole short book, but not a full library.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the size of your desk - you can only work with the documents that fit on it at one time.

## Related Concepts

- [[tokenization|Tokenization]]
- [[transformer-architecture|Transformer Architecture]]
- [[attention|Attention]]

title: coreference-resolution
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Finding which words refer to the same entity. Essential for understanding pronouns.

## 📋 Concrete Example

In Mary said she was tired, coreference resolution links she to Mary.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a detective connecting nicknames, pronouns, and names to figure out who is who in a story.

## Related Concepts

- [[named-entity-recognition|Named Entity Recognition]]
- [[semantics|Semantics]]

title: corpus
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A large collection of text used for training. The bigger and more diverse, the better the model learns.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Wikipedia, news articles, and books together form a corpus for training a language model.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a library the model studies - the more books it reads, the more it knows.

## Related Concepts

- [[dataset|Dataset]]
- [[language-model|Language Model]]
- [[pre-training|Pre-Training]]

title: decoder
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The part of a transformer that generates the output sequence one token at a time, using encoder context.

## 📋 Concrete Example

In translation, the decoder generates the English translation word by word, guided by the encoder output.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a writer who takes the understanding and writes it out in a new language, one word at a time.

## Related Concepts

- [[encoder|Encoder]]
- [[transformer-architecture|Transformer Architecture]]
- [[seq2seq|Seq2Seq]]

title: dependency-parsing
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Analyzes the grammatical structure by finding relationships (head and dependent) between words.

## 📋 Concrete Example

In I eat rice, eat is the head, I is the subject dependent, and rice is the object dependent.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like drawing arrows between words to show who depends on whom in a sentence.

## Related Concepts

- [[part-of-speech-tagging|Part of Speech Tagging]]
- [[syntax|Syntax]]
- [[chunking|Chunking]]

title: distributed-representation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Representing meaning as a pattern across many dimensions, not a single symbol. Embeddings do this.

## 📋 Concrete Example

The meaning of king is spread across 300 numbers, not stored in one slot labeled king.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like describing a color by its RGB values instead of just its name - more detailed and comparable.

## Related Concepts

- [[embedding|Embedding]]
- [[word2vec|Word2Vec]]
- [[vector|Vector]]

title: embedding
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Turns words or tokens into vectors of numbers so the computer can measure meaning and similarity.

## 📋 Concrete Example

The word happy might become [0.8, -0.1, 0.5, ...]. Words with similar meaning get similar vectors.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like giving each word a fingerprint - similar words have similar prints, different words have different ones.

## Related Concepts

- [[word2vec|Word2Vec]]
- [[glove|GloVe]]
- [[vector|Vector]]
- [[tokenization|Tokenization]]

title: encoder
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The part of a transformer that reads and understands the input, turning it into rich representations.

## 📋 Concrete Example

In translation, the encoder reads the Chinese sentence and produces a set of context vectors capturing its meaning.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a reader who absorbs a story and forms a deep understanding of it in their mind.

## Related Concepts

- [[decoder|Decoder]]
- [[transformer-architecture|Transformer Architecture]]
- [[self-attention|Self-Attention]]

title: evaluation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Measuring how good an NLP model is. Metrics include accuracy, F1, BLEU, and perplexity.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A translation model is evaluated with BLEU score comparing its output to human translations.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a report card with different grades for different subjects - each metric measures a different aspect.

## Related Concepts

- [[perplexity|Perplexity]]
- [[bleu-score|BLEU Score]]
- [[f1-score|F1 Score]]

title: f1-score
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The harmonic mean of precision and recall. Balances both into one number for classification tasks.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Precision 0.8, recall 0.6 -> F1 = 2 * (0.8*0.6)/(0.8+0.6) = 0.68. A single balanced score.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a judge who weighs both how many correct answers you got (precision) and how many you missed (recall).

## Related Concepts

- [[evaluation|Evaluation]]
- [[precision|Precision]]
- [[recall|Recall]]

title: few-shot-learning
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Giving the model a few examples in the prompt to help it understand the task before asking it to perform.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Prompt: Here are 3 examples of formal vs informal text... Now classify this new sentence. The model follows the pattern.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like showing a new employee 3 example emails before asking them to write one - they learn the style quickly.

## Related Concepts

- [[zero-shot-learning|Zero-Shot Learning]]
- [[prompt-engineering|Prompt Engineering]]
- [[language-model|Language Model]]

title: fine-tuning
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Training a pre-trained language model further on a specific dataset so it specializes in a task or domain.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Fine-tune GPT on Hong Kong legal documents to make a legal assistant chatbot.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a general doctor taking extra training to become a heart specialist.

## Related Concepts

- [[pre-training|Pre-Training]]
- [[transfer-learning|Transfer Learning]]
- [[language-model|Language Model]]

title: glove
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Global Vectors: learns embeddings from word co-occurrence counts across the whole corpus.

## 📋 Concrete Example

GloVe looks at how often ice and steam appear near each other versus with other words, and places them accordingly.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a popularity chart - words that hang out together in many books get similar scores.

## Related Concepts

- [[word2vec|Word2Vec]]
- [[embedding|Embedding]]
- [[vector|Vector]]

title: gpt
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Generative Pre-trained Transformer. Autoregressive decoder that generates text token by token.

## 📋 Concrete Example

GPT reads your prompt and generates a response one token at a time, always looking left only.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a storyteller who builds the tale word by word, each new word based on everything said so far.

## Related Concepts

- [[causal-language-modeling|Causal Language Modeling]]
- [[decoder|Decoder]]
- [[next-token-prediction|Next Token Prediction]]
- [[transformer-architecture|Transformer Architecture]]

title: greedy-decoding
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Always picks the most likely next token. Fast but can produce repetitive or suboptimal text.

## 📋 Concrete Example

The model always picks the highest-probability word. It might get stuck repeating the same phrase.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like always choosing the shortest path at each turn without looking ahead - you might hit a dead end.

## Related Concepts

- [[beam-search|Beam Search]]
- [[sampling|Sampling]]
- [[decoder|Decoder]]

title: hallucination
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When a language model confidently states false information as if it were true. A major challenge in NLP.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A model might say Hong Kong was founded in 1843 (wrong, it was 1842) with full confidence.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a student who makes up an answer on an exam and writes it confidently - sounds right, but is wrong.

## Related Concepts

- [[language-model|Language Model]]
- [[evaluation|Evaluation]]
- [[gpt|GPT]]

title: information-extraction
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Pulling structured facts from unstructured text. NER, relation extraction, and event extraction.

## 📋 Concrete Example

From Apple was founded in 1976, extract: (Apple, founded, 1976). Turns text into a database.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like panning for gold - you sift through raw text to find the valuable structured nuggets.

## Related Concepts

- [[named-entity-recognition|Named Entity Recognition]]
- [[relation-extraction|Relation Extraction]]

title: language-model
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A model that assigns probabilities to sequences of text. Can predict the next word. The core of chatbots.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Given The sky is, a language model says blue is most likely (0.8), green less likely (0.05).

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a super-smart autocomplete on your phone that has read millions of books.

## Related Concepts

- [[n-gram|N-Gram]]
- [[perplexity|Perplexity]]
- [[transformer-architecture|Transformer Architecture]]
- [[next-token-prediction|Next Token Prediction]]

title: lemmatization
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Reduces words to their dictionary root form (lemma). Slower than stemming but more accurate.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Better becomes good. Running becomes run. Studies becomes study. All are real dictionary words.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like looking up a word in a dictionary to find its base form - accurate but takes a moment.

## Related Concepts

- [[stemming|Stemming]]
- [[preprocessing|Preprocessing]]
- [[part-of-speech-tagging|Part of Speech Tagging]]

title: machine-translation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Automatically translates text from one language to another. Google Translate and DeepL use this.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Input: Good morning. Output (Chinese): zao shang hao. The model learns mappings between languages.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a bilingual friend who reads a Chinese text and tells you what it means in English.

## Related Concepts

- [[seq2seq|Seq2Seq]]
- [[encoder|Encoder]]
- [[decoder|Decoder]]
- [[attention|Attention]]

title: masked-language-modeling
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Hides some tokens and asks the model to predict them. How BERT is trained.

## 📋 Concrete Example

The [MASK] sat on the mat. The model learns to predict cat from the surrounding context.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a fill-in-the-blank quiz - the model learns language by guessing the hidden words.

## Related Concepts

- [[language-model|Language Model]]
- [[bert|BERT]]
- [[pre-training|Pre-Training]]

title: multi-head-attention
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Runs several attention mechanisms in parallel, each focusing on different relationships, then combines results.

## 📋 Concrete Example

One head might focus on grammar, another on emotion, another on named entities - all at once.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a team of detectives each looking at different clues (motive, alibi, evidence) and then pooling findings.

## Related Concepts

- [[self-attention|Self-Attention]]
- [[transformer-architecture|Transformer Architecture]]

title: n-gram
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A sequence of N consecutive tokens. Used to model local word patterns and predict the next word.

## 📋 Concrete Example

In I love AI so much, the bigrams (2-grams) are: I love, love AI, AI so, so much.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like looking at words two or three at a time, like reading through a magnifying glass that shows a small window.

## Related Concepts

- [[tokenization|Tokenization]]
- [[bag-of-words|Bag of Words]]
- [[language-model|Language Model]]

title: named-entity-recognition
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Finds and classifies names in text: people, places, organizations, dates, etc.

## 📋 Concrete Example

In Tim Cook visited Apple Park in Cupertino, NER finds: Tim Cook (PERSON), Apple Park (ORG), Cupertino (LOC).

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a highlighter that marks every proper noun and labels what kind of thing it is.

## Related Concepts

- [[part-of-speech-tagging|Part of Speech Tagging]]
- [[information-extraction|Information Extraction]]

title: next-token-prediction
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The fundamental task of autoregressive language models: guess the next token from the context so far.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Input: Hong Kong is famous for its. Model predicts: dim sum (0.3), skyline (0.2), harbor (0.15), ...

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a guessing game where you predict the next word in a sentence your friend is saying.

## Related Concepts

- [[causal-language-modeling|Causal Language Modeling]]
- [[language-model|Language Model]]
- [[gpt|GPT]]

title: part-of-speech-tagging
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Labels each word with its grammatical role: noun, verb, adjective, etc. Helps disambiguate meaning.

## 📋 Concrete Example

In I book a ticket, book is a verb. In I read a book, book is a noun. Same word, different tags.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like labeling each word in a sentence with a name tag saying I am a noun or I am a verb.

## Related Concepts

- [[lemmatization|Lemmatization]]
- [[named-entity-recognition|Named Entity Recognition]]
- [[syntax|Syntax]]

title: perplexity
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Measures how surprised a language model is by text. Lower perplexity means the model expected the text better.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A good language model has low perplexity on well-written English and high perplexity on random gibberish.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a prediction game - if you guessed the text right, you are not perplexed; if it shocked you, perplexity is high.

## Related Concepts

- [[language-model|Language Model]]
- [[cross-entropy|Cross-Entropy]]
- [[evaluation|Evaluation]]

title: positional-encoding
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Adds position information to tokens since attention has no built-in sense of order.

## 📋 Concrete Example

The model adds a position pattern to each token: token 1 gets pattern A, token 2 gets pattern B, etc.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like numbering the pages of a book - the text on each page needs a page number so you know the order.

## Related Concepts

- [[transformer-architecture|Transformer Architecture]]
- [[self-attention|Self-Attention]]
- [[embedding|Embedding]]

title: pre-training
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Training a language model on a massive text corpus before any specific task. Gives general language understanding.

## 📋 Concrete Example

GPT is pre-trained on web text, books, and code. Then it is fine-tuned or prompted for specific tasks.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a student doing broad reading for years before specializing in one subject at university.

## Related Concepts

- [[fine-tuning|Fine-Tuning]]
- [[transfer-learning|Transfer Learning]]
- [[corpus|Corpus]]

title: precision
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Of the items the model predicted as positive, how many were actually positive. Measures quality of positive predictions.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Model predicts 10 emails are spam, 8 actually are. Precision = 8/10 = 0.8. 2 were false alarms.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a fisherman checking his catch - of the 10 fish he kept, how many were the target species.

## Related Concepts

- [[f1-score|F1 Score]]
- [[recall|Recall]]
- [[evaluation|Evaluation]]

title: preprocessing
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Cleaning and preparing raw text before feeding it to a model. Tokenization, lowercasing, removing noise.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Raw HTML gets tags stripped, text lowercased, tokenized, and stop words removed before analysis.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like washing and chopping vegetables before cooking - you prepare the ingredients first.

## Related Concepts

- [[tokenization|Tokenization]]
- [[stop-words|Stop Words]]
- [[stemming|Stemming]]
- [[lemmatization|Lemmatization]]

title: prompt-engineering
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Crafting the input prompt to get the best output from a language model. A key skill for using LLMs.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Adding Be specific and give 3 examples to a prompt can dramatically improve the response quality.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like asking a teacher the right question - a well-phrased question gets a much better answer.

## Related Concepts

- [[language-model|Language Model]]
- [[gpt|GPT]]
- [[next-token-prediction|Next Token Prediction]]

title: question-answering
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Given a question and a context passage, the model finds or generates the answer.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Question: When was Hong Kong established? Context: Hong Kong was established in 1842. Answer: 1842.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a student reading a passage then answering comprehension questions from it.

## Related Concepts

- [[text-classification|Text Classification]]
- [[embedding|Embedding]]
- [[bert|BERT]]

title: recall
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Of all the actual positive items, how many the model found. Measures completeness.

## 📋 Concrete Example

There are 15 real spam emails. Model finds 8. Recall = 8/15 = 0.53. It missed 7.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a search and rescue team - of all the lost hikers, how many did they find.

## Related Concepts

- [[f1-score|F1 Score]]
- [[precision|Precision]]
- [[evaluation|Evaluation]]

title: relation-extraction
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Finding relationships between entities in text. Builds knowledge graphs.

## 📋 Concrete Example

From Steve Jobs co-founded Apple, extract: (Steve Jobs, co-founded, Apple).

## 🔗 Analogy

Like connecting dots in a detective board - link people, companies, and events with strings.

## Related Concepts

- [[named-entity-recognition|Named Entity Recognition]]
- [[information-extraction|Information Extraction]]

title: self-attention
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Each token looks at all other tokens in the same sequence to understand its own meaning in context.

## 📋 Concrete Example

In The bark was loud, self-attention helps the model know bark means dog sound (not tree bark) by looking at loud.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a group discussion where each person listens to everyone else to decide what they themselves mean.

## Related Concepts

- [[attention-mechanism|Attention Mechanism]]
- [[transformer-architecture|Transformer Architecture]]
- [[multi-head-attention|Multi-Head Attention]]

title: semantics
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The meaning of words and sentences. NLP aims to capture semantics, not just syntax.

## 📋 Concrete Example

The cat sat on the mat and The feline rested on the rug have different syntax but similar semantics.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the difference between what a sentence says (syntax) and what it means (semantics).

## Related Concepts

- [[syntax|Syntax]]
- [[embedding|Embedding]]
- [[word2vec|Word2Vec]]

title: sentiment-analysis
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Determines if text is positive, negative, or neutral. Used for reviews, social media, and feedback.

## 📋 Concrete Example

This movie is great! is positive. The food was terrible and cold is negative.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a mood ring for text - it tells you if the writer is happy, angry, or neutral.

## Related Concepts

- [[classification|Classification]]
- [[text-classification|Text Classification]]
- [[embedding|Embedding]]

title: seq2seq
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Sequence-to-sequence models take an input sequence and produce an output sequence of different length.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Translation: input 5 Chinese words, output 7 English words. The lengths differ, and that is fine.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a translator who reads a 3-line Chinese poem and writes a 4-line English version.

## Related Concepts

- [[encoder|Encoder]]
- [[decoder|Decoder]]
- [[machine-translation|Machine Translation]]
- [[attention|Attention]]

title: stemming
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Cuts off word endings to get a root form. Fast but crude - results may not be real words.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Running, runs, runner all stem to run. Studies might stem to studi (not a real word).

## 🔗 Analogy

Like pruning a tree with hedge clippers - quick and rough, not always pretty.

## Related Concepts

- [[lemmatization|Lemmatization]]
- [[preprocessing|Preprocessing]]
- [[stop-words|Stop Words]]

title: stop-words
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Common words like the, is, a that appear everywhere but carry little meaning. Often removed to save space.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Removing stop words from The cat sat on the mat gives cat sat mat. The core meaning stays.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like skimming a book and skipping filler words like um and uh to get to the real content.

## Related Concepts

- [[bag-of-words|Bag of Words]]
- [[tf-idf|TF-IDF]]
- [[preprocessing|Preprocessing]]

title: subword-tokenization
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Splits text into pieces smaller than words but bigger than characters. Handles rare and new words well.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Unbelievable might split into [Un, believe, able]. ChatGPT splits text into subword units like this.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like breaking a big Lego build into medium modules - flexible enough to build anything, efficient to store.

## Related Concepts

- [[tokenization|Tokenization]]
- [[bpe|BPE]]
- [[wordpiece|WordPiece]]
- [[vocabulary|Vocabulary]]

title: summarization
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Producing a shorter version of a longer text while keeping the key points.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Input: 3-page news article. Output: 2-sentence summary capturing the headline event.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like writing a TL;DR at the top of a long email - the essence in a fraction of the words.

## Related Concepts

- [[text-generation|Text Generation]]
- [[seq2seq|Seq2Seq]]
- [[encoder|Encoder]]

title: syntax
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The rules governing sentence structure and word order. Different from semantics (meaning).

## 📋 Concrete Example

Colorless green ideas sleep furiously is syntactically valid but semantically nonsensical.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like the grammar rules of a language - they tell you if a sentence is well-formed, not if it makes sense.

## Related Concepts

- [[part-of-speech-tagging|Part of Speech Tagging]]
- [[dependency-parsing|Dependency Parsing]]
- [[semantics|Semantics]]

title: temperature
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Controls randomness in text generation. Low temperature is focused and safe; high temperature is creative and risky.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Temperature 0.1: model always picks likely words (boring but safe). Temperature 1.5: more random, sometimes creative, sometimes weird.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a thermostat for creativity - low means stay calm and predictable, high means get wild and experimental.

## Related Concepts

- [[sampling|Sampling]]
- [[top-k-sampling|Top-K Sampling]]
- [[language-model|Language Model]]

title: text-classification
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Assigning a category to a piece of text. Spam detection, sentiment analysis, and topic labeling are examples.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Email text -> model -> spam or not spam. News article -> model -> sports, politics, or tech.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like sorting mail into labeled folders - each piece of text goes into one category.

## Related Concepts

- [[classification|Classification]]
- [[sentiment-analysis|Sentiment Analysis]]
- [[embedding|Embedding]]

title: text-generation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Producing new text token by token. The core capability of chatbots and writing assistants.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Prompt: Write a poem about Hong Kong. The model generates: Victoria Harbour gleams at night ...

## 🔗 Analogy

Like an author writing a story - each sentence builds on the last, creating something new.

## Related Concepts

- [[language-model|Language Model]]
- [[next-token-prediction|Next Token Prediction]]
- [[decoder|Decoder]]

title: tf-idf
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Term Frequency x Inverse Document Frequency. Highlights words that are important in a document but rare overall.

## 📋 Concrete Example

The appears in every document (low IDF, ignored). Quantum might appear in one physics paper (high TF-IDF, important).

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a word's VIP score - frequent in this document but rare elsewhere means it is a keyword.

## Related Concepts

- [[bag-of-words|Bag of Words]]
- [[vectorization|Vectorization]]
- [[information-retrieval|Information Retrieval]]

title: tokenization
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Computers cannot read whole sentences at once. We must split text into smaller pieces called tokens first.

## 📋 Concrete Example

The sentence I love AI splits into tokens: [I, love, AI]. Each token gets a number from the vocabulary.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like cutting a long sandwich into bite-size pieces before serving - easier to eat and count.

## Related Concepts

- [[word-tokenization|Word Tokenization]]
- [[subword-tokenization|Subword Tokenization]]
- [[character-level-tokenization|Character-Level Tokenization]]
- [[vocabulary|Vocabulary]]

title: top-k-sampling
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Only samples from the K most likely next tokens, ignoring the long tail of unlikely ones.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Top-K = 40 means the model only considers the top 40 candidates and samples among them.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a talent show where only the top 40 contestants get to perform - the rest are cut.

## Related Concepts

- [[temperature|Temperature]]
- [[sampling|Sampling]]
- [[language-model|Language Model]]

title: top-p-sampling
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Samples from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches P (nucleus sampling).

## 📋 Concrete Example

Top-P = 0.9 means take tokens in order of probability until they add up to 90%, then sample from that set.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like packing a suitcase - take the most important items first until you reach 90% full, then pick randomly from the rest.

## Related Concepts

- [[top-k-sampling|Top-K Sampling]]
- [[temperature|Temperature]]
- [[sampling|Sampling]]

title: transformer-architecture
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The neural network design based entirely on attention, no recurrence. Powers all modern LLMs.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A transformer uses self-attention layers and feed-forward layers, processing all tokens at once in parallel.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a round-table meeting where everyone speaks and listens at once, instead of a phone chain where messages pass one by one.

## Related Concepts

- [[self-attention|Self-Attention]]
- [[positional-encoding|Positional Encoding]]
- [[encoder|Encoder]]
- [[decoder|Decoder]]

title: vectorization
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Converting text into numerical vectors that a model can process. Bag of words, TF-IDF, and embeddings all do this.

## 📋 Concrete Example

I love AI becomes [0.2, 0.8, 0.1, ...] via embedding. Now the computer can do math on it.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like translating a poem into numbers - each word and its meaning become coordinates on a map.

## Related Concepts

- [[bag-of-words|Bag of Words]]
- [[tf-idf|TF-IDF]]
- [[embedding|Embedding]]

title: vocabulary
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The set of all tokens a model knows. Each token maps to an ID number. Unknown tokens cause problems.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A vocabulary of 50000 subwords covers most English. A word outside it gets split into known subwords.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a dictionary the model has memorized - if a word is not in it, the model has to describe it with smaller known pieces.

## Related Concepts

- [[tokenization|Tokenization]]
- [[bpe|BPE]]
- [[embedding|Embedding]]

title: word-tokenization
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Splitting text by spaces and punctuation into individual words. The simplest tokenization method.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Hello, world! becomes [Hello, ,, world, !]. Punctuation marks are often separate tokens.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like tearing a sentence into individual word cards, one word per card.

## Related Concepts

- [[tokenization|Tokenization]]
- [[subword-tokenization|Subword Tokenization]]
- [[vocabulary|Vocabulary]]

title: word2vec
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Learns word embeddings by predicting words from context. Similar words end up with similar vectors.

## 📋 Concrete Example

After training, vector(king) - vector(man) + vector(woman) is close to vector(queen). Famous word analogy.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a GPS for meaning - words that mean similar things end up close together on the map.

## Related Concepts

- [[embedding|Embedding]]
- [[glove|GloVe]]
- [[vector|Vector]]
- [[distributed-representation|Distributed Representation]]

title: wordpiece
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Like BPE but builds vocabulary for language understanding (BERT). Uses ## prefix for non-starting pieces.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Playing splits to [Play, `##ing`]. The double-hash marks that `ing` attaches to the previous piece.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like labeling puzzle pieces - the piece with ## is a connector that must follow another piece.

## Related Concepts

- [[bpe|BPE]]
- [[subword-tokenization|Subword Tokenization]]
- [[vocabulary|Vocabulary]]

title: zero-shot-learning
text:
> **Domain:** [[_nlp-fundamentals-moc|NLP Fundamentals]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The model performs a task it has never been explicitly trained on, using only its general knowledge and the prompt.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Ask a model to classify sentiment of Cantonese text even if it was never trained on a sentiment task in Cantonese.

## 🔗 Analogy

Like a student tackling a brand new question type on an exam using general reasoning, never having practiced it.

## Related Concepts

- [[few-shot-learning|Few-Shot Learning]]
- [[prompt-engineering|Prompt Engineering]]
- [[language-model|Language Model]]
