title: agent-adaptation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The agent adjusts its behavior based on the current task, user, or context - not one-size-fits-all.

## 📋 Concrete Example

For a beginner user: agent explains step by step with simple language. For an expert: agent is concise and technical. Same agent, different behavior based on context.

## 🔗 Analogy

A teacher adapting to different classes - for beginners, they explain basics slowly. For advanced students, they go fast and deep. Agent adaptation customizes behavior to the situation.

## Related Concepts

- [[dynamic-prompting|Dynamic Prompting]]
- [[personalization|Personalization]]
- [[context-aware|Context-Aware]]

title: agent-benchmarking
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Systematically comparing different agent architectures on standardized tasks to find the best design.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Benchmark: 5 architectures x 10 tasks x 3 runs = 150 evaluations. Measure: success rate, steps, tokens, time. Architecture X wins on coding, Architecture Y wins on research.

## 🔗 Analogy

Car comparison testing - 5 cars x 10 road types (highway, city, off-road). Measure speed, fuel, comfort. Find the best car for each road type. Agent benchmarking finds the best architecture for each task type.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-benchmark|Agent Benchmark]]
- [[performance-metric|Performance Metric]]
- [[evaluation|Evaluation]]

title: agent-composition
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Building complex agents by combining simpler agents, like building with blocks.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Compose: SearchAgent + SummarizeAgent + TranslateAgent = NewsTranslator. SearchAgent finds news, SummarizeAgent condenses, TranslateAgent translates. Three simple agents composed into one complex agent.

## 🔗 Analogy

Building with Lego - a wheel + axle + chassis = a car. Simple pieces composed into complex structures. Agent composition builds complex agents from simpler ones.

## Related Concepts

- [[multi-agent-architecture|Multi-Agent Architecture]]
- [[agent-pipeline|Agent Pipeline]]
- [[modular-design|Modular Design]]

title: agent-discovery
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Finding and selecting the right agent for a task from the registry. May involve capability matching and availability checks.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Task: 'Write Python tests.' Discovery: search registry for agents with `python` and `testing` skills, that are available. Find TestAgent. Assign task.

## 🔗 Analogy

Finding a plumber - you search online directories for 'plumber near me, available today.' You find one with good reviews and assign the job. Agent discovery does this for AI agents.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-registry|Agent Registry]]
- [[task-assignment|Task Assignment]]
- [[multi-agent-architecture|Multi-Agent Architecture]]

title: agent-feedback-loop
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Collecting user feedback on agent performance and using it to improve future behavior.

## 📋 Concrete Example

User rates agent's code: '4/5, good but missing comments.' Feedback stored. Next time, agent adds comments. The feedback loop improves the agent over time.

## 🔗 Analogy

Restaurant comment cards - customers rate food and service. The manager reads them and improves. Next time, the food is better. Agent feedback loops use user ratings to improve.

## Related Concepts

- [[improvement-loop|Improvement Loop]]
- [[learning-agent|Learning Agent]]
- [[reflection|Reflection]]

title: agent-pipeline
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A fixed sequence of agents where each one's output feeds into the next, like an assembly line.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Pipeline: Research Agent -> Outline Agent -> Draft Agent -> Edit Agent -> Publish Agent. Each takes the previous output, processes it, and passes to the next.

## 🔗 Analogy

A car assembly line - chassis station -> engine station -> paint station -> inspection station. Each station takes the car from the previous one, adds its part, passes it on. Agent pipelines are assembly lines for tasks.

## Related Concepts

- [[sequential-execution|Sequential Execution]]
- [[prompt-chaining|Prompt Chaining]]
- [[multi-agent-architecture|Multi-Agent Architecture]]

title: agent-protocol
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The rules and formats agents use to communicate - message structure, response formats, error handling.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Protocol: messages are JSON with {from, to, type, content, timestamp}. Type can be `request`, `response`, `status`, `error`. All agents follow this protocol for reliable communication.

## 🔗 Analogy

Radio communication protocols - `over` means I am done speaking, `copy` means I understood, 'stand by' means wait. Everyone follows these rules. Agent protocols are the communication rules for AI agents.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-communication|Agent Communication]]
- [[multi-agent-architecture|Multi-Agent Architecture]]
- [[message-format|Message Format]]

title: agent-registry
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A directory of available agents, their capabilities, and how to contact them. Essential for multi-agent coordination.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Registry: {`CoderAgent`: {skills: [`python`, `javascript`], endpoint: 'agent://coder', available: true}, `TestAgent`: {skills: [`pytest`, `unittest`], endpoint: 'agent://tester', available: false}}

## 🔗 Analogy

A company directory - 'Marketing: Jane (SEO, social media), Engineering: Bob (Python, Java).' You look up who has the skills you need. An agent registry does this for AI agents.

## Related Concepts

- [[multi-agent-architecture|Multi-Agent Architecture]]
- [[tool-registration|Tool Registration]]
- [[agent-discovery|Agent Discovery]]

title: agent-scalability
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

How well an agent architecture handles increasing workload - more tasks, more users, more data.

## 📋 Concrete Example

1 task: ReAct works great. 100 tasks: need parallelism. 10,000 tasks: need distributed agents. The architecture must scale from 1 to 10,000 without breaking.

## 🔗 Analogy

A restaurant kitchen - 5 orders: one chef handles it. 50 orders: need more chefs. 500 orders: need a full kitchen brigade. The system must scale to handle growth.

## Related Concepts

- [[scalability|Scalability]]
- [[distributed-agent|Distributed Agent]]
- [[load-balancing|Load Balancing]]

title: agent-specialization
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Designing each agent to excel at one specific type of task rather than being a generalist.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A general coding agent: writes code at 70% quality. A specialized Python agent: writes Python at 95%. A specialized SQL agent: writes SQL at 95%. Specialization makes each agent an expert in its domain.

## 🔗 Analogy

Medical specialists - a general doctor treats common illnesses, but a cardiologist treats hearts better, and a neurologist treats brains better. Specialization makes each agent an expert in its narrow field.

## Related Concepts

- [[multi-agent-architecture|Multi-Agent Architecture]]
- [[role-assignment|Role Assignment]]
- [[expert-system|Expert System]]

title: agent-swarming
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Many simple agents working together like a swarm, each doing small tasks, with emergent collective intelligence.

## 📋 Concrete Example

100 simple agents each search one page of documentation. Individually simple, but together they cover 100 pages. The collective result is comprehensive.

## 🔗 Analogy

Ants building a colony - each ant does simple tasks (carry dirt, feed larvae). No single ant knows the plan. Together, they build a complex colony. Agent swarms achieve complex results through simple individual actions.

## Related Concepts

- [[multi-agent-architecture|Multi-Agent Architecture]]
- [[emergent-behavior|Emergent Behavior]]
- [[parallel-processing|Parallel Processing]]

title: agent-topology
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The communication structure between agents: star (hub-spoke), ring, mesh, tree, or custom.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Star: all agents talk to orchestrator only. Ring: A->B->C->A. Mesh: every agent talks to every other. Tree: hierarchical parent-child. Topology affects speed, reliability, and complexity.

## 🔗 Analogy

Office communication structures - star (everyone goes through the boss), ring (pass messages around the team), mesh (everyone talks to everyone), tree (managers and subordinates). Topology shapes how agents communicate.

## Related Concepts

- [[multi-agent-architecture|Multi-Agent Architecture]]
- [[agent-communication|Agent Communication]]
- [[network-topology|Network Topology]]

title: agent-verification
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

After an agent completes a task, verifying the result is correct before accepting it.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent says 'I fixed the bug.' Verification: run the tests. Tests pass? Yes -> accept. No -> reject and ask agent to try again. Verification ensures quality.

## 🔗 Analogy

A teacher grading homework - the student says 'I am done.' The teacher checks the work. Correct? Accept. Wrong? Hand back for revision. Agent verification does this for AI outputs.

## Related Concepts

- [[self-evaluation|Self-Evaluation]]
- [[quality-assessment|Quality Assessment]]
- [[testing|Testing]]

title: agentic-workflow
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The designed flow of an agent's actions: what triggers it, what steps it takes, what tools it uses, and how it terminates.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Workflow: 1) Receive code review request. 2) Read code files. 3) Run static analysis. 4) Check for security issues. 5) Write review comments. 6) Submit. Each step is designed and documented.

## 🔗 Analogy

A restaurant's order-to-table workflow - receive order, prep ingredients, cook, plate, garnish, serve. Each step is designed. Agentic workflows structure how agents work from start to finish.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]
- [[task-planning|Task Planning]]
- [[agent-architecture|Agent Architecture]]

title: architecture-selection
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Choosing the right agent architecture for a specific task based on requirements.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Simple Q&A: Reflex agent (fast, simple). Multi-step coding: ReAct (adaptive). Large project: Hierarchical (delegates). High-stakes: Semi-autonomous (human approval). Match architecture to needs.

## 🔗 Analogy

Choosing transportation - to school: walk (simple). To Kowloon: MTR (medium). To Shenzhen: high-speed rail (complex). Match the vehicle to the distance. Architecture selection matches the agent to the task.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-benchmarking|Agent Benchmarking]]
- [[hybrid-architecture|Hybrid Architecture]]
- [[task-planning|Task Planning]]

title: autonomous-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An agent that can operate independently for extended periods, making decisions without human intervention.

## 📋 Concrete Example

An autonomous monitoring agent: watches server logs 24/7, detects anomalies, diagnoses issues, applies fixes, and reports daily. It operates independently with minimal human oversight.

## 🔗 Analogy

A night security guard - they patrol, check doors, respond to alarms, and call police if needed. They work independently all night. Autonomous agents do this for digital tasks.

## Related Concepts

- [[autonomy|Autonomy]]
- [[agent-lifecycle|Agent Lifecycle]]
- [[guardrails|Guardrails]]

title: blackboard-architecture
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A shared knowledge base (blackboard) that multiple agents read from and write to. Agents contribute partial solutions that build up over time.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Blackboard: {topic: 'AI ethics', research: '...', outline: '...', draft: '...'}. Research Agent adds research. Outline Agent reads research, adds outline. Draft Agent reads both, adds draft. All share the same space.

## 🔗 Analogy

A group whiteboard in a brainstorming session - each person adds ideas, reads others' ideas, and builds on them. Nobody talks directly; they all write on the board. Blackboard architecture does this for agents.

## Related Concepts

- [[multi-agent-architecture|Multi-Agent Architecture]]
- [[shared-state|Shared State]]
- [[agent-communication|Agent Communication]]

title: context-aware-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The agent considers context - who the user is, what they asked before, what tools are available - when deciding actions.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Context: user is 14 years old, asked 3 Python questions today, prefers short answers. Agent adapts: gives brief, Python-specific, teen-friendly answers. Context shapes every decision.

## 🔗 Analogy

A tour guide who reads their group - families with kids get fun, simple tours. Adult history buffs get detailed, academic tours. Context-aware agents adapt to their user and situation.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-adaptation|Agent Adaptation]]
- [[dynamic-prompting|Dynamic Prompting]]
- [[agent-memory|Agent Memory]]

title: crew-architecture
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A team of agents with defined roles working together, like a film crew. Each member has a specific job.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Crew: Captain (planner), Researcher (info gatherer), Engineer (coder), QA (tester), Reviewer (quality checker). The Captain coordinates; each member does their part.

## 🔗 Analogy

A film production crew - director (captain), camera operator, sound engineer, lighting, makeup. Each has a role. Together they make a film. Crew architecture gives agents defined crew roles.

## Related Concepts

- [[multi-agent-architecture|Multi-Agent Architecture]]
- [[role-assignment|Role Assignment]]
- [[hierarchical-agent|Hierarchical Agent]]

title: deterministic-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An agent whose behavior is fully predictable - same input always produces same actions. Useful for testing and safety.

## 📋 Concrete Example

With temperature 0 and fixed seed, the agent always takes the same actions for the same input. Deterministic agents are reproducible and auditable.

## 🔗 Analogy

A vending machine - press A1, always get the same snack. No randomness. Deterministic agents are like vending machines: same input, same output, every time.

## Related Concepts

- [[deterministic-output|Deterministic Output]]
- [[reproducibility|Reproducibility]]
- [[state-machine-agent|State Machine Agent]]

title: distributed-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An agent that runs across multiple machines, coordinating over a network. Enables larger-scale tasks.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A web-crawling agent runs on 10 servers: Server 1 crawls pages 1-1000, Server 2 crawls 1001-2000, etc. Results are merged centrally. One task, distributed across machines.

## 🔗 Analogy

A chain of restaurants - each branch (machine) cooks the same menu but serves a different area. Together, they serve the whole city. Distributed agents scale across machines.

## Related Concepts

- [[parallel-processing|Parallel Processing]]
- [[multi-agent-architecture|Multi-Agent Architecture]]
- [[scalability|Scalability]]

title: emergent-behavior
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Complex, intelligent behavior arising from many simple agents following simple rules - without any central controller.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Each agent: 'if you find a bug, fix it and tell neighbors.' 100 agents on a codebase: they find and fix 500 bugs, coordinate without overlap, and clean up the codebase. No one directed this - it emerged.

## 🔗 Analogy

A flock of birds - each bird follows simple rules (stay close, do not collide, match speed). No leader. Yet the flock moves as one fluid shape. Emergent behavior is complexity from simplicity.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-swarming|Agent Swarming]]
- [[multi-agent-architecture|Multi-Agent Architecture]]
- [[self-organization|Self-Organization]]

title: expert-system
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An agent (or system) that encodes human expert knowledge in a specific domain and uses it to make expert-level decisions.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Medical expert system: symptoms -> possible diagnoses -> recommended tests -> treatment options. It encodes a doctor's decision-making process.MYCIN was an early expert system for bacterial infections.

## 🔗 Analogy

A senior doctor who has seen 10,000 patients - their experience (encoded knowledge) lets them diagnose quickly. Expert systems encode this experience as rules or patterns.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-specialization|Agent Specialization]]
- [[knowledge-base|Knowledge Base]]
- [[rule-based-system|Rule-Based System]]

title: finite-state-machine
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A model with a finite number of states, transitions between them, and actions associated with each state/transition. Useful for designing agent behavior.

## 📋 Concrete Example

FSM for a code agent: states={IDLE, READING, CODING, TESTING, DONE}, transitions={IDLE->READING (task received), READING->CODING (files read), CODING->TESTING (code written), TESTING->DONE (tests pass)}.

## 🔗 Analogy

A vending machine - states: waiting for money, money inserted, dispensing, done. Insert coin: waiting -> money inserted. Press button: money inserted -> dispensing. FSM gives agents predictable, testable behavior.

## Related Concepts

- [[state-machine-agent|State Machine Agent]]
- [[state-transition|State Transition]]
- [[deterministic-behavior|Deterministic Behavior]]

title: goal-based-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The agent has explicit goals and searches for action sequences that achieve them, rather than just reacting.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Goal: 'deploy the app.' The agent searches for a path: build -> test -> containerize -> push -> deploy. It evaluates which actions move toward the goal.

## 🔗 Analogy

A navigator with a destination - they do not just turn left when they see a left sign. They plan a route to their destination (goal) and follow it. Goal-based agents navigate toward goals.

## Related Concepts

- [[goal-oriented|Goal-Oriented]]
- [[task-planning|Task Planning]]
- [[search-algorithm|Search Algorithm]]

title: hierarchical-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Complex tasks are managed by a top-level agent that delegates sub-tasks to lower-level specialist agents.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Top agent: 'Build a web app.' Delegates to: Design Agent (UI), Backend Agent (API), Database Agent (schema). Each sub-agent handles its specialty and reports back.

## 🔗 Analogy

A CEO delegating to department heads - the CEO (top agent) says 'launch a product.' Engineering (sub-agent) builds it, Marketing (sub-agent) promotes it, Sales (sub-agent) sells it. Each department reports to the CEO.

## Related Concepts

- [[multi-agent-system|Multi-Agent System]]
- [[role-assignment|Role Assignment]]
- [[task-decomposition|Task Decomposition]]

title: hybrid-architecture
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Combining multiple architectures: e.g., a hierarchical agent that uses ReAct for planning and rule-based for safety checks.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Top: Orchestrator (hierarchical). Middle: Specialist agents (multi-agent). Each specialist: ReAct loop with rule-based safety guardrails. Combines strengths of each architecture.

## 🔗 Analogy

A hybrid car - it uses both gasoline engine and electric motor, switching between them for optimal performance. Hybrid architectures combine multiple approaches for the best overall result.

## Related Concepts

- [[react-architecture|ReAct Architecture]]
- [[hierarchical-agent|Hierarchical Agent]]
- [[rule-based-system|Rule-Based System]]

title: learning-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An agent that improves over time by learning from its experiences - successes, failures, and feedback.

## 📋 Concrete Example

First time: agent writes code with bugs. User says 'this has a bug.' Agent learns: 'check for null pointers.' Next time: code is cleaner. Over many interactions, it gets better.

## 🔗 Analogy

A new employee who learns from feedback - their first report has mistakes. A colleague points them out. Next report is better. Over months, they improve. Learning agents do this automatically.

## Related Concepts

- [[improvement-loop|Improvement Loop]]
- [[reflection|Reflection]]
- [[feedback-loop|Feedback Loop]]

title: load-balancing
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Distributing tasks across multiple agents so no single agent is overwhelmed while others are idle.

## 📋 Concrete Example

10 tasks arrive. Load balancer assigns: Agent A gets tasks 1-3, B gets 4-6, C gets 7-10. If A is slow, new tasks go to B and C. Balanced workload = faster overall.

## 🔗 Analogy

A supermarket checkout - 10 registers open. A manager directs customers to the shortest line. No single cashier is overwhelmed. Load balancing does this for agents.

## Related Concepts

- [[scalability|Scalability]]
- [[distributed-agent|Distributed Agent]]
- [[task-assignment|Task Assignment]]

title: mesh-topology
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Every agent can communicate with every other agent directly. Most flexible but most complex.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent A can talk to B, C, D directly. B can talk to A, C, D. No hub needed. Great for collaboration but many communication channels to manage.

## 🔗 Analogy

A group chat where everyone can message everyone - fast and flexible, but with 20 people, there are 190 possible conversations. Hard to track. Mesh topology is flexible but complex at scale.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-topology|Agent Topology]]
- [[agent-communication|Agent Communication]]
- [[multi-agent-architecture|Multi-Agent Architecture]]

title: message-format
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The structure of messages agents exchange. A clear format prevents misunderstanding.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Format: {`from`: `CoderAgent`, `to`: `TestAgent`, `type`: `task_complete`, `content`: {`file`: `app.py`, `status`: `ready_for_testing`}, `timestamp`: '2025-08-03T14:30:00Z'}

## 🔗 Analogy

A formal letter format - Date, Recipient, Subject, Body, Signature. Everyone knows where to look for each piece of information. Message formats do this for agent communication.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-protocol|Agent Protocol]]
- [[agent-communication|Agent Communication]]
- [[json|JSON]]

title: model-based-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The agent maintains an internal model of the world and uses it to make better decisions than a reflex agent.

## 📋 Concrete Example

The agent tracks: 'File A was modified at 2pm. Tests last passed at 1pm. So tests might fail now.' It uses its world model to predict outcomes before acting.

## 🔗 Analogy

A chess player who thinks several moves ahead - they maintain a mental model of the board and predict what happens after each move. Model-based agents do this with their environment.

## Related Concepts

- [[reflex-architecture|Reflex Architecture]]
- [[world-model|World Model]]
- [[state-tracking|State Tracking]]

title: modular-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An agent built from independent modules (planner, memory, tools, evaluator) that can be swapped or upgraded independently.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Swap the planner module: from ReAct to Plan-and-Execute. Memory module: from simple to RAG. Each module is independent - upgrade one without changing others.

## 🔗 Analogy

A gaming PC - swap the graphics card, add more RAM, upgrade the CPU. Each part is modular. Upgrade one without replacing the whole computer. Modular agents work the same way.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-composition|Agent Composition]]
- [[modular-design|Modular Design]]
- [[agent-framework|Agent Framework]]

title: multi-agent-architecture
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Multiple agents collaborate, each with specialized roles. More complex but handles larger, more diverse tasks.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Team: Researcher Agent (finds info), Coder Agent (writes code), Tester Agent (tests), Reviewer Agent (reviews). They communicate and coordinate to build software together.

## 🔗 Analogy

A film crew - director, camera operator, sound engineer, editor. Each specializes. Together they make a movie that no single person could make alone. Multi-agent architectures work the same way.

## Related Concepts

- [[multi-agent-system|Multi-Agent System]]
- [[hierarchical-agent|Hierarchical Agent]]
- [[agent-communication|Agent Communication]]

title: non-deterministic-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An agent that may take different actions for the same input due to temperature, timing, or learning. More creative but harder to debug.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Same prompt, different runs: Run 1 writes code one way, Run 2 writes it differently. Both work, but the approach varies. Non-determinism brings creativity but makes debugging harder.

## 🔗 Analogy

A chef cooking without a recipe - same ingredients, but each time the dish is slightly different. Sometimes better, sometimes worse. Non-deterministic agents are creative but unpredictable.

## Related Concepts

- [[temperature|Temperature]]
- [[deterministic-agent|Deterministic Agent]]
- [[creativity|Creativity]]

title: orchestrator-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A central agent that coordinates other agents - deciding who does what, when, and combining results.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Orchestrator receives: 'Build a landing page.' Assigns: Design Agent (mockup), Coder Agent (HTML/CSS), Copy Agent (text). Collects results, combines them, delivers final page.

## 🔗 Analogy

A symphony conductor - they do not play any instrument, but they coordinate all musicians. Each musician plays their part; the conductor ensures they work together. The orchestrator conducts the agent orchestra.

## Related Concepts

- [[hierarchical-agent|Hierarchical Agent]]
- [[multi-agent-architecture|Multi-Agent Architecture]]
- [[task-assignment|Task Assignment]]

title: plan-and-execute-architecture
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

First create a complete plan, then execute each step sequentially. More structured than ReAct but less adaptive.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Step 1: Plan = [research, write outline, draft, edit, publish]. Steps 2-6: execute each. If step 3 fails, you might need to re-plan from step 3.

## 🔗 Analogy

A builder following blueprints - first the architect draws complete plans (plan), then the builder executes each step. If a wall is wrong, they revise the blueprint before continuing.

## Related Concepts

- [[task-planning|Task Planning]]
- [[sequential-execution|Sequential Execution]]
- [[react-architecture|ReAct Architecture]]

title: react-architecture
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Reasoning + Acting interleaved: the agent thinks, acts, observes, thinks again. The simplest and most common agent pattern.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Thought: user wants weather. Action: call weather_api(`HK`). Observation: 28C sunny. Thought: nice weather, suggest outdoor activity. Action: respond to user.

## 🔗 Analogy

A cook tasting as they go - taste (observe), add salt (act), taste again (observe), adjust (act). They interleave tasting and adjusting until the dish is right.

## Related Concepts

- [[react-prompting|ReAct Prompting]]
- [[action-observation-loop|Action-Observation Loop]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]

title: reflex-architecture
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The simplest agent: no planning, no memory. It directly maps observations to actions. Fast but limited.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Observation: 'user says hello' -> Action: 'respond with greeting'. No planning, no memory of past interactions. Like a reflex - knee tap triggers kick.

## 🔗 Analogy

A reflex action - doctor taps your knee, your leg kicks. No thinking involved. Reflex agents map input to output directly, like a reflex.

## Related Concepts

- [[reactive-behavior|Reactive Behavior]]
- [[simple-agent|Simple Agent]]
- [[stimulus-response|Stimulus-Response]]

title: reflexion-architecture
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

After each attempt, the agent reflects on failures and adds self-critique to memory, improving on the next try.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Attempt 1: code fails. Reflection: 'Forgot to handle empty input.' Attempt 2: code with empty input handling. Reflection: 'Now works but slow.' Attempt 3: optimized. Each attempt is better.

## 🔗 Analogy

A student taking practice tests - after each test, they note which questions they missed and why. Before the next test, they study those areas. Each practice test improves their score.

## Related Concepts

- [[reflection|Reflection]]
- [[self-evaluation|Self-Evaluation]]
- [[improvement-loop|Improvement Loop]]

title: router-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An agent that classifies incoming requests and routes them to the right specialist agent.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Router sees: 'Fix this Python bug.' Routes to: Coding Agent. Sees: 'Translate this.' Routes to: Translation Agent. Sees: 'Summarize this.' Routes to: Summarization Agent.

## 🔗 Analogy

A hospital triage nurse - they assess each patient and route them to the right department: broken bone to orthopedics, chest pain to cardiology. The router agent triages requests to specialists.

## Related Concepts

- [[orchestrator-agent|Orchestrator Agent]]
- [[multi-agent-architecture|Multi-Agent Architecture]]
- [[classification|Classification]]

title: rule-based-system
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An agent that follows explicit if-then rules. Predictable and explainable but limited to what the rules cover.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Rules: IF temp > 38 AND cough = true THEN suggest 'see doctor'. IF temp < 37 AND cough = false THEN suggest `healthy`. Each rule covers a specific scenario.

## 🔗 Analogy

A recipe - IF water boils THEN add pasta. IF pasta is soft THEN drain. Each step is an if-then rule. Rule-based systems follow recipes of rules, predictable but inflexible.

## Related Concepts

- [[expert-system|Expert System]]
- [[deterministic-behavior|Deterministic Behavior]]
- [[knowledge-base|Knowledge Base]]

title: scalability
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The ability to handle more work by adding more agents or resources. A scalable architecture grows without breaking.

## 📋 Concrete Example

10 tasks: 1 agent finishes in 100s. 100 tasks: add 9 more agents, finish in 100s (not 1000s). The architecture scales horizontally by adding more agents.

## 🔗 Analogy

A scalable restaurant - 10 customers: 1 chef handles it. 100 customers: add 9 more chefs. Each chef works independently. The restaurant scales by adding more chefs, not by making one chef work 10x faster.

## Related Concepts

- [[distributed-agent|Distributed Agent]]
- [[parallel-processing|Parallel Processing]]
- [[load-balancing|Load Balancing]]

title: self-organization
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Agents organize themselves without a central controller, adapting to changes dynamically.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agents discover: 3 are good at Python, 2 at SQL, 5 at testing. They self-organize: Python agents take Python tasks, SQL agents take SQL tasks. No manager assigned roles - they figured it out.

## 🔗 Analogy

Students forming study groups - nobody assigns groups. Students find others with similar interests and form groups naturally. Self-organization lets agents adapt without central control.

## Related Concepts

- [[emergent-behavior|Emergent Behavior]]
- [[agent-swarming|Agent Swarming]]
- [[multi-agent-coordination|Multi-Agent Coordination]]

title: semi-autonomous-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An agent that works independently on safe tasks but asks for human approval on risky ones.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent auto-reads files, searches, and drafts code (autonomous). But to delete a file or deploy to production, it asks: 'I want to delete old_logs/. Approve?' (semi-autonomous).

## 🔗 Analogy

A learner driver with a permit - they drive independently on quiet roads but must have a licensed adult for highways. Semi-autonomous agents handle easy tasks alone, ask for help on risky ones.

## Related Concepts

- [[autonomous-agent|Autonomous Agent]]
- [[human-in-the-loop|Human-in-the-Loop]]
- [[approval-workflow|Approval Workflow]]

title: sequential-execution
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Agents run one after another, each waiting for the previous to finish. Simple and predictable but slower.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent A (10s) -> Agent B (15s) -> Agent C (5s) = 30s total. Each starts only after the previous finishes. No overlap.

## 🔗 Analogy

Baking a cake - mix ingredients (step 1), then bake (step 2), then decorate (step 3). Each step must finish before the next. Sequential execution is step-by-step, no shortcuts.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-pipeline|Agent Pipeline]]
- [[parallel-processing|Parallel Processing]]
- [[efficiency|Efficiency]]

title: shared-state
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A common data store that multiple agents can read and write to, enabling coordination without direct communication.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Shared state: {`task`: 'build app', `design`: `done`, `code`: `in_progress`, `tests`: `pending`}. All agents can see the overall progress and know what to work on next.

## 🔗 Analogy

A shared Google Doc - multiple people edit simultaneously. Everyone sees what others have written. No need to email updates. Shared state lets agents coordinate through a common data store.

## Related Concepts

- [[blackboard-architecture|Blackboard Architecture]]
- [[multi-agent-coordination|Multi-Agent Coordination]]
- [[agent-memory|Agent Memory]]

title: single-agent-architecture
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

One agent handles everything: planning, tool use, memory, response. Simple to build but can be overwhelmed by complex tasks.

## 📋 Concrete Example

One agent: reads the request, plans, searches the web, writes code, tests it, fixes bugs, and responds. No delegation - all roles in one agent.

## 🔗 Analogy

A solo entrepreneur - they do marketing, coding, accounting, and customer service all by themselves. It works for small projects but gets overwhelming for large ones.

## Related Concepts

- [[multi-agent-system|Multi-Agent System]]
- [[agent-framework|Agent Framework]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]

title: star-topology
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

One central hub agent communicates with all others. Simple to manage but the hub is a bottleneck.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Orchestrator communicates with: Coder, Tester, Reviewer, Deployer. They do not talk to each other directly - all communication goes through the orchestrator.

## 🔗 Analogy

A star network in a classroom - all students raise hands and talk to the teacher (hub). Students do not talk to each other; everything goes through the teacher. Simple but the teacher can become a bottleneck.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-topology|Agent Topology]]
- [[orchestrator-agent|Orchestrator Agent]]
- [[multi-agent-architecture|Multi-Agent Architecture]]

title: state-machine-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The agent operates as a state machine: it has defined states, and transitions between them based on conditions.

## 📋 Concrete Example

States: IDLE -> RESEARCHING -> CODING -> TESTING -> DONE. Transitions: IDLE + new_task -> RESEARCHING. RESEARCHING + info_found -> CODING. CODING + code_ready -> TESTING. TESTING + tests_pass -> DONE.

## 🔗 Analogy

A washing machine - states: fill, wash, rinse, spin, done. It transitions based on conditions (water level, timer). State machine agents work the same way: defined states, condition-based transitions.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-architecture|Agent Architecture]]
- [[state-transition|State Transition]]
- [[finite-state-machine|Finite State Machine]]

title: state-transition
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Moving from one state to another when a condition is met. The transition rules define the agent's behavior.

## 📋 Concrete Example

State: TESTING. Condition: tests fail. Transition: -> DEBUGGING. State: DEBUGGING. Condition: bug fixed. Transition: -> TESTING. The cycle continues until tests pass.

## 🔗 Analogy

Traffic lights - green (go) transitions to yellow (slow down) after a timer, yellow transitions to red (stop), red transitions to green. Each transition is triggered by a condition. Agent state transitions work similarly.

## Related Concepts

- [[state-machine-agent|State Machine Agent]]
- [[finite-state-machine|Finite State Machine]]
- [[condition|Condition]]

title: sub-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A smaller, focused agent spawned by a parent agent for a specific sub-task. It reports back and then terminates.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Parent: 'Research AI trends.' Spawns Sub-Agent A: 'Find 2024 AI papers.' Sub-Agent B: 'Find AI startup funding.' Each returns results. Parent combines them.

## 🔗 Analogy

A manager delegating to interns - 'you research competitors, you research market size.' Each intern (sub-agent) does focused research and reports back. The manager combines the findings.

## Related Concepts

- [[hierarchical-agent|Hierarchical Agent]]
- [[task-decomposition|Task Decomposition]]
- [[worker-agent|Worker Agent]]

title: supervisor-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

An agent that monitors other agents, ensuring they stay on task, follow rules, and produce quality output.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Supervisor watches: CoderAgent is spending too many tokens. Supervisor intervenes: 'You are over budget. Wrap up and submit what you have.' It oversees and corrects.

## 🔗 Analogy

A floor manager in a factory - they walk around, check that workers are productive and safe, and intervene if something is wrong. Supervisor agents oversee other agents' work.

## Related Concepts

- [[orchestrator-agent|Orchestrator Agent]]
- [[guardrails|Guardrails]]
- [[agent-observability|Agent Observability]]

title: utility-based-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When multiple actions could achieve a goal, the agent picks the one with the highest utility (best outcome).

## 📋 Concrete Example

Two paths to deploy: Path A (fast but risky) utility=0.6, Path B (slower but safe) utility=0.8. The agent chooses Path B because it has higher utility.

## 🔗 Analogy

A shopper comparing products - two phones meet your needs (goal), but you pick the one with better battery life and lower price (higher utility). Utility-based agents optimize for the best outcome.

## Related Concepts

- [[goal-based-agent|Goal-Based Agent]]
- [[utility-function|Utility Function]]
- [[decision-theory|Decision Theory]]

title: worker-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architectures-moc|Agent Architectures]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A specialized agent that receives tasks from an orchestrator, does the work, and returns results.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Orchestrator: 'Write a Python function to sort a list.' Worker: writes the function, tests it, returns: 'def sort_list(lst): return sorted(lst) # Tested with 5 cases, all pass.'

## 🔗 Analogy

A construction worker receiving instructions from the foreman - 'build a wall here.' The worker builds it and reports back. Worker agents execute specific tasks assigned by the orchestrator.

## Related Concepts

- [[orchestrator-agent|Orchestrator Agent]]
- [[hierarchical-agent|Hierarchical Agent]]
- [[task-assignment|Task Assignment]]

title: api-design
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Designing APIs and tools that are easy to use, hard to misuse, and well-documented. Good design makes agents more effective.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Good: get_weather(city: str) -> WeatherResult. Clear name, simple parameter, structured return. Bad: do_thing(x, y, z, flag1, flag2) -> any. Unclear what it does or how to use it.

## 🔗 Analogy

Designing a control panel - good design: clearly labelled buttons with intuitive layouts. Bad design: unlabeled buttons in random order. API design is about making tools intuitive for agents.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-definition|Tool Definition]]
- [[schema|Schema]]
- [[documentation|Documentation]]

title: api-integration
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Connecting external APIs as agent tools - weather, stock prices, maps, databases - extends the agent's capabilities infinitely.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Register tools: get_weather (OpenWeather API), get_stock (Yahoo Finance API), get_directions (Google Maps API). Now the agent can check weather, stocks, and directions.

## 🔗 Analogy

Adding apps to your phone - each app (API) adds a new capability: maps for navigation, banking for payments, social media for sharing. API integration gives agents new capabilities the same way.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[rest-api|REST API]]
- [[function-calling|Function Calling]]

title: backward-compatibility
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When a tool is updated, old agent code should still work. Backward compatibility ensures updates do not break existing behavior.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Tool v2 adds an optional `detailed` parameter: get_weather(city, detailed=False). Old calls without `detailed` still work. New calls can use it. Backward compatible.

## 🔗 Analogy

A new phone keeping old chargers - the new phone has new features but still works with your old charger (backward compatible). If it needed a new charger, that would break compatibility.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-versioning|Tool Versioning]]
- [[api-design|API Design]]
- [[migration|Migration]]

title: browser-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A tool that lets the agent browse websites, click links, fill forms, and extract information - like a human using a browser.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent: navigate to `amazon.com`, search for `laptop`, filter by price < 5000, extract top 5 results with prices. It can comparison shop autonomously.

## 🔗 Analogy

A personal shopper going to stores - they walk in, browse shelves, compare prices, and pick the best deal. Browser tools let agents be personal shoppers on the web.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[web-scraping|Web Scraping]]
- [[web-search-tool|Web Search Tool]]

title: budget-management
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Setting and enforcing spending limits for tools. The agent stops using paid tools when the budget is reached.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Budget: $1.00/day. At $0.85 spent, agent warns: 'Approaching budget limit.' At $1.00, it stops: 'Budget exhausted. Free tools only.' It manages its own spending.

## 🔗 Analogy

A prepaid phone card - you have $50 credit. Each call costs money. When credit runs out, you cannot call anymore. Budget management gives agents a prepaid card for tool spending.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-cost-tracking|Tool Cost Tracking]]
- [[cost-optimization|Cost Optimization]]
- [[guardrails|Guardrails]]

title: calculator-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A tool for exact arithmetic. LLMs are bad at math (they approximate); calculators are exact.

## 📋 Concrete Example

LLM alone: 'What is 2347 * 891?' might say '2,091,000' (wrong). With calculator: exact answer 2,091,177. The calculator tool eliminates math errors.

## 🔗 Analogy

A student using a calculator vs mental math - mental math might give 'about 2 million' (LLM approximation). A calculator gives the exact answer. Calculator tools make agents precise at math.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[code-interpreter|Code Interpreter]]
- [[precision|Precision]]

title: calendar-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A tool that lets the agent view, create, and manage calendar events. Useful for scheduling and reminders.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent: check calendar for free slots, schedule a meeting at 3pm Friday, send invites. It manages time and scheduling.

## 🔗 Analogy

A personal assistant with a planner - they check your schedule, find free time, book appointments, and remind you. Calendar tools let agents manage schedules.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[api-integration|API Integration]]
- [[scheduling|Scheduling]]

title: code-execution
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Actually running code that the agent generated. This is different from the agent just writing code - execution produces real results.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent writes: `print(2**10)`. Execution returns: 1024. Without execution, the agent might guess 512 or 2048. With execution, the answer is exact.

## 🔗 Analogy

A scientist running an experiment - writing the procedure is not enough. You must actually run it to get results. Code execution is running the agent's code to get real outputs.

## Related Concepts

- [[code-interpreter|Code Interpreter]]
- [[tool-execution|Tool Execution]]
- [[sandbox|Sandbox]]

title: code-interpreter
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A tool that lets the agent write and execute code in real-time. Essential for math, data analysis, and complex reasoning.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent writes Python: `import statistics; data = [85, 90, 78, 92, 88]; print(statistics.mean(data))` -> executes -> 86.6. It can do precise calculations that the LLM alone cannot.

## 🔗 Analogy

A student using a calculator during an exam - they do not do mental math for complex problems. They write the formula and compute. A code interpreter is the agent's calculator.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[code-execution|Code Execution]]
- [[sandbox|Sandbox]]

title: crud
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Create, Read, Update, Delete - the four basic operations for managing data. Most tools and APIs revolve around CRUD.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A student database tool: create_student (C), get_student (R), update_student (U), delete_student (D). Every data management tool does these four operations.

## 🔗 Analogy

Managing a contact list - add a contact (Create), look up a number (Read), change an address (Update), remove a contact (Delete). CRUD covers all data operations.

## Related Concepts

- [[http-method|HTTP Method]]
- [[rest-api|REST API]]
- [[database-operation|Database Operation]]

title: database-query-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A tool that lets the agent query databases (SQL, NoSQL) to retrieve, insert, or update data.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent calls: query_database(sql='SELECT name, grade FROM students WHERE grade > 80') -> returns: [(`Alice`, 95), (`Bob`, 85)]. It can answer data questions precisely.

## 🔗 Analogy

A librarian searching the catalog - you ask 'Do you have books about space?' They search the database and tell you what is available. Database query tools let agents search digital data catalogs.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[sql|SQL]]
- [[crud|CRUD]]

title: dynamic-configuration
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The agent's tools, memory, and behavior can be changed at runtime without restarting. Enables flexible, adaptive agents.

## 📋 Concrete Example

At runtime: add a new tool `translate_text`, change temperature to 0.5, increase max_steps to 100. The agent adapts without restarting.

## 🔗 Analogy

Adjusting your phone settings - turn on WiFi, change brightness, add a new app. All without restarting the phone. Dynamic configuration lets agents adjust on the fly.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-discovery|Tool Discovery]]
- [[agent-adaptation|Agent Adaptation]]
- [[modular-agent|Modular Agent]]

title: email-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A tool that lets the agent send, read, and manage emails. Powerful for automation but needs safety guardrails.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent: read latest 5 emails, summarize each, draft replies for important ones, send replies after user approval. It manages email workflows.

## 🔗 Analogy

A postal worker - they collect mail (read), sort it (organize), and deliver responses (send). Email tools let agents be digital postal workers.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[api-integration|API Integration]]
- [[guardrails|Guardrails]]

title: endpoint
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A specific URL where an API can be accessed. Each endpoint handles a different operation.

## 📋 Concrete Example

GET /api/students -> list all. GET /api/students/123 -> get one. POST /api/students -> create. PUT /api/students/123 -> update. Each URL is a different endpoint.

## 🔗 Analogy

Extensions in an office phone system - dial 101 for Sales, 102 for Engineering, 103 for HR. Each extension (endpoint) reaches a different department. API endpoints work the same way.

## Related Concepts

- [[rest-api|REST API]]
- [[http-method|HTTP Method]]
- [[url|URL]]

title: file-system-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Tools that let the agent read, write, and manage files on disk. Essential for coding agents.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Tools: read_file(path), write_file(path, content), list_dir(path), delete_file(path). A coding agent uses these to navigate code, edit files, and manage projects.

## 🔗 Analogy

A filing cabinet - you can open drawers (list_dir), take out files (read_file), put in new files (write_file), and throw away old ones (delete_file). File system tools give agents a digital filing cabinet.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[file-i-o|File I-O]]
- [[code-generation|Code Generation]]

title: function-calling
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

LLMs can not directly execute code or APIs. Function calling lets the model output a structured request to call a function, which the application then executes.

## 📋 Concrete Example

User: 'What is the weather in HK?' Model outputs: call get_weather(city='Hong Kong'). Application executes get_weather, returns '28C sunny'. Model uses result to answer.

## 🔗 Analogy

A restaurant customer ordering - the customer (model) says 'I want the chicken rice' (function call). The waiter (application) takes the order to the kitchen (executes). The food comes back, and the customer eats.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[structured-output|Structured Output]]
- [[json|JSON]]
- [[api|API]]

title: function-chaining
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The output of one function call becomes the input to the next. The model chains tools together for complex workflows.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Step 1: get_stock_price(`AAPL`) -> $185. Step 2: calculate_change(185, 180) -> +2.8%. Step 3: format_report(`AAPL`, 185, 2.8) -> 'AAPL: $185 (+2.8%)'. Chain of functions.

## 🔗 Analogy

An assembly line - each station takes the previous station's output and adds something. Station 1 makes the frame, Station 2 adds wheels, Station 3 paints. Function chaining is an assembly line for tool calls.

## Related Concepts

- [[function-calling|Function Calling]]
- [[sequential-execution|Sequential Execution]]
- [[pipeline|Pipeline]]

title: http-method
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The type of action in an HTTP request: GET (read), POST (create), PUT (update), DELETE (remove).

## 📋 Concrete Example

GET /users/123: retrieve user 123. POST /users: create a new user. PUT /users/123: update user 123. DELETE /users/123: delete user 123. Each method is a different action.

## 🔗 Analogy

CRUD operations in a library - Read (GET a book), Create (POST a new book record), Update (PUT new info on a book), Delete (DELETE a book). HTTP methods are CRUD for the web.

## Related Concepts

- [[rest-api|REST API]]
- [[crud|CRUD]]
- [[endpoint|Endpoint]]

title: image-generation-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A tool that lets the agent generate images from text descriptions. Combines language understanding with visual creation.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent calls: generate_image(prompt='a red panda wearing a space suit, digital art') -> returns an image URL. The agent can create visual content.

## 🔗 Analogy

A graphic designer - you describe what you want ('a logo with a blue circle and white text'), and they create it. Image generation tools let agents be graphic designers.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[text-to-image|Text-to-Image]]
- [[multimodal|Multimodal]]

title: least-privilege
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Give an agent the minimum tools it needs. Do not give delete access to a coding agent that only writes code.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A coding agent needs: read_file, write_file, run_code. It does NOT need: delete_file, send_email, make_payment. Least privilege limits potential damage if the agent makes a mistake.

## 🔗 Analogy

A hotel room key - it opens your room only, not every room. You get the minimum access needed. Least privilege gives agents the minimum tools needed for their task.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-permission|Tool Permission]]
- [[security|Security]]
- [[guardrails|Guardrails]]

title: multimodal-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A tool that handles multiple types of input/output: text, images, audio, video. Makes the agent capable beyond text.

## 📋 Concrete Example

A multimodal agent: reads text (articles), views images (diagrams), listens to audio (podcasts), and watches video (lectures). It can process any content type.

## 🔗 Analogy

An all-in-one media center - it plays music (audio), shows movies (video), displays photos (images), and reads text (news). Multimodal tools give agents all-media capabilities.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[image-generation-tool|Image Generation Tool]]
- [[speech-to-text-tool|Speech-to-Text Tool]]

title: parallel-function-calling
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The model can call multiple functions at once when they are independent, speeding up execution.

## 📋 Concrete Example

User: 'Weather in HK and Tokyo?' Model calls get_weather(`HK`) and get_weather(`Tokyo`) simultaneously. Both results come back, and the model compares them.

## 🔗 Analogy

Ordering multiple items at a restaurant - you say 'I want the soup, the chicken, and the rice' all at once. The kitchen prepares them in parallel. Faster than ordering one at a time.

## Related Concepts

- [[function-calling|Function Calling]]
- [[parallel-processing|Parallel Processing]]
- [[efficiency|Efficiency]]

title: parameter-extraction
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The model must extract the right parameters from the user's natural language request and fill them into the function call.

## 📋 Concrete Example

User: 'What is the weather like in Tokyo tomorrow?' Model extracts: city=`Tokyo`, date=`tomorrow`. It fills the schema: get_weather(city=`Tokyo`, date='2025-08-04').

## 🔗 Analogy

A barista taking an order - 'I want a large iced latte with oat milk, less sugar.' The barista extracts: size=large, temperature=iced, drink=latte, milk=oat, sugar=less. Parameter extraction fills the order form.

## Related Concepts

- [[function-calling|Function Calling]]
- [[schema|Schema]]
- [[natural-language-understanding|Natural Language Understanding]]

title: rate-limiting-tools
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Tools that call external APIs may have rate limits. The agent must respect these limits to avoid being blocked.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Weather API allows 60 calls/minute. Agent tracks call count: calls 55, then waits 60s before calling more. Rate limiting tools prevents getting blocked.

## 🔗 Analogy

A water tower limiting flow - the valve only lets so much water through per minute. Too much, and the pipes burst. Rate limiting tools control the flow of API calls to prevent overloading.

## Related Concepts

- [[rate-limit|Rate Limit]]
- [[retry-logic|Retry Logic]]
- [[backoff-strategy|Backoff Strategy]]

title: rest-api
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A common type of web API where tools make HTTP requests (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to interact with external services.

## 📋 Concrete Example

GET https://api.weather.com/v1/current?city=HK -> returns JSON with weather data. The agent wraps this as a tool: get_weather(city) makes this GET request internally.

## 🔗 Analogy

A library check-out system - you request a book (GET), borrow it (POST), return it (PUT), cancel membership (DELETE). REST APIs work the same way with web resources.

## Related Concepts

- [[api-integration|API Integration]]
- [[http-method|HTTP Method]]
- [[endpoint|Endpoint]]

title: sandbox
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A safe, isolated environment where code can run without affecting the main system. Essential for code interpreter tools.

## 📋 Concrete Example

The code interpreter runs in a Docker container with no network access, limited CPU and memory. If the agent's code crashes or has an infinite loop, only the sandbox is affected.

## 🔗 Analogy

A sandbox playground - kids can dig, build, and play freely. If they make a mess, it stays in the sandbox. The rest of the park is unaffected. Code sandboxes contain potential damage.

## Related Concepts

- [[code-interpreter|Code Interpreter]]
- [[isolation|Isolation]]
- [[security|Security]]

title: scheduling
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The agent plans when to execute tasks, considering deadlines, dependencies, and priorities.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent schedules: 9am - write tests, 10am - run tests, 11am - fix bugs, 2pm - deploy. It creates a timeline and follows it.

## 🔗 Analogy

A school timetable - Math 9am, English 10am, PE 11am. Each subject has a time slot. Scheduling gives agents a timetable for their tasks.

## Related Concepts

- [[calendar-tool|Calendar Tool]]
- [[task-planning|Task Planning]]
- [[time-management|Time Management]]

title: schema
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A formal description of what parameters a function accepts - their names, types, and whether they are required. This structure lets the model fill in arguments correctly.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Schema for get_weather: {`city`: {`type`: `string`, `description`: 'City name', `required`: True}, `unit`: {`type`: `string`, `enum`: [`C`,`F`], `default`: `C`}}.

## 🔗 Analogy

A form template - Name (required, text), Age (required, number), Email (optional, text). The schema tells the model what fields to fill and what type each value should be.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-definition|Tool Definition]]
- [[type-hint|Type Hint]]
- [[validation|Validation]]

title: shell-command-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A tool that lets the agent execute shell commands (ls, cd, grep, git, pip). Powerful but dangerous - needs guardrails.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent runs: `git status` -> sees modified files. Runs: `pytest` -> sees test results. Runs: `pip install requests` -> installs a package. Shell tools give agents full system access.

## 🔗 Analogy

Giving someone the keys to your computer - they can run any command. Powerful, but you need trust and guardrails. Shell command tools give agents the same power, with safety checks.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[terminal|Terminal]]
- [[guardrails|Guardrails]]

title: simulation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Running the agent in a simulated environment with mock tools to test behavior before deploying with real tools.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Simulate: agent plans a trip. Mock tools return flight prices, hotel availability, weather. Agent makes decisions. You verify it behaves correctly before giving it real booking tools.

## 🔗 Analogy

A military training exercise - soldiers practice with simulated weapons and scenarios before real deployment. Simulation lets agents practice safely before using real tools.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-mocking|Tool Mocking]]
- [[testing|Testing]]
- [[sandbox|Sandbox]]

title: speech-to-text-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A tool that converts audio to text. Lets the agent understand spoken input.

## 📋 Concrete Example

User sends a voice message. Agent calls: speech_to_text(audio_file) -> 'What time is it in Tokyo?' The agent processes the transcribed text and responds.

## 🔗 Analogy

A secretary taking dictation - the boss speaks, the secretary types it out. Speech-to-text tools let agents convert spoken words into text they can process.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[speech-recognition|Speech Recognition]]
- [[multimodal|Multimodal]]

title: sql
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Structured Query Language - the standard language for querying relational databases. A powerful tool for data retrieval.

## 📋 Concrete Example

`SELECT name, age FROM students WHERE age > 15 ORDER BY name` - gets names and ages of students over 15, sorted alphabetically. SQL lets you ask precise data questions.

## 🔗 Analogy

Asking a librarian in their specialized language - 'Find me all fiction books published after 2020 by Chinese authors, sorted by title.' SQL is the specialized language for asking databases questions.

## Related Concepts

- [[database-query-tool|Database Query Tool]]
- [[query-language|Query Language]]
- [[relational-database|Relational Database]]

title: task-prioritization
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Deciding which tasks are most important or urgent and should be done first.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Priority 1 (urgent): fix production bug. Priority 2 (important): write tests. Priority 3 (nice to have): refactor code. The agent does P1 first, then P2, then P3 if time allows.

## 🔗 Analogy

A fire brigade triage - rescue trapped people first (P1), then put out the fire (P2), then investigate the cause (P3). Task prioritization orders work by urgency and importance.

## Related Concepts

- [[time-management|Time Management]]
- [[task-planning|Task Planning]]
- [[urgency|Urgency]]

title: text-to-speech-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A tool that converts text to audio. Useful for accessibility, language learning, and content creation.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent calls: text_to_speech(text='Hello, how are you?', voice=`en-US`) -> returns an audio file. The agent can produce spoken content.

## 🔗 Analogy

A radio announcer reading a script - the text (script) is converted to audio (broadcast). Text-to-speech tools let agents convert their text responses into spoken audio.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[speech-synthesis|Speech Synthesis]]
- [[accessibility|Accessibility]]

title: time-management
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The agent prioritizes tasks, allocates time, and avoids spending too long on any single step.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent: 'I have 30 minutes. Testing takes 10, debugging takes 15, deployment takes 5. I will skip documentation for now.' It manages time within constraints.

## 🔗 Analogy

Budgeting your study time - 2 hours total: 45 min math (hardest), 30 min English, 30 min science, 15 min break. Time management lets agents budget their time wisely.

## Related Concepts

- [[scheduling|Scheduling]]
- [[efficiency|Efficiency]]
- [[task-prioritization|Task Prioritization]]

title: tool-caching
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Storing tool results so repeated calls with the same parameters return instantly without re-calling the tool.

## 📋 Concrete Example

First call: get_weather(`HK`) -> 28C (takes 2s, API call). Cache stores {`HK`: '28C'}. Second call: get_weather(`HK`) -> 28C (instant, from cache). Saves time and API quota.

## 🔗 Analogy

Keeping a note of bus schedules - instead of checking the app every time, you remember 'Bus 1A comes at 3:15.' Next time, you check your note (cache) instead of the app. Faster and saves data.

## Related Concepts

- [[efficiency|Efficiency]]
- [[lru-cache|LRU Cache]]
- [[token-management|Token Management]]

title: tool-combination
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Using multiple tools together to accomplish a task that no single tool could handle alone.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent: search_web (find article) + code_interpreter (analyze data from article) + write_file (save results). Three tools combined accomplish a research task.

## 🔗 Analogy

Using multiple kitchen tools - blender (mix), oven (bake), fridge (chill). No single tool makes a cake. Tool combination lets agents tackle complex, multi-step tasks.

## Related Concepts

- [[function-chaining|Function Chaining]]
- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[multi-step-reasoning|Multi-Step Reasoning]]

title: tool-cost-tracking
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Some tools cost money per use (API calls, cloud services). Tracking cost per tool call helps manage budgets.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Cost log: search_web: $0.001/call x 50 calls = $0.05. Image generation: $0.02/call x 5 = $0.10. Total: $0.15. If budget is $0.20, 5 more searches are OK. Cost tracking prevents overspending.

## 🔗 Analogy

Tracking spending on a trip - taxi: $30, lunch: $50, tickets: $20. Total: $100. If budget is $150, you have $50 left. Tool cost tracking budgets agent spending.

## Related Concepts

- [[cost-optimization|Cost Optimization]]
- [[budget-management|Budget Management]]
- [[api-key|API Key]]

title: tool-definition
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Before an agent can use a tool, you must define it: name, description, parameters, and return type. The model uses this to decide when and how to call it.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Define: get_weather(city: str, unit: str=`C`) -> str. Description: 'Get current weather for a city.' The model sees this definition and knows it can check weather.

## 🔗 Analogy

A tool catalog in a workshop - each tool has a label: 'Hammer - for driving nails. Input: nail + surface. Output: nail driven in.' The catalog tells workers what each tool does and how to use it.

## Related Concepts

- [[function-calling|Function Calling]]
- [[tool-registration|Tool Registration]]
- [[schema|Schema]]

title: tool-discovery
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The agent dynamically discovers available tools at runtime rather than having them hard-coded.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent starts, queries: 'What tools are available?' MCP server responds: [read_file, write_file, search_web, calculator]. Agent registers them dynamically.

## 🔗 Analogy

A tourist arriving at a hotel - they check what amenities are available (pool, gym, spa) upon arrival. They use what they find. Tool discovery lets agents find and use available tools at runtime.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-registration|Tool Registration]]
- [[mcp|MCP]]
- [[dynamic-configuration|Dynamic Configuration]]

title: tool-documentation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Each tool should have clear documentation: what it does, parameters, return value, errors, and examples. The agent reads this to use the tool correctly.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Docs: 'get_weather(city): Returns current weather. Parameters: city (str, required) - city name. Returns: dict with temperature, condition, humidity. Errors: CityNotFoundError, TimeoutError.'

## 🔗 Analogy

An instruction manual for a gadget - explains what it does, how to use it, what the buttons mean, and what to do if it breaks. Tool documentation is the manual for each agent tool.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-definition|Tool Definition]]
- [[api-design|API Design]]
- [[docstring|Docstring]]

title: tool-error-handling
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When a tool call fails (API down, invalid parameters, timeout), the agent must handle the error gracefully.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Tool call: get_weather(`Mars`) -> Error: 'City not found.' Agent handles: 'I could not find weather for Mars. Did you mean a city on Earth?' It does not crash; it adapts.

## 🔗 Analogy

A delivery driver getting a flat tire - they do not abandon the delivery. They call for help, find alternative transport, or notify the customer. Tool error handling is the agent adapting when tools fail.

## Related Concepts

- [[error-recovery|Error Recovery]]
- [[function-calling|Function Calling]]
- [[graceful-degradation|Graceful Degradation]]

title: tool-execution
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

When the model calls a function, the application executes it. The tool runs real code - an API call, a file read, a calculation - and returns the result.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Model calls: calculate_compound_interest(principal=1000, rate=0.05, years=10). Application runs the actual Python function, gets 1628.89, returns it to the model.

## 🔗 Analogy

A cashier processing an order - the customer says what they want (function call), the cashier actually rings it up and processes payment (execution), then gives the receipt (return value).

## Related Concepts

- [[function-calling|Function Calling]]
- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[action-space|Action Space]]

title: tool-mocking
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

For testing, replace real tools with fake (mock) versions that return predetermined results. Enables testing without real API calls.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Mock get_weather: always returns '28C sunny' without calling the real API. Test the agent's logic: does it suggest outdoor activities when sunny? Mock tools make testing fast and free.

## 🔗 Analogy

A flight simulator - you practice flying without leaving the ground. Mock tools let agents be tested without real API calls, costs, or risks.

## Related Concepts

- [[testing|Testing]]
- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[simulation|Simulation]]

title: tool-permission
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Not all agents should have access to all tools. Permissions control which agents can use which tools.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Permissions: JuniorAgent can use read_file and search_web. SeniorAgent can also use write_file and delete_file. AdminAgent can use shell_command. Least privilege: give only what is needed.

## 🔗 Analogy

School access levels - students can read books, teachers can add books, librarians can remove books. Each role has different permissions. Tool permissions do this for agents.

## Related Concepts

- [[guardrails|Guardrails]]
- [[security|Security]]
- [[least-privilege|Least Privilege]]

title: tool-result
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The output returned to the model after tool execution. The model uses this to continue reasoning and respond to the user.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Tool result: {`temperature`: 28, `condition`: `sunny`, `humidity`: 65}. Model reads this and responds: 'It is 28 degrees and sunny in Hong Kong today.'

## 🔗 Analogy

A lab technician running a test - the doctor orders a blood test (function call). The technician runs it (execution). The results come back (tool result). The doctor interprets them for the patient.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-execution|Tool Execution]]
- [[observation|Observation]]
- [[action-observation-loop|Action-Observation Loop]]

title: tool-selection
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

The model must choose the right tool from many available options. Good tool descriptions are critical for correct selection.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Available: search_web, calculator, read_file, send_email. User asks: 'What is 15% of 240?' Model selects calculator (not search_web) because it is a math question.

## 🔗 Analogy

Choosing the right tool from a toolbox - to hammer a nail, you pick the hammer (not the saw). To cut wood, you pick the saw. Tool selection is the model picking the right tool for each task.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-definition|Tool Definition]]
- [[function-calling|Function Calling]]
- [[decision-making|Decision Making]]

title: tool-timeout
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

If a tool takes too long, the agent should give up rather than wait forever. A timeout prevents hanging.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Tool timeout: 30 seconds. If get_weather takes 31s, the agent stops waiting and says 'Weather service is slow, try again later.' It does not hang indefinitely.

## 🔗 Analogy

A bus wait limit - if the bus does not come in 10 minutes, you walk. You do not wait forever. Tool timeouts set a maximum wait time for tool responses.

## Related Concepts

- [[error-handling|Error Handling]]
- [[stop-condition|Stop Condition]]
- [[latency|Latency]]

title: tool-versioning
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Tools change over time. Versioning tracks which version of a tool the agent is using, preventing compatibility issues.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Tool v1: get_weather(city) -> temperature only. Tool v2: get_weather(city) -> temperature, humidity, wind. Agent must know which version it is using to parse results correctly.

## 🔗 Analogy

Software updates on your phone - v1 of an app has basic features, v2 adds more. You need to know which version you have to use it correctly. Tool versioning tracks this for agents.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-definition|Tool Definition]]
- [[semantic-versioning|Semantic Versioning]]
- [[backward-compatibility|Backward Compatibility]]

title: web-scraping
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

Extracting data from web pages. A tool that parses HTML to pull out specific information.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent scrapes a news site: extract all headlines and dates. Returns: [('AI Breakthrough', '2025-08-03'), ('New Phone Released', '2025-08-02')]. Structured data from unstructured web pages.

## 🔗 Analogy

Clipping newspaper articles - you cut out articles you want and paste them in a scrapbook. Web scraping does this digitally: extracting specific information from web pages.

## Related Concepts

- [[browser-tool|Browser Tool]]
- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[html-parsing|HTML Parsing]]

title: web-search-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-function-calling-moc|Tools & Function Calling]]

## 🎯 Motivation

A tool that lets the agent search the internet for current information. Overcomes the knowledge cutoff limitation.

## 📋 Concrete Example

Agent searches: 'latest Python version 2025' -> results: 'Python 3.13 released October 2025.' The agent uses this to give an accurate, current answer.

## 🔗 Analogy

A student using the library - instead of relying only on their textbook (training data), they search the library (web search) for the latest information. Web search gives agents access to current knowledge.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-use|Tool Use]]
- [[knowledge-cutoff|Knowledge Cutoff]]
- [[rag|RAG]]
