title: persistent-memory
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

Hermes remembers facts about you and your environment across conversations. This means you do not have to reintroduce yourself every time. Memory makes interactions feel continuous.

## Concrete Example

On Monday you tell Hermes your name is Alex. On Friday, Hermes greets you as Alex without being reminded.

## Analogy

Like your school ID card. The school remembers who you are every day, so you do not have to sign in each morning.

## Related Concepts

- [[what-makes-hermes-different|What Makes Hermes Different]]
- [[memory-provider|Memory Provider]]
- [[self-improving-agent|Self-Improving Agent]]

title: platform-adapters
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

Each messaging platform has an adapter, a piece of code that translates between that platform format and Hermes. This is why the same agent can talk on Telegram, Discord, and Email.

## Concrete Example

The Telegram adapter receives a text message and turns it into a Hermes request. The Discord adapter does the same but handles Discord slash commands.

## Analogy

Like translators at a meeting. Each one speaks a different language but passes the same message to the boss.

## Related Concepts

- [[gateway|Gateway]]
- [[multi-platform-agent|Multi-Platform Agent]]

title: plugins
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

Plugins are extra packages that add new features to Hermes, such as a memory provider or a tool integration. You install them with a command and they hook into the system.

## Concrete Example

You install a plugin that adds Spotify control. Now Hermes can play songs and manage your playlists.

## Analogy

Like adding a mod to Minecraft. The base game stays the same, but you get new blocks and items.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills|Skills]]
- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[mcp-servers|MCP Servers]]

title: profiles
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

A profile is a separate Hermes instance with its own config, sessions, skills, and memory. You can have one for school, one for gaming, one for experiments. They never mix.

## Concrete Example

You create a profile called school with a serious model and a profile called fun with a cheaper model for casual chat.

## Analogy

Like having two Octopus cards: one personal, one for school trips. The balances stay separate.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]
- [[persistent-memory|Persistent Memory]]
- [[multi-platform-agent|Multi-Platform Agent]]

title: provider-agnostic
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

Hermes does not lock you to one AI company. You can switch between OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, Google, local models, and more, often without changing your setup. This gives you freedom and saves money.

## Concrete Example

You start using a free DeepSeek model, then switch to a stronger Anthropic model for a harder task, all with one command.

## Analogy

Like choosing different MTR lines to reach the same station. You pick the route that suits you best.

## Related Concepts

- [[model-config|Model Config]]
- [[what-is-hermes-agent|What is Hermes Agent]]
- [[credential-pools|Credential Pools]]

title: reasoning-levels
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

Some models can show their thinking steps before answering. Hermes lets you set a reasoning level, from none to extra high. Higher levels take longer but give more thorough answers.

## Concrete Example

You set reasoning to high for a tough maths problem. Hermes writes out each step before giving the final answer.

## Analogy

Like a teacher who shows full working on the board versus one who just writes the answer.

## Related Concepts

- [[model-config|Model Config]]
- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]

title: self-improving-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

Hermes gets better the more you use it. When it solves a tricky problem or learns a new workflow, it can save that knowledge as a skill. Next time it faces the same task, it loads the skill and works faster.

## Concrete Example

After Hermes helps you set up a Python project three times, it creates a skill called project-setup. The fourth time, it follows that saved recipe automatically.

## Analogy

Like a kitchen helper who writes down a recipe after cooking a dish once, so next time they do not need to ask how to make it.

## Related Concepts

- [[learning-loop|Learning Loop]]
- [[skill-creation|Skill Creation]]
- [[skill-curator|Skill Curator]]

title: session-search
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

Session search is a tool that lets Hermes look through your past conversations for relevant context. This is separate from web search; it only looks at your own history.

## Concrete Example

You ask Hermes to continue a coding task from last week. It searches past sessions, finds the code you wrote, and picks up where you left off.

## Analogy

Like using Ctrl+F to find a word in your notes, but across all your notebooks at once.

## Related Concepts

- [[sessions-db|Sessions DB]]
- [[session|Session]]
- [[persistent-memory|Persistent Memory]]

title: session
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

A session is one conversation from start to finish. Hermes saves every session, so you can resume, search, or export it later. Sessions are stored in a local database.

## Concrete Example

You start a session on Monday about a history essay. On Wednesday you resume it and Hermes remembers everything you discussed.

## Analogy

Like a notebook where each conversation is a page. You can flip back to any page anytime.

## Related Concepts

- [[sessions-db|Sessions DB]]
- [[session-search|Session Search]]
- [[persistent-memory|Persistent Memory]]

title: sessions-db
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

All sessions are saved in a local SQLite database with full-text search. This means Hermes can search past conversations by keyword, not just list them.

## Concrete Example

You ask Hermes to recall what you said about climate change last month. It searches the database and finds the exact messages.

## Analogy

Like a diary with an index. You can search for a word and jump straight to that entry.

## Related Concepts

- [[session|Session]]
- [[session-search|Session Search]]

title: skill-creation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

A skill is a saved set of instructions that Hermes can load when a similar task comes up. Anyone can create one, including Hermes itself. Skills are the main way Hermes improves.

## Concrete Example

You teach Hermes how to format a lab report. It saves a skill called lab-report. Next time you say write my lab report, it follows that saved format.

## Analogy

Like writing a cheat sheet for an exam. Once you write it, you can use it again and again.

## Related Concepts

- [[learning-loop|Learning Loop]]
- [[skills|Skills]]
- [[skill-curator|Skill Curator]]

title: skill-curator
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

The curator is a background helper that keeps your skills tidy. It tracks which skills you use, marks unused ones as stale, and archives them. It never deletes, so nothing is lost.

## Concrete Example

You installed ten skills last month but only used three. The curator archives the seven idle ones to keep your list clean.

## Analogy

Like a librarian who moves books nobody borrows to the back shelf, but never throws them away.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills|Skills]]
- [[learning-loop|Learning Loop]]
- [[skill-creation|Skill Creation]]

title: skill-hub
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

The Skill Hub is an online library where the community shares skills. You can browse, search, and install skills with one command, so you do not have to write everything yourself.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes skills search git and find a skill that teaches Hermes how to resolve merge conflicts. You install it with one click.

## Analogy

Like the App Store, but for Hermes skills. Browse, tap install, and you are ready.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills|Skills]]
- [[skill-creation|Skill Creation]]
- [[skill-curator|Skill Curator]]

title: skills
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

Skills are reusable knowledge modules. Each skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file describing how to do something. Hermes scans your skills folder and loads relevant ones automatically.

## Concrete Example

You install a skill for making PowerPoint slides. When you ask Hermes to build a presentation, it reads that skill and follows the steps.

## Analogy

Like apps on your phone. You install the ones you need, and they are ready whenever you open them.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill-creation|Skill Creation]]
- [[skill-hub|Skill Hub]]
- [[learning-loop|Learning Loop]]

title: terminal-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

The most common way to use Hermes is in a terminal, a text-based screen where you type commands. This is fast, lightweight, and works on almost any computer, even a cheap server.

## Concrete Example

You open a terminal, type hermes, and start chatting. No mouse, no heavy window, just text.

## Analogy

Like a walkie-talkie compared to a smartphone. Simple, but quick and reliable.

## Related Concepts

- [[desktop-app|Desktop App]]
- [[cli-vs-gateway|CLI vs Gateway]]
- [[what-is-hermes-agent|What is Hermes Agent]]

title: terminal-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

The terminal tool lets Hermes run shell commands on your computer. This is how it installs software, runs scripts, and manages files. It is the most powerful and most used tool.

## Concrete Example

You ask Hermes to check your Python version. It runs python3 --version and reads the output.

## Analogy

Like giving Hermes the keys to your computer keyboard. It can type any command you could.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[tool-calling|Tool Calling]]
- [[command-approval|Command Approval]]

title: tool-calling
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

Tools are the hands and eyes of Hermes. Each tool does one job, like reading a file, running a command, or searching the web. Hermes picks the right tool for each step of a task.

## Concrete Example

Hermes uses the read_file tool to open your essay, then uses the write_file tool to save a corrected version.

## Analogy

Like a toolbox where you grab a screwdriver for screws and a hammer for nails. Hermes chooses the right tool automatically.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]
- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[terminal-tool|Terminal Tool]]

title: toolsets
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

Tools are grouped into toolsets, each covering a category: web, terminal, file, vision, and more. You can turn toolsets on or off depending on what you want Hermes to be able to do.

## Concrete Example

You turn off the browser toolset during an exam so Hermes can only read local files, not go online.

## Analogy

Like turning off data roaming on your phone when you travel, so you only use Wi-Fi.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-calling|Tool Calling]]
- [[terminal-tool|Terminal Tool]]
- [[web-toolset|Web Toolset]]

title: vision-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

The vision tool lets Hermes look at images and understand what is in them. This is useful for reading diagrams, analysing screenshots, or describing photos.

## Concrete Example

You send Hermes a photo of a maths problem on the whiteboard. It reads the equations and solves them.

## Analogy

Like a friend who can look at your drawing and tell you what they see.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[tool-calling|Tool Calling]]

title: voice-mode
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

Hermes can listen to your voice and speak back. This uses speech-to-text and text-to-speech tools. It is handy when you cannot type, like when cooking or walking.

## Concrete Example

You send a voice message on Telegram asking Hermes to set a reminder. It replies with a spoken confirmation.

## Analogy

Like a walkie-talkie. You talk, it talks back, no typing needed.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[multi-platform-agent|Multi-Platform Agent]]

title: web-toolset
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

The web toolset gives Hermes the ability to search the internet and read web pages. This is essential for research, looking up current events, or finding documentation.

## Concrete Example

You ask Hermes for the latest news about a typhoon. It searches the web, reads the Observatory website, and summarises the warning.

## Analogy

Like a librarian who can dash out to the newsstand, grab a paper, and read you the headline.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[tool-calling|Tool Calling]]
- [[browser-toolset|Browser Toolset]]

title: webhooks
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

Webhooks let external services trigger Hermes. When something happens on another website, it sends a message to Hermes, which then runs a task.

## Concrete Example

You set a webhook so that when a new GitHub issue is opened, Hermes reads it and posts a summary to your Discord.

## Analogy

Like a doorbell connected to a camera. When someone rings, the camera turns on automatically.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-jobs|Cron Jobs]]
- [[gateway|Gateway]]

title: what-is-hermes-agent
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

Hermes Agent is an open-source AI agent made by Nous Research. Unlike a chatbot that only talks, Hermes can run commands, read and write files, search the web, and remember things across conversations. It lives in your terminal, on your phone through messaging apps, or on a server.

## Concrete Example

You type a message asking Hermes to summarise your homework notes into bullet points. Hermes reads the files, writes a summary file, and tells you it is done.

## Analogy

Think of Hermes like a class monitor who does not just listen but actually carries out tasks for you, like collecting homework and writing the summary on the board.

## Related Concepts

- [[ai-agent-vs-chatbot|AI Agent vs Chatbot]]
- [[nous-research|Nous Research]]
- [[open-source|Open Source]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]

title: what-makes-hermes-different
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

Three things set Hermes apart: it learns from experience (skills), it remembers you across sessions (memory), and it runs on many platforms at once. Most chatbots do none of these.

## Concrete Example

After a week of use, Hermes knows you prefer Python, remembers your school project folder, and can fix bugs in code it helped you write before.

## Analogy

Like a tutor who has taught you for months and knows your strengths, versus a stranger you meet once.

## Related Concepts

- [[self-improving-agent|Self-Improving Agent]]
- [[persistent-memory|Persistent Memory]]
- [[multi-platform-agent|Multi-Platform Agent]]

title: worktree-mode
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

In worktree mode, Hermes works in a separate copy of your git project. This means it can make changes without touching your main files, which is great for parallel experiments.

## Concrete Example

You start two Hermes agents in worktree mode. One tries a new design, the other fixes bugs. Neither breaks the other.

## Analogy

Like photocopying your homework so you can try two different answers and keep the better one.

## Related Concepts

- [[profiles|Profiles]]
- [[delegation-tool|Delegation Tool]]

title: yolo-mode
text:
> **Domain:** [[_hermes-fundamentals-moc|Hermes Fundamentals]]

## Motivation

Yolo mode skips all command approval prompts. It is faster but riskier, because Hermes will run any command without asking. Use it only when you trust the task fully.

## Concrete Example

You turn on yolo mode for a quick file rename task. Hermes runs the command instantly without pausing to ask.

## Analogy

Like riding a bike with no helmet. Faster, but you had better be sure of the road.

## Related Concepts

- [[command-approval|Command Approval]]
- [[global-flags|Global Flags]]

title: api-keys
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

An API key is a secret string that proves you are allowed to use a service. You get one from the AI provider website and put it in your .env file. Hermes uses it to call the AI model.

## Concrete Example

You sign up at OpenRouter, copy your API key, and paste it into .env as OPENROUTER_API_KEY.

## Analogy

Like the secret code for your locker. Only you have it, and it lets you open the door.

## Related Concepts

- [[env-file|Env File]]
- [[credential-pools|Credential Pools]]
- [[setup-wizard|Setup Wizard]]

title: auth-file
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

The auth.json file stores OAuth tokens and credential pool info. It is separate from .env so you can have both API keys (in .env) and OAuth tokens (in auth.json) at the same time.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes auth list and see your Nous Portal token stored in auth.json, plus your OpenAI key from .env.

## Analogy

Like a wallet with two sections: one for cards (OAuth), one for cash (API keys).

## Related Concepts

- [[credential-pools|Credential Pools]]
- [[oauth-login|OAuth Login]]
- [[env-file|Env File]]

title: backup-before-update
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

Before a major update, it is wise to back up your .hermes folder. This way, if the new version breaks something, you can restore the old setup.

## Concrete Example

You copy ~/.hermes to ~/.hermes-backup, then run hermes update. If something breaks, you restore the backup.

## Analogy

Like saving your game before a boss fight. If you lose, you reload and try again.

## Related Concepts

- [[updating-hermes|Updating Hermes]]
- [[hermes_home|HERMES_HOME]]
- [[checkpoints|Checkpoints]]

title: bot-token
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

A bot token is a secret string from a platform like Telegram that identifies your bot. You get it from BotFather on Telegram. Hermes uses it to receive and send messages as your bot.

## Concrete Example

On Telegram you message @BotFather, create a bot, and receive a token like 123456:ABC-DEF. You paste it into Hermes gateway setup.

## Analogy

Like the membership number on your Octopus card. It uniquely identifies your card to the system.

## Related Concepts

- [[gateway-setup|Gateway Setup]]
- [[platform-adapters|Platform Adapters]]
- [[auth-file|Auth File]]

title: code-execution-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

The code execution tool lets Hermes run Python code on demand. It can be sandboxed or run directly. This is how Hermes does maths, processes data, and writes scripts.

## Concrete Example

You ask Hermes to calculate the average of your test scores. It writes a Python script, runs it, and tells you the answer.

## Analogy

Like a calculator that can also write its own programs and run them.

## Related Concepts

- [[sandboxed-execution|Sandboxed Execution]]
- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[terminal-tool|Terminal Tool]]

title: config-yaml
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

config.yaml is the main settings file for Hermes. It uses a format called YAML, which is text with indentation. All your preferences, from model choice to display theme, live here.

## Concrete Example

You open config.yaml and see neat sections: model, terminal, memory, display. You change display.skin to dark.

## Analogy

Like the settings file for a video game. Edit a value and the game looks or plays differently.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]
- [[config-file|Config File]]
- [[env-file|Env File]]

title: curl-install
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

On Linux, macOS, WSL2, and Android Termux, you install Hermes using the curl command. Curl downloads the install script and bash runs it. This is the standard method for these platforms.

## Concrete Example

On your Linux laptop you run the curl command. The script prints progress as it downloads and configures Hermes.

## Analogy

Like using a vending machine. You press one button (curl) and the drink (Hermes) drops out ready.

## Related Concepts

- [[install-script|Install Script]]
- [[powershell-install|PowerShell Install]]
- [[platform-support|Platform Support]]

title: dependencies
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

Dependencies are other software packages that Hermes needs to run, like libraries for web requests, file handling, and AI model calls. The install script downloads and installs them all into the venv.

## Concrete Example

The install log shows dozens of packages being installed: requests, pyyaml, prompt_toolkit, and more.

## Analogy

Like the ingredients list for a recipe. You need flour, eggs, and sugar to bake a cake.

## Related Concepts

- [[venv|Venv]]
- [[prerequisites|Prerequisites]]
- [[install-script|Install Script]]

title: disk-space
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

Hermes and its dependencies need a few hundred megabytes of disk space. If your drive is almost full, the install may fail. Make sure you have at least 1 GB free.

## Concrete Example

You check with df -h and see you have 5 GB free. Plenty. The install finishes without issue.

## Analogy

Like checking your bag has room before buying groceries. No space, no room for the food.

## Related Concepts

- [[prerequisites|Prerequisites]]
- [[install-logs|Install Logs]]

title: env-file
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

The .env file stores your API keys and tokens. Hermes reads it at startup. Without the right keys, Hermes cannot talk to AI models or use some tools.

## Concrete Example

You open .env and add a line OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-your-key-here. Save it, and Hermes can now reach the model.

## Analogy

Like the battery in your phone. Without it, the phone looks fine but will not turn on.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-file|Config File]]
- [[credential-pools|Credential Pools]]
- [[setup-wizard|Setup Wizard]]

title: environment-setup
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

Environment setup means preparing your computer so Hermes can run. This includes having the right Python version, enough disk space, and the needed system tools. The install script handles most of this.

## Concrete Example

The install script checks that Python 3.11 is present. If not, it prints a message telling you to install it first.

## Analogy

Like packing your bag before a field trip. You need the right items or the trip will not go smoothly.

## Related Concepts

- [[prerequisites|Prerequisites]]
- [[python-version|Python Version]]
- [[venv|Venv]]

title: first-run
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

After install, your first hermes command launches the setup wizard if no config exists. This ensures you pick a model and add at least one key before chatting.

## Concrete Example

You type hermes for the first time. Instead of chatting, the setup wizard opens to guide you.

## Analogy

Like turning on a new phone for the first time. It walks you through setup before you can use it.

## Related Concepts

- [[setup-wizard|Setup Wizard]]
- [[hermes-setup|Hermes Setup]]
- [[install-script|Install Script]]

title: gateway-setup
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

Gateway setup (hermes gateway setup) connects Hermes to messaging platforms. It asks for bot tokens and configuration for each platform you want to use.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes gateway setup, choose Telegram, paste your bot token from BotFather, and now your Telegram bot is linked to Hermes.

## Analogy

Like pairing Bluetooth headphones. You put them in pairing mode and enter a code to connect.

## Related Concepts

- [[gateway|Gateway]]
- [[platform-adapters|Platform Adapters]]
- [[setup-wizard|Setup Wizard]]

title: hermes-desktop
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

Hermes Desktop is a graphical installer and app for Windows and macOS. If you prefer clicking buttons over typing commands, this is the easiest path. It installs both the CLI and the desktop window.

## Concrete Example

You download the Hermes Desktop installer from the website, double-click, and a wizard with pictures guides you through setup.

## Analogy

Like buying a computer from a store with setup included, versus building one yourself from parts.

## Related Concepts

- [[install-script|Install Script]]
- [[setup-wizard|Setup Wizard]]
- [[terminal-agent|Terminal Agent]]

title: hermes-doctor
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

hermes doctor checks your Hermes installation for problems. It looks for missing dependencies, broken config, and missing API keys. It can even try to fix issues with the --fix flag.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes doctor and it reports that your Python version is too old. You update Python and run it again. All green.

## Analogy

Like a health check at the clinic. The doctor lists what is wrong and can prescribe fixes.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-status|Hermes Status]]
- [[setup-wizard|Setup Wizard]]
- [[prerequisites|Prerequisites]]

title: hermes-setup
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

The hermes setup command launches the setup wizard. You can run it for all sections or just one, like hermes setup model to only configure the model.

## Concrete Example

You already have a model but want to add Telegram. You run hermes setup gateway and follow just that part.

## Analogy

Like going to a specific counter at the post office instead of waiting in the general line.

## Related Concepts

- [[setup-wizard|Setup Wizard]]
- [[hermes-doctor|Hermes Doctor]]
- [[hermes-status|Hermes Status]]

title: hermes-status
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

hermes status shows you what parts of Hermes are running and connected. It tells you if the gateway is up, which tools are enabled, and which providers are set.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes status and see a table: Gateway running, Telegram connected, Model set to DeepSeek. Everything looks good.

## Analogy

Like the dashboard of a car. One glance tells you fuel, speed, and engine status.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-doctor|Hermes Doctor]]
- [[gateway-service|Gateway Service]]
- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]

title: hermes_home
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

HERMES_HOME is the folder where Hermes stores everything: config, sessions, skills, logs. By default it is ~/.hermes. You can change it to run multiple independent setups.

## Concrete Example

You set HERMES_HOME to /home/alex/my-hermes. Now all of Hermes data lives in that folder instead of the default.

## Analogy

Like choosing which locker to put your books in. Change the locker number and everything goes there instead.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-file|Config File]]
- [[profiles|Profiles]]
- [[per-user-vs-root-install|Per-User vs Root Install]]

title: install-logs
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

During installation, the script prints logs showing each step. If something fails, these logs tell you exactly where. Reading them helps you fix problems quickly.

## Concrete Example

The install log shows Downloading... Done. Creating venv... Done. Installing dependencies... Error: no disk space.

## Analogy

Like a receipt that lists every item. If the total is wrong, you check each line.

## Related Concepts

- [[install-script|Install Script]]
- [[hermes-doctor|Hermes Doctor]]
- [[prerequisites|Prerequisites]]

title: install-script
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

The fastest way to get Hermes is the install script. It is one command you paste into your terminal. The script downloads Hermes, sets up a Python environment, and gets everything ready.

## Concrete Example

You paste curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.sh | bash and wait about a minute. Then you type hermes and it works.

## Analogy

Like a meal kit delivered to your door. One delivery, and you have all the ingredients and the recipe.

## Related Concepts

- [[curl-install|Curl Install]]
- [[prerequisites|Prerequisites]]
- [[setup-wizard|Setup Wizard]]

title: migration-from-openclaw
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

If you used OpenClaw before, Hermes has a migration command (hermes claw migrate) that imports your settings and sessions so you do not lose your work.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes claw migrate. It reads your old OpenClaw config and copies the compatible settings into Hermes.

## Analogy

Like transferring your phone contacts to a new phone. Your old friends come with you.

## Related Concepts

- [[updating-hermes|Updating Hermes]]
- [[config-file|Config File]]

title: model-picker
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

The model picker (hermes model) is an interactive menu that lists available providers and models. You scroll, pick one, and Hermes saves it as your default.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes model. A menu shows OpenRouter, Anthropic, DeepSeek, and more. You pick DeepSeek and press Enter.

## Analogy

Like choosing your character in a fighting game. Each has different stats and abilities.

## Related Concepts

- [[model-config|Model Config]]
- [[setup-wizard|Setup Wizard]]
- [[provider-agnostic|Provider-Agnostic]]

title: multi-instance-setup
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

You can run more than one Hermes on the same machine using profiles or different HERMES_HOME values. This is useful for separating school and personal use.

## Concrete Example

You set HERMES_HOME=/home/alex/school-hermes for one terminal and the default for another. Two independent Hermes instances run side by side.

## Analogy

Like having two lockers in different buildings. Each holds different things and they never mix.

## Related Concepts

- [[profiles|Profiles]]
- [[hermes_home|HERMES_HOME]]
- [[per-user-vs-root-install|Per-User vs Root Install]]

title: network-requirements
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

The install script needs internet access to download Hermes and its dependencies. If you are behind a firewall or proxy, you may need to configure it to allow the download.

## Concrete Example

On school Wi-Fi the install fails. You switch to mobile data and it works, because the school firewall blocked the download.

## Analogy

Like needing signal to send a message. No signal, no delivery.

## Related Concepts

- [[install-script|Install Script]]
- [[prerequisites|Prerequisites]]
- [[curl-install|Curl Install]]

title: nix-setup
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

Nix is a special package manager that creates reproducible environments. Hermes has a Nix setup for users who already use Nix or NixOS. It handles dependencies in a declarative way.

## Concrete Example

On NixOS you add Hermes to your configuration.nix, rebuild, and Hermes is ready with all dependencies pinned.

## Analogy

Like a recipe with exact gram measurements. Every time you cook, the result is identical.

## Related Concepts

- [[platform-support|Platform Support]]
- [[venv|Venv]]
- [[dependencies|Dependencies]]

title: nous-portal
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

Nous Portal is the official service from Nous Research. One login gives you access to a model and the four Tool Gateway tools (web, image, TTS, browser). It is the easiest way to start.

## Concrete Example

You use hermes setup --portal, log in to Nous Portal, and Hermes is ready to chat, search, draw, and speak.

## Analogy

Like a school all-in-one card: library, canteen, and computer room access in one tap.

## Related Concepts

- [[setup-portal|Setup Portal]]
- [[oauth-login|OAuth Login]]
- [[provider-agnostic|Provider-Agnostic]]

title: oauth-login
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

OAuth is a secure way to log in without sharing your password. Hermes uses OAuth for some providers like Nous Portal and OpenAI Codex. You authorise once and Hermes gets a token.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes auth add nous. A browser opens, you log in to Nous Portal, and Hermes gets a token saved in auth.json.

## Analogy

Like tapping your student ID to enter the school gate. The gate checks you are a student without you typing a password.

## Related Concepts

- [[setup-portal|Setup Portal]]
- [[credential-pools|Credential Pools]]
- [[env-file|Env File]]

title: per-user-vs-root-install
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

Hermes can be installed just for your user account (per-user) or for the whole system (root). Per-user is safer and recommended. Root install is for shared servers where many people use Hermes.

## Concrete Example

On your personal laptop you choose per-user install. Hermes lives in your home folder and only you can run it.

## Analogy

Like having your own locker versus a shared storeroom. Your own locker is safer and simpler.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes_home|HERMES_HOME]]
- [[install-script|Install Script]]
- [[platform-support|Platform Support]]

title: platform-support
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

Hermes runs on Linux, macOS, Windows (native and WSL2), and Android (Termux). Each platform has a recommended install method. The docs have a full support matrix showing what works where.

## Concrete Example

You check the platform support table and see that your Chromebook running Linux works, but iOS does not yet.

## Analogy

Like a transit map showing which lines reach which stations. You check before you travel.

## Related Concepts

- [[curl-install|Curl Install]]
- [[powershell-install|PowerShell Install]]
- [[wsl2-install|WSL2 Install]]

title: powershell-install
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

On native Windows, you use PowerShell instead of curl. The command is slightly different but does the same thing: downloads and installs Hermes for you.

## Concrete Example

You open PowerShell, paste the install command, and watch it set up Hermes in your Windows user folder.

## Analogy

Like the same vending machine but with a different button layout for a different country.

## Related Concepts

- [[install-script|Install Script]]
- [[curl-install|Curl Install]]
- [[platform-support|Platform Support]]

title: prerequisites
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

Before installing Hermes, your computer needs a few things: Python 3.11 or newer, curl or PowerShell, and basic build tools. The install script checks and warns you if anything is missing.

## Concrete Example

The install script prints: Python 3.11 found. git found. All prerequisites met. Installing...

## Analogy

Like checking you have your ID and ticket before entering Ocean Park. No ticket, no entry.

## Related Concepts

- [[environment-setup|Environment Setup]]
- [[python-version|Python Version]]
- [[install-script|Install Script]]

title: provider-setup
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

Each provider may need different setup. Some need an API key in .env, others need an OAuth login via hermes auth. The setup wizard and docs guide you through each one.

## Concrete Example

For OpenRouter you paste a key into .env. For Nous Portal you run hermes auth add nous and log in via browser.

## Analogy

Like different MTR lines needing different tickets. The Airport Express needs a special ticket, the Tsuen Wan Line uses a standard one.

## Related Concepts

- [[api-keys|API Keys]]
- [[oauth-login|OAuth Login]]
- [[model-picker|Model Picker]]

title: python-version
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

Hermes needs Python 3.11 or newer. Python is the programming language Hermes is written in. If your system has an older version, you must upgrade before installing.

## Concrete Example

You run python3 --version and see 3.11.15. Good to go. If it said 3.9, you would need to upgrade first.

## Analogy

Like needing the latest game update to play online. Old version, no match.

## Related Concepts

- [[prerequisites|Prerequisites]]
- [[venv|Venv]]
- [[environment-setup|Environment Setup]]

title: sandboxed-execution
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

Hermes can run Python code in a sandbox, an isolated space that cannot touch your real files. This is safer when running untrusted code or experimenting.

## Concrete Example

Hermes runs a script in the sandbox. The script tries to delete a file, but the sandbox blocks it. Your real files are safe.

## Analogy

Like a practice room with rubber walls. You can throw things around and nothing breaks.

## Related Concepts

- [[venv|Venv]]
- [[command-approval|Command Approval]]
- [[code-execution-tool|Code Execution Tool]]

title: setup-portal
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

The setup portal (hermes setup --portal) is the fastest path to a working agent. One OAuth login covers a model plus web search, image generation, text-to-speech, and browser tools.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes setup --portal, log in once with Nous Portal, and all five tools are ready. No need to hunt for separate API keys.

## Analogy

Like an all-in-one transport pass. One tap opens MTR gates, bus doors, and ferry terminals.

## Related Concepts

- [[setup-wizard|Setup Wizard]]
- [[credential-pools|Credential Pools]]
- [[model-config|Model Config]]

title: setup-wizard
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

After installing, the setup wizard (hermes setup) walks you through choosing a model, connecting tools, and setting up messaging. It asks simple questions and configures everything for you.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes setup. It asks which AI company to use, whether you want web search, and whether to connect Telegram. You answer and it saves your choices.

## Analogy

Like the first-time setup of a new phone. It asks your language, Wi-Fi, and account, step by step.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-doctor|Hermes Doctor]]
- [[config-file|Config File]]
- [[env-file|Env File]]

title: shell-completions
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

Hermes can install shell completions so that pressing Tab auto-fills commands and options. This saves typing and prevents typos. Supports bash and zsh.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes completion bash and add the output to your .bashrc. Now typing hermes c and pressing Tab shows chat, config, cron.

## Analogy

Like autocorrect on your phone. Start typing and it finishes the word for you.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-setup|Hermes Setup]]
- [[terminal-agent|Terminal Agent]]

title: systemd-linger
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

On Linux, if you log out, your background services may stop. Enabling linger with loginctl lets your user services keep running even when you are logged out. This is needed for a 24/7 gateway.

## Concrete Example

You run sudo loginctl enable-linger alex. Now your Hermes gateway stays on after you close your SSH session.

## Analogy

Like telling the school guard to keep the lights on in your club room even after you leave campus.

## Related Concepts

- [[systemd-service|Systemd Service]]
- [[gateway-service|Gateway Service]]

title: systemd-service
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

On Linux, the gateway can run as a systemd service. This means it starts automatically when your computer boots and stays running in the background. Use hermes gateway install to set it up.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes gateway install. Now every time you boot your server, the Hermes gateway starts automatically and your Telegram bot is online.

## Analogy

Like the school bell that rings automatically at the same time every day, no one needs to press a button.

## Related Concepts

- [[gateway-service|Gateway Service]]
- [[gateway-setup|Gateway Setup]]

title: termux-install
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

Termux is a terminal app for Android. You can install Hermes on your phone using the same curl method, turning your phone into a portable AI agent.

## Concrete Example

You open Termux on your Android phone, paste the curl command, and a minute later you are chatting with Hermes.

## Analogy

Like turning your phone into a mini computer. Same power, smaller screen.

## Related Concepts

- [[curl-install|Curl Install]]
- [[platform-support|Platform Support]]
- [[terminal-agent|Terminal Agent]]

title: uninstalling-hermes
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

If you want to remove Hermes, the hermes uninstall command cleans up the installed files. Your config and sessions may remain unless you delete the .hermes folder yourself.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes uninstall. It removes the program. You then delete ~/.hermes to wipe all data.

## Analogy

Like uninstalling a game. The game is gone, but your save files stay until you delete them too.

## Related Concepts

- [[updating-hermes|Updating Hermes]]
- [[hermes_home|HERMES_HOME]]

title: updating-hermes
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

Hermes gets better over time with updates. You run hermes update to download and install the latest version. Updates can add new tools, fix bugs, and improve speed.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes update. It downloads the new version, restarts, and you now have the latest features.

## Analogy

Like updating an app from the App Store. New version, new improvements.

## Related Concepts

- [[install-script|Install Script]]
- [[hermes-doctor|Hermes Doctor]]

title: venv
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

A venv (virtual environment) is an isolated Python folder. Hermes installs its packages inside a venv so they do not clash with other Python projects on your computer.

## Concrete Example

The install script creates a venv at ~/.hermes/venv. All Hermes dependencies live there, separate from your school Python projects.

## Analogy

Like a lunch box with dividers. Your rice does not touch your soup. Each stays in its own section.

## Related Concepts

- [[python-version|Python Version]]
- [[dependencies|Dependencies]]
- [[environment-setup|Environment Setup]]

title: wsl2-install
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

WSL2 lets you run Linux inside Windows. Installing Hermes on WSL2 means you use the Linux curl method, which often works more smoothly than the native Windows method for developers.

## Concrete Example

You open WSL2, run the curl install command, and Hermes works as if you were on a Linux machine.

## Analogy

Like running a Japanese app inside a Japanese-mode emulator on your English computer. It just works better.

## Related Concepts

- [[curl-install|Curl Install]]
- [[platform-support|Platform Support]]
- [[powershell-install|PowerShell Install]]

title: wsl2-systemd
text:
> **Domain:** [[_installation-setup-moc|Installation & Setup]]

## Motivation

WSL2 needs systemd=true in /etc/wsl.conf for systemd services to work. Without it, the gateway falls back to nohup and may stop when you close the WSL window.

## Concrete Example

You add [boot] systemd=true to /etc/wsl.conf, restart WSL, and now hermes gateway install works properly.

## Analogy

Like enabling the engine mode in a remote-control car. Without it, the car runs but cannot use advanced features.

## Related Concepts

- [[wsl2-install|WSL2 Install]]
- [[systemd-service|Systemd Service]]

title: checkpoints-flag
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The --checkpoints flag enables filesystem checkpoints for this session. Hermes will snapshot your files before risky changes, so you can roll back with /rollback.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes chat --checkpoints. Before Hermes edits your project, it saves a snapshot. If things go wrong, /rollback restores everything.

## Analogy

Like wearing a seatbelt. You hope you never need it, but it is there if you do.

## Related Concepts

- [[checkpoints|Checkpoints]]
- [[file-toolset|File Toolset]]
- [[hermes-chat|Hermes Chat]]

title: config-check
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

hermes config check scans your config for missing or outdated settings. It tells you if something is wrong or if new options are available after an update.

## Concrete Example

After updating Hermes you run hermes config check. It says three new options are available and offers to add them.

## Analogy

Like a teacher checking your homework and marking the missing parts.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-config|Hermes Config]]
- [[config-set|Config Set]]
- [[hermes-doctor|Hermes Doctor]]

title: config-edit
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

hermes config edit opens your config.yaml file in a text editor. You can change any setting directly. This is for users who want full control over every option.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes config edit. Your text editor opens. You change max_turns from 90 to 120 and save.

## Analogy

Like opening the hood of a car to tune the engine. Full control, but you need to know what you are doing.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-config|Hermes Config]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[config-set|Config Set]]

title: config-migrate
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

hermes config migrate updates your config file to include new options added in recent Hermes versions. It preserves your existing settings and only adds the new defaults.

## Concrete Example

You update Hermes and run hermes config migrate. New sections appear in your config with default values, old settings untouched.

## Analogy

Like a phone update that adds new toggles to settings without resetting your old ones.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-check|Config Check]]
- [[updating-hermes|Updating Hermes]]

title: config-path
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

hermes config path prints the location of your config.yaml file. This is handy when you want to find, copy, or share your config.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes config path and it prints /home/alex/.hermes/config.yaml. You now know exactly where the file is.

## Analogy

Like a map pin showing where your locker is. One command, exact location.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-config|Hermes Config]]
- [[config-file|Config File]]
- [[hermes_home|HERMES_HOME]]

title: config-set
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

hermes config set KEY VALUE changes one setting at a time from the command line. It is safer than editing the whole file, because it only touches the key you name.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes config set memory.memory_enabled true. Memory is now on. No need to open an editor.

## Analogy

Like adjusting the volume with a button instead of opening the sound menu.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-config|Hermes Config]]
- [[config-edit|Config Edit]]
- [[config-check|Config Check]]

title: continue-flag
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The --continue flag (or -c) resumes the most recent session, or a named one. It is a shortcut when you do not remember the session ID but want to keep going.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes --continue. Your last chat opens. Hermes says Welcome back, we were talking about your essay.

## Analogy

Like pressing Continue on a game save screen. It loads your last save automatically.

## Related Concepts

- [[resume-flag|Resume Flag]]
- [[session|Session]]
- [[hermes-chat|Hermes Chat]]

title: global-flags
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

Global flags work with any hermes command. They include --resume, --continue, --worktree, --skills, --profile, --yolo, and --version. You combine them to control how Hermes starts.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes --profile school --skills lab-report --continue. Three flags at once: switch profile, load a skill, resume last session.

## Analogy

Like toppings on a pizza. Pick and combine the ones you want for this order.

## Related Concepts

- [[resume-flag|Resume Flag]]
- [[continue-flag|Continue Flag]]
- [[profile-flag|Profile Flag]]

title: hermes-acp
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes acp command starts Hermes as an ACP server, which lets IDEs like VS Code connect to it. This is how Hermes integrates with your code editor.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes acp. Your VS Code extension connects to it. Now you can chat with Hermes inside the editor while coding.

## Analogy

Like plugging a second monitor into your laptop. Same computer, bigger workspace.

## Related Concepts

- [[terminal-agent|Terminal Agent]]
- [[desktop-app|Desktop App]]
- [[plugins|Plugins]]

title: hermes-auth
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes auth command group manages credentials. Subcommands include add, list, and remove. You use it to add OAuth logins or API keys and see what is stored.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes auth add nous. A browser opens for login. Then hermes auth list shows the Nous token is saved.

## Analogy

Like the accounts section in your phone settings. Add, view, remove logins.

## Related Concepts

- [[credential-pools|Credential Pools]]
- [[oauth-login|OAuth Login]]
- [[auth-file|Auth File]]

title: hermes-chat
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes chat command starts an interactive conversation with Hermes. If you just type hermes with no command, it defaults to chat. This is the main way you talk to Hermes in the terminal.

## Concrete Example

You type hermes and a chat prompt opens. You type a question, press Enter, and Hermes replies. You can keep the conversation going for hours.

## Analogy

Like opening WhatsApp and starting to text a friend. The conversation stays open until you close it.

## Related Concepts

- [[single-query-mode|Single Query Mode]]
- [[global-flags|Global Flags]]
- [[terminal-agent|Terminal Agent]]

title: hermes-claw-migrate
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes claw migrate command imports settings and sessions from OpenClaw, an older tool. If you are moving from OpenClaw to Hermes, this saves your old work.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes claw migrate. It reads your OpenClaw config, copies compatible settings, and imports your session history.

## Analogy

Like a moving company that packs your old house and unpacks it into the new one.

## Related Concepts

- [[migration-from-openclaw|Migration from OpenClaw]]
- [[config-file|Config File]]
- [[hermes-update|Hermes Update]]

title: hermes-completion
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes completion command generates shell completion scripts for bash or zsh. You add the output to your shell config file and Tab auto-fills Hermes commands.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes completion bash >> ~/.bashrc. Next time you open a terminal, typing hermes c and Tab shows chat, config, cron.

## Analogy

Like training your phone keyboard to predict your most-used words.

## Related Concepts

- [[shell-completions|Shell Completions]]
- [[hermes-setup|Hermes Setup]]

title: hermes-config
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes config command group lets you view, edit, and check your configuration. Subcommands include edit, set, path, and check. It is your control panel for all settings.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes config set display.skin dark. The theme changes. You run hermes config to see all current settings.

## Analogy

Like the settings app on your phone. One place to view and change everything.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-file|Config File]]
- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]
- [[config-edit|Config Edit]]

title: hermes-cron
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes cron command group manages scheduled tasks. Subcommands include list, create, edit, pause, resume, run, and remove. You set a schedule and Hermes runs tasks automatically.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes cron create every-9am with the prompt to check weather and message you. Every morning at 9, Hermes runs the task.

## Analogy

Like setting a recurring alarm. But instead of just ringing, it does a whole task.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-jobs|Cron Jobs]]
- [[gateway|Gateway]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]

title: hermes-curator
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes curator command manages the skill lifecycle in the background. Subcommands include status, run, pause, resume, pin, archive, restore, prune, backup, and rollback.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes curator status. It shows 3 skills are stale and 1 is pinned. You run hermes curator run to clean up.

## Analogy

Like a garden keeper. They prune dead branches, water the healthy plants, and keep everything tidy.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill-curator|Skill Curator]]
- [[skills|Skills]]
- [[learning-loop|Learning Loop]]

title: hermes-doctor-command
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

hermes doctor runs a full health check on your Hermes installation. It checks Python version, dependencies, config, API keys, and gateway status. Add --fix to auto-repair where possible.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes doctor --fix. It finds a missing dependency, installs it, and reports all systems green.

## Analogy

Like a car service. The mechanic checks everything and fixes what they can on the spot.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-status|Hermes Status]]
- [[config-check|Config Check]]
- [[prerequisites|Prerequisites]]

title: hermes-gateway
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes gateway command group controls the messaging gateway. Subcommands include run, install, start, stop, restart, status, and setup. This is how you connect Hermes to Telegram, Discord, etc.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes gateway start. The gateway begins. You run hermes gateway status and see Telegram connected.

## Analogy

Like the power switches for different appliances in your home. Turn on the TV, turn off the lamp.

## Related Concepts

- [[gateway|Gateway]]
- [[gateway-service|Gateway Service]]
- [[gateway-setup|Gateway Setup]]

title: hermes-honcho
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes honcho command manages the Honcho memory integration. Honcho is a more advanced memory provider. Subcommands include setup and status.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes honcho setup. It configures Honcho as your memory provider. Now memory uses Honcho instead of the built-in file store.

## Analogy

Like upgrading from a notebook to a filing cabinet. More space, better organisation.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-provider|Memory Provider]]
- [[hermes-memory|Hermes Memory]]
- [[plugins|Plugins]]

title: hermes-insights
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes insights command shows usage analytics: how many tokens you used, how many sessions, which tools were called. Use --days N to set the time range.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes insights --days 7. A summary shows you used 50,000 tokens and called the web tool 30 times this week.

## Analogy

Like a fitness tracker for your Hermes usage. See your stats over time.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-status|Hermes Status]]
- [[hermes-sessions|Hermes Sessions]]

title: hermes-kanban
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes kanban command manages the multi-agent task board. Subcommands include init, create, list, show, assign, link, comment, complete, and archive.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes kanban init to create a board. Then hermes kanban create with the task title Write tests. You assign it to a worker profile.

## Analogy

Like a Trello board for a group project. Cards move from To Do to Doing to Done.

## Related Concepts

- [[kanban-board|Kanban Board]]
- [[profiles|Profiles]]
- [[delegation-tool|Delegation Tool]]

title: hermes-mcp
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes mcp command group manages MCP servers. Subcommands include serve, add, remove, list, test, and configure. MCP servers add external tools to Hermes.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes mcp add google-drive --url .... Then hermes mcp test google-drive confirms it works. Hermes can now read your Drive files.

## Analogy

Like adding a new appliance to your smart home. Plug it in, test the connection, configure settings.

## Related Concepts

- [[mcp-servers|MCP Servers]]
- [[plugins|Plugins]]
- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]

title: hermes-memory
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes memory command manages the memory system. Subcommands include setup, status, and off. You use it to choose a memory provider and check if memory is working.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes memory status. It shows memory is enabled, provider is built-in, and 42 facts are stored.

## Analogy

Like checking the capacity of your brain. How much do you remember and where is it stored.

## Related Concepts

- [[persistent-memory|Persistent Memory]]
- [[memory-provider|Memory Provider]]
- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]

title: hermes-model
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes model command opens an interactive menu to pick or change your AI model and provider. You can also use it to just see what is currently set.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes model. A menu appears. You scroll to Anthropic Claude and press Enter. Hermes now uses that model.

## Analogy

Like the character select screen in a game. Pick a character and the next match uses them.

## Related Concepts

- [[model-config|Model Config]]
- [[model-picker|Model Picker]]
- [[provider-agnostic|Provider-Agnostic]]

title: hermes-pairing
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes pairing command manages DM authorisation. When someone messages your Hermes bot, they must be approved. Subcommands include list, approve, and revoke.

## Concrete Example

A classmate messages your Telegram bot. You run hermes pairing approve alice. Now Alice can chat with your Hermes.

## Analogy

Like approving a friend request. Until you accept, they cannot message you.

## Related Concepts

- [[gateway|Gateway]]
- [[platform-adapters|Platform Adapters]]
- [[bot-token|Bot Token]]

title: hermes-plugins
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes plugins command manages plugins. Subcommands include list, install, and remove. Plugins add bundles of new features, tools, or integrations.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes plugins install spotify-control. The plugin adds Spotify tools. Now Hermes can play your playlists.

## Analogy

Like installing an expansion pack for a game. New content appears in the main menu.

## Related Concepts

- [[plugins|Plugins]]
- [[skills|Skills]]
- [[mcp-servers|MCP Servers]]

title: hermes-profile
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes profile command group manages multiple Hermes profiles. Subcommands include list, create, use, delete, show, rename, export, and import. Profiles keep different setups isolated.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes profile create school. Then hermes profile use school. Now all commands use the school profile.

## Analogy

Like having different user accounts on a shared computer. Each person has their own desktop and files.

## Related Concepts

- [[profiles|Profiles]]
- [[hermes_home|HERMES_HOME]]
- [[config-file|Config File]]

title: hermes-sessions
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes sessions command group manages your saved conversations. Subcommands include list, browse, export, rename, delete, and prune. You never lose a conversation.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes sessions list and see your last ten chats. You run hermes sessions export homework.json to save one.

## Analogy

Like a photo album. Browse, rename, delete, or export your memories.

## Related Concepts

- [[session|Session]]
- [[sessions-db|Sessions DB]]
- [[session-search|Session Search]]

title: hermes-skills
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes skills command group manages your skill library. Subcommands include list, search, install, inspect, update, and uninstall. It is how you grow what Hermes can do.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes skills search git. A list of git-related skills appears. You run hermes skills install git-helper to add one.

## Analogy

Like browsing the App Store. Search, read reviews, install, update.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills|Skills]]
- [[skill-hub|Skill Hub]]
- [[skill-creation|Skill Creation]]

title: hermes-status-command
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

hermes status shows a quick snapshot of what is running and connected. It is faster than doctor and focuses on runtime state, not installation health.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes status. A table shows: Gateway running, Model DeepSeek, 3 tools enabled, 2 profiles exist.

## Analogy

Like glancing at the MTR next-train display. Quick, current, actionable.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-doctor-command|Hermes Doctor Command]]
- [[gateway|Gateway]]
- [[hermes-config|Hermes Config]]

title: hermes-tools
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes tools command opens an interactive menu to enable or disable toolsets. You can also use list, enable, and disable subcommands for scripting.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes tools. A checklist appears. You toggle the browser toolset off and press Enter. Web browsing is now disabled.

## Analogy

Like the toggles in your phone settings. Turn Wi-Fi on, Bluetooth off, etc.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[tool-calling|Tool Calling]]
- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]

title: hermes-uninstall
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes uninstall command removes the Hermes program from your system. Your data in .hermes may remain. To fully clean up, delete that folder manually afterwards.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes uninstall. The program is removed. You then run rm -rf ~/.hermes to delete all data.

## Analogy

Like returning a library book and then clearing your bookmark file. Two steps to fully clean up.

## Related Concepts

- [[uninstalling-hermes|Uninstalling Hermes]]
- [[hermes_home|HERMES_HOME]]
- [[updating-hermes|Updating Hermes]]

title: hermes-update
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes update command downloads and installs the latest version of Hermes. It is the easiest way to get new features and bug fixes. Run it every few weeks.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes update. It downloads, installs, and prints Version 2.2.0 installed. You restart Hermes to use it.

## Analogy

Like tapping Update in the App Store. A minute later, new version ready.

## Related Concepts

- [[updating-hermes|Updating Hermes]]
- [[backup-before-update|Backup Before Update]]
- [[config-migrate|Config Migrate]]

title: hermes-webhook
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The hermes webhook command group manages webhook subscriptions. Subcommands include subscribe, list, remove, and test. Webhooks let external services trigger Hermes tasks.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes webhook subscribe github-issues. Now GitHub can POST to your Hermes when an issue is opened, and Hermes runs a task.

## Analogy

Like setting up a doorbell that also texts you when someone rings it.

## Related Concepts

- [[webhooks|Webhooks]]
- [[cron-jobs|Cron Jobs]]
- [[gateway|Gateway]]

title: model-flag
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The --model flag (or -m) lets you override the model for just this one session, without changing your config. Handy when a task needs a stronger or cheaper model temporarily.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes chat -m anthropic/claude-sonnet-4. This session uses Claude, but your default stays DeepSeek.

## Analogy

Like renting a bigger locker for one day. Tomorrow, you are back to your regular one.

## Related Concepts

- [[model-config|Model Config]]
- [[hermes-model|Hermes Model]]
- [[global-flags|Global Flags]]

title: pass-session-id-flag
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The --pass-session-id flag includes the session ID in the system prompt. This is mainly for advanced workflows where external tools need to know the session identifier.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes --pass-session-id. The session ID appears in the context, so a webhook or script can reference it.

## Analogy

Like wearing a name badge at a conference. Others can identify and reference you.

## Related Concepts

- [[session|Session]]
- [[global-flags|Global Flags]]

title: profile-flag
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The --profile flag (or -p) tells Hermes to use a named profile for this session. This overrides the default profile, so you can switch contexts with one flag.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes -p school. This session uses the school profile: its model, memory, and sessions. Your personal profile is untouched.

## Analogy

Like swiping a different Octopus card. Same gate, different account.

## Related Concepts

- [[profiles|Profiles]]
- [[hermes-profile|Hermes Profile]]
- [[hermes_home|HERMES_HOME]]

title: provider-flag
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The --provider flag forces a specific provider (openrouter, anthropic, nous, etc.) for this session. It is used together with --model when you want exact control.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes chat --provider openai -m gpt-4o. This session uses OpenAI GPT-4o, regardless of your default.

## Analogy

Like choosing a specific courier company for one delivery, instead of your usual.

## Related Concepts

- [[model-flag|Model Flag]]
- [[provider-agnostic|Provider-Agnostic]]
- [[model-config|Model Config]]

title: quiet-flag
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The --quiet flag (or -Q) hides the banner, spinner, and tool previews. Output is just the answer. This is great for scripts where you only want the result.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes chat -q -Q with the question what is 2 plus 2. It prints just 4, no banner, no extra text.

## Analogy

Like a library where everyone whispers. Only the essential words, nothing else.

## Related Concepts

- [[verbose-flag|Verbose Flag]]
- [[single-query-mode|Single Query Mode]]
- [[hermes-chat|Hermes Chat]]

title: resume-flag
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The --resume flag (or -r) lets you continue a specific past session by its ID or title. This is how you pick up an old conversation exactly where you left off.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes --resume 20260804_homework. The old session opens and Hermes remembers the full context.

## Analogy

Like opening a bookmarked book to the exact page you stopped at.

## Related Concepts

- [[session|Session]]
- [[continue-flag|Continue Flag]]
- [[hermes-sessions|Hermes Sessions]]

title: single-query-mode
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The -q flag lets you ask Hermes one question and get an answer without entering interactive chat. This is perfect for quick lookups from a script or shortcut.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes chat -q with the question about the capital of France, and Hermes prints Paris, then exits.

## Analogy

Like a fortune-telling machine. You insert a coin, ask one question, get an answer, done.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-chat|Hermes Chat]]
- [[global-flags|Global Flags]]

title: skills-flag
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The --skills flag (or -s) preloads one or more skills at startup. This is useful when you know you will need a specific skill and want it ready immediately.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes -s git-helper,lab-report. Both skills load at startup. When you ask about git, Hermes uses the skill instantly.

## Analogy

Like packing specific textbooks in your bag before class. They are ready when you need them.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills|Skills]]
- [[skill-creation|Skill Creation]]
- [[hermes-skills|Hermes Skills]]

title: source-flag
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The --source flag tags the session with a label, like cli, telegram, or cron. This helps you filter sessions later by where they came from.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes chat --source school-project. Later, hermes sessions list can filter sessions tagged school-project.

## Analogy

Like colour-coding your notebooks by subject. Easy to find the one you need.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-sessions|Hermes Sessions]]
- [[session|Session]]

title: toolsets-flag
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The --toolsets flag (or -t) lets you pick exactly which toolsets are active for this session. You pass a comma-separated list. This overrides your default toolset config.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes chat -t terminal,file. Only terminal and file tools are available. No web, no browser, locked down.

## Analogy

Like choosing only pens and pencils for an exam, leaving the calculator behind.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[hermes-tools|Hermes Tools]]
- [[global-flags|Global Flags]]

title: verbose-flag
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The --verbose flag (or -v) makes Hermes print extra detail: tool calls, timings, and internal steps. It is useful for learning how Hermes works or debugging a problem.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes chat -v. Now each tool call prints its name, arguments, and result before Hermes continues.

## Analogy

Like a teacher showing every step of a maths solution, not just the answer.

## Related Concepts

- [[quiet-flag|Quiet Flag]]
- [[hermes-chat|Hermes Chat]]
- [[global-flags|Global Flags]]

title: version-flag
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The --version flag (or -V) prints the installed Hermes version and exits. Useful for checking what you are running or reporting a bug.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes --version. It prints Hermes Agent 2.1.0. You now know which version to report in a bug ticket.

## Analogy

Like checking the edition number on a textbook. Quick, one line, done.

## Related Concepts

- [[global-flags|Global Flags]]
- [[hermes-update|Hermes Update]]

title: worktree-flag
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The --worktree flag (or -w) starts Hermes in an isolated git worktree. This means file changes happen in a copy, not your main project. Great for experiments and parallel agents.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes -w in your project. Hermes makes a worktree copy. It can edit files freely without touching the original.

## Analogy

Like photocopying a worksheet to try answers in pencil. The original stays clean.

## Related Concepts

- [[worktree-mode|Worktree Mode]]
- [[profiles|Profiles]]
- [[delegation-tool|Delegation Tool]]

title: yolo-flag
text:
> **Domain:** [[_cli-commands-moc|CLI & Commands]]

## Motivation

The --yolo flag skips all command approval prompts. Hermes will run any command, including risky ones, without asking. Use it only when you fully trust the task.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes --yolo and ask it to clean up temp files. Hermes runs rm commands without pausing to confirm each one.

## Analogy

Like a green light at every intersection. Fast, but you better be a careful driver.

## Related Concepts

- [[yolo-mode|Yolo Mode]]
- [[command-approval|Command Approval]]
- [[global-flags|Global Flags]]
