title: agent-config
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The agent section of config.yaml. Controls max_turns, tool_use_enforcement, reasoning level, personality.

## Concrete Example

agent: max_turns: 30, tool_use_enforcement: strict, reasoning: medium, personality: SOUL.md. The agent section controls how Hermes behaves in conversations.

## Analogy

A job description - it defines how an employee should work, their limits, and their style. The agent config is Hermes job description.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]

title: auxiliary-models
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

Models used for non-chat tasks: vision, compression, session search, command safety analysis. Configured separately from the main model.

## Concrete Example

model.vision: gpt-4o (image analysis). model.compression: deepseek-v3 (summarizing). model.session_search: text-embedding-3-small (searching). Each auxiliary model specializes.

## Analogy

Assistants in a company - the main worker (default model) does the main job, but assistants (auxiliary models) handle specific tasks like filing, translating, etc.

## Related Concepts

- [[model-config|Model Config]]
- [[models-providers|Models & Providers]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]

title: checkpoints-config
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The checkpoints section: enabled, max_snapshots, interval. Controls filesystem snapshots.

## Concrete Example

checkpoints: enabled: true, max_snapshots: 50, interval: 0. Hermes takes snapshots before risky changes. Up to 50 saved. The checkpoints config controls this.

## Analogy

A security camera settings - recording on/off, how many days saved, recording interval. Checkpoints config sets the filesystem camera.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[checkpoints|Checkpoints]]

title: compression-config
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The compression section: enabled, threshold, target_ratio. Controls automatic context compression.

## Concrete Example

compression: enabled: true, threshold: 0.50, target_ratio: 0.20. At 50% of context, compress to 20% of capacity. Keeps conversations going without hitting limits.

## Analogy

A thermostat - you set when the AC turns on (threshold) and the target temperature (target_ratio). Compression config sets when and how much to compress.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[context-compression|Context Compression]]

title: compression-model
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

An auxiliary model used for context compression. Summarizes old messages to free context space.

## Concrete Example

model.compression: openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v3. At compression threshold, this model summarizes 80K tokens of history into 20K. Fast and cheap.

## Analogy

A note-taker in a meeting - they summarize the 2-hour discussion into 1 page. The compression model summarizes old context into a brief summary.

## Related Concepts

- [[auxiliary-models|Auxiliary Models]]
- [[model-config|Model Config]]
- [[context-compression|Context Compression]]

title: compression-threshold
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The percentage of context window at which compression triggers. Default: 0.50 (50%).

## Concrete Example

compression.threshold: 0.50. At 50% of 200K = 100K tokens, compression starts. Old messages are summarized to make room for new ones.

## Analogy

A water tank alarm - when the tank is 50% full, the alarm triggers. Compression threshold triggers when context is 50% full.

## Related Concepts

- [[compression-config|Compression Config]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[context-compression|Context Compression]]

title: config-backup
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

Saving a copy of config.yaml before making changes. Useful for rollback.

## Concrete Example

cp config.yaml config.yaml.bak. Make changes. If things break: cp config.yaml.bak config.yaml. Back to working state.

## Analogy

Backing up your phone before an update - if the update fails, you restore the backup. Config backup saves your settings before changes.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[config-edit|Config Edit]]
- [[config-migrate|Config Migrate]]

title: config-check
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

Check config for missing or outdated options. Command: hermes config check.

## Concrete Example

hermes config check. Output: OK: model.default set. WARNING: memory.provider not set (default: built-in). Identifies issues without fixing them.

## Analogy

A car diagnostic tool - it scans the engine and reports problems. hermes config check scans your config and reports issues.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[config-migrate|Config Migrate]]
- [[hermes-doctor|Hermes Doctor]]

title: config-defaults
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

Default values used when a config option is not set. Hermes has sensible defaults for everything.

## Concrete Example

No config? Hermes uses: model=openrouter auto, max_turns=30, compression=on, memory=off. Everything works out of the box. Config is optional.

## Analogy

Default settings on a new phone - it works without any setup. You can customize later. Hermes defaults let it work immediately.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]
- [[hermes-config|Hermes Config]]

title: config-diff
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

Show what changed since the default config. Command: hermes config diff.

## Concrete Example

hermes config diff. Output: model.default: default=openrouter/auto, yours=anthropic/claude-sonnet-4. memory.enabled: default=false, yours=true. Shows your customizations.

## Analogy

A diff between your essay and the template - it shows what you changed. Config diff shows what you customized vs defaults.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[config-defaults|Config Defaults]]
- [[hermes-config|Hermes Config]]

title: config-edit
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

Open the config file in your editor. Command: hermes config edit. Opens config.yaml in $EDITOR (vim, nano, etc.).

## Concrete Example

hermes config edit. Vim opens with config.yaml. You change model.default to gpt-4o. Save and quit. Next session uses gpt-4o.

## Analogy

Customizing your phone settings - you open the settings app and change options. hermes config edit opens the settings file for Hermes.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[config-set|Config Set]]
- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]

title: config-env-path
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

Show the location of the .env file. Command: hermes config env-path.

## Concrete Example

hermes config env-path. Output: /home/alice/.hermes/.env. The .env file holds API keys and secrets, separate from config.yaml.

## Analogy

Finding where you keep your spare keys - you need the location. hermes config env-path tells you where the secrets file is.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[env-file|Env File]]
- [[secrets-management|Secrets Management]]

title: config-export
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

Saving your config to a shareable file. Useful for backups or sharing with others.

## Concrete Example

hermes config export my-config.yaml. Your config.yaml is copied to my-config.yaml. Share it with colleagues or back it up.

## Analogy

Exporting your contacts to a file - you save them for backup or sharing. Config export saves your settings for backup or sharing.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[config-import|Config Import]]
- [[hermes-config|Hermes Config]]

title: config-import
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

Loading a config from another source. Useful when setting up a new machine or sharing configs.

## Concrete Example

hermes config import my-config.yaml. Your config is replaced with my-config.yaml. All settings transferred in one command.

## Analogy

Importing contacts to a new phone - you load a file and all contacts appear. Config import loads settings from a file.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[config-export|Config Export]]
- [[hermes-config|Hermes Config]]

title: config-migrate
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

Update config.yaml with new options after a Hermes update. Command: hermes config migrate.

## Concrete Example

hermes update -> new version adds delegation.max_spawn_depth. hermes config migrate adds it with the default value. Config is now compatible with the new version.

## Analogy

Renewing your ID card when the format changes - new fields are added. Config migrate adds new fields to your config after an update.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[config-check|Config Check]]
- [[hermes-update|Hermes Update]]

title: config-path
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

Show the location of config.yaml. Command: hermes config path.

## Concrete Example

hermes config path. Output: /home/alice/.hermes/config.yaml. Useful when you need to find the file manually or back it up.

## Analogy

Asking for an address - you need to know where something is. hermes config path tells you where config.yaml lives.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[hermes-config|Hermes Config]]
- [[config-edit|Config Edit]]

title: config-reset
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

Resetting config to factory defaults. Command: hermes config reset. All custom settings are lost.

## Concrete Example

hermes config reset. Are you sure? y. Config is reset to defaults. All custom model, memory, and security settings are gone. Fresh start.

## Analogy

Factory reset on a phone - everything goes back to how it was when you bought it. Config reset puts Hermes back to defaults.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[config-defaults|Config Defaults]]
- [[hermes-config|Hermes Config]]

title: config-sections
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The major sections of config.yaml: model, agent, terminal, compression, display, stt, tts, memory, security, delegation, checkpoints.

## Concrete Example

config.yaml sections: model: (which LLM), agent: (behavior), terminal: (shell), compression: (context), display: (UI), stt: (voice input), tts: (voice output), memory: (persistence), security: (protection), delegation: (subagents), checkpoints: (snapshots).

## Analogy

Different departments in a school - math, science, English, PE. Each manages its own area. Config sections each manage their own feature area.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[config-edit|Config Edit]]
- [[config-set|Config Set]]

title: config-set
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

Change a single config value from the command line. Command: hermes config set KEY VALUE.

## Concrete Example

hermes config set model.default anthropic/claude-sonnet-4. One line, one change. No editor needed. Faster than config edit for single values.

## Analogy

A quick dial on a combination lock - you change one number at a time. hermes config set changes one config value at a time.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[config-edit|Config Edit]]
- [[hermes-config|Hermes Config]]

title: config-validation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

Hermes validates config.yaml on startup. Invalid values are rejected with helpful error messages.

## Concrete Example

config: max_turns: -5. Hermes: ERROR: max_turns must be positive. Fix: hermes config set agent.max_turns 30. Invalid config is caught early.

## Analogy

A bouncer at a club - they check IDs at the door. Invalid IDs are rejected. Config validation checks values at startup.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[config-check|Config Check]]
- [[hermes-config|Hermes Config]]

title: config-yaml
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The main configuration file for Hermes. Located at ~/.hermes/config.yaml. Controls every aspect of agent behavior.

## Concrete Example

config.yaml has sections: model, agent, terminal, compression, display, stt, tts, memory, security, delegation, checkpoints. Each section controls different features. Edit with: hermes config edit.

## Analogy

A remote control with buttons for every TV feature - volume, channels, brightness, input. config.yaml is the remote control for Hermes.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-edit|Config Edit]]
- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]
- [[hermes-config|Hermes Config]]

title: context-length
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The maximum number of tokens the model can process. Configured per-model in config.yaml.

## Concrete Example

model.context_length: 200000. The model handles up to 200K tokens. If conversation exceeds this, compression triggers. Different models have different limits.

## Analogy

A backpack capacity - it holds 20L. If you try to put in 25L, something must come out. Context length is the backpack capacity for the model.

## Related Concepts

- [[model-config|Model Config]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[context-window|Context Window]]

title: context-window
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The active portion of context length being used for the current conversation. Changes as the conversation grows.

## Concrete Example

Start: 2K tokens (system prompt). After 10 messages: 15K. After 50 messages: 80K. Context window grows. At threshold, compression shrinks it.

## Analogy

A backpack being packed - it starts empty, fills up as you add items. The context window fills as the conversation grows.

## Related Concepts

- [[context-length|Context Length]]
- [[context-compression|Context Compression]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]

title: delegation-config
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The delegation section: enabled, max_spawn_depth, max_concurrent_children, model.

## Concrete Example

delegation: enabled: true, max_spawn_depth: 1, max_concurrent_children: 3. Hermes can spawn up to 3 subagents, each with depth 1. The delegation config controls subagents.

## Analogy

A company org chart - how many teams, how many levels, who reports to whom. Delegation config sets the org chart for Hermes subagents.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[delegate-task|Delegate Task]]

title: display-config
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The display section: skin, tool_progress, show_reasoning, show_cost, show_models.

## Concrete Example

display: skin: default, tool_progress: true, show_reasoning: medium, show_cost: true. The display section controls what you see in the TUI.

## Analogy

A phone display settings - brightness, dark mode, font size. Display config controls what you see in the Hermes interface.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[skin|Skin]]

title: display-indicator
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

A TUI element showing agent status: thinking, running tool, idle. Configured in display section.

## Concrete Example

display.indicator: spinner. When Hermes is thinking: [thinking...] When running a tool: [running terminal...] When idle: ready. Visual feedback.

## Analogy

A status light on a printer - green (ready), yellow (processing), red (error). The display indicator shows Hermes status.

## Related Concepts

- [[display-config|Display Config]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[tui|TUI]]

title: egress-proxy
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

A proxy server for all Hermes network traffic. Configured in config.yaml. Useful for monitoring and compliance.

## Concrete Example

Config: egress_proxy: http://proxy.school.edu:8080. All HTTP requests go through the school proxy. The proxy can log and filter traffic.

## Analogy

A customs checkpoint - all goods pass through. Officers inspect and filter. An egress proxy is customs for Hermes network traffic.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[network-security|Network Security]]
- [[configuration|Configuration]]

title: env-file
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

A file (~/.hermes/.env) storing API keys and secrets. Separate from config.yaml for security.

## Concrete Example

.env: OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-xxx, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-xxx. Hermes reads these for authentication. The model never sees them (redacted).

## Analogy

A locked drawer in your desk - you keep valuables (API keys) there, not on the desk. The .env file is the locked drawer for secrets.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[secrets-management|Secrets Management]]
- [[secret-redaction|Secret Redaction]]

title: global-flags
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

Command-line flags that work with all hermes commands: --resume, --continue, --worktree, --skills, --profile, --yolo.

## Concrete Example

hermes --profile work chat. Or: hermes --yolo chat. Or: hermes --skills debugging,github chat. Global flags modify how any command runs.

## Analogy

Universal settings on a camera - flash, timer, resolution work with any photo mode. Global flags work with any hermes command.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[cli|CLI]]
- [[hermes-config|Hermes Config]]

title: hermes-config
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The CLI command group for managing configuration. Subcommands: edit, set, check, migrate, path, env-path.

## Concrete Example

hermes config edit (open editor). hermes config set model.default X (change one value). hermes config check (validate). All config management in one command group.

## Analogy

A settings app on your phone - one app with many options. hermes config is the settings app for Hermes.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[config-edit|Config Edit]]
- [[config-set|Config Set]]

title: managed-scope
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

A mode where certain config settings are locked and cannot be changed. Used in enterprise or educational deployments.

## Concrete Example

Managed scope: security.redact_secrets locked to true. Students cannot disable it. The teacher (admin) manages it. Ensures policies are enforced.

## Analogy

School uniform rules - students cannot change them. Managed scope locks certain Hermes settings so users cannot change them.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[security-config|Security Config]]
- [[configuration|Configuration]]

title: max-turns
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The maximum number of agent loop iterations per conversation. Prevents infinite loops. Default: 30.

## Concrete Example

agent.max_turns: 30. If the agent loops 30 times without finishing, it stops. Prevents runaway loops that waste API credits.

## Analogy

A chess game timer - each player has limited moves. Max turns limits how many times the agent can loop before stopping.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-config|Agent Config]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]

title: memory-config
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The memory section: enabled, provider, char_limit. Controls persistent memory.

## Concrete Example

memory: enabled: true, provider: built-in, char_limit: 2000. Hermes remembers your preferences across sessions. The memory config controls how.

## Analogy

A notebook settings - size, type, sections. Memory config sets how Hermes memory works.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[persistent-memory|Persistent Memory]]

title: model-config
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The model section of config.yaml. Controls which LLM to use, context length, and auxiliary models.

## Concrete Example

model: default: openrouter/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4, context_length: 200000, vision: openrouter/.../gpt-4o, compression: openrouter/.../deepseek-v3. The model section picks all LLMs.

## Analogy

Choosing players for a sports team - you pick the starting player (default), a substitute (compression), and a specialist (vision). The model config picks all LLMs for different roles.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[models-providers|Models & Providers]]

title: personality
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

A custom personality for Hermes. Defined in SOUL.md. Controls tone, style, and behavior.

## Concrete Example

SOUL.md: You are a patient, encouraging tutor. Explain simply, use analogies, praise effort. Hermes adopts this personality in all conversations.

## Analogy

An actor playing a character - they adopt the character personality in every scene. SOUL.md lets Hermes play a specific character.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-config|Agent Config]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[soulmd|SOUL.md]]

title: profile-flag
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

A global flag that selects which profile to use. Profiles have separate config, skills, sessions, and memory.

## Concrete Example

hermes --profile work chat. Hermes uses the work profile: work config, work skills, work memory. Completely separate from the default profile.

## Analogy

A school ID vs a library card - different cards for different contexts. The profile flag picks which context (profile) Hermes uses.

## Related Concepts

- [[global-flags|Global Flags]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[profiles|Profiles]]

title: reasoning-levels
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

How much the model reasons before responding. Levels: none, minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh. Higher = more thinking.

## Concrete Example

agent.reasoning: high. The model thinks deeply: considers options, plans steps, evaluates trade-offs. Lower levels think less. Higher levels are smarter but slower.

## Analogy

A student deciding how to solve a problem - quick guess (none) vs careful analysis (high). Reasoning levels control how much the model thinks before answering.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-config|Agent Config]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[show-reasoning|Show Reasoning]]

title: security-config
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The security section: tirith_enabled, redact_secrets, website_blocklist. Controls all security features.

## Concrete Example

security: tirith_enabled: true, redact_secrets: true, website_blocklist: [evil.com]. Three security layers. The security config controls all protection.

## Analogy

A security system settings - alarm, cameras, door codes. Security config sets all Hermes security features.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[security-overview|Security Overview]]

title: session-search-model
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

An auxiliary model used for searching past sessions. Usually an embedding model.

## Concrete Example

model.session_search: text-embedding-3-small. You search: docker debugging. The model embeds your query, finds similar past sessions, returns results.

## Analogy

A search engine indexing old emails - you type a keyword and it finds matching emails. The session search model indexes and searches past conversations.

## Related Concepts

- [[auxiliary-models|Auxiliary Models]]
- [[model-config|Model Config]]
- [[session-search|Session Search]]

title: show-cost
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

A display setting that shows token usage and cost after each response.

## Concrete Example

display.show_cost: true. After each response: Tokens: 1,234 in, 567 out. Cost: $0.012. You see how much each message costs.

## Analogy

A receipt after shopping - you see how much you spent. Show cost displays the token and dollar cost of each response.

## Related Concepts

- [[display-config|Display Config]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[display-config|Display Config]]

title: show-reasoning
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

A display setting that shows the model reasoning process. Levels: none, minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh.

## Concrete Example

display.show_reasoning: medium. You see: Reasoning: The user wants... I should use the terminal tool... The thought process is visible.

## Analogy

Showing your work in math class - the teacher sees each step. Show reasoning displays the model thought process.

## Related Concepts

- [[display-config|Display Config]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[reasoning-levels|Reasoning Levels]]

title: skills-flag
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

A global flag that pre-loads specific skills for the session.

## Concrete Example

hermes --skills debugging,tdd chat. Hermes starts with the debugging and TDD skills loaded. No need to /skill load them manually.

## Analogy

Pre-loading apps before a trip - you download maps and translation before you go. The skills flag pre-loads skills before the session starts.

## Related Concepts

- [[global-flags|Global Flags]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[skills-system|Skills System]]

title: skin
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

Visual theme for the TUI. Controls colors, borders, and layout. Configured in display section.

## Concrete Example

display.skin: default. Or: minimal, dark, retro. Each skin changes how the TUI looks. Colors, borders, status bar style - all controlled by skin.

## Analogy

A phone case - you pick a color and style. The phone works the same, but looks different. Skins change how Hermes looks, not how it works.

## Related Concepts

- [[display-config|Display Config]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[tui|TUI]]

title: soulmd
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

A file defining Hermes personality. Located at ~/.hermes/SOUL.md. Contains instructions for tone, style, and behavior.

## Concrete Example

SOUL.md: You are Hermes, a helpful and friendly assistant. Be concise. Use Hong Kong examples. Speak formally. Hermes reads this and adopts the personality.

## Analogy

A role description for an actor - it tells them how to play the character. SOUL.md tells Hermes how to play its role.

## Related Concepts

- [[personality|Personality]]
- [[agent-config|Agent Config]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]

title: status-bar
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

A TUI element showing session info: model name, token count, cost, turn number.

## Concrete Example

Status bar: Model: claude-sonnet-4 | Tokens: 12K/200K | Cost: $0.05 | Turn: 5. Always visible at the bottom of the TUI.

## Analogy

A car dashboard - always shows speed, fuel, temperature. The status bar always shows model, tokens, cost.

## Related Concepts

- [[display-config|Display Config]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[tui|TUI]]

title: stt-config
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The stt section: provider, model, language. Controls speech-to-text.

## Concrete Example

stt: provider: faster_whisper, model: base, language: en. When you send a voice message, faster_whisper transcribes it. The stt config picks the transcriber.

## Analogy

A subtitle settings on a video - you pick the language and style. STT config picks how voice messages are transcribed.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[stt|STT]]

title: target-ratio
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The target context usage after compression. Default: 0.20 (20%).

## Concrete Example

compression.target_ratio: 0.20. After compression, context is reduced to 20% of capacity = 40K tokens. 60K tokens freed for new messages.

## Analogy

A diet target - after cutting, you want to reach 20% body fat. Target ratio is the target context level after compression.

## Related Concepts

- [[compression-config|Compression Config]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[context-compression|Context Compression]]

title: terminal-config
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The terminal section of config.yaml. Controls shell, timeout, backend (local vs SSH).

## Concrete Example

terminal: shell: /bin/bash, timeout: 180, backend: local. The terminal section controls how shell commands are executed.

## Analogy

Settings on a microwave - power level, timer, mode. The terminal config sets how the terminal tool operates.

## Related Concepts

- [[config-sections|Config Sections]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[terminal-backend|Terminal Backend]]

title: tool-progress
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

A display setting that shows tool execution progress in real-time. Configured in display section.

## Concrete Example

display.tool_progress: true. When Hermes runs a tool, you see: Running terminal... Done. Running read_file... Done. Real-time feedback.

## Analogy

A progress bar on a download - you see how it is going. Tool progress shows each tool as it runs.

## Related Concepts

- [[display-config|Display Config]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[display-config|Display Config]]

title: tool-use-enforcement
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

How strictly Hermes enforces tool calling. Modes: strict, permissive. Configured in agent section.

## Concrete Example

agent.tool_use_enforcement: strict. The model must use tools when appropriate. If it tries to answer without checking, Hermes forces it to use tools first.

## Analogy

A teacher requiring students to show their work - they cannot just write the answer. Tool use enforcement requires the model to use tools before answering.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-config|Agent Config]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[tool-calling|Tool Calling]]

title: tts-config
text:
> **Domain:** [[_configuration-moc|Configuration]]

## Motivation

The tts section: provider, voice, speed. Controls text-to-speech.

## Concrete Example

tts: provider: edge, voice: en-US-JennyNeural, speed: 1.0. Hermes replies are spoken in Jennie voice. The tts config picks the narrator.

## Analogy

title: credential-pools
text:
> **Domain:** [[_models-providers-moc|Models & Providers]]

## Motivation

Multiple API keys for the same provider. Hermes rotates across them to avoid rate limits.

## Concrete Example

Pool: [key1, key2, key3]. key1 hits rate limit -> switch to key2. key2 expires -> key3. When key1 resets -> switch back. No interruption.

## Analogy

A fleet of delivery scooters - when one runs out of fuel, switch to another. Credential pools ensure uninterrupted service.

## Related Concepts

title: credential-rotation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_models-providers-moc|Models & Providers]]

## Motivation

Automatically switching between API keys in a pool when one becomes exhausted or rate-limited.

## Concrete Example

key1: 50 req/min. At req 51 -> key2. At key2 limit -> key3. When key1 resets -> back to key1. Continuous rotation = no downtime.

## Analogy

Shift workers at a 24-hour restaurant - when one finishes, another takes over. Credential rotation keeps the agent running 24/7.

## Related Concepts

Choosing transportation: MTR for speed, bus for cost, taxi for convenience. Different providers for different needs.

- [[provider-agnostic|Provider Agnostic]]
- [[hermes-model|Hermes Model]]
- [[provider|Provider]]

title: qwen-oauth
text:
> **Domain:** [[_models-providers-moc|Models & Providers]]

## Motivation

Alibaba Qwen models accessible via OAuth instead of API key. Easier authentication.

## Concrete Example

hermes auth add qwen --oauth. Browser opens, you log in. Token is saved. No API key needed. Qwen is now available.

## Analogy

Using a student ID to access campus services - no need for a separate pass. Qwen OAuth uses login instead of API keys.

## Related Concepts

- [[oauth|OAuth]]
- [[alibaba-dashscope|Alibaba DashScope]]
- [[auth-json|Auth JSON]]

title: rate-limiting
text:
> **Domain:** [[_models-providers-moc|Models & Providers]]

## Motivation

When a provider limits how many requests you can make per minute. Credential pools help avoid this.

## Concrete Example

OpenAI: 50 req/min. At req 51 -> error: rate limit exceeded. Solution: credential pool with 3 keys = 150 req/min. Or switch providers.

## Analogy

A water meter limiting flow - you can only use so much per hour. Rate limiting limits how many API calls you can make.

## Related Concepts

- [[credential-pools|Credential Pools]]
- [[credential-rotation|Credential Rotation]]
- [[provider|Provider]]

title: streaming
text:
> **Domain:** [[_models-providers-moc|Models & Providers]]

## Motivation

Receiving the model response token by token as it is generated, rather than waiting for the full response.

## Concrete Example

Streaming: You see each word appear: The... weather... is... sunny. Like watching someone type. Faster perceived response vs waiting for full text.

## Analogy

Watching a live sports broadcast vs a recording - live is more exciting. Streaming shows the response as it is generated.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-model|Hermes Model]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]
- [[models-providers|Models & Providers]]

title: token-cost
text:
> **Domain:** [[_models-providers-moc|Models & Providers]]

## Motivation

The cost of using an LLM. Measured in tokens. Different providers have different prices.

## Concrete Example

Claude: $3/1M input, $15/1M output. GPT-4o: $2.50/1M input, $10/1M output. DeepSeek: $0.14/1M input, $0.28/1M output. Prices vary widely.

## Analogy

Parking fees - different carparks have different rates. Token costs vary by provider. Choose based on budget.

## Related Concepts

- [[provider-selection|Provider Selection]]
- [[show-cost|Show Cost]]
- [[models-providers|Models & Providers]]

title: tool-use-support
text:
> **Domain:** [[_models-providers-moc|Models & Providers]]

## Motivation

Whether a model supports function/tool calling. Most modern models do, but quality varies.

## Concrete Example

Claude: excellent tool use. GPT-4o: good. Some smaller models: poor or no tool use. Tool use is essential for agents.

## Analogy

A worker who can use tools vs one who can only talk. Tool use support determines if a model can be an agent.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-calling|Tool Calling]]
- [[provider-selection|Provider Selection]]
- [[models-providers|Models & Providers]]

title: vision-support
text:
> **Domain:** [[_models-providers-moc|Models & Providers]]

## Motivation

Whether a model can analyze images. GPT-4o, Claude, and Gemini support vision.

## Concrete Example

GPT-4o: send a photo, it describes what it sees. Claude: same. Some models: text only, no vision. Vision support enables image analysis.

## Analogy

A friend who can see vs one who is blind. Vision support lets the model see and analyze images.

## Related Concepts

- [[vision-model|Vision Model]]
- [[provider-selection|Provider Selection]]
- [[models-providers|Models & Providers]]

title: vllm
text:
> **Domain:** [[_models-providers-moc|Models & Providers]]

## Motivation

A high-throughput LLM serving engine. Runs models locally with optimized inference.

## Concrete Example

vLLM: python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server --model llama-3.3-70b. High throughput, OpenAI-compatible API. Hermes connects via base_url.

## Analogy

An espresso machine for a cafe - high volume, fast, professional. vLLM is for serving models to many users at high speed.

## Related Concepts

- [[local-model|Local Model]]
- [[provider|Provider]]
- [[models-providers|Models & Providers]]

title: xai-grok
text:
> **Domain:** [[_models-providers-moc|Models & Providers]]

## Motivation

Elon Musk AI company. Grok models. Known for real-time knowledge and humor.

## Concrete Example

xai/grok-2: real-time X/Twitter knowledge. hermes model set xai/grok-2. Grok can access current events via X.

## Analogy

A news channel with live updates - always current. Grok has real-time knowledge from X.

## Related Concepts

- [[provider|Provider]]
- [[models-providers|Models & Providers]]
- [[hermes-model|Hermes Model]]

title: zai-glm
text:
> **Domain:** [[_models-providers-moc|Models & Providers]]

## Motivation

Zhipu AI (Z.AI) models. GLM-4, GLM-5. Known for strong Chinese and English bilingual support.

## Concrete Example

zai/glm-4-plus: excellent for Chinese and English. hermes model set zai/glm-4-plus. Great for Hong Kong students who use both languages.

## Analogy

A bilingual teacher - fluent in both Chinese and English. Z.AI GLM is the bilingual LLM.

- [[provider|Provider]]
- [[models-providers|Models & Providers]]
- [[hermes-model|Hermes Model]]

title: background-tasks
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

Long-running tasks started with terminal(background=true). Tracked by the process tool. Can be polled, waited on, or killed.

## Concrete Example

terminal(command=python train.py, background=true). Task runs in background. process(action=poll). Check progress. process(action=wait). Block until done.

## Analogy

Running a download in the background - you continue working while it downloads. Background tasks let Hermes work while long tasks run.

## Related Concepts

- [[process-tool|Process Tool]]
- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[terminal-backend|Terminal Backend]]

title: browser-back
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool that navigates back to the previous page in browser history.

## Concrete Example

browser_back(). Goes back to the previous page. Like pressing the Back button in your browser.

## Analogy

The back button on a browser - you go to the previous page. Browser back lets Hermes navigate backward.

## Related Concepts

- [[browser-tool|Browser Tool]]
- [[web-toolset|Web Toolset]]
- [[browser-navigate|Browser Navigate]]

title: browser-click
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool that clicks an element on a web page by its ref ID.

## Concrete Example

browser_click(ref=@e5). Clicks the element with ref @e5 (e.g., a Submit button). The page updates. New snapshot available.

## Analogy

Pressing a button on an elevator - you press floor 5, the elevator goes there. Browser click presses buttons on web pages.

## Related Concepts

- [[browser-tool|Browser Tool]]
- [[web-toolset|Web Toolset]]
- [[browser-snapshot|Browser Snapshot]]

title: browser-console
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool that gets browser console output and JavaScript errors. Also evaluates JS expressions.

## Concrete Example

browser_console(expression=document.title). Returns: Example Domain. JavaScript executed in the page. Console errors visible.

## Analogy

Opening Developer Tools in a browser - you see console messages and errors. Browser console lets Hermes see page internals.

## Related Concepts

- [[browser-tool|Browser Tool]]
- [[web-toolset|Web Toolset]]
- [[browser-snapshot|Browser Snapshot]]

title: browser-get-images
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool that lists all images on the current page with URLs and alt text.

## Concrete Example

browser_get_images(). Returns: [{url: img1.jpg, alt: Logo}, {url: img2.jpg, alt: Photo}]. All images listed.

## Analogy

A photo gallery - you see all photos with labels. Browser get images lists all images on a page.

## Related Concepts

- [[browser-tool|Browser Tool]]
- [[web-toolset|Web Toolset]]
- [[vision-tool|Vision Tool]]

title: browser-press
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool that presses a keyboard key. Useful for submitting forms (Enter), navigating (Tab).

## Concrete Example

browser_press(key=Enter). Submits the form. Or: browser_press(key=Tab). Moves to the next field. Keyboard interaction.

## Analogy

Pressing keys on a keyboard - Enter to submit, Tab to move. Browser press lets Hermes use the keyboard on web pages.

## Related Concepts

- [[browser-tool|Browser Tool]]
- [[web-toolset|Web Toolset]]
- [[browser-type|Browser Type]]

title: browser-scroll
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool that scrolls the page up or down to reveal more content.

## Concrete Example

browser_scroll(direction=down). Page scrolls down. More content visible. New snapshot available. Useful for long pages.

## Analogy

Scrolling on your phone - you swipe up to see more. Browser scroll lets Hermes see more of a long page.

## Related Concepts

- [[browser-tool|Browser Tool]]
- [[web-toolset|Web Toolset]]
- [[browser-snapshot|Browser Snapshot]]

title: browser-snapshot
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool that captures the current page accessibility tree. Returns interactive elements with ref IDs for clicking.

## Concrete Example

browser_snapshot(). Returns: button [ref=@e5] Submit, textbox [ref=@e3] Search. Each element has a ref for clicking.

## Analogy

A map of a room - it shows where everything is. Browser snapshot maps the page so Hermes knows what to click.

## Related Concepts

- [[browser-tool|Browser Tool]]
- [[web-toolset|Web Toolset]]
- [[browser-click|Browser Click]]

title: browser-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool for web browser automation. Navigate, click, type, screenshot. Uses Browserbase, Camofox, or local Chromium.

## Concrete Example

browser_navigate(url=https://example.com). browser_click(ref=@e5). browser_type(ref=@e3, text=Hello). Full browser automation.

## Analogy

A remote-controlled hand - it navigates, clicks, and types on web pages. The browser tool lets Hermes browse the web.

## Related Concepts

- [[web-toolset|Web Toolset]]
- [[browser-automation|Browser Automation]]
- [[browserbase|Browserbase]]

title: browser-type
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool that types text into an input field on a web page.

## Concrete Example

browser_type(ref=@e3, text=Hello World). Types Hello World into the text field with ref @e3. Like filling in a form.

## Analogy

Writing on a form with a pen - you fill in the blanks. Browser type fills in web forms.

## Related Concepts

- [[browser-tool|Browser Tool]]
- [[web-toolset|Web Toolset]]
- [[browser-snapshot|Browser Snapshot]]

title: browser-vision
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool that takes a screenshot for visual analysis. Useful for CAPTCHAs, complex layouts, visual verification.

## Concrete Example

browser_vision(question=What does this page look like?). Screenshot taken. Analysis: The page has a blue header with a login form. Visual understanding.

## Analogy

Taking a photo of a screen - you can see what is displayed. Browser vision lets Hermes see what the web page looks like.

## Related Concepts

- [[browser-tool|Browser Tool]]
- [[web-toolset|Web Toolset]]
- [[vision-tool|Vision Tool]]

title: clarify-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool for asking the user a question when the model needs clarification.

## Concrete Example

clarify(question=Which database?, choices=[PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite]). User picks PostgreSQL. Model proceeds with PostgreSQL.

## Analogy

Raising your hand in class to ask a question - you need more info before proceeding. The clarify tool lets the model ask the user.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[user-interaction|User Interaction]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]

title: code-execution
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool for running Python code programmatically. Used for multi-step logic, data processing, loops.

## Concrete Example

execute_code(code=print(2+2)). Returns: 4. Used for: filtering data, conditional logic, loops, calculations. More flexible than single tool calls.

## Analogy

A calculator that can do complex math - not just 2+2 but full equations with variables. Code execution lets Hermes run Python programs.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[terminal|Terminal]]
- [[sandbox-security|Sandbox Security]]

title: core-tools
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

The essential tools that Hermes always has: terminal, read_file, write_file, patch, search_files, browser, web_search, web_extract, todo, memory, session_search, skills, delegate_task, cronjob, clarify, text_to_speech, vision_analyze, image_generate.

## Concrete Example

Core tools: always available. terminal (shell), read_file/write_file (files), web_search (internet), browser (web automation), todo (task list), memory (persistence). The foundation.

## Analogy

The basic tools in a toolbox - hammer, screwdriver, wrench. Always there. Core tools are the basic set Hermes always has.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[tool-registry|Tool Registry]]
- [[tool-calling|Tool Calling]]

title: cronjob-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool for creating and managing scheduled tasks. The model can set up recurring jobs.

## Concrete Example

cronjob(action=create, schedule=every 2h, prompt=Check server status). A cron job is created. Every 2 hours, Hermes checks the server.

## Analogy

An alarm clock that repeats - you set it and it goes off regularly. The cronjob tool lets the model set recurring tasks.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[cron-jobs|Cron Jobs]]
- [[automation|Automation]]

title: delegation-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool for spawning subagents. The model can delegate tasks to isolated subagents.

## Concrete Example

delegate_task(goal=Debug the auth module, context=File: auth.py). A subagent is spawned. It works in isolation. Result returned when done.

## Analogy

A manager delegating tasks to team members - each works independently. The delegation tool lets the model spawn subagents.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[delegate-task|Delegate Task]]
- [[subagent|Subagent]]

title: discord-admin-toolset
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

Tools for Discord server administration: manage roles, channels, bans.

## Concrete Example

discord_admin: ban user, create role, delete channel. Administrative actions on Discord. Available when Hermes is a Discord admin.

## Analogy

A moderator badge at an event - you can manage crowd, remove troublemakers. Discord admin tools let Hermes moderate a Discord server.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[discord|Discord]]
- [[gateway|Gateway]]

title: file-tools
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

Tools for file operations: read_file, write_file, patch, search_files. Part of the terminal toolset.

## Concrete Example

read_file: cat with line numbers. write_file: create/overwrite. patch: find-and-replace. search_files: grep/find. All file operations.

## Analogy

A filing cabinet with tools - you read, write, modify, and search files. File tools give Hermes a filing cabinet.

## Related Concepts

- [[terminal-toolset|Terminal Toolset]]
- [[read-file|Read File]]
- [[write-file|Write File]]

title: hermes-core-tools
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

The set of tools always loaded. Defined in toolsets.py as _HERMES_CORE_TOOLS. Cannot be disabled.

## Concrete Example

_CORE_TOOLS: [terminal, read_file, write_file, patch, search_files, browser_*, web_search, todo, memory, session_search, skills, delegate_task, cronjob, clarify, tts, vision, image_generate]. Always available.

## Analogy

The foundation of a house - always there, cannot be removed. Core tools are always loaded and cannot be disabled.

## Related Concepts

- [[core-tools|Core Tools]]
- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[tool-registry|Tool Registry]]

title: hermes-tools
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

The CLI command for managing tools. Subcommands: list, search, enable, disable, check.

## Concrete Example

hermes tools list: shows all tools and status. hermes tools enable web_search: turns on a tool. hermes tools disable tts: turns off a tool. All tool management in one command.

## Analogy

A control panel for appliances - you see all appliances and can turn them on/off. hermes tools manages all Hermes tools.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[tool-enable|Tool Enable]]
- [[tool-disable|Tool Disable]]

title: image-generation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool for creating images from text descriptions. Text-to-image using FAL, OpenAI, or other backends.

## Concrete Example

image_generate(prompt=a cat in a space suit, aspect_ratio=square). Returns: image URL. Text became an image.

## Analogy

A magic paintbrush - you describe what you want, it paints it. Image generation creates images from text descriptions.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[image-gen|Image Gen]]
- [[fal|FAL]]

title: kanban-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool for managing a Kanban board with columns and cards. Visual task management.

## Concrete Example

kanban(add card=Fix auth bug to column=Todo). kanban(move card=Fix auth bug to column=Doing). Visual project management.

## Analogy

A whiteboard with sticky notes - you move tasks from To Do to Doing to Done. The Kanban tool is a digital whiteboard for tasks.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[task-management|Task Management]]
- [[cron-jobs|Cron Jobs]]

title: lsp-diagnostics
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

Language Server Protocol integration. Hermes can get code diagnostics (errors, warnings) from LSP servers.

## Concrete Example

When editing Python, LSP checks: line 5: undefined variable foo. Hermes sees this and fixes it. Real-time code analysis.

## Analogy

A spell checker for code - it underlines errors as you type. LSP diagnostics give Hermes real-time code error checking.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[code-execution|Code Execution]]
- [[ide-integration|IDE Integration]]

title: memory-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool for reading and writing persistent memory. The model can save facts and recall them later.

## Concrete Example

memory(action=add, target=user, content=User prefers Python). Fact saved. Next session: fact is recalled. Persistent across sessions.

## Analogy

A sticky note on your desk - you write something and it stays. The memory tool lets the model write and read sticky notes.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[persistent-memory|Persistent Memory]]
- [[memory-operations|Memory Operations]]

title: messaging-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

Tools for sending messages across platforms. The model can send messages to Telegram, Discord, etc.

## Concrete Example

send_message(platform=telegram, chat_id=123, text=Hello). Message sent to Telegram chat. Cross-platform messaging from within the agent.

## Analogy

A messaging app on your phone - you send messages to contacts. The messaging tool lets Hermes send messages to platforms.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[gateway|Gateway]]
- [[platforms|Platforms]]

title: moa-toolset
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

Mixture of Agents toolset. Sends queries to multiple models and synthesizes results.

## Concrete Example

moa ask: What is 2+2? Claude: 4. GPT-4o: 4. Gemini: 4. Synthesis: 4 (all agree). Multiple models, one answer.

## Analogy

A panel of experts - you ask 3 experts and combine their answers. The moa toolset queries multiple models.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[mixture-of-agents|Mixture of Agents]]
- [[model-routing|Model Routing]]

title: notify-on-complete
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A flag for background tasks. When true, Hermes notifies the user when the task finishes.

## Concrete Example

terminal(command=pytest, background=true, notify_on_complete=true). Tests run in background. When done: notification sent. You know without polling.

## Analogy

A delivery notification - you get a text when your package arrives. notify_on_complete tells you when a background task finishes.

## Related Concepts

- [[background-tasks|Background Tasks]]
- [[process-tool|Process Tool]]
- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]

title: patch-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool for targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Uses fuzzy matching. Used instead of sed/awk.

## Concrete Example

patch(path=file.py, old=print(hello), new=print(world)). Finds print(hello) in file.py, replaces with print(world). Targeted edit.

## Analogy

A correction pen - you fix a specific word without rewriting the whole page. The patch tool fixes specific text without rewriting the whole file.

## Related Concepts

- [[file-tools|File Tools]]
- [[read-file|Read File]]
- [[write-file|Write File]]

title: process-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool for managing background processes. Actions: list, poll, log, wait, kill, write, submit, close.

## Concrete Example

process(action=list). Shows all background processes. process(action=kill, session_id=xxx). Kills a process. Full background process management.

## Analogy

A task manager on your computer - you see running processes and can stop them. The process tool manages background tasks.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[background-tasks|Background Tasks]]
- [[terminal-backend|Terminal Backend]]

title: read-file
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool that reads file contents with line numbers. Pagination supported. Used instead of cat.

## Concrete Example

read_file(path=/home/alice/notes.txt). Returns: 1|Hello 2|World 3|Foo. Line numbers included. Pagination for large files.

## Analogy

A photocopier that also numbers pages - you copy a document and each page is numbered. read_file reads files with line numbers.

## Related Concepts

- [[file-tools|File Tools]]
- [[write-file|Write File]]
- [[terminal-toolset|Terminal Toolset]]

title: safe-toolset
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A restricted toolset with only safe tools. No terminal, no file deletion. Used in educational or restricted environments.

## Concrete Example

safe toolset: [read_file, web_search, todo, memory]. No terminal (no shell commands). No write_file (no file changes). Safe for students.

## Analogy

Training wheels on a bicycle - you can ride but cannot fall. The safe toolset lets the model work but not break anything.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[tool-disable|Tool Disable]]
- [[security-overview|Security Overview]]

title: search-files
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool for searching file contents or finding files by name. Ripgrep-backed. Used instead of grep/find.

## Concrete Example

search_files(pattern=TODO, target=content). Returns: file.py:15: TODO fix this. search_files(pattern=*.py, target=files). Returns: file1.py, file2.py.

## Analogy

A search engine for your computer - you type a keyword and find matching files or content. search_files searches your filesystem.

## Related Concepts

- [[file-tools|File Tools]]
- [[terminal-toolset|Terminal Toolset]]
- [[read-file|Read File]]

title: session-search-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool for searching past conversation history. FTS5-backed full-text search.

## Concrete Example

session_search(query=docker debugging, limit=3). Returns: 3 past sessions about Docker debugging. The model can recall past conversations.

## Analogy

A search engine for your chat history - you type a keyword and find past conversations. Session search lets the model recall past chats.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[sessions|Sessions]]
- [[session-search-model|Session Search Model]]

title: skills-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool for loading and using skills. The model can browse, load, and follow skill instructions.

## Concrete Example

Model: I need to debug. /skill debugging. Skill loaded. Model follows the debugging steps. The skills tool gives access to the skill library.

## Analogy

A library card - you browse, check out, and read books. The skills tool lets the model browse and use skills.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[skills-system|Skills System]]
- [[skill-loading|Skill Loading]]

title: terminal-backend
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

The backend used by the terminal tool. Options: local (direct shell), SSH (remote shell). Configured in terminal section.

## Concrete Example

terminal.backend: local. Commands run on the local machine. terminal.backend: ssh. Commands run on a remote server via SSH. Flexible.

## Analogy

A kitchen at home vs a restaurant kitchen - you can cook locally or remotely. The terminal backend chooses where commands run.

## Related Concepts

- [[terminal-config|Terminal Config]]
- [[terminal-toolset|Terminal Toolset]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]

title: terminal-toolset
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

Tools for shell and file operations: terminal, read_file, write_file, patch, search_files.

## Concrete Example

terminal: run shell commands. read_file: read files with line numbers. write_file: create/edit files. patch: find-and-replace. search_files: grep/find. Full filesystem access.

## Analogy

A terminal window on your computer - you run commands, edit files, search. The terminal toolset gives Hermes a terminal.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[terminal|Terminal]]
- [[read-file|Read File]]

title: todo-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool for managing a task list within the session. The model can track multi-step tasks.

## Concrete Example

todo(todos=[{id:1, content:Read file, status:done}, {id:2, content:Fix bug, status:in_progress}]). Task list tracked. Progress visible.

## Analogy

A checklist on your desk - you list tasks and check them off. The todo tool lets the model track its task list.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[task-management|Task Management]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]

title: tool-calling
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

The mechanism by which the LLM requests to use a tool. The model outputs a structured tool call; Hermes executes it and returns the result.

## Concrete Example

Model: I need to check the weather. call weather_api(city=HK). Hermes executes weather_api, gets 28C sunny, returns result. Model uses it to answer.

## Analogy

A customer ordering at a restaurant - they tell the waiter what they want. The waiter (Hermes) brings it. The model orders tools, Hermes executes them.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-dispatch|Tool Dispatch]]
- [[tool-registry|Tool Registry]]
- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[mcp-bridge|MCP Bridge]]
- [[entry-points-pattern|Entry Points Pattern]]

title: tool-check
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

Verify that a tool is working correctly. Command: hermes tools check TOOL_NAME.

## Concrete Example

hermes tools check terminal. Output: terminal: OK (backend: local, shell: bash). hermes tools check web_search: OK (provider: hosted). Verify tools before relying on them.

## Analogy

A diagnostic test on a car - you check if each part works. Tool check verifies each tool is functional.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-tools|Hermes Tools]]
- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[tool-handler|Tool Handler]]

title: tool-disable
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

Turn off a specific tool. Command: hermes tools disable TOOL_NAME. Or /tools disable in session.

## Concrete Example

hermes tools disable terminal. The model can no longer run shell commands. Safer for restricted environments. /tools disable tts. No voice output.

## Analogy

Turning off a light switch - the light is off, cannot be used. Tool disable turns off a specific tool so the model cannot use it.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-tools|Hermes Tools]]
- [[tool-enable|Tool Enable]]
- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]

title: tool-dispatch
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

The process of routing a tool call to the correct handler. Located in model_tools.py. Called when the model outputs a tool_call.

## Concrete Example

Model calls: terminal(command=ls). handle_function_call routes to terminal handler. Handler executes ls. Returns: file listing. Result appended to conversation.

## Analogy

A switchboard operator - you say connect me to billing, they route your call. Tool dispatch routes model requests to the correct tool handler.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-calling|Tool Calling]]
- [[tool-registry|Tool Registry]]
- [[tool-handler|Tool Handler]]

title: tool-enable
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

Turn on a specific tool. Command: hermes tools enable TOOL_NAME. Or /tools enable in session.

## Concrete Example

hermes tools enable web_search. web_search is now available. The model can use it. /tools enable image_gen. Enabled for this session.

## Analogy

Turning on a light switch - the light is now available. Tool enable turns on a specific tool for the model to use.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-tools|Hermes Tools]]
- [[tool-disable|Tool Disable]]
- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]

title: tool-handler
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

The Python function that executes when a tool is called. Located in tools/*.py. Each tool has its own handler.

## Concrete Example

terminal handler: def terminal(command, timeout=180): # executes shell command, returns output. The handler does the actual work.

## Analogy

The chef in a kitchen - the order (tool call) comes in, the chef (handler) cooks it. Each tool has its own chef (handler).

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-dispatch|Tool Dispatch]]
- [[tool-registry|Tool Registry]]
- [[tool-schema|Tool Schema]]

title: tool-isolation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

Tools operate with limited scope. The terminal tool cannot access .env. The file tool cannot write to system directories.

## Concrete Example

terminal: cannot cat .env (redacted). file: cannot write to /etc/. Each tool has boundaries that protect the system.

## Analogy

Different keycards in a hotel - your room key opens your room only. Tool isolation gives each tool limited access.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[security-overview|Security Overview]]
- [[sandbox-security|Sandbox Security]]

title: tool-progress-display
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A visual indicator showing which tool is running and its progress. Configured in display section.

## Concrete Example

Tool running: [terminal] ls -la... Done. [read_file] notes.txt... Done. [web_search] AI news... Running... Real-time feedback.

## Analogy

A progress bar on a download - you see what is happening. Tool progress display shows each tool as it runs.

## Related Concepts

- [[display-config|Display Config]]
- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[tui|TUI]]

title: tool-registry
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

Central registry of all tools. Located in tools/registry.py. Tools register at import time. The master list of available tools.

## Concrete Example

registry.register(name=terminal, schema=..., handler=...). At startup, all tools/*.py are imported. Each registers itself. The registry is the master list.

## Analogy

A phone directory - every number is listed with a name. The tool registry lists every tool with its name, schema, and handler.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-dispatch|Tool Dispatch]]
- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[tool-handler|Tool Handler]]

title: tool-requirements
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

Some tools require specific config or setup. Hermes checks requirements before enabling a tool.

## Concrete Example

web_search requires: API key or Tool Gateway. spotify requires: Spotify Premium account. vision requires: vision model configured. Requirements checked at startup.

## Analogy

Prerequisites for a class - you need a textbook before attending. Tool requirements must be met before a tool can be used.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[hermes-tools|Hermes Tools]]
- [[tool-check|Tool Check]]

title: tool-result-truncation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

When tool output is too long, it is truncated to fit in context. The model sees a summary instead of full output.

## Concrete Example

terminal output: 50,000 lines. Too long. Truncated to: first 100 lines + ... + last 100 lines (500 lines total). Fits in context.

## Analogy

A summary of a long book - instead of reading 500 pages, you read a 5-page summary. Tool result truncation summarizes long outputs.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[context-window|Context Window]]
- [[context-compression|Context Compression]]

title: tool-schema
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

The JSON schema describing a tool parameters and return type. The model uses this to know how to call the tool.

## Concrete Example

Schema: {name: terminal, parameters: {command: string, timeout: int}}. The model sees this and knows: I need to provide a command string. Structured interface.

## Analogy

A recipe format - it tells you what ingredients to provide and in what order. The tool schema tells the model what parameters to provide.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-calling|Tool Calling]]
- [[tool-registry|Tool Registry]]
- [[tool-handler|Tool Handler]]

title: tool-search
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

Search for tools by keyword. Command: hermes tools search KEYWORD.

## Concrete Example

hermes tools search file. Results: read_file, write_file, patch, search_files. Find the right tool fast.

## Analogy

Searching an app store - you type a keyword and see matching apps. Tool search finds matching tools by keyword.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-tools|Hermes Tools]]
- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[tool-enable|Tool Enable]]

title: tool-timeout
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

The maximum time a tool can run before being killed. Configured per-tool or globally.

## Concrete Example

terminal timeout: 180s. If a command runs longer than 180s, it is killed. Prevents hanging. web_search timeout: 30s. Different timeouts for different tools.

## Analogy

A timer on an exam - when time is up, you must stop. Tool timeout stops tools that run too long.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[terminal-config|Terminal Config]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]

title: toolsets
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

Named groups of tools. Examples: web, terminal, file, vision, image_gen, tts, skills, memory, delegation, cronjob. Each toolset is a category.

## Concrete Example

toolset terminal: [terminal, read_file, write_file, patch, search_files]. toolset web: [web_search, web_extract, browser_navigate]. Groups for easy management.

## Analogy

A toolbox with compartments - screwdrivers in one, wrenches in another, hammers in a third. Toolsets group tools by category.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-registry|Tool Registry]]
- [[tool-calling|Tool Calling]]
- [[tool-enable|Tool Enable]]

title: tts-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool for converting text to speech audio. Multiple providers supported.

## Concrete Example

text_to_speech(text=Hello, how are you?). Returns: audio file. On Telegram, sent as a voice message. Text became audio.

## Analogy

An audiobook narrator - they read text aloud. The TTS tool reads Hermes text responses aloud.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[tts|TTS]]
- [[edge-tts|Edge TTS]]

title: vision-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool for analyzing images. The model can see and understand images. Uses the vision auxiliary model.

## Concrete Example

vision_analyze(image_url=photo.jpg, question=What is in this image?). Returns: A cat sitting on a desk. Image understood.

## Analogy

A friend who describes what they see - you show them a photo, they tell you what is in it. The vision tool lets Hermes see images.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[vision-model|Vision Model]]
- [[vision-support|Vision Support]]

title: watch-patterns
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A flag for background tasks. Hermes watches for specific strings in the output and notifies when they appear.

## Concrete Example

terminal(command=server.py, background=true, watch_patterns=[Startup complete]). When server prints Startup complete, you are notified.

## Analogy

A baby monitor - it alerts you when the baby cries. Watch patterns alert you when specific text appears in task output.

## Related Concepts

- [[background-tasks|Background Tasks]]
- [[process-tool|Process Tool]]
- [[notify-on-complete|Notify On Complete]]

title: web-toolset
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

Tools for web interaction: web_search, web_extract, browser_navigate, browser_click, browser_type, browser_snapshot, browser_vision.

## Concrete Example

web_search: find information. web_extract: read web pages. browser_navigate: open URLs. browser_click: click elements. Full web interaction.

## Analogy

A web browser on your computer - you search, read, click, type. The web toolset gives Hermes a web browser.

## Related Concepts

- [[toolsets|Toolsets]]
- [[web-search|Web Search]]
- [[browser|Browser]]

title: write-file
text:
> **Domain:** [[_tools-toolsets-moc|Tools & Toolsets]]

## Motivation

A tool that writes content to a file, overwriting if it exists. Creates parent directories. Used instead of echo/cat.

## Concrete Example

write_file(path=/home/alice/notes.txt, content=Hello World). File created with content. If it exists, overwritten. Simple file creation.

## Analogy

A pen and paper - you write content on the page. If the page has old content, you erase it first. write_file writes content to files.

## Related Concepts

- [[file-tools|File Tools]]
- [[read-file|Read File]]
- [[patch-tool|Patch Tool]]
