title: curator-archive
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

The curator moves a stale skill to an archive folder instead of deleting it. Archived skills can be restored later.

## Concrete Example

The curator archives unused-skill-v1 to ~/.hermes/skills/.archive/. It is out of the active library but not gone. You can restore it if needed.

## Analogy

Moving old clothes to a storage box in the attic - you are not wearing them but they are not thrown away. You can retrieve them if needed. Archiving skills works the same way.

## Related Concepts

- [[curator-restore|Curator Restore]]
- [[stale-skills|Stale Skills]]
- [[curator|Curator]]

title: curator-backup
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Saving a snapshot of all skills before the curator makes changes, so you can undo if something goes wrong.

## Concrete Example

Before archiving 3 skills, the curator creates a backup: skills-backup-2026-08-04.tar.gz. If the changes were wrong, you can restore from this backup.

## Analogy

Saving a game before a risky mission - if things go wrong, you reload the save. Curator backup saves the skill library state before making changes.

## Related Concepts

- [[curator-rollback|Curator Rollback]]
- [[curator-archive|Curator Archive]]
- [[curator|Curator]]

title: curator-pause
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Temporarily stopping the curator from making changes. Useful when you are actively working on skills and do not want them moved.

## Concrete Example

hermes curator pause stops automatic maintenance. Now your skills stay exactly as they are until you resume. Useful when editing multiple SKILL.md files.

## Analogy

Pausing an alarm system while you are home - you do not want it triggering while you are moving around. Curator pause prevents changes while you are actively editing.

## Related Concepts

- [[curator-resume|Curator Resume]]
- [[curator-status|Curator Status]]
- [[curator|Curator]]

title: curator-pin
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Marking a skill as protected so the curator will never archive or modify it. Pinned skills stay forever.

## Concrete Example

hermes curator pin github-pr-workflow marks it as pinned. The curator sees the pin and skips it during cleanup. Even if unused for a year, it stays.

## Analogy

Putting a do not remove sticker on a box in storage - the cleaners see it and leave that box alone. Pinning protects a skill from being cleaned up.

## Related Concepts

- [[curator-unpin|Curator Unpin]]
- [[skill-pinning|Skill Pinning]]
- [[curator|Curator]]

title: curator-prune
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

The curator permanently deletes very old archived skills that have not been restored. Pruning keeps the archive from growing forever.

## Concrete Example

hermes curator prune deletes skills archived over 6 months ago that were never restored. This frees up disk space and keeps the archive manageable.

## Analogy

Throwing out clothes you have not worn in years - you kept them in storage, but eventually you donate them. Pruning permanently removes old archived skills.

## Related Concepts

- [[curator-archive|Curator Archive]]
- [[curator-backup|Curator Backup]]
- [[curator|Curator]]

title: curator-restore
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Bringing an archived skill back into the active library. Useful if you need a skill you previously archived.

## Concrete Example

hermes curator restore unused-skill-v1 moves it from .archive back to the active skills directory. It is available again for the agent to load and use.

## Analogy

Taking winter clothes out of storage when cold weather returns - you packed them away, now you bring them back. Restore does this for archived skills.

## Related Concepts

- [[curator-archive|Curator Archive]]
- [[curator|Curator]]
- [[skills-list|Skills List]]

title: curator-resume
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Restarting the curator after a pause so it resumes automatic maintenance of the skill library.

## Concrete Example

hermes curator resume un-pauses the curator. It will run on its next scheduled time. Any changes you made to skills during the pause are now visible to it.

## Analogy

Turning the alarm back on after leaving the house - you paused it while inside, now you resume it as you leave. Curator resume restarts maintenance.

## Related Concepts

- [[curator-pause|Curator Pause]]
- [[curator-status|Curator Status]]
- [[curator|Curator]]

title: curator-rollback
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Undoing curator changes by restoring from a backup. If the curator archived something you needed, rollback brings it back.

## Concrete Example

hermes curator rollback skills-backup-2026-08-04 restores all skills to how they were on that date. The wrongly-archived skill comes back.

## Analogy

Pressing undo after a bad edit - you revert to the previous version. Curator rollback undoes the curator changes by restoring a backup.

## Related Concepts

- [[curator-backup|Curator Backup]]
- [[curator-archive|Curator Archive]]
- [[curator|Curator]]

title: curator-run
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Manually triggering the curator to do a maintenance pass right now, instead of waiting for the next scheduled run.

## Concrete Example

hermes curator run starts a pass immediately. It scans all skills, archives stale ones, updates descriptions, and reports: Archived 1, updated 2, no issues found.

## Analogy

Pressing the clean now button on a robot vacuum - instead of waiting for the scheduled time, you tell it to clean right now. Curator run triggers immediate maintenance.

## Related Concepts

- [[curator|Curator]]
- [[curator-status|Curator Status]]
- [[stale-skills|Stale Skills]]

title: curator-status
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Checking what the curator is doing or has done: is it running, paused, what changes has it made recently?

## Concrete Example

hermes curator status shows: State: running / Last run: 2 hours ago / Actions: archived 2 stale skills, updated 3 descriptions. You see the curator recent activity.

## Analogy

Checking a cleaning schedule - the cleaner logged: vacuumed living room, cleaned kitchen, skipped garage. Curator status shows what maintenance was done.

## Related Concepts

- [[curator|Curator]]
- [[curator-run|Curator Run]]
- [[curator-pause|Curator Pause]]

title: curator-unpin
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Removing the pin protection from a skill so the curator can manage it normally again (archive if stale, update descriptions).

## Concrete Example

hermes curator unpin old-experiment removes the pin. Now if it goes stale, the curator may archive it. You unpin when a skill is no longer critical.

## Analogy

Removing the do not remove sticker - the cleaners can now clear that box if it is old. Unpinning lets the curator manage the skill normally again.

## Related Concepts

- [[curator-pin|Curator Pin]]
- [[skill-pinning|Skill Pinning]]
- [[curator|Curator]]

title: curator
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

A background process that manages the skill library automatically: archiving stale skills, updating descriptions, and keeping things tidy.

## Concrete Example

The curator notices you have not used old-python-2-tool in 3 months. It archives it. It also updates a skill description that was too vague. The curator keeps the library healthy.

## Analogy

A museum curator who organises exhibits - they rotate old pieces into storage, clean dusty displays, and arrange new items. The skill curator organises the skill library.

## Related Concepts

- [[curator-status|Curator Status]]
- [[stale-skills|Stale Skills]]
- [[skill-lifecycle|Skill Lifecycle]]

title: external-skill-dirs
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Skills do not have to live only in the default folder. You can add external directories so skills can be shared across projects.

## Concrete Example

You set skills_dirs to include /mnt/shared/team-skills/. Now both your agent and your teammate agent can use the same shared skills without copying.

## Analogy

A shared network drive at school - instead of each student having their own copy of files, everyone accesses the shared drive. External skill dirs are shared skill locations.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-config|Skills Config]]
- [[skill-loading|Skill Loading]]
- [[skills-list|Skills List]]

title: reload-skills
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

A command to refresh the skill list after adding or editing skills, so the agent sees the changes without restarting.

## Concrete Example

You just edited a SKILL.md file. Typing /reload-skills makes the agent re-scan the skills directory and pick up your changes immediately.

## Analogy

Refreshing a web page after the content changes - you hit F5 to see the latest version. /reload-skills refreshes the agent view of skills.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-command|Skills Command]]
- [[skill-loading|Skill Loading]]
- [[skills-check|Skills Check]]

title: skill-assets
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Static files within a skill: images, data files, config examples. Assets are used but not executed, unlike scripts.

## Concrete Example

A pixel-art skill has assets/nes-palette.json containing the NES colour palette. The agent reads this file when generating pixel art but never runs it. It is data, not code.

## Analogy

Ingredients in a kitchen - flour, sugar, eggs are assets. You use them to cook but they are not tools (scripts). Skill assets are the raw materials a skill uses.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill-scripts|Skill Scripts]]
- [[skill-references|Skill References]]
- [[skillmd|SKILL.md]]

title: skill-auto-discovery
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

The agent automatically finds and loads relevant skills based on the task, without you manually specifying which skill to use.

## Concrete Example

You ask: Help me deploy to Kubernetes. The agent scans skill descriptions, finds k8s-troubleshooting and helm-chart-deployment, and loads them automatically. No manual command needed.

## Analogy

A smart phone suggesting the right app - when you get on a plane, it offers the airline app. When you arrive at a restaurant, it suggests the menu app. Auto-discovery suggests the right skill.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill-dispatch|Skill Dispatch]]
- [[skill-loading|Skill Loading]]
- [[skills-config|Skills Config]]

title: skill-categories
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Skills can be grouped into categories like devops, data-science, or mlops. Categories help organise the skill library and find what you need fast.

## Concrete Example

Under the devops category you find dockerfile-optimization, k8s-troubleshooting, helm-chart-deployment. Under creative you find ascii-art, pixel-art, p5js. Categories keep things tidy.

## Analogy

A library with section signs - Fiction here, Science there, History in the back. You go straight to the right section instead of searching every shelf. Categories do this for skills.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill-frontmatter|Skill Frontmatter]]
- [[skills-list|Skills List]]
- [[skills-browse|Skills Browse]]

title: skill-command
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

A slash command that manually loads a specific skill into the current session, even if the agent did not auto-discover it.

## Concrete Example

Typing /skill debugging loads the debugging skill right now. The agent reads SKILL.md and follows its steps for the rest of the conversation.

## Analogy

Asking a friend to pull out their recipe book - they might not have planned to cook that dish, but you request it, so they get the recipe out. /skill is a manual request.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-command|Skills Command]]
- [[skill-loading|Skill Loading]]
- [[skill-dispatch|Skill Dispatch]]

title: skill-conflict-resolution
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

When two skills cover the same task, the agent needs rules to pick the right one. Conflict resolution prevents confusion.

## Concrete Example

Two skills both handle git commits. The agent picks the one with a more specific description match, or the one with higher usage. Conflict resolution chooses the best match.

## Analogy

Two friends giving you different directions to the same place - you pick the one who knows the area better. Conflict resolution picks the better skill.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill-dispatch|Skill Dispatch]]
- [[skill-auto-discovery|Skill Auto-Discovery]]
- [[skills-list|Skills List]]

title: skill-creation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

When a task succeeds after several steps, you save the approach as a skill so the agent can repeat it without rediscovering the method each time.

## Concrete Example

You fixed a tricky Docker bug after 5 attempts. You save the working steps as a skill called docker-troubleshooting. Next time, the agent loads it and fixes similar bugs fast.

## Analogy

A student who figured out a great study method and writes it down - next exam, they just follow their notes instead of starting from scratch.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill|Skill]]
- [[skillmd|SKILL.md]]
- [[skill-lifecycle|Skill Lifecycle]]
- [[skill-templates|Skill Templates]]

title: skill-customisation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Editing a skill to fit your specific workflow. Customised skills work better for your particular setup than generic ones.

## Concrete Example

You install a github-pr skill, then customise it: change the PR template to match your team style, add a step to run your specific linter. Now it fits your team perfectly.

## Analogy

Tailoring a suit - you buy one off the rack (install), then the tailor adjusts it to fit you perfectly (customise). Skill customisation tailors a skill to your needs.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill-creation|Skill Creation]]
- [[skillmd|SKILL.md]]
- [[skill-templates|Skill Templates]]

title: skill-dependencies
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Some skills depend on others or on external tools. Declaring dependencies ensures the agent checks before using the skill.

## Concrete Example

A skill declares: requires: [git, gh-cli]. Before loading, the agent checks git and gh are installed. If not, it tells you to install them first.

## Analogy

A recipe that needs a specific pan - before starting, you check you have it. If not, you buy it first. Skill dependencies are checked before the skill runs.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-check|Skills Check]]
- [[skill-scripts|Skill Scripts]]
- [[skill-validation|Skill Validation]]

title: skill-description-quality
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

A good skill description is specific enough for auto-discovery to match it correctly. Vague descriptions lead to wrong skill choices.

## Concrete Example

Bad: Helps with stuff. Good: Deploy Helm charts to Kubernetes, integrate CRDs, manage releases. The good description has keywords the agent can match to deployment tasks.

## Analogy

A clear shop sign - Sushi Restaurant is better than Food Place. A clear description helps people (and the agent) find the right skill.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill-frontmatter|Skill Frontmatter]]
- [[skill-auto-discovery|Skill Auto-Discovery]]
- [[skill-dispatch|Skill Dispatch]]

title: skill-dispatch
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

The agent deciding which skill to use for a task based on the task description and skill descriptions. Dispatch matches need to skill.

## Concrete Example

User asks: Fix my Kubernetes pod. The agent reads skill descriptions, matches k8s-troubleshooting, and dispatches (activates) that skill. Wrong match means wrong approach.

## Analogy

A dispatcher at a taxi company - a call comes in, they match it to the nearest available driver. Skill dispatch matches the task to the right skill.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill-loading|Skill Loading]]
- [[skills-list|Skills List]]
- [[skill-command|Skill Command]]

title: skill-export
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Saving a skill as a shareable file or archive so you can move it to another machine or share with a colleague.

## Concrete Example

hermes skills export debugging creates debugging-skill.tar.gz. You send it to a colleague who runs hermes skills import on their machine. The skill transfers cleanly.

## Analogy

Exporting a presentation as a file - instead of sharing online, you save it as a file someone can open on their computer. Skill export packages a skill for transfer.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill-import|Skill Import]]
- [[skills-publish|Skills Publish]]
- [[skill-sharing|Skill Sharing]]

title: skill-frontmatter
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

YAML metadata at the top of SKILL.md that gives the agent key info: the skill name, a short description, and optional tags for organising.

## Concrete Example

Frontmatter looks like: name: github-pr-workflow / description: Branch, commit, open PR, check CI / tags: [git, github]. The agent reads this first to decide if the skill is relevant.

## Analogy

The label on a file folder tab - before opening the folder, you read the tab to know what is inside. Frontmatter is the tab label for a skill.

## Related Concepts

- [[skillmd|SKILL.md]]
- [[skill-categories|Skill Categories]]
- [[skill-creation|Skill Creation]]

title: skill-import
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Bringing a skill from a file or archive into the skill library, without using the hub. Useful for offline or private skills.

## Concrete Example

hermes skills import ~/downloads/my-private-skill.tar.gz unpacks the archive into the skills directory. The skill is now available, no internet needed.

## Analogy

Importing contacts from a file - instead of adding them one by one online, you load a file. Skill import loads a skill from a file without the hub.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-install|Skills Install]]
- [[skills-export|Skills Export]]
- [[external-skill-dirs|External Skill Dirs]]

title: skill-lifecycle
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

A skill goes through stages: created, active, stale, archived, pruned. Understanding the lifecycle helps you manage skills well.

## Concrete Example

A skill is created (you write it), becomes active (agent uses it), goes stale (not used in months), gets archived (curator moves it), then pruned (deleted after long unused).

## Analogy

A product in a store: new arrival, on display, moved to clearance, sent to warehouse, eventually discontinued. Skills have a similar lifecycle.

## Related Concepts

- [[stale-skills|Stale Skills]]
- [[curator-archive|Curator Archive]]
- [[skill-creation|Skill Creation]]

title: skill-loading
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

The process of reading a SKILL.md file and bringing its instructions into the agent working memory so it can follow the steps.

## Concrete Example

When the agent decides to debug, it loads the debugging skill: reads SKILL.md, loads any referenced scripts, and now knows the 4-phase debugging method.

## Analogy

Opening a textbook to a chapter - the knowledge goes from the shelf (disk) into your mind (memory). Skill loading moves instructions from file to active use.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill-dispatch|Skill Dispatch]]
- [[skill-references|Skill References]]
- [[reload-skills|Reload Skills]]

title: skill-moc
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

A Map of Content that lists all skills in a domain, helping you navigate the skill library visually.

## Concrete Example

The Skills System MOC lists all 60 concepts in this domain as links. You click any concept to read its note. The MOC is the index page for the domain.

## Analogy

A table of contents in a textbook - it lists all chapters and page numbers. You use it to find what you need. A skill MOC is the table of contents for skills.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-list|Skills List]]
- [[skills-browse|Skills Browse]]
- [[skill-categories|Skill Categories]]

title: skill-pinning
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Manually marking a skill as important so it is never archived. Different from curator pin - this is a user action to protect a favourite skill.

## Concrete Example

You pin debugging and tdd because you use them constantly. Even if usage drops temporarily, they stay in the active library. Pinning gives you control.

## Analogy

Bookmarking a webpage - you mark it as important so it never gets deleted from your history. Pinning marks a skill as permanent.

## Related Concepts

- [[curator-pin|Curator Pin]]
- [[curator-unpin|Curator Unpin]]
- [[skill-lifecycle|Skill Lifecycle]]

title: skill-provenance
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Tracking whether a skill was created by the agent itself, installed from the hub, or written by a human. Provenance tells you where a skill came from.

## Concrete Example

A skill shows provenance: created_by: agent (auto-saved after a successful task) vs created_by: hub (installed from community). You trust agent-created skills differently from hub ones.

## Analogy

A food label showing country of origin - Made in Japan vs Made locally. Provenance tells you the origin of a skill, which affects how much you trust it.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill-creation|Skill Creation]]
- [[skills-hub|Skills Hub]]
- [[skill-lifecycle|Skill Lifecycle]]

title: skill-references
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Files linked from SKILL.md that provide extra detail: API docs, configuration examples, or reference tables. They keep SKILL.md focused.

## Concrete Example

SKILL.md says: For full API details, see references/api.md. The agent loads references/api.md when it needs the complete API documentation. SKILL.md stays concise.

## Analogy

A textbook with a references section at the back - the main chapter gives the overview, but detailed tables and formulas are in the appendix. Skill references are the appendix.

## Related Concepts

- [[skillmd|SKILL.md]]
- [[skill-templates|Skill Templates]]
- [[skill-scripts|Skill Scripts]]

title: skill-scripts
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Executable scripts (Python, shell) within a skill that the agent can run to perform specific actions. Scripts do the heavy lifting.

## Concrete Example

A debugging skill has scripts/trace.sh that adds trace logging to a Python file. The agent runs this script instead of manually editing the file. Scripts automate repetitive work.

## Analogy

Power tools in a workshop - instead of cutting wood by hand (manual steps), you use a saw (script) to do it faster and more consistently. Skill scripts are power tools for the agent.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill-references|Skill References]]
- [[skill-templates|Skill Templates]]
- [[skill-assets|Skill Assets]]

title: skill-sharing
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Sharing skills between teammates or projects by placing them in a shared directory or publishing to the hub.

## Concrete Example

Your team puts a shared skill in /mnt/shared/team-skills/code-review. Everyone on the team configures this as an external skill dir. All agents can now use the same review process.

## Analogy

Sharing notes with classmates - you put them in a shared Google Drive folder, and everyone can access them. Skill sharing makes a skill available to others.

## Related Concepts

- [[external-skill-dirs|External Skill Dirs]]
- [[skills-publish|Skills Publish]]
- [[skills-hub|Skills Hub]]

title: skill-templates
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Pre-built template files within a skill that the agent can copy and fill in. Templates save time and ensure consistent output.

## Concrete Example

A github-pr skill has templates/pull-request-template.md. The agent copies it, fills in the PR description, and creates a well-structured pull request every time.

## Analogy

A form letter template - you do not write from scratch. You fill in the blanks. Skill templates give the agent a starting structure to fill in.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill-references|Skill References]]
- [[skill-scripts|Skill Scripts]]
- [[skillmd|SKILL.md]]

title: skill-usage-tracking
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Recording how often each skill is used and when. This data helps identify stale skills and popular ones.

## Concrete Example

The agent records each time it loads a skill. github-pr-workflow: used 15 times this week. old-python-2-tool: used 0 times in 3 months. Usage tracking feeds the curator.

## Analogy

A shop tracking which products sell well and which sit on shelves. Popular items stay stocked; unpopular ones get clearance. Usage tracking does this for skills.

## Related Concepts

- [[stale-skills|Stale Skills]]
- [[usage-json|Usage JSON]]
- [[curator|Curator]]

title: skill-validation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Checking that a newly created or modified skill is valid: frontmatter is correct, referenced files exist, scripts are executable.

## Concrete Example

After editing SKILL.md, you run validation. It checks: frontmatter has name and description - OK. references/api.md exists - OK. scripts/deploy.sh is executable - FIXED (chmod +x).

## Analogy

Proofreading an essay before submitting - you check spelling, grammar, and that all references are cited. Skill validation checks a skill is ready for use.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-check|Skills Check]]
- [[skillmd|SKILL.md]]
- [[skill-frontmatter|Skill Frontmatter]]

title: skill-versioning
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Tracking skill versions so you know which version you have and can update when improvements are released.

## Concrete Example

A skill shows version: 2.1.0. The hub has 2.2.0 with a bug fix. You update to get the fix. Versioning tracks what changed between versions.

## Analogy

Software version numbers on apps - v1.0, v1.1, v2.0. Each number tells you what version you have and what is newer. Skill versioning does the same.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-update|Skills Update]]
- [[skills-hub|Skills Hub]]
- [[skills-publish|Skills Publish]]

title: skill
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

An AI agent needs reusable procedures for recurring tasks. Skills are packaged instructions that teach the agent how to do a specific job well, like a manual the agent can open and follow.

## Concrete Example

A skill called git-workflow tells the agent how to branch, commit, and open a PR. When the agent sees a coding task, it loads the skill and follows the steps.

## Analogy

A recipe card in a kitchen - the chef doesn't memorise every dish. They pull the recipe card (skill) when they need to cook that dish, follow the steps, and put it back.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill-creation|Skill Creation]]
- [[skillmd|SKILL.md]]
- [[skill-loading|Skill Loading]]
- [[skill-dispatch|Skill Dispatch]]

title: skillmd
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Every skill needs a main file that describes what it does, when to use it, and the steps to follow. SKILL.md is that file - the heart of every skill.

## Concrete Example

A SKILL.md starts with YAML frontmatter (name, description) then has numbered steps: 1. Run npm test 2. Check coverage 3. Fix failing tests. The agent reads this to know exactly what to do.

## Analogy

A recipe page with a title at the top (frontmatter), ingredients list, and step-by-step instructions (body). SKILL.md is the recipe page for an agent skill.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill|Skill]]
- [[skill-frontmatter|Skill Frontmatter]]
- [[skill-creation|Skill Creation]]
- [[skill-references|Skill References]]

title: skills-browse
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Exploring the skills hub to discover new skills without knowing a specific name. Browse by category or popularity.

## Concrete Example

hermes skills browse shows categories: devops (12 skills), creative (8 skills), mlops (15 skills). You pick devops and browse the list to find something useful.

## Analogy

Browsing shelves in a bookstore - you walk through sections, pick up books that look interesting, and discover something new. Skills browse does this for the hub.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-hub|Skills Hub]]
- [[skills-search|Skills Search]]
- [[skill-categories|Skill Categories]]

title: skills-check
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Verifying that all installed skills are valid - SKILL.md exists, frontmatter is correct, no broken links. Catches problems early.

## Concrete Example

hermes skills check scans all skills and reports: OK: github-pr-workflow / WARNING: old-skill missing description / ERROR: broken-skill no SKILL.md found. You fix the issues.

## Analogy

A health check at the doctor - they run tests on everything and tell you what is fine and what needs attention. Skills check does a health check on your skill library.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-config|Skills Config]]
- [[skillmd|SKILL.md]]
- [[skill-frontmatter|Skill Frontmatter]]

title: skills-command
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

A slash command that lists all available skills in the current session, showing which are loaded and which are available to load.

## Concrete Example

Typing /skills shows: Loaded: debugging, tdd / Available: github-pr-workflow, dockerfile-optimization. You see what is active and what you can activate.

## Analogy

Opening your backpack and seeing what is inside - some books are already on your desk (loaded), others are in the bag (available). /skills shows your skill inventory.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill-command|Skill Command]]
- [[skills-list|Skills List]]
- [[skill-loading|Skill Loading]]

title: skills-config
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Configuring skill settings: which directories to scan, whether auto-discovery is on, and other preferences.

## Concrete Example

hermes skills config shows: skills_dirs: [~/.hermes/skills, ./skills] / auto_discover: true / max_skills: 100. You can change these to fit your setup.

## Analogy

Settings on your phone - you configure which apps can send notifications, how they are grouped, and where they appear. Skills config sets up how skills behave.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-tap|Skills Tap]]
- [[external-skill-dirs|External Skill Dirs]]
- [[skills-check|Skills Check]]

title: skills-hub
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

A central online repository where the community shares skills. Think of it as an app store for agent skills.

## Concrete Example

The hub has hundreds of skills: github tools, docker helpers, creative generators. You search, install, and use. Popular skills get many installs and reviews.

## Analogy

The Apple App Store or Google Play Store - a central place where developers publish apps and users download them. The skills hub is the app store for agent skills.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-install|Skills Install]]
- [[skills-publish|Skills Publish]]
- [[skills-tap|Skills Tap]]

title: skills-inspect
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Looking at the details of a skill before using it - what it does, what files it contains, and how it works.

## Concrete Example

hermes skills inspect debugging shows: Name: debugging / Description: 4-phase root cause debugging / Files: SKILL.md, scripts/trace.sh / Author: agent. You see the full picture.

## Analogy

Reading the back of a box before buying - ingredients, instructions, warnings. Skills inspect shows you what is inside a skill before you commit to using it.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-list|Skills List]]
- [[skillmd|SKILL.md]]
- [[skill-references|Skill References]]

title: skills-install
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Adding a new skill to your agent from the skills hub or a local path. After install, the agent can use it immediately.

## Concrete Example

hermes skills install github-pr-workflow downloads the skill from the hub, places it in the skills directory, and confirms: Installed github-pr-workflow successfully.

## Analogy

Downloading an app from the App Store - you tap install, it downloads and appears on your phone ready to use. Skills install does this for agent skills.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-hub|Skills Hub]]
- [[skills-uninstall|Skills Uninstall]]
- [[skills-tap|Skills Tap]]

title: skills-list
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

The command to see all installed skills at a glance. Shows skill names and short descriptions so you know what is available.

## Concrete Example

Running hermes skills list outputs: github-pr-workflow - Branch, commit, open PR / debugging - Systematic 4-phase debugging / tdd - Test-driven development. A quick inventory.

## Analogy

Checking your phone's app drawer - you see all installed apps with their icons and names. Skills list shows all installed skills with names and descriptions.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-search|Skills Search]]
- [[skills-browse|Skills Browse]]
- [[skill-categories|Skill Categories]]

title: skills-publish
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Sharing a skill you created with the community by uploading it to the skills hub so others can install and use it.

## Concrete Example

You created a great skill for Moodle plugin testing. hermes skills publish moodle-plugin-testing uploads it to the hub. Others can now hermes skills install it.

## Analogy

Publishing a recipe on a cooking website - you share your dish so anyone in the world can try it. Skills publish shares your skill with the whole community.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-hub|Skills Hub]]
- [[skills-install|Skills Install]]
- [[skill-creation|Skill Creation]]

title: skills-search
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

When you have many skills, searching by keyword finds the right one faster than scrolling through a long list.

## Concrete Example

hermes skills search deploy finds: k8s-troubleshooting, vllm-deployment, helm-chart-deployment. Searching docker finds dockerfile-optimization and k8s-troubleshooting.

## Analogy

Using a search bar in an app store - instead of scrolling through thousands of apps, you type deploy and see only deployment-related results.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-list|Skills List]]
- [[skills-install|Skills Install]]
- [[skills-browse|Skills Browse]]

title: skills-tap
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Adding a source repository to your skills hub so you can install skills from that source. Tapping is like adding a new store.

## Concrete Example

hermes skills tap nousresearch/skills adds the Nous Research skill repository as a source. Now you can install skills from that repo alongside the default hub.

## Analogy

Adding a new bookstore to your reading app - previously you only had one store. Now you tap to add another, so you can browse and buy from both.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-hub|Skills Hub]]
- [[skills-install|Skills Install]]
- [[skills-config|Skills Config]]

title: skills-uninstall
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Removing a skill you no longer need. Keeps the skill library clean and saves space.

## Concrete Example

hermes skills uninstall old-python-2-tool removes the skill files and confirms removal. The agent will no longer load or suggest this skill.

## Analogy

Deleting an app from your phone - press and hold, tap delete, it is gone. Skills uninstall removes a skill you do not need anymore.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-install|Skills Install]]
- [[skills-update|Skills Update]]
- [[skill-lifecycle|Skill Lifecycle]]

title: skills-update
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Fetching the latest version of skills from the hub. Skills get improved over time, and update keeps you current.

## Concrete Example

hermes skills update checks all installed skills for newer versions. If github-pr-workflow has a v2, it downloads and replaces the old version. You get bug fixes and improvements.

## Analogy

Updating apps on your phone - developers release new versions with fixes and features. You tap update to get the latest. Skills update does this for agent skills.

## Related Concepts

- [[skills-install|Skills Install]]
- [[skills-hub|Skills Hub]]
- [[stale-skills|Stale Skills]]

title: stale-skills
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

Skills that have not been used in a long time. They clutter the library and may contain outdated instructions. The curator identifies and archives them.

## Concrete Example

A skill called old-docker-compose was last used 4 months ago. The curator flags it as stale. If still unused, it gets archived to keep the library clean.

## Analogy

Food in the fridge that is past its expiry date - it takes up space and might not be good anymore. Stale skills take up space and may be outdated.

## Related Concepts

- [[curator|Curator]]

title: usage-json
text:
> **Domain:** [[_skills-system-moc|Skills System]]

## Motivation

A small file (.usage.json) next to each skill that records usage statistics: times used, last used date, success rate.

## Concrete Example

debugging/.usage.json contains: {used_count: 42, last_used: 2026-08-03, success_rate: 0.88}. The curator reads this to decide if the skill is stale.

## Analogy

A mileage log in a car - it tracks total miles, last trip date, fuel efficiency. .usage.json tracks a skill usage stats the same way.

title: agentsmd
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

A file that tells the agent about the project: what it is, conventions to follow, and things to watch out for. Like a briefing document.

## Concrete Example

AGENTS.md says: This is a Flask web app. Use Python 3.11. Tests go in tests/. Never commit to main branch. The agent follows these rules when working on the project.

## Analogy

A briefing packet for a new employee - here is the project, here are the rules, here is what to watch out for. AGENTS.md briefs the agent on the project.

## Related Concepts

- [[context-files|Context Files]]
- [[claudemd|CLAUDE.md]]
- [[cursor-rules|Cursor Rules]]

title: built-in-memory
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

The default memory provider. Stores memories locally in files. Simple, no setup needed, but limited features.

## Concrete Example

Built-in memory saves facts to MEMORY.md and USER.md on your machine. No external service needed. It works out of the box but does not have smart search or sharing.

## Analogy

A notebook you keep in your bag - always there, no internet needed, but you have to flip through pages manually. Built-in memory is the simple local notebook.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-provider|Memory Provider]]
- [[memorymd|MEMORY.md]]
- [[usermd|USER.md]]

title: claudemd
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

A context file originally for Claude Code but widely adopted. Tells the agent coding standards, style preferences, and project-specific instructions.

## Concrete Example

CLAUDE.md contains: Use 4-space indentation. Add type hints to all functions. Prefer composition over inheritance. The agent follows these when writing code.

## Analogy

A style guide for a school newspaper - headline rules, font size, citation format. Writers follow it for consistency. CLAUDE.md is a style guide for the agent.

## Related Concepts

- [[context-files|Context Files]]
- [[agentsmd|AGENTS.md]]
- [[cursor-rules|Cursor Rules]]

title: compress-command
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

A slash command that manually triggers context compression. Useful when you know the conversation is long and want to compress before the automatic threshold.

## Concrete Example

Typing /compress immediately summarizes older messages. The agent shows: Compressed 30 messages into a summary. Context now at 40 percent. You have room to continue.

## Analogy

Pressing save on a document to reduce its working state - you compress the history into a saved version. /compress compresses conversation history manually.

## Related Concepts

- [[context-compression|Context Compression]]
- [[compression-threshold|Compression Threshold]]
- [[context-window|Context Window]]

title: compression-threshold
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

The point at which context compression triggers. When the conversation length exceeds this threshold, the agent compresses automatically.

## Concrete Example

Threshold set to 80 percent of context window. When the conversation fills 80 percent, compression kicks in. Below that, no compression needed.

## Analogy

A water tank alarm - when water reaches 80 percent capacity, the alarm triggers. The compression threshold triggers when context reaches its limit.

## Related Concepts

- [[context-compression|Context Compression]]
- [[target-ratio|Target Ratio]]
- [[context-window|Context Window]]

title: context-budget
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

The total context space available. The agent must budget it across system prompt, memory, conversation, and files. Running out means compression or loss.

## Concrete Example

Budget: 128K tokens. System prompt: 2K, memory: 5K, conversation: 100K, files: 21K. Total: 128K. If conversation grows, something else must shrink (compression).

## Analogy

A monthly allowance - you budget across food, transport, and fun. If one grows, another shrinks. Context budget allocates tokens across all context sources.

## Related Concepts

- [[context-window|Context Window]]
- [[context-prioritisation|Context Prioritisation]]
- [[context-compression|Context Compression]]

title: context-compression
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

When a conversation gets very long, the agent compresses older messages into a summary to fit within its context window. You keep the meaning but use less space.

## Concrete Example

After 50 messages, the agent compresses messages 1-40 into: User asked about Python lists, dicts, and loops. Decided to build a calculator. Now the context has room for new messages.

## Analogy

Summarising a long meeting into bullet points - instead of keeping the full 2-hour transcript, you write 5 key points. Same information, much less space.

## Related Concepts

- [[compression-threshold|Compression Threshold]]
- [[target-ratio|Target Ratio]]
- [[context-window|Context Window]]
- [[compress-command|Compress Command]]

title: context-files
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Files the agent reads at the start of each session to get context: AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules. They set rules and provide project context.

## Concrete Example

The agent starts a session, reads AGENTS.md (project conventions), CLAUDE.md (coding standards). Now it knows the project rules before you even ask a question.

## Analogy

Reading the house rules when you check into a hotel - wifi password, breakfast time, checkout. Before you start your stay, you read the rules. Context files are the house rules.

## Related Concepts

- [[agentsmd|AGENTS.md]]
- [[claudemd|CLAUDE.md]]
- [[cursor-rules|Cursor Rules]]

title: context-freshness
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Recent context is more relevant than old context. The agent weights recent messages and memory higher when deciding what matters now.

## Concrete Example

You switched from Python to JavaScript last week. The agent weights this recent switch higher than your Python preferences from 3 months ago. Freshness keeps the agent current.

## Analogy

News - today headlines matter more than last week. The agent treats recent context as more relevant, like how you prioritise recent news.

## Related Concepts

- [[context-prioritisation|Context Prioritisation]]
- [[memory-decay|Memory Decay]]
- [[context-window|Context Window]]

title: context-injection
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Automatically inserting relevant context (memories, files, past session info) into the conversation before the agent responds.

## Concrete Example

You ask: Help me continue my project. The agent injects: your project details from MEMORY.md, your skills from USER.md, and the last session summary. Now it has full context to help.

## Analogy

A waiter who knows your usual order - before you speak, they already know you want the set lunch with iced tea. Context injection pre-loads what the agent needs.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-retrieval|Memory Retrieval]]
- [[context-files|Context Files]]
- [[context-references|Context References]]

title: context-loss
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

When information falls out of the context window and is forgotten. Compression helps, but some detail is always lost in very long conversations.

## Concrete Example

After a 200-message conversation, the agent does not remember the exact code from message 5. It remembers the summary (you were debugging a sort function) but not the exact code.

## Analogy

Forgetting the beginning of a long movie by the end - you remember the plot but not every line of dialogue. Context loss is the agent forgetting old details.

## Related Concepts

- [[context-window|Context Window]]
- [[context-compression|Context Compression]]
- [[compression-threshold|Compression Threshold]]

title: context-prioritisation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

When context is limited, the agent prioritises what to keep: recent messages, important memories, and active instructions come first.

## Concrete Example

With limited context, the agent keeps: the last 10 messages (recent), your user profile (important), and the current task instruction (active). Old tangents get compressed first.

## Analogy

Packing a backpack for a hike - you pack the essentials first (water, map, first aid), then nice-to-haves. Context prioritisation packs the most important context first.

## Related Concepts

- [[context-window|Context Window]]
- [[context-compression|Context Compression]]
- [[memory-retrieval|Memory Retrieval]]

title: context-references
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Ways the agent can pull in external context: file references, URL references, and session links. This extends what the agent knows beyond the conversation.

## Concrete Example

You type: Look at @agents.md and @session:work/42. The agent reads AGENTS.md for project rules and session 42 for past context. References pull in extra information.

## Analogy

Footnotes in a book - they reference other pages or sources. You flip to them for more context. Context references let the agent pull in external context.

## Related Concepts

- [[context-files|Context Files]]
- [[session-links|Session Links]]
- [[session-search-tool|Session Search Tool]]

title: context-snapshot
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

A saved snapshot of the current context (messages, memory, files) at a point in time. Useful for debugging or resuming.

## Concrete Example

Before a risky operation, the agent saves a context snapshot. If something goes wrong, it can roll back to this snapshot and try a different approach.

## Analogy

A save point in a video game - before a boss fight, you save. If you lose, you reload from the save point. Context snapshots are save points for agent context.

## Related Concepts

- [[context-loss|Context Loss]]
- [[context-budget|Context Budget]]
- [[memory-export|Memory Export]]

title: context-window
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

The maximum amount of text the agent can consider at once. Like short-term memory - it holds the current conversation but has a limit.

## Concrete Example

If the context window is 128K tokens (about 100,000 words), and your conversation is 150,000 words, the oldest messages fall out of the window and are forgotten unless compressed.

## Analogy

A person short-term memory - you can hold a conversation in mind, but if it goes on for hours, the earliest parts fade. The context window is the agent short-term memory.

## Related Concepts

- [[context-compression|Context Compression]]
- [[compression-threshold|Compression Threshold]]
- [[token|Token]]

title: cursor-rules
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

A file (.cursorrules) that defines how the agent should behave in a project. Originally for Cursor IDE but can be read by other agents.

## Concrete Example

.cursorrules says: Always write tests before implementation. Use descriptive variable names. Comment complex logic. The agent treats these as rules to follow.

## Analogy

Rules posted in a computer lab - no food, log off when done, save files to the shared drive. Cursor rules are the lab rules for the agent.

## Related Concepts

- [[context-files|Context Files]]
- [[agentsmd|AGENTS.md]]
- [[claudemd|CLAUDE.md]]

title: honcho-memory
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

A memory provider that lets multiple agents share the same memory. Good for teams where several agents help the same user.

## Concrete Example

With Honcho, agent A learns you like Python, and agent B (using the same Honcho) also knows this. Shared memory means consistent service across multiple agents.

## Analogy

A shared family calendar - when mom adds an event, dad and kids all see it. Honcho memory lets multiple agents share what they know about you.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-provider|Memory Provider]]
- [[mem0-memory|Mem0 Memory]]
- [[built-in-memory|Built-in Memory]]

title: mem0-memory
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

A smart memory provider that uses AI to organise, summarise, and retrieve memories intelligently. Finds relevant memories even with fuzzy queries.

## Concrete Example

Mem0 stores 100 facts about you. You ask about your coding project. Mem0 finds the 3 relevant memories (your Python level, your project topic, your deadline) and surfaces them.

## Analogy

A smart photo album that tags faces and places - when you search beach, it finds all beach photos even without that word in the filename. Mem0 finds relevant memories smartly.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-provider|Memory Provider]]
- [[honcho-memory|Honcho Memory]]
- [[built-in-memory|Built-in Memory]]

title: memory-accuracy
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Ensuring stored memories are correct. Inaccurate memories lead to wrong personalisation. The agent verifies before saving.

## Concrete Example

Agent hears: I got a B on my math test. It saves: User received a B on the math test (verified from user statement). It does not guess or assume details it was not told.

## Analogy

A journalist fact-checking before publishing - they verify the claim before printing it. Memory accuracy means the agent saves only verified facts.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-operations|Memory Operations]]
- [[memory-conflict|Memory Conflict]]
- [[memory-consolidation|Memory Consolidation]]

title: memory-add
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Adding a new fact to memory. The agent does this when it learns something new and worth remembering.

## Concrete Example

Agent learns: User has a dog named Rex. It calls memory add: User has a dog named Rex. Now every future session knows about Rex.

## Analogy

Writing a new entry in your diary - today I learned something new, so I add it. Memory add writes a new fact into the agent memory.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-operations|Memory Operations]]
- [[memory-replace|Memory Replace]]
- [[memory-remove|Memory Remove]]

title: memory-batch-operations
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Adding, replacing, or removing multiple memories in one action. Faster than doing them one at a time.

## Concrete Example

The agent learns 5 things in one conversation. Instead of 5 separate memory calls, it batches: add 3, replace 1, remove 1. One operation, multiple changes.

## Analogy

Going to the grocery store with a list - instead of 5 trips for 5 items, you do one trip and get everything. Batch operations handle multiple memories at once.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-operations|Memory Operations]]
- [[memory-add|Memory Add]]
- [[memory-tool|Memory Tool]]

title: memory-char-limit
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

A maximum character count for each memory entry. Prevents overly long memories that bloat files and slow loading.

## Concrete Example

A memory entry is limited to 500 characters. The agent wants to save a long story but must compress it: User is building a Flask chatbot for a school project. Concise and under the limit.

## Analogy

Twitter character limit - you cannot write an essay in a tweet. You must be concise. Memory char limit forces the agent to be brief and clear.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-operations|Memory Operations]]
- [[memorymd|MEMORY.md]]
- [[memory-tool|Memory Tool]]

title: memory-clear
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Deleting all stored memories. A fresh start. Useful when the agent has accumulated too many outdated or incorrect memories.

## Concrete Example

hermes memory clear wipes all memories. The agent starts the next session knowing nothing about you. Use carefully - this cannot be undone.

## Analogy

Factory reset on a phone - everything is wiped, back to the start. Memory clear resets the agent memory to empty.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-off|Memory Off]]
- [[memory-remove|Memory Remove]]
- [[memory-operations|Memory Operations]]

title: memory-confidence
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Some memories are certain (user explicitly stated a fact), others are inferred. Confidence tracks how sure the agent is about each memory.

## Concrete Example

User said: I am 15 years old. Confidence: high (explicit). Agent inferred: User likes coding (from multiple coding questions). Confidence: medium (inferred). The agent trusts high-confidence memories more.

## Analogy

A witness who saw it with their own eyes (high confidence) vs one who heard it second-hand (low confidence). Memory confidence tracks the reliability of each memory.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-accuracy|Memory Accuracy]]
- [[memory-operations|Memory Operations]]
- [[memory-retrieval|Memory Retrieval]]

title: memory-conflict
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

When two memories contradict each other. The agent needs rules to resolve which one is current and correct.

## Concrete Example

Memory A: User likes dark mode. Memory B: User switched to light mode. The agent uses the most recent (B) and may remove the outdated (A). Conflict resolution keeps memory consistent.

## Analogy

Two friends telling you different times for a meeting - you check which message is more recent and trust that one. Memory conflict picks the most recent memory.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-replace|Memory Replace]]
- [[memory-remove|Memory Remove]]
- [[memory-operations|Memory Operations]]

title: memory-consolidation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Combining several related memories into one cleaner, more complete memory. Reduces clutter and redundancy.

## Concrete Example

Three memories: User knows Python, User knows HTML, User knows CSS. Consolidation merges them: User knows Python, HTML, and CSS (web development basics). One memory instead of three.

## Analogy

Merging duplicate contacts on your phone - instead of three entries for the same person, you merge them into one complete contact. Memory consolidation merges related memories.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-operations|Memory Operations]]
- [[memory-replace|Memory Replace]]
- [[memorymd|MEMORY.md]]

title: memory-decay
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Old memories that have not been referenced in a long time may become less relevant. Decay reduces their priority in retrieval.

## Concrete Example

A memory from 6 months ago about a project you finished has low priority. A memory from yesterday about your current project has high priority. Decay ranks memories by recency.

## Analogy

Forgetting details of a movie you watched years ago but remembering one you saw last week. Memory decay naturally prioritises recent memories.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-provider|Memory Provider]]
- [[mem0-memory|Mem0 Memory]]
- [[memory-operations|Memory Operations]]

title: memory-enabled
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

A setting that turns persistent memory on or off. When enabled, the agent saves and recalls facts across sessions. When off, each session is a blank slate.

## Concrete Example

memory_enabled: true in config. The agent now saves what it learns about you. Set it to false for a one-off session where you want total privacy and no remembering.

## Analogy

The remember passwords checkbox in a browser - check it to save (enabled), uncheck to forget each time (disabled). Memory enabled controls whether the agent remembers.

## Related Concepts

- [[persistent-memory|Persistent Memory]]
- [[memory-provider|Memory Provider]]
- [[memory-setup|Memory Setup]]

title: memory-export
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Saving all memories to a file so you can back them up, move them to another machine, or share with another agent.

## Concrete Example

hermes memory export creates memories-backup.json with all 42 memories. You can import this on another machine to transfer your agent memory.

## Analogy

Exporting your contacts to a file - you save them so you can import them on a new phone. Memory export saves memories for transfer or backup.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-provider|Memory Provider]]
- [[memory-setup|Memory Setup]]
- [[usermd|USER.md]]

title: memory-import
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Loading memories from a previously exported file. Useful when setting up a new agent or restoring from backup.

## Concrete Example

hermes memory import memories-backup.json loads 42 memories into the agent. Your new agent now knows everything the old one did.

## Analogy

Importing contacts to a new phone - you load the file and all your contacts appear. Memory import loads saved memories into the agent.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-export|Memory Export]]
- [[memory-provider|Memory Provider]]
- [[memory-setup|Memory Setup]]

title: memory-off
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Turning memory completely off. The agent will not save or recall any facts. Useful for sensitive or one-time sessions.

## Concrete Example

hermes memory off disables all memory. The agent forgets everything after this session. Use this when working on something private where you want zero retention.

## Analogy

Incognito mode in a browser - no history saved, no cookies stored. Memory off is incognito mode for the agent.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-enabled|Memory Enabled]]
- [[memory-status|Memory Status]]
- [[persistent-memory|Persistent Memory]]

title: memory-operations
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

The three core actions on memory: add (new fact), replace (update fact), remove (delete fact). Together they keep memory accurate and useful.

## Concrete Example

In one session the agent: adds your new project, replaces your old grade, removes an outdated preference. Three operations, one clean memory.

## Analogy

Editing a document - you can add text, replace words, or delete paragraphs. Memory operations are add, replace, delete for agent memory.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-add|Memory Add]]
- [[memory-replace|Memory Replace]]
- [[memory-remove|Memory Remove]]
- [[memory-tool|Memory Tool]]

title: memory-permissions
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Controls who can read or write memories. Important for shared agents where multiple users interact with the same agent.

## Concrete Example

User A memories are private. User B cannot see them. An admin can manage all memories. Permissions keep each user data separate and secure.

## Analogy

User accounts on a shared computer - each person logs in and sees only their own files. Memory permissions keep each user memories private.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-privacy|Memory Privacy]]
- [[memory-scope|Memory Scope]]
- [[memory-provider|Memory Provider]]

title: memory-privacy
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Concerns about what the agent remembers and who can access it. Memory can contain personal info, so privacy controls matter.

## Concrete Example

Your memory contains your real name, school, and grades. You can turn off memory for sensitive sessions, or clear all memory when sharing the agent with others.

## Analogy

A personal journal with a lock - you control who reads it. Memory privacy controls let you decide what the agent remembers and when to forget.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-off|Memory Off]]
- [[memory-enabled|Memory Enabled]]
- [[usermd|USER.md]]

title: memory-provider
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

The system that stores and retrieves memories. Different providers have different features: built-in is simple, Honcho is shared, Mem0 is smart.

## Concrete Example

Config: memory_provider: builtin (simple, local). Or memory_provider: honcho (shared across agents). Or memory_provider: mem0 (AI-organised memories). Each has trade-offs.

## Analogy

Choosing a cloud storage service - Google Drive (built-in, simple), Dropbox (shared), or iCloud (smart integration). Memory providers are storage services for agent memories.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-enabled|Memory Enabled]]
- [[built-in-memory|Built-in Memory]]
- [[honcho-memory|Honcho Memory]]
- [[mem0-memory|Mem0 Memory]]

title: memory-remove
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Deleting a memory that is no longer correct or relevant. Keeps memory clean and accurate.

## Concrete Example

Memory says: User is learning Scratch. But you have moved on to Python. The agent calls memory remove to delete the Scratch fact. Memory stays current.

## Analogy

Crossing out an old todo item that is no longer relevant - you remove it so your list stays clean. Memory remove deletes outdated memories.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-operations|Memory Operations]]
- [[memory-add|Memory Add]]
- [[memory-replace|Memory Replace]]

title: memory-replace
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Updating an existing memory with new information. Prevents outdated facts from confusing the agent.

## Concrete Example

Old memory: User is in F3. New fact: User is now in F4. The agent calls memory replace to update F3 to F4. No stale information remains.

## Analogy

Updating a contact in your phone - your friend changed their number, so you replace the old one. Memory replace updates outdated facts.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-operations|Memory Operations]]
- [[memory-add|Memory Add]]
- [[memory-remove|Memory Remove]]

title: memory-retrieval
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

How the agent finds the right memories at the right time. Good retrieval surfaces relevant facts without flooding the context with everything.

## Concrete Example

You ask about your web project. The agent retrieves: project details, your Python level, and the framework you chose. It does NOT retrieve your math exam date (irrelevant).

## Analogy

A librarian who finds you the right book - you ask for a mystery novel, they do not bring you cookbooks. Memory retrieval brings relevant memories only.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-provider|Memory Provider]]
- [[memory-tool|Memory Tool]]
- [[context-window|Context Window]]

title: memory-scope
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Memories can be global (apply everywhere) or scoped to a project or profile. Scope prevents memories from one project leaking into another.

## Concrete Example

A memory scoped to project A: Use PostgreSQL. This does not appear when working on project B (which uses SQLite). Scope keeps project memories separate.

## Analogy

Folders in your notebook - math notes in the math folder, English notes in the English folder. You do not mix them. Memory scope keeps memories in the right context.

title: memory-setup
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Configuring memory: choosing a provider, enabling it, and setting preferences. Run once to get memory working.

## Concrete Example

hermes memory setup asks: Which provider? (builtin/mem0/honcho). Enable user profile? (y/n). After answering, memory is configured and ready to use.

## Analogy

Setting up a new phone - you choose a language, sign in, set preferences. After setup, the phone is personalised. Memory setup personalises the agent memory system.

- [[memory-provider|Memory Provider]]
- [[memory-enabled|Memory Enabled]]
- [[memory-status|Memory Status]]

title: memory-size-management
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Too many memories slow down loading and fill context. Managing memory size keeps it lean and fast.

## Concrete Example

After 200 memories, the agent consolidates and removes outdated ones, bringing the count to 120. Loading is faster, and the most relevant memories fit in context easily.

## Analogy

Cleaning out your closet periodically - too many clothes make it hard to find what you want. You donate old ones to keep it manageable. Memory size management keeps memory lean.

## Related Concepts

- [[memory-consolidation|Memory Consolidation]]
- [[memory-decay|Memory Decay]]
- [[memory-char-limit|Memory Char Limit]]

title: memory-status
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Checking whether memory is on, which provider is active, and how many memories are stored. A quick health check for memory.

## Concrete Example

hermes memory status shows: Memory: enabled / Provider: builtin / Memories stored: 42 / Last updated: 2026-08-03. You see the full memory status at a glance.

## Analogy

Checking your phone storage - how much space is used, what is stored, last backup date. Memory status shows the agent memory state.

- [[memory-setup|Memory Setup]]
- [[memory-enabled|Memory Enabled]]
- [[memory-provider|Memory Provider]]

title: memory-tagging
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Labelling memories with tags (project, personal, skill) so they can be filtered and retrieved by category.

## Concrete Example

A memory is tagged: [project:chatbot, skill:flask]. When you work on the chatbot project, the agent retrieves memories tagged project:chatbot. Tagging makes retrieval precise.

## Analogy

Hashtags on social media - you search `#travel` to find travel posts. Memory tagging lets the agent filter memories by category.

- [[memory-scope|Memory Scope]]
- [[memory-retrieval|Memory Retrieval]]

title: memory-target
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Deciding whether a memory is about the user (goes to USER.md) or general context (goes to MEMORY.md). Correct targeting keeps memory organised.

## Concrete Example

User name and grade go to USER.md (user target). Project decisions go to MEMORY.md (memory target). The agent picks the right target for each fact.

## Analogy

Sorting mail into different trays - personal letters in one, work documents in another. Memory target sorts facts into the right file.

title: memory-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

The built-in tool the agent uses to add, replace, or remove memories. The agent calls this tool automatically when it learns something worth remembering.

## Concrete Example

The agent learns you are preparing for a math exam. It calls the memory tool: add memory: User is preparing for a math exam. Next session, it asks how the exam went.

## Analogy

A secretary with a notebook - during a meeting, they jot down important points. The memory tool is the agent secretary, jotting down what matters.

title: memorymd
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

A file where the agent stores general memories: things it learned, decisions made, and context worth keeping. The agent reads it at the start of each session.

## Concrete Example

MEMORY.md contains: User prefers concise answers. Working on a chatbot project using Flask. Decided to use PostgreSQL. The agent reads this and starts the session already informed.

## Analogy

A personal diary - you write down what happened and what matters. Next time you need to remember, you flip back and read. MEMORY.md is the agent diary.

title: persistent-memory
text:
> **Domain:** [[_memory-context-moc|Memory & Context]]

## Motivation

Without memory, every conversation starts from scratch. Persistent memory lets the agent remember facts about you across sessions, so it does not ask the same questions twice.

## Concrete Example

You tell the agent: I prefer Python and I am learning web development. Next session, you ask for a coding example. The agent uses Python and picks a web project, remembering your preferences.

## Analogy

A friend who remembers your birthday and favourite food - you do not remind them every time. Persistent memory lets the agent remember you between conversations.

title: session-links
text:

## Motivation

A way to reference a past session by its ID, like @session:work/42. The agent can read that session for context from a previous conversation.

## Concrete Example

You type: Remember what we decided in @session:default/15. The agent loads session 15, reads the decisions, and continues from where that session left off.

A hyperlink to a previous email thread - you click it to see what was discussed before. Session links connect the current conversation to past ones.

text:

A tool that lets the agent search past sessions by keyword. Finds relevant context from previous conversations without you having to remember session IDs.

Agent calls session_search(query=docker fix) and finds 3 past sessions where you fixed Docker issues. It reads them and uses the solutions to help you now.

A search bar in your email - instead of scrolling through hundreds of emails, you type docker and find the relevant ones. Session search finds past conversations by keyword.

title: target-ratio
text:

## Motivation

After compression, the agent aims for a target ratio of used context. For example, compress to 50 percent so there is room for more conversation.

Context was at 90 percent. After compression, it targets 50 percent. The summary takes 50 percent, leaving 50 percent for new messages before needing another compression.

## Analogy

A suitcase you pack to half full - after compressing clothes (rolling them), you aim for the suitcase to be half full so you have room for souvenirs. Target ratio is the target fullness.

user_profile_enabled: true means the agent tracks: you are a student, you know Python basics, you prefer concise answers. This profile shapes every response.

A loyalty card at a shop - they track what you buy and tailor offers to you. User profile enabled lets the agent tailor responses based on what it knows about you.
