A global flag to resume a specific session. Usage: hermes --resume SESSION_ID.

## Concrete Example

hermes --resume a1b2c3d4 chat. Loads session a1b2c3d4. Full history restored. You continue the previous conversation.

## Analogy

A bookmark in a book - you open to the marked page. --resume opens the marked session.

## Related Concepts

- [[resume-session|Resume Session]]
- [[global-flags|Global Flags]]
- [[sessions|Sessions]]

title: resume-session
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

Continue a previous session. Command: hermes --resume ID. Or: --continue (resumes most recent).

## Concrete Example

hermes --resume a1b2c3d4. Previous session loads. All messages restored. You continue where you left off. --continue resumes the last session.

## Analogy

Opening a saved game - you continue from where you saved. --resume continues a saved conversation.

## Related Concepts

- [[sessions|Sessions]]
- [[session-id|Session ID]]
- [[continue-flag|Continue Flag]]

title: retry
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

Regenerate the last response. Command: /retry. The model generates a new response to the last message.

## Concrete Example

Hermes gave a confusing answer. /retry. Hermes generates a new answer. Different approach, hopefully clearer.

## Analogy

Asking a teacher to explain again - you get a different explanation. /retry asks the model to answer again.

## Related Concepts

- [[sessions|Sessions]]
- [[conversation-history|Conversation History]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]

title: running-multiple-agents
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

Run multiple Hermes profiles simultaneously. Each is independent. Useful for parallel work.

## Concrete Example

Terminal 1: hermes --profile work chat. Terminal 2: hermes --profile school chat. Two agents running simultaneously. Independent.

## Analogy

Two cooks in two kitchens - they cook independently. Running multiple agents lets you work on multiple tasks simultaneously.

## Related Concepts

- [[profiles|Profiles]]
- [[profile-isolation|Profile Isolation]]
- [[delegate-task|Delegate Task]]

title: session-branching
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

Create a copy of the current session to explore a different path. Command: /branch or /fork.

## Concrete Example

/branch. Session A: original. Session B: branch. In B, try a risky approach. If it fails, A is safe. Two independent paths.

## Analogy

A choose-your-own-adventure book - you bookmark a page, explore a path, go back if it fails. Session branching bookmarks conversations.

## Related Concepts

- [[session-fork|Session Fork]]
- [[sessions|Sessions]]
- [[safety-net|Safety Net]]

title: session-browse
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

Browse sessions interactively. Command: hermes sessions browse. Shows a list with previews.

## Concrete Example

hermes sessions browse. List: 1. Docker Fix (Aug 3, 15 msgs) 2. Python Project (Aug 2, 30 msgs). Arrow keys to navigate. Enter to resume.

## Analogy

Browsing a photo gallery - you scroll through photos. Session browse lets you scroll through conversations.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-sessions|Hermes Sessions]]
- [[sessions|Sessions]]
- [[resume-session|Resume Session]]

title: session-compression-history
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

When a session is compressed, the old messages are replaced by a summary. The summary is part of the conversation history.

## Concrete Example

Session: 200 messages (100K tokens). Compression: summarizes first 150 messages into 5K tokens. Now: summary + 50 recent messages = 30K tokens. More room.

## Analogy

A meeting summary - instead of 2 hours of transcript, you have a 1-page summary. Compression history replaces old messages with summaries.

## Related Concepts

- [[sessions|Sessions]]
- [[context-compression|Context Compression]]
- [[conversation-history|Conversation History]]

title: session-delete
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

Delete a session. Command: hermes sessions delete --id ID.

## Concrete Example

hermes sessions delete --id a1b2c3d4. Session and all its messages are deleted. Permanent. Frees space.

## Analogy

Deleting a photo from your album - it is gone. Session delete removes a conversation permanently.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-sessions|Hermes Sessions]]
- [[sessions|Sessions]]
- [[session-prune|Session Prune]]

title: session-export
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

Export a session to a file. Command: hermes sessions export --id ID. Formats: JSONL, JSON.

## Concrete Example

hermes sessions export --id a1b2c3d4 --format jsonl. File: session-a1b2c3d4.jsonl. Contains all messages, tool calls, and metadata. Shareable.

## Analogy

Saving a chat log - you export the conversation to a file. Session export saves conversations for sharing or backup.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-sessions|Hermes Sessions]]
- [[session-id|Session ID]]
- [[sessions|Sessions]]

title: session-fork
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

A forked (branched) session. An exact copy at the fork point. Changes in the fork do not affect the original.

## Concrete Example

Session A: Build web app. /fork -> Session B (copy). In B: try Flask. In A: continue with Django. Two independent paths.

## Analogy

A fork in a hiking trail - the path splits. Both explore independently. Session fork splits the conversation.

## Related Concepts

- [[session-branching|Session Branching]]
- [[sessions|Sessions]]
- [[safety-net|Safety Net]]

title: session-id
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

A unique identifier for each session. Used to resume, export, or delete sessions.

## Concrete Example

Session ID: a1b2c3d4. hermes --resume a1b2c3d4. Or: hermes sessions export --id a1b2c3d4. The ID uniquely identifies one conversation.

## Analogy

A student ID number - it uniquely identifies one student. The session ID uniquely identifies one conversation.

## Related Concepts

- [[sessions|Sessions]]
- [[hermes-sessions|Hermes Sessions]]
- [[session-store|Session Store]]

title: session-prune
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

Delete old sessions to free space. Command: hermes sessions prune. Options: --older-than DAYS, --keep N.

## Concrete Example

hermes sessions prune --older-than 30. Deletes sessions older than 30 days. hermes sessions prune --keep 50. Keeps only the 50 most recent.

## Analogy

Cleaning out old notebooks - you throw away notes from last semester. Session prune deletes old conversations.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-sessions|Hermes Sessions]]
- [[sessions|Sessions]]
- [[session-store|Session Store]]

title: session-rename
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

Rename a session. Command: hermes sessions rename --id ID --title TITLE.

## Concrete Example

hermes sessions rename --id a1b2c3d4 --title My Project. Session a1b2c3d4 is now called My Project. Easier to find later.

## Analogy

Renaming a file - you give it a better name. Session rename gives a conversation a better name.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-sessions|Hermes Sessions]]
- [[session-title|Session Title]]
- [[sessions|Sessions]]

title: session-source-tag
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

A tag indicating where the session started: CLI, telegram, discord, matrix, etc.

## Concrete Example

Session source: telegram. You started this conversation on Telegram. Source: cli. You started it in the terminal. Tags track origins.

## Analogy

A stamp on a letter showing where it was sent from. The session source tag shows where the conversation started.

## Related Concepts

- [[sessions|Sessions]]
- [[session-title|Session Title]]
- [[hermes-sessions|Hermes Sessions]]

title: session-stats
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

Show statistics about sessions. Command: hermes sessions stats.

## Concrete Example

hermes sessions stats. Output: Total: 150 sessions. Oldest: 2025-01-15. Newest: 2025-08-04. Total messages: 3,200. Average: 21 msg/session.

## Analogy

A fitness app summary - total steps, average per day. Session stats summarize your conversation history.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-sessions|Hermes Sessions]]
- [[sessions|Sessions]]
- [[session-store|Session Store]]

title: session-store
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

The database where sessions are stored. Located at ~/.hermes/state.db. SQLite with FTS5 full-text search.

## Concrete Example

state.db: SQLite database. Stores all messages, tool calls, and metadata. FTS5 enables fast text search across all sessions. hermes sessions list reads from here.

## Analogy

A filing cabinet - every document is stored in a drawer. The session store is the filing cabinet for conversations.

## Related Concepts

- [[sessions|Sessions]]
- [[state-db|State DB]]
- [[sqlite-fts5|SQLite FTS5]]

title: session-title
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

A human-readable name for a session. Auto-generated or manually set. Helps you find sessions later.

## Concrete Example

Session 1: Python Web Scraper (auto-generated). Session 2: Docker Debugging (auto). /title My Project Debugging (manual). Titles make sessions findable.

## Analogy

Labeling a notebook cover - Math, English, Science. You find the right notebook fast. Session titles label conversations.

## Related Concepts

- [[sessions|Sessions]]
- [[hermes-sessions|Hermes Sessions]]
- [[session-id|Session ID]]

title: sessions
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

Each conversation with Hermes is a session. Sessions are stored in SQLite. You can resume, branch, and export them.

## Concrete Example

You chat with Hermes about a Python project (Session A). Later, you start a new session about a different topic (Session B). Session A is saved. You can resume it anytime.

## Analogy

Notebooks for different subjects - math notes in one, English in another. Each session is a notebook for one conversation topic.

## Related Concepts

- [[session-store|Session Store]]
- [[session-id|Session ID]]
- [[hermes-sessions|Hermes Sessions]]

title: sqlite-fts5
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

Full-Text Search version 5. A SQLite extension that enables fast text search. Hermes uses it for session search.

## Concrete Example

FTS5: you search docker debugging. It finds all sessions containing docker or debugging. Ranked by relevance. Fast, like Google for your chats.

## Analogy

A search engine index - it catalogs every word in every document. FTS5 catalogs every word in every session for fast search.

## Related Concepts

- [[session-store|Session Store]]
- [[session-search-tool|Session Search Tool]]
- [[state-db|State DB]]

title: state-db
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

The main Hermes database: ~/.hermes/state.db. SQLite. Stores sessions, messages, and search index.

## Concrete Example

state.db: tables include sessions, messages, tool_calls. FTS5 virtual table for full-text search. All conversation data in one file.

## Analogy

A school records office - all student records in one place. state.db is the records office for Hermes.

## Related Concepts

- [[session-store|Session Store]]
- [[sessions|Sessions]]
- [[sqlite-fts5|SQLite FTS5]]

title: undo
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

Remove the last exchange from the conversation. Command: /undo. The model forgets the last interaction.

## Concrete Example

You asked Hermes to rename a file. It did. You realize: wrong name! /undo. The rename command and result are removed from the conversation.

## Analogy

An eraser on a pencil - you erase the last thing you wrote. /undo erases the last exchange from the conversation.

## Related Concepts

- [[safety-net|Safety Net]]
- [[conversation-history|Conversation History]]
- [[sessions|Sessions]]

title: write-json-snapshots
text:
> **Domain:** [[_sessions-profiles-moc|Sessions & Profiles]]

## Motivation

A config option: write_json_snapshots. When true, Hermes saves a JSON snapshot after each session.

## Concrete Example

config: write_json_snapshots: true. After each session, a JSON file is saved. Useful for backup and debugging.

## Analogy

An autosave feature in a game - it saves automatically. write_json_snapshots autosaves session data.

## Related Concepts

- [[json-snapshots|JSON Snapshots]]
- [[config-yaml|Config YAML]]
- [[sessions|Sessions]]

title: agent-loop
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

The agent loop is the heart of Hermes. It keeps the conversation going turn after turn until the task is done or a limit is reached.

## Concrete Example

Each turn the agent reads the latest messages, builds a prompt, calls the model, and handles the response. If the model requests a tool, the loop runs again.

## Analogy

Like a dishwasher cycle: fill, wash, rinse, drain, repeat until the dishes are clean.

## Related Concepts

- [[run_conversation|run_conversation]]
- [[max_turns|max_turns]]
- [[iteration|iteration]]
- [[tool-dispatch|tool dispatch]]

title: audit-log
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

The audit log records every tool call, model response, and user input for debugging and review.

## Concrete Example

You can look at the audit log to see exactly which tools were called and what they returned at each step.

## Analogy

Like a CCTV recording in a shop: you can replay it to see what happened and when.

## Related Concepts

- [[conversation-state|Conversation State]]
- [[error-recovery|error recovery]]
- [[memory-store|Memory Store]]

title: busy
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

The busy flag tells the interface that the agent is working so it shows a loading state.

## Concrete Example

When the agent runs a long tool the busy indicator turns on, then turns off when done.

## Analogy

Like a shop sign that flips to Back in 5 minutes while the staff restock.

## Related Concepts

- [[indicator|/indicator]]
- [[statusbar|/statusbar]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]

title: config-layers
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Hermes loads settings from multiple layers: defaults, config file, environment variables, and runtime overrides.

## Concrete Example

The default model is A, the config file sets it to B, and a runtime flag sets it to C. The last layer wins, so C is used.

## Analogy

Like school rules layered on top of government rules: the more specific one applies.

## Related Concepts

- [[system-prompt|system prompt]]
- [[environment-hints|environment hints]]
- [[personality|personality]]

title: context-compression-trigger
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

When the conversation gets too long, a compression trigger shrinks old messages so the prompt stays within the model limit.

## Concrete Example

After 20 tool calls the prompt is huge. The trigger summarizes early messages into a compact note, freeing space for new ones.

## Analogy

Like cleaning your backpack: you remove old worksheets and keep only what you still need.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]
- [[prompt-builder|prompt builder]]
- [[prompt-caching|prompt caching]]

title: context-window
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can see at once. It limits how much history fits in one prompt.

## Concrete Example

A model with a 32k window can hold about 24 pages of text. If the conversation is longer, old parts get compressed.

## Analogy

Like the size of a whiteboard: once it is full you have to erase old notes to write new ones.

## Related Concepts

- [[token-budget|Token Budget]]
- [[context-compression-trigger|context compression trigger]]
- [[prompt-caching|prompt caching]]

title: conversation-state
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

The conversation state tracks all messages, tool results, and metadata across turns so the agent knows what happened so far.

## Concrete Example

The state holds 12 messages: 3 from you, 5 from the assistant, and 4 tool results. The agent uses this history to stay on track.

## Analogy

Like a scoreboard recording every point so the referee knows the current score.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]
- [[message-role-alternation|message role alternation]]
- [[context-compression-trigger|context compression trigger]]

title: environment-hints
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Environment hints tell the model about the world around it: the operating system, current folder, date, and available tools.

## Concrete Example

The prompt includes lines like Host: Linux and Current working directory: /home/student so the model knows where it is running.

## Analogy

Like a map pinned to the classroom wall showing which building you are in and where the exits are.

## Related Concepts

- [[prompt-builder|prompt builder]]
- [[tool-dispatch|tool dispatch]]
- [[system-prompt|system prompt]]

title: error-recovery
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

When a tool call fails or the model gives a bad response, error recovery handles it gracefully and lets the loop continue.

## Concrete Example

The terminal tool returns an error because the file is missing. Hermes tells the model, which tries a different path.

## Analogy

Like having an eraser handy: when you make a mistake you erase and try again.

## Related Concepts

- [[handle_function_call|handle_function_call]]
- [[tool_call-response|tool_call response]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]

title: fallback-chain
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

If the primary model fails, Hermes can fall back to a backup model so the conversation keeps going.

## Concrete Example

Model A is down. Hermes automatically switches to Model B and continues the chat without interruption.

## Analogy

Like a backup generator: when the power cuts out, the generator kicks in so the lights stay on.

## Related Concepts

- [[model-selection|Model Selection]]
- [[error-recovery|error recovery]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]

title: footer
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

The footer shows extra info at the very bottom: version number, shortcuts, or tips.

## Concrete Example

The footer reads Press Tab to autocomplete so you learn shortcuts while chatting.

## Analogy

Like the small print at the bottom of a textbook page with helpful footnotes.

## Related Concepts

- [[statusbar|/statusbar]]
- [[indicator|/indicator]]
- [[skin|/skin]]

title: graceful-shutdown
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

When you exit Hermes, it saves state, finishes running tools, and closes connections cleanly.

## Concrete Example

You type exit. Hermes finishes the current tool, saves the memory, and closes the gateway before quitting.

## Analogy

Like a shop closing routine: count the cash, lock the doors, turn off the lights.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]
- [[conversation-state|Conversation State]]
- [[memory-store|Memory Store]]

title: handle_function_call
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

This step takes a single tool call from the model, runs the actual tool function, and returns the result back to the conversation.

## Concrete Example

The model calls read_file. handle_function_call opens the file, reads the content, and hands the text back as a tool result message.

## Analogy

Like a librarian fetching a book you requested: you ask, they go get it, and hand it to you.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-dispatch|tool dispatch]]
- [[tool_call-response|tool_call response]]
- [[text-response|text response]]

title: idle-state
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

When the agent is not working on anything, it is in idle state, waiting for your next message.

## Concrete Example

The indicator shows a steady dot. No tools are running. The agent is ready for input.

## Analogy

Like a taxi waiting at a stand: engine off, ready to go when a passenger arrives.

## Related Concepts

- [[busy|/busy]]
- [[indicator|/indicator]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]

title: indicator-states
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

The indicator can show several states: thinking, tool running, waiting for input, error, and idle.

## Concrete Example

A pulsing dot means thinking. A gear icon means a tool is running. A red dot means an error occurred.

## Analogy

Like traffic lights: green means go, red means stop, yellow means slow down.

## Related Concepts

- [[indicator|/indicator]]
- [[busy|/busy]]
- [[idle-state|Idle State]]

title: indicator
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

The indicator is a small icon or dot that shows what the agent is doing: thinking, running a tool, or idle.

## Concrete Example

A spinning circle means the model is thinking. A checkmark means it is done.

## Analogy

Like the status dot on a messaging app: green for online, red for busy.

## Related Concepts

- [[statusbar|/statusbar]]
- [[busy|/busy]]
- [[footer|/footer]]

title: iteration
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Each pass through the agent loop is one iteration. The model thinks, tools run, and results come back in each iteration.

## Concrete Example

Turn 1 the model searches. Turn 2 it reads a file. Turn 3 it gives the answer. That is three iterations.

## Analogy

Like laps around a running track: each lap is one iteration until you finish the race.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]
- [[max_turns|max_turns]]
- [[run_conversation|run_conversation]]

title: max_turns
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

max_turns stops the agent from looping forever. It is a safety limit on how many turns one conversation can take.

## Concrete Example

If max_turns is 25, the agent stops after 25 turns even if the model keeps asking for more tools.

## Analogy

Like a game with extra time: when the whistle blows the game ends no matter what.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]
- [[iteration|iteration]]
- [[run_conversation|run_conversation]]

title: memory-store
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

The memory store saves facts and preferences between conversations so the agent remembers you next time.

## Concrete Example

Hermes remembers your name is Alex and you prefer Python. Next session it greets you by name and defaults to Python.

## Analogy

Like a diary the agent writes in and reads from to remember past conversations.

## Related Concepts

- [[conversation-state|Conversation State]]
- [[context-compression-trigger|context compression trigger]]
- [[profile-system|Profile System]]

title: message-role-alternation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Messages must alternate between user and assistant roles. The model expects this pattern to follow the conversation correctly.

## Concrete Example

The sequence goes user, assistant, tool, assistant, tool, assistant. Hermes keeps this order so the model does not get confused.

## Analogy

Like a tennis rally: the ball goes back and forth between two sides in a steady rhythm.

## Related Concepts

- [[prompt-builder|prompt builder]]
- [[tool_call-response|tool_call response]]
- [[text-response|text response]]

title: mixture-of-agents
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Instead of one model doing everything, a mixture of agents uses different models for different parts of the task.

## Concrete Example

One model drafts code, another reviews it, and a third writes tests. Together they produce better results.

## Analogy

Like a group project where the writer, artist, and presenter each do what they are best at.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]
- [[delegate_task|delegate_task]]
- [[personality|personality]]

title: model-selection
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Hermes can switch between different AI models. Each model has different strengths, speeds, and costs.

## Concrete Example

You pick a fast small model for simple chat and a powerful large model for complex coding tasks.

## Analogy

Like choosing a pen: a fine tip for neat writing, a thick marker for posters.

## Related Concepts

- [[reasoning-levels|Reasoning Levels]]
- [[mixture-of-agents|Mixture of Agents]]
- [[config-layers|Config Layers]]

title: multi-tool-call
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Sometimes the model calls several tools in one turn. Hermes runs them and collects all results before continuing.

## Concrete Example

The model calls read_file on three files at once. Hermes runs all three and returns three results in one turn.

## Analogy

Like a waiter carrying three plates to the kitchen at once instead of making three trips.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-dispatch|tool dispatch]]
- [[handle_function_call|handle_function_call]]
- [[tool_call-response|tool_call response]]

title: personality
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

This command lets you switch the agent personality on the fly without restarting.

## Concrete Example

Type /personality friendly tutor and the agent immediately changes its speaking style.

## Analogy

Like changing costumes backstage between scenes in a school play.

## Related Concepts

- [[personality|personality]]
- [[soulmd|SOUL.md]]
- [[reasoning|/reasoning]]

title: plugin-system
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Plugins extend Hermes with new tools, skills, or platform connectors without changing the core code.

## Concrete Example

You install a plugin that adds Spotify control. Now the agent can play music without any code changes.

## Analogy

Like adding apps to your phone: each app gives new features without replacing the phone.

## Related Concepts

- [[skill-loading|Skill Loading]]
- [[tool-registration|Tool Registration]]
- [[mixture-of-agents|Mixture of Agents]]

title: profile-system
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Profiles let you keep separate setups: different models, skills, and memories for different purposes.

## Concrete Example

You have a study profile for homework and a game profile for fun. Switching profiles changes everything at once.

## Analogy

Like having different binders for different subjects: each one has its own notes and tools.

## Related Concepts

- [[soulmd|SOUL.md]]
- [[personality|personality]]
- [[config-layers|Config Layers]]

title: prompt-builder
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

The prompt builder assembles all the pieces into one big prompt each turn: system prompt, conversation history, tool definitions, and environment hints.

## Concrete Example

Hermes collects your messages, the tool list, the current working folder, and the system prompt, then packs them into one request to the model.

## Analogy

Like packing a lunchbox: you put rice, meat, vegetables, and a note together before heading to school.

## Related Concepts

- [[system-prompt|system prompt]]
- [[environment-hints|environment hints]]
- [[tool-dispatch|tool dispatch]]
- [[prompt-caching|prompt caching]]

title: prompt-caching
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Prompt caching saves the unchanged part of the prompt so it does not need to be processed again, making responses faster and cheaper.

## Concrete Example

The system prompt and tool definitions stay the same every turn. The cache reuses them so only new messages are processed fresh.

## Analogy

Like saving a draft email: next time you only type the new part instead of rewriting everything.

## Related Concepts

- [[prompt-builder|prompt builder]]
- [[environment-hints|environment hints]]
- [[context-compression-trigger|context compression trigger]]

title: reasoning-display
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

This controls whether the reasoning steps are shown to you or hidden. Showing them helps you learn how the model thinks.

## Concrete Example

With show you see the thinking steps. With hide you only see the final answer.

## Analogy

Like a teacher who either talks through the solution on the board or just writes the final answer.

## Related Concepts

- [[reasoning-levels|Reasoning Levels]]
- [[verbose|/verbose]]
- [[reasoning|/reasoning]]

title: reasoning-hide
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

When reasoning is hidden, only the final answer appears. The thinking happens behind the scenes.

## Concrete Example

You just see The file has 42 lines without seeing the intermediate planning steps.

## Analogy

Like ordering at a restaurant: you get the dish without seeing the kitchen work.

## Related Concepts

- [[reasoning-display|Reasoning Display]]
- [[reasoning-show|Reasoning Show]]

title: reasoning-high
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Level high gives deep thinking for complex problems that need careful step-by-step reasoning.

## Concrete Example

For a tricky math proof the high level breaks the problem into parts and verifies each step carefully.

## Analogy

Like solving a chess puzzle: you think several moves ahead before deciding.

## Related Concepts

- [[reasoning-levels|Reasoning Levels]]
- [[reasoning-medium|reasoning medium]]
- [[reasoning-xhigh|reasoning xhigh]]

title: reasoning-levels
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Reasoning levels control how much the model thinks before answering. Higher levels mean more thinking steps for harder problems.

## Concrete Example

Level none gives quick answers. Level medium thinks through steps. Level high spends extra effort on tough math or coding.

## Analogy

Like choosing walking or running: walk for short trips, sprint when you are late for the exam.

## Related Concepts

- [[reasoning-display|reasoning display]]
- [[system-prompt|system prompt]]
- [[reasoning|/reasoning]]

title: reasoning-low
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Level low adds a short thinking block. Useful for straightforward tasks that benefit from a moment of planning.

## Concrete Example

Before summarizing a short paragraph the model spends a few seconds planning its answer.

## Analogy

Like checking your homework answers once before handing them in.

## Related Concepts

- [[reasoning-levels|Reasoning Levels]]
- [[reasoning-minimal|reasoning minimal]]
- [[reasoning-medium|reasoning medium]]

title: reasoning-medium
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Level medium gives moderate thinking. A balanced choice for most everyday tasks.

## Concrete Example

For a coding question the medium level plans the approach, writes the code, and double-checks the logic.

## Analogy

Like doing a rough draft before the final copy of an essay.

## Related Concepts

- [[reasoning-levels|Reasoning Levels]]
- [[reasoning-low|reasoning low]]
- [[reasoning-high|reasoning high]]

title: reasoning-minimal
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Level minimal gives a tiny bit of thinking. Good for easy tasks that need just a quick check.

## Concrete Example

The model does one quick mental step before answering a yes or no question.

## Analogy

Like glancing both ways before crossing a quiet side street.

## Related Concepts

- [[reasoning-levels|Reasoning Levels]]
- [[reasoning-none|Reasoning none]]
- [[reasoning-low|reasoning low]]

title: reasoning-none
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Level none means no extra thinking steps. The model answers directly, which is fast but less thorough.

## Concrete Example

For a simple greeting like hi the model just says Hello back without any deep reasoning.

## Analogy

Like answering roll call: you just say present and move on.

## Related Concepts

- [[reasoning-levels|Reasoning Levels]]
- [[reasoning-minimal|reasoning minimal]]
- [[reasoning|/reasoning]]

title: reasoning-show
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

When reasoning is shown, you can see the model thinking process step by step before the final answer.

## Concrete Example

You see lines like Let me check the file first then I will count the lines before the answer appears.

## Analogy

Like watching a chef cook: you see every step from chopping to plating.

## Related Concepts

- [[reasoning-display|Reasoning Display]]
- [[reasoning-hide|Reasoning Hide]]
- [[verbose|/verbose]]

title: reasoning-xhigh
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Level xhigh is the deepest reasoning. Reserved for the hardest problems needing maximum effort.

## Concrete Example

For a complex algorithm design the model spends extra turns exploring options and checking edge cases.

## Analogy

Like a student spending an hour on one competition math problem to find the best solution.

## Related Concepts

- [[reasoning-levels|Reasoning Levels]]
- [[reasoning-high|reasoning high]]
- [[reasoning|/reasoning]]

title: reasoning
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

This command changes the reasoning level during a conversation.

## Concrete Example

Type /reasoning high before a hard math question and the model thinks deeper for the next answer.

## Analogy

Like a video game difficulty selector: you raise it when the boss fight starts.

## Related Concepts

- [[reasoning-levels|Reasoning Levels]]
- [[reasoning-display|Reasoning Display]]
- [[verbose|/verbose]]

title: response-parsing
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

After the model returns a response, Hermes parses it to find tool calls, text, or reasoning blocks.

## Concrete Example

The response has a tool_call block and a text block. Hermes separates them, runs the tool, and shows the text.

## Analogy

Like sorting mail into bills, letters, and ads so each type goes to the right place.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool_call-response|tool_call response]]
- [[text-response|text response]]
- [[handle_function_call|handle_function_call]]

title: run_conversation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

This is the main function that drives the whole agent loop. Without it the agent would only answer one message and stop.

## Concrete Example

You type a question. run_conversation starts, calls the model, runs tools, and loops until the model gives a final text answer with no tool calls.

## Analogy

Like the conductor of an orchestra who keeps the music flowing until the piece ends.

## Related Concepts

- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]
- [[max_turns|max_turns]]
- [[system-prompt|system prompt]]
- [[text-response|text response]]

title: skill-loading
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Skills are reusable instruction sets. Hermes loads relevant skills before answering to follow proven workflows.

## Concrete Example

When you ask about GitHub, Hermes loads the github-pr-workflow skill so it follows the correct PR steps.

## Analogy

Like a student pulling out the right textbook before starting a specific assignment.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-dispatch|tool dispatch]]
- [[system-prompt|system prompt]]
- [[memory-store|Memory Store]]

title: skin
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

This command switches the visual skin or theme of the interface.

## Concrete Example

Type /skin midnight and the colors change to a dark blue palette.

## Analogy

Like swapping your phone case for a new color.

## Related Concepts

- [[skins-and-themes|Skins and Themes]]
- [[statusbar|/statusbar]]
- [[footer|/footer]]

title: skins-and-themes
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Skins change how the Hermes interface looks: colors, layout, and visual style. Themes are preset skin bundles.

## Concrete Example

You pick a dark theme for night study and a light theme for daytime. The layout and colors change instantly.

## Analogy

Like changing your phone wallpaper and icon pack to match your mood.

## Related Concepts

- [[skin|/skin]]
- [[statusbar|/statusbar]]
- [[indicator|/indicator]]

title: soulmd
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

SOUL.md is a file that stores the deep identity and values of the agent. It goes beyond a simple system prompt.

## Concrete Example

SOUL.md might say I am Hermes, a curious and patient assistant who always shows working steps and admits mistakes.

## Analogy

Like a personal mission statement that defines your core values and guides every decision you make.

## Related Concepts

- [[personality|personality]]
- [[system-prompt|system prompt]]
- [[personality|/personality]]

title: statusbar
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

The status bar shows live info at the bottom of the screen: model name, token count, and connection status.

## Concrete Example

You glance at the status bar and see Model: GLM-5.2 and Tokens: 1200 so you know your session status.

## Analogy

Like the HUD in a racing game showing speed and lap number.

## Related Concepts

- [[indicator|/indicator]]
- [[footer|/footer]]
- [[busy|/busy]]

title: streaming-response
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Instead of waiting for the full answer, streaming sends text to you piece by piece as the model generates it.

## Concrete Example

You see words appearing one by one on screen while the model is still writing the rest.

## Analogy

Like watching a live text broadcast of a sports match instead of waiting for the final summary.

## Related Concepts

- [[text-response|text response]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]
- [[busy|/busy]]

title: system-message-construction
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Hermes builds the system message by combining the base prompt, personality, environment hints, and tool list into one coherent instruction set.

## Concrete Example

The final system message reads: You are Hermes, a helpful agent. Host: Linux. Tools: terminal, read_file, write_file. Be concise and friendly.

## Analogy

Like a job description that combines role, rules, and tools into one document.

## Related Concepts

- [[system-prompt|system prompt]]
- [[prompt-builder|prompt builder]]
- [[environment-hints|environment hints]]

title: system-prompt
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

The system prompt tells the model who it is and how it should behave. It sets the rules for the whole conversation.

## Concrete Example

Hermes builds a system prompt saying you are a helpful agent with these tools and this personality. The model follows those rules every turn.

## Analogy

Like a school badge and uniform rules: they define who you are and how you act before you even speak.

## Related Concepts

- [[prompt-builder|prompt builder]]
- [[personality|personality]]
- [[soulmd|SOUL.md]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]

title: text-response
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

A text response is the final answer the model gives when it has no more tool calls to make. This ends the current turn.

## Concrete Example

After checking the weather with a tool, the model writes Today is 28 degrees and sunny. That text goes to you as the answer.

## Analogy

Like the teacher saying class dismissed after finishing the lesson: no more actions needed.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool_call-response|tool_call response]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]
- [[run_conversation|run_conversation]]

title: token-budget
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

The token budget is how many tokens the model can process in one turn. Longer conversations use more tokens.

## Concrete Example

A model with a 128000 token budget can handle a long chat, but when it gets close to the limit, old messages get compressed.

## Analogy

Like a data plan on your phone: when you use too much, the system warns you and slows things down.

## Related Concepts

- [[context-compression-trigger|context compression trigger]]
- [[prompt-caching|prompt caching]]
- [[max_turns|max_turns]]

title: tool-dispatch
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

When the model asks to use a tool, tool dispatch figures out which tool to run and sends the request to it.

## Concrete Example

The model says use terminal with command ls. Tool dispatch finds the terminal tool, runs it, and collects the output.

## Analogy

Like a school office routing forms: you drop a form at the counter and the staff send it to the right department.

## Related Concepts

- [[handle_function_call|handle_function_call]]
- [[tool_call-response|tool_call response]]
- [[prompt-builder|prompt builder]]

title: tool-registration
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Tools must be registered before the agent can use them. Registration tells Hermes the tool name, schema, and function.

## Concrete Example

The terminal tool is registered at startup. The search_files tool is registered too. The model can now call either one.

## Analogy

Like signing up for a club: once registered you can participate in activities.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-dispatch|tool dispatch]]
- [[tool-schema|Tool Schema]]
- [[tool_use_enforcement|tool_use_enforcement]]

title: tool-schema
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

Each tool has a schema that describes its name, what it does, and what parameters it accepts. The model reads schemas to know how to call tools.

## Concrete Example

The terminal tool schema says it needs a command string and has an optional timeout number. The model follows this format to call it.

## Analogy

Like a recipe card listing ingredients and steps so anyone can follow it.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-dispatch|tool dispatch]]
- [[handle_function_call|handle_function_call]]
- [[prompt-builder|prompt builder]]

title: tool_call-response
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

After a tool runs, its result goes back to the model as a tool_call response so the model can decide what to do next.

## Concrete Example

The terminal tool returns a folder listing. That listing becomes a tool role message. The model reads it and decides to open a file.

## Analogy

Like getting your exam paper back with marks: you read the feedback and decide what to study next.

## Related Concepts

- [[handle_function_call|handle_function_call]]
- [[text-response|text response]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]

title: tool_use_enforcement
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

This rule makes sure the model actually uses tools when needed instead of guessing answers or making things up.

## Concrete Example

The system prompt says you MUST use tools to read files. If the model tries to answer without reading, the loop sends it back to use a tool.

## Analogy

Like a teacher who says show your working: you cannot just write the answer, you must prove each step.

## Related Concepts

- [[tool-dispatch|tool dispatch]]
- [[system-prompt|system prompt]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]

title: turn-timeout
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

A turn timeout stops a single turn from running too long, protecting against tools that hang or freeze.

## Concrete Example

If a tool call takes more than 300 seconds the timeout fires and the turn ends with an error message.

## Analogy

Like an exam timer: when the bell rings you must stop writing.

## Related Concepts

- [[max_turns|max_turns]]
- [[error-recovery|error recovery]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]

title: verbose
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

This command toggles how much detail the agent shows: tool inputs, outputs, and reasoning steps.

## Concrete Example

Turn verbose on to see every tool call and result. Turn it off for a clean, quiet chat.

## Analogy

Like turning subtitles on or off while watching a movie.

## Related Concepts

- [[reasoning-display|Reasoning Display]]
- [[statusbar|/statusbar]]
- [[indicator|/indicator]]

title: warm-start
text:
> **Domain:** [[_agent-architecture-moc|Agent Architecture]]

## Motivation

A warm start reuses cached prompts and loaded tools from a previous run, making the next conversation start faster.

## Concrete Example

After one chat ends, the next one starts in 1 second instead of 5 because the system prompt is already cached.

## Analogy

Like a warm-up before exercise: your muscles are ready so you perform better from the start.

## Related Concepts

- [[prompt-caching|prompt caching]]
- [[agent-loop|Agent Loop]]
- [[config-layers|Config Layers]]

Like a bouncer at a club door letting someone in after checking the guest list.

BlueBubbles is a bridge that lets Hermes send and receive iMessages from Apple devices.

You set up BlueBubbles on a Mac and connect Hermes. Now you can iMessage your agent and get replies.

Like a mail forwarding service that sends your letters between two different post offices.

- [[gateway|gateway]]

A bot token is a secret key that lets Hermes connect to a platform as a bot. Keep it private.

You get a token from Telegram BotFather and put it in the config. Hermes uses it to log in as your bot.

Like a house key: only the person with the key can open the door.

- [[platform-connection|platform connection]]

## Motivation

Broadcast sends the same message to all connected platforms at once.

You broadcast a weather alert. It goes to Telegram, Discord, and Slack simultaneously.

Like a school announcement over the PA system reaching every classroom at once.

## Related Concepts

- [[delivery-options|delivery options]]
- [[home-channels|home channels]]
- [[gateway|gateway]]

title: commands
text:

This command lists all available gateway commands you can use in chat.

You type /commands and see a list: /platforms, /gateway, /restart, /sethome, /approve, /deny.

Like a restaurant menu showing all the options you can order.

## Related Concepts

- [[platforms|/platforms]]
- [[gateway|/gateway]]

title: connection-pool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_gateway-platforms-moc|Gateway & Platforms]]

## Motivation

The connection pool manages multiple platform connections efficiently, reusing connections instead of making new ones.

## Concrete Example

Hermes keeps 5 Telegram connections in a pool. When a message arrives it uses a free connection instead of opening a new one.

## Analogy

Like a carpool: instead of everyone driving separately, you share rides to save resources.

## Related Concepts

- [[platform-connection|platform connection]]
- [[gateway|gateway]]
- [[platform-adapter|platform adapter]]

Delivery options control where the agent sends its output: the original chat, local terminal, all platforms, or a specific platform.

A cron job can deliver results to the Telegram home channel only, or to all connected platforms.

Like choosing delivery method: standard mail, express, or pickup at the counter.

- [[home-channels|home channels]]
- [[platform-connection|platform connection]]

## Motivation

This command rejects a pending pairing request, blocking that user or device.

An unknown user tries to connect. You type /deny and they are blocked from messaging the agent.

## Analogy

Like a security guard turning away someone without an ID badge.

## Related Concepts

- [[pairing|pairing]]
- [[approve|/approve]]
- [[dm-authorization|DM authorization]]

DingTalk is a business messaging app used in China. Hermes can connect to it for workplace communication.

You connect DingTalk and ask Hermes to check tomorrow schedule in the DingTalk chat.

## Analogy

Like having a personal assistant in your work group chat.

title: automation-chain
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

Multiple automated tasks can be chained: one triggers the next, creating a full workflow without human input.

## Concrete Example

A webhook triggers a code review, which on success triggers a deployment, which triggers a notification.

## Analogy

Like dominoes standing in a line: pushing the first one knocks down the rest in sequence.

## Related Concepts

- [[context_from-chaining|context_from (Chaining)]]
- [[webhooks|webhooks]]
- [[event-driven-architecture|event-driven architecture]]

title: automation-safety
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

Automation can be powerful but risky. Safety limits like timeouts, retries, and restricted tools prevent disasters.

## Concrete Example

A cron job that deletes old files has a restricted toolset and a 60-second timeout so it cannot accidentally delete everything.

## Analogy

Like safety guards on a power saw: they prevent accidents while still letting you cut wood.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-job-enabled_toolsets|Cron Job enabled_toolsets]]
- [[cron-job-timeout|Cron Job Timeout]]
- [[3-minute-interrupt|3-minute interrupt]]

title: background-tasks
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

Background tasks run without blocking the main conversation, letting the agent do work while still chatting with you.

## Concrete Example

You ask the agent to run a long build. It starts it in the background and you can keep chatting while it compiles.

## Analogy

Like cooking rice in a rice cooker while you do your homework: both happen at the same time.

## Related Concepts

- [[terminal-background-mode|terminal background mode]]
- [[notify_on_complete|notify_on_complete]]
- [[delegate_task|delegate_task]]

title: context_from-chaining
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

context_from lets one cron job receive the output of a previous job, chaining them together.

## Concrete Example

Job A fetches the news. Job B uses context_from A to summarize the news that Job A collected.

## Analogy

Like a relay race: each runner passes the baton to the next so they build on the same effort.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]
- [[hermes-cron-create|hermes cron create]]
- [[cron-job-skills|Cron Job Skills]]

title: cron-delivery-framing
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

The delivery framing wraps the cron job output with context so the message makes sense when it arrives.

## Concrete Example

The message arrives as Cron job weather-check result: Today is 28C and sunny instead of just the raw output.

## Analogy

Like a teacher framing a handout with a title and instructions so students understand what they received.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-job-delivery|Cron Job delivery]]
- [[delivery-options|delivery options]]
- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]

title: cron-job-delivery
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

Delivery controls where the cron job result goes: the origin chat, local terminal, all platforms, or a specific one.

## Concrete Example

A cron job set to delivery platform sends its result to Telegram only, not to every connected platform.

## Analogy

Like choosing where to send a photo: to one friend, to a group, or to everyone.

## Related Concepts

- [[delivery-options|delivery options]]
- [[home-channels|home channels]]
- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]

title: cron-job-enabled_toolsets
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

You can restrict which tools a cron job can use, limiting it to only what it needs for safety.

## Concrete Example

A report cron job only has read_file and terminal enabled. It cannot write files or delete anything.

## Analogy

Like giving a substitute teacher only the keys to the classroom, not the whole school.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]
- [[tool-dispatch|tool dispatch]]
- [[hermes-cron-create|hermes cron create]]

title: cron-job-model-override
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

You can set a specific model for a cron job, different from your default, to save cost or use a specialized model.

## Concrete Example

The daily summary job uses a small fast model while the weekly analysis job uses a powerful model.

## Analogy

Like choosing different tools for different jobs: a scissors for paper, a saw for wood.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]
- [[model-selection|Model Selection]]
- [[hermes-cron-create|hermes cron create]]

title: cron-job-priority
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

Cron jobs can have priority levels so important jobs run first when multiple are due at the same time.

## Concrete Example

At 9am two jobs are due. The high-priority report runs first, then the low-priority cleanup job.

## Analogy

Like a VIP line at an airport: priority passengers board first.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]
- [[cron-tick-lock|Cron Tick Lock]]
- [[hermes-cron-create|hermes cron create]]

title: cron-job-retry
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

If a cron job fails, it can automatically retry a few times before giving up and reporting an error.

## Concrete Example

A weather API call fails. The job retries 3 times with 1-minute gaps before marking itself as failed.

## Analogy

Like calling a busy hotline: you try a few times before giving up.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]
- [[3-minute-interrupt|3-minute interrupt]]
- [[error-recovery|error recovery]]

title: cron-job-script
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

Instead of an AI task, a cron job can run a shell script directly for simple automated tasks.

## Concrete Example

A cron job runs backup.sh every night at midnight to copy files to an external drive.

## Analogy

Like a vending machine: you set it up once and it dispenses the same item every time you press the button.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]
- [[no_agent-mode|no_agent mode]]
- [[hermes-cron-create|hermes cron create]]

title: cron-job-skills
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

You can attach a skill to a cron job so it runs with specific instructions every time.

## Concrete Example

A daily report cron job uses the github-pr-workflow skill so it always follows the correct PR review steps.

## Analogy

Like a recipe attached to a timer: when the timer goes off, the recipe is ready to follow.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]
- [[hermes-cron-create|hermes cron create]]
- [[skill-loading|Skill Loading]]

title: cron-job-timeout
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

Each cron job has a timeout that stops it if it takes too long, preventing one slow job from blocking others.

## Concrete Example

A job with a 60-second timeout gets killed if it runs longer than a minute.

## Analogy

Like an egg timer: when it dings you take the egg out whether it is done or not.

## Related Concepts

- [[3-minute-interrupt|3-minute interrupt]]
- [[cron-tick-lock|Cron Tick Lock]]
- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]

title: cron-job-workdir
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

You can set a working directory for a cron job so it runs in the right project folder.

## Concrete Example

A cron job set to workdir /projects/homework runs git commands inside the homework folder.

## Analogy

Like a stage manager setting up the right stage before the actors perform.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]
- [[hermes-cron-create|hermes cron create]]
- [[no_agent-mode|no_agent mode]]

title: cron-jobs
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

Cron jobs are scheduled tasks that run automatically at set times. They let Hermes do things even when you are not chatting.

## Concrete Example

You create a cron job that checks the weather every morning at 7am and sends you a summary on Telegram.

## Analogy

Like an alarm clock that not only rings but also makes your breakfast for you.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-cron-create|hermes cron create]]
- [[cronjob-tool|cronjob tool]]
- [[schedule-formats|schedule formats]]

title: cron-missed-runs
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

If the gateway is down when a cron job is scheduled, the missed run can be detected and optionally caught up.

## Concrete Example

The gateway was down at 7am. When it starts at 8am it sees the missed weather job and can run it immediately.

## Analogy

Like a DVR recording a show you missed: you can watch it when you get home.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]
- [[hermes-gateway-status|hermes gateway status]]
- [[cron-tick-lock|Cron Tick Lock]]

title: cron-tick-lock
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

The tick lock prevents two copies of the same cron job from running at the same time.

## Concrete Example

Job A is still running when the next tick fires. The lock blocks the second run until the first finishes.

## Analogy

Like a fitting room lock: only one person can use it at a time.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]
- [[gatewaylock|gateway.lock]]
- [[hermes-cron-run|hermes cron run]]

title: cronjob-tool
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

The cronjob tool is a built-in tool that lets the agent create, list, and manage cron jobs during a conversation.

## Concrete Example

You ask the agent to remind me to study every day at 8pm. The agent uses the cronjob tool to create it.

## Analogy

Like a personal assistant who can set up their own reminders without you filling out forms.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]
- [[hermes-cron-create|hermes cron create]]
- [[schedule-formats|schedule formats]]

title: delegate_task
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

This tool lets the agent spawn a sub-agent to handle a task independently, then report back.

## Concrete Example

The main agent delegates write unit tests to a sub-agent while it continues working on the main code.

## Analogy

Like a manager assigning tasks to team members and collecting their reports later.

## Related Concepts

- [[delegation-config|delegation config]]
- [[leaf-vs-orchestrator-role|leaf vs orchestrator role]]
- [[background-tasks|background tasks]]

title: delegation-config
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

Delegation config controls how sub-agents are spawned: what tools they get, what model they use, and their limits.

## Concrete Example

You set delegation config to allow sub-agents with read-only tools and a fast model for quick lookups.

## Analogy

Like a job description for a temp worker: it defines what they can do and what tools they can use.

## Related Concepts

- [[delegate_task|delegate_task]]
- [[leaf-vs-orchestrator-role|leaf vs orchestrator role]]
- [[max_spawn_depth|max_spawn_depth]]

title: duration-schedule
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

A duration schedule runs a job after a fixed time interval, repeating automatically.

## Concrete Example

You set a duration of 30 minutes. The job runs every 30 minutes: 10:00, 10:30, 11:00, and so on.

## Analogy

Like a bus that comes every 15 minutes on a fixed loop.

## Related Concepts

- [[schedule-formats|schedule formats]]
- [[every-phrase-schedule|every phrase schedule]]
- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]

title: event-driven-architecture
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

In event-driven architecture, actions happen in response to events instead of on a fixed schedule.

## Concrete Example

A PR opens (event) which triggers a code review (action). No cron schedule needed, the event drives it.

## Analogy

Like a restaurant kitchen: orders come in as events and the chef cooks each one as it arrives.

## Related Concepts

- [[webhooks|webhooks]]
- [[webhook-routes|webhook routes]]
- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]

title: every-phrase-schedule
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

An every phrase schedule uses natural language like every day at 9am or every Monday.

## Concrete Example

You write every Friday at 3pm and the job runs every Friday at 3pm without needing cron syntax.

## Analogy

Like telling a friend call me every Sunday noon in plain words instead of setting a complex alarm.

## Related Concepts

- [[schedule-formats|schedule formats]]
- [[duration-schedule|duration schedule]]
- [[5-field-cron-schedule|5-field cron schedule]]

title: hermes-cron-create
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

This command creates a new cron job with a schedule and a task description.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes cron create with schedule every day at 7am and task summarize the news. The job is now active.

## Analogy

Like adding a new recurring event to your calendar.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]
- [[schedule-formats|schedule formats]]
- [[hermes-cron-list|hermes cron list]]

title: hermes-cron-edit
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

This command lets you change an existing cron job: its schedule, task, or settings.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes cron edit weather-check and change the time from 7am to 6:30am.

## Analogy

Like editing a calendar event to move it to a different time.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-cron-create|hermes cron create]]
- [[hermes-cron-pause|hermes cron pause]]
- [[schedule-formats|schedule formats]]

title: hermes-cron-list
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

This command shows all your cron jobs, their schedules, and whether they are active.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes cron list and see: weather-check (daily 7am, active), report (weekly Mon 9am, paused).

## Analogy

Like a timetable showing all your classes and whether they are happening or cancelled.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]
- [[hermes-cron-create|hermes cron create]]
- [[hermes-cron-status|hermes cron status]]

title: hermes-cron-pause
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

This command temporarily stops a cron job without deleting it. You can resume it later.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes cron pause weather-check before a holiday. It stops running until you resume.

## Analogy

Like snoozing an alarm: it stops for now but you can turn it back on.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-cron-resume|hermes cron resume]]
- [[hermes-cron-list|hermes cron list]]
- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]

title: hermes-cron-remove
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

This command permanently deletes a cron job. It cannot be recovered.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes cron remove old-report and the job is gone forever.

## Analogy

Like tearing a page out of your planner: it is gone for good.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-cron-pause|hermes cron pause]]
- [[hermes-cron-list|hermes cron list]]
- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]

title: hermes-cron-resume
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

This command restarts a paused cron job so it runs on its schedule again.

## Concrete Example

After your holiday you run hermes cron resume weather-check and it starts running at 7am again.

## Analogy

Like turning your alarm back on after a break.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-cron-pause|hermes cron pause]]
- [[hermes-cron-list|hermes cron list]]
- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]

title: hermes-cron-run
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

This command runs a cron job immediately, regardless of its schedule, to test or trigger it on demand.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes cron run weather-check and it executes right now instead of waiting for 7am.

## Analogy

Like pressing the test button on a fire alarm to check it works.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-cron-create|hermes cron create]]
- [[hermes-cron-status|hermes cron status]]
- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]

title: hermes-cron-status
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

This command shows the status of a specific cron job: last run, next run, and any errors.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes cron status weather-check and see: Last run 7am today, next run 7am tomorrow, no errors.

## Analogy

Like tracking a package: you see where it is and when it arrives next.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-cron-list|hermes cron list]]
- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]
- [[hermes-cron-run|hermes cron run]]

title: hermes-webhook-list
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

This command shows all registered webhooks and their routes.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes webhook list and see: github-push (active), payment-alert (paused).

## Analogy

Like a subscriptions page showing all the newsletters you are signed up for.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-webhook-subscribe|hermes webhook subscribe]]

text:

## Motivation

This command deletes a webhook subscription so Hermes no longer listens for those events.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes webhook remove old-webhook and Hermes stops responding to those events.

## Analogy

Like unsubscribing from a mailing list: you stop receiving those emails.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-webhook-subscribe|hermes webhook subscribe]]
- [[hermes-webhook-list|hermes webhook list]]
- [[webhooks|webhooks]]

title: hermes-webhook-subscribe
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

This command registers a webhook endpoint so Hermes can receive events from an external service.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes webhook subscribe github-push and get a URL to put in GitHub settings.

## Analogy

Like registering your phone number with a delivery service so they text you when your package arrives.

## Related Concepts

- [[webhooks|webhooks]]
- [[hermes-webhook-list|hermes webhook list]]
- [[webhook-routes|webhook routes]]

title: hermes-webhook-test
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

This command sends a test event to a webhook to verify it is working correctly.

## Concrete Example

You run hermes webhook test github-push and see Hermes receive and process the test event.

## Analogy

Like a fire drill: you test the alarm to make sure it works before a real emergency.

## Related Concepts

- [[hermes-webhook-subscribe|hermes webhook subscribe]]
- [[webhooks|webhooks]]
- [[webhook-routes|webhook routes]]

title: iso-timestamp-schedule
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

An ISO timestamp schedule runs a job once at a specific date and time in ISO format.

## Concrete Example

You write 2026-08-04T14:30:00 to run the job once at 2:30pm on August 4 2026.

## Analogy

Like setting a one-time alarm for a specific date instead of a recurring one.

## Related Concepts

- [[schedule-formats|schedule formats]]
- [[5-field-cron-schedule|5-field cron schedule]]
- [[duration-schedule|duration schedule]]

title: kanban-board
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

A Kanban board is a visual task tracker with columns like To Do, Doing, and Done. Hermes can manage one for projects.

## Concrete Example

The agent creates a Kanban board for your project with 5 tasks in To Do and 2 in Doing.

## Analogy

Like a whiteboard with sticky notes that you move from left to right as tasks progress.

## Related Concepts

- [[kanban-cli-verbs|kanban CLI verbs]]
- [[kanban-dispatch|kanban dispatch]]
- [[kanban-worker-toolset|kanban worker toolset]]

title: kanban-cli-verbs
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

Hermes Kanban has CLI commands to create, move, and manage tasks on the board.

## Concrete Example

You run kanban add write tests, kanban move task-3 doing, kanban done task-2 to manage the board.

## Analogy

Like a remote control for your task board: each button does one action.

## Related Concepts

- [[kanban-board|Kanban Board]]
- [[kanban-dispatch|kanban dispatch]]
- [[kanban-worker-toolset|kanban worker toolset]]

title: kanban-dispatch
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

Dispatch assigns a Kanban task to a worker agent that picks it up and works on it independently.

## Concrete Example

You dispatch task-3 to a worker. The worker agent picks it up and starts coding the solution.

## Analogy

Like a taxi dispatcher sending the nearest available driver to pick up a passenger.

## Related Concepts

- [[kanban-board|Kanban Board]]
- [[kanban-worker-toolset|kanban worker toolset]]
- [[delegate_task|delegate_task]]

title: kanban-worker-toolset
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

A Kanban worker gets a specific set of tools to do its assigned task, limited to what it needs.

## Concrete Example

A worker assigned to fix a bug gets terminal, read_file, and patch tools but not email or web tools.

## Analogy

Like giving a plumber only plumbing tools: they have what they need without carrying the whole toolbox.

## Related Concepts

- [[kanban-board|Kanban Board]]
- [[kanban-dispatch|kanban dispatch]]
- [[delegation-config|delegation config]]

title: leaf-vs-orchestrator-role
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

A leaf agent does tasks directly. An orchestrator agent delegates tasks to leaf agents and coordinates results.

## Concrete Example

The orchestrator breaks a big project into parts and delegates each to a leaf agent, then combines the results.

## Analogy

Like a conductor (orchestrator) who does not play an instrument but directs the musicians (leaves) who do.

## Related Concepts

- [[delegate_task|delegate_task]]
- [[delegation-config|Delegation Config]]
- [[max_concurrent_children|max_concurrent_children]]

title: max_concurrent_children
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

This limits how many sub-agents can run at the same time, preventing resource overload.

## Concrete Example

With a limit of 3, the orchestrator can run 3 sub-agents in parallel. A 4th must wait until one finishes.

## Analogy

Like a classroom with 3 computers: only 3 students can use them at once, others wait their turn.

## Related Concepts

- [[delegate_task|delegate_task]]
- [[max_spawn_depth|max_spawn_depth]]
- [[background-tasks|background tasks]]

title: max_spawn_depth
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

This limits how many levels deep agents can spawn sub-agents, preventing infinite chains.

## Concrete Example

Depth 2 means the main agent can spawn a sub-agent, and that sub-agent can spawn one more, but no deeper.

## Analogy

Like a family tree limit: you can have children and grandchildren but no great-grandchildren.

## Related Concepts

- [[delegate_task|delegate_task]]
- [[leaf-vs-orchestrator-role|leaf vs orchestrator role]]
- [[max_concurrent_children|max_concurrent_children]]

title: no_agent-mode
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

In no_agent mode the cron job runs a script or command without calling the AI model at all, saving time and cost.

## Concrete Example

A no_agent job runs git pull every hour to fetch the latest code. No AI thinking needed.

## Analogy

Like an automatic door: it opens when someone approaches, no decision-making required.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-job-script|Cron Job Script]]
- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]
- [[hermes-cron-create|hermes cron create]]

title: notify_on_complete
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

When a background task finishes, this setting sends a notification to the agent so it can report the result.

## Concrete Example

A 10-minute build finishes and the agent gets notified, then tells you the build succeeded.

## Analogy

Like a timer that beeps when your food is ready so you know to take it out.

## Related Concepts

- [[background-tasks|background tasks]]
- [[terminal-background-mode|Terminal Background Mode]]
- [[watch_patterns|watch_patterns]]

title: orchestrator-coordination
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

The orchestrator agent coordinates multiple sub-agents, assigning tasks and collecting their results.

## Concrete Example

The orchestrator sends 3 tasks to 3 workers, waits for all to finish, then combines their outputs into one report.

## Analogy

Like a project manager who assigns work to 3 team members and compiles their parts into the final report.

## Related Concepts

- [[delegate_task|delegate_task]]
- [[leaf-vs-orchestrator-role|leaf vs orchestrator role]]
- [[max_concurrent_children|max_concurrent_children]]

title: parallel-execution
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

Multiple sub-agents can run at the same time, completing tasks faster than doing them one by one.

## Concrete Example

Three sub-agents review 3 different files simultaneously. The whole review finishes in 1 minute instead of 3.

## Analogy

Like 3 cashiers serving 3 customers at once instead of 1 cashier serving everyone in a single line.

## Related Concepts

- [[delegate_task|delegate_task]]
- [[max_concurrent_children|max_concurrent_children]]
- [[background-tasks|background tasks]]

title: process-management
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

Hermes can track and manage background processes: list them, check status, and kill them if needed.

## Concrete Example

You list running processes, see one is stuck, and kill it to free up resources.

## Analogy

Like a task manager on your computer showing all running apps with the option to close them.

## Related Concepts

- [[background-tasks|background tasks]]
- [[terminal-background-mode|Terminal Background Mode]]
- [[notify_on_complete|notify_on_complete]]

title: schedule-formats
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

Cron jobs can use several schedule formats: duration, every phrase, 5-field cron, or ISO timestamp.

## Concrete Example

You can write every 2 hours, or 0 */2 * * *, or 2026-08-04T10:00:00. All are valid schedule formats.

## Analogy

Like writing dates in different formats: 4/8/2026 or August 4 2026 or 2026-08-04 all mean the same day.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]
- [[hermes-cron-create|hermes cron create]]
- [[cronjob-tool|cronjob tool]]

title: scheduled-reports
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

Cron jobs are great for generating and delivering reports on a schedule without anyone asking.

## Concrete Example

Every Friday at 5pm a cron job generates a weekly summary and sends it to your Telegram.

## Analogy

Like a weekly newsletter that arrives automatically every Friday without you having to request it.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]
- [[cron-job-delivery|Cron Job delivery]]
- [[home-channels|home channels]]

title: skip_memory
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

When skip_memory is on, the cron job does not save its conversation to memory, keeping history clean.

## Concrete Example

A quick status check job uses skip_memory so it does not clutter your memory with repeated checks.

## Analogy

Like using scratch paper for rough work that you throw away instead of saving in your notebook.

## Related Concepts

- [[cron-jobs|cron jobs]]
- [[memory-store|Memory Store]]
- [[hermes-cron-create|hermes cron create]]

title: sub-agent-isolation
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

Sub-agents run in isolated spaces with their own context, so they do not interfere with the main conversation.

## Concrete Example

A sub-agent runs a code review in its own space. Its tool calls and results do not clutter your main chat.

## Analogy

Like individual study carrels in a library: each student works in their own space without disturbing others.

## Related Concepts

- [[delegate_task|delegate_task]]
- [[leaf-vs-orchestrator-role|leaf vs orchestrator role]]
- [[background-tasks|background tasks]]

title: task-handoff
text:
> **Domain:** [[_automation-scheduling-moc|Automation & Scheduling]]

## Motivation

When a sub-agent finishes, it hands its result back to the parent agent in a structured format.

## Concrete Example

The sub-agent completes the code review and sends back a summary with 3 findings and suggested fixes.

## Analogy

Like a student handing in homework: the teacher receives it and can review or grade it.

## Related Concepts

- [[delegate_task|delegate_task]]
- [[sub-agent-isolation|Sub-Agent Isolation]]
